en: Śrī.
Now begins the fourth maṇḍala.
In the fourth Maṇḍala of the Vāmadevya [book], there are five Anuvākas.
Among them, in the first Anuvāka, there are ten Sūktas;
of these, the first Sūkta, consisting of eighty verses, begins with "tvām hy agne madin."
Here is the table of contents (anukramaṇikā): “O Agni, [this hymn] consists of twenty-one verses; the first eight are Jagatīs, while the last four are optionally addressed to Varuṇa.
The seer (ṛṣi) who perceived these mantras is Vāmadeva.

The first verse is an Aṣṭi of fifty-four syllables; the second is an Atijagatī of fifty-two syllables; the third is a Dhṛti of seventy-two syllables; and the remaining seventeen, by the rule of default designation, are Triṣṭubhs.

By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "the deity of the *maṇḍala* and so forth is Agni," the deity of the entire hymn (*sūkta*) is Agni; alternatively, the second through fourth [verses] have Varuṇa as their deity.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn is based on its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*).
The first [verse] is employed in the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) of the chapter (*adhyāya*) and in the *maṇḍala*-opening oblation (*maṇḍalādi-homa*).

For the gods, ever-minded, have established you, O Agni, as the immortal messenger among the immortals; with wisdom they have established you. They have generated the worshipful one among mortals, the god who gladdens all; they have generated the wise one, the god who gladdens all.

For indeed, O Agni, the gods of one mind have ever established you, the god, as their messenger; they have established you with wisdom. They have established the immortal among mortals for worship. They have brought forth the wise god from among the gods; they have brought forth the all-wise one from among the gods. 1.
Vāmadeva praises:
O Agni, you who possess all wealth!
*Manyu* is rivalry.
Accompanied by her— meaning competing with those equal to themselves—
the gods (devāsaḥ), Indra and the other deities who possess divine nature, have indeed always desired you, the shining one (devam), the swift traveler (varatim), for exhilaration (madam).
"Indeed, they urge you on in battle caused by rivalry.
The word *iti* has the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*).
Since the gods urge you intensely toward battle, therefore the sacrificers have urged you on with *kratu*, that is, by means of the ritual action characterized by praise.

Indeed, it is the invocation of the gods to bring the oblation (*havis*) to them during the sacrificial rite that impels you most strongly. O Agni, worthy of worship, they generated you—the immortal, deathless one, or rather, the all-pervading, radiant, and wise one—among mortals performing the sacrifice; that is, among men, they brought you forth as the one who comes to the divine assembly for the purpose of cooking the oblation.

Likewise, the gods made you, the wise one who knows the ritual acts and who attends at various sacrifices, their messenger simultaneously at all those sacrifices that require the simultaneous instruction of knowledge, for the purpose of bringing the oblation.
Nyerira: from the root *īr* meaning "to go.
Because it is a mantra, the suffix *ām* does not occur in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*).
The compound is formed by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) for *saha*;
because it is joined with *hi*, there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*).
[The word is] *kratvā*.

The absence of the substitution [of *na* for *ni*] is due to the rule "In the case of *jas* and so forth, in Vedic usage, there is optionally no [substitution]," and thus the *yaṇ* substitution [of *i* for *y*] occurs.

1. *Ta-vāmadeve* refers to the fourth *maṇḍala*; that is, in the fourth *vāmadeva-maṇḍala*. 2. *Ta-dvāsaptatyakṣarā*: consisting of seventy-two syllables. 3. *La*: for the purpose of bringing [them] twice. 4. *Ga-na-karmaṇo’bhijñam*: one who is skilled in the ritual action of *ga* and *na*.

Turn hither first toward Varuṇa, our kinsman, toward the gods with your favor, toward the one who delights in sacrifice, the eldest who delights in sacrifice—the Āditya who upholds the cosmic order (*ṛta*), the king who sustains the people.

O Agni, turn toward Varuṇa, our father, toward the gods with favor; toward him who loves the sacrifice, the most excellent lover of sacrifice, the upholder of cosmic order, the Āditya who sustains the people, the king who sustains the people. 2.
O Agni, such as you are, you choose Varuṇa as your brother through dwelling in the same place;
Varuṇa is so called because he encompasses (vṛṇoti) the waters.

O God, turn toward and bring face-to-face those gods who delight in sacrifice—the one who is to be honored with sacrifices, offerings, and oblations, the possessor of the forest of sacrifice (*yajñavanasa*), the distributor of sacrifice, the eldest and most preeminent, the observer of cosmic order (*ṛtāvān*), the possessor of waters by virtue of being their lord (or the possessor of truth), the son of Aditi, the sustainer of men through the bestowing of water, the sustainer of people through his excellent wisdom, the one supported by the people, the shining King—turn toward these gods, O Varuṇa, and make them favorable to us.
*vavṛtsva* [is derived from] *vṛt* in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*).
In the *loṭ* (imperative) mood, by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is the elision (*ślu*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The *nighāta* (elision of accent).
In *sumati*, the final syllable is acute (*udātta*) by the rule "In mantras, [words ending in] *vṛṣan* etc. which prescribes the suffix *kvip*.
By the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is a long vowel of the same quality as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) for the third case ending;
it receives the accent of the single substitute (*ekādeśasvara*).
Thus: *jyeṣṭham*.
In the sense of "praiseworthy," there is the substitution of *jya* by the rule "ijya ca" [Pāṇini 5.3.61]. Being a *nī*, it is udātta on the first syllable.
This is the accent of the single substitute (ekādeśasvara).
Regarding *yajñavana-sam*: the root *van* (in the sense of "to enjoy" or "to possess") takes the suffix *asun* in the sense of both the object and the agent (*karmakartari*).

The accent of the first member [of the compound] is applied by the rule: "There is also the preservation of the original accent of the first member even when [the compound denotes] a destination (gati) or an agent (kāraka). Thus, it is the accent of the first member.
In the subsequent chapter concerning the Pravargya and Abhiṣava rites, there is this verse: "O friend, turn toward your friend.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'O friend, turn toward your friend; lift us up for our protection' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.7)."
O Friend, turn toward your friend as swiftly as a wheel follows a swift horse, like a chariot-rider with speed—O Wondrous One, with speed for us!
O Agni, together with Varuṇa, find favor among the all-shining Maruts; for our progeny and for our strength, O Radiant One, grant us well-being; O Wondrous One, grant us well-being!

O Friend, turn toward your friend, as a wheel follows the swift horse, with speed like that of chariot-racers—O Wondrous One, with speed for us! O Agni, together with Varuṇa, find grace; among the all-illuminating Maruts, grant welfare to our progeny and to our strength. O Wondrous One, grant us welfare; grant us welfare! 3.
1. By *ca* and *eka*, [it means] by dwelling in one place; by *ta* and *na*, [it means] not dwelling in one place.
2. The letter *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*, and the word *varuṇa* do not exist.
3. By *ṇa*, [it means] the preparation for sacrifice (*yajñasaṃbhāra*).
4. [The syllables] ṇa, su, ma, ti, [and] sumati;
5. [the syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, pha, bha, sa, [and] devān; [the syllables] ta, na, la, [and] stotṛn devān. 494.
O friend, O renowned one, O wondrous and beautiful Agni, you— turn Varuṇa, your friend, who is worthy of constant service and purposeful, toward our light; there,
an illustration [is given].
Like two horses yoked to a chariot, excellent in their speed and movement, which swiftly turn the wheel toward the target region—that is, toward the place of aim—so it is with you.
O Agni, in your company, as your companion, you have found (*vidaḥ*) the gracious oblation (*mṛḷīkam havir*) that brings happiness;
likewise, among those of great power (*mahrāsu*) whose splendor pervades everywhere (*viśvabhānuṣu*), you have found that which brings happiness.
The meaning here is that you are the protector against fire for the two functions of the fire-drills (araṇis).
O Agni, shining brightly (*śuśucāna*), [be so] for the child (*toka*). That by which the mother is tormented (*tujyate*) and afflicted through dwelling in the womb is called *toka*, namely, the son.
For him, the *tuka*—
so called because he goes (*gacchati*) by means of this [lineage] to fulfill his debt to his father— is the grandson;
for him, *śam*, happiness, *kṛdhi*, perform.
O wondrous and beautiful Agni, bring us peace; that is, create happiness for us.
[The word *ratheva* is explained as follows: in the sense of "these two of a chariot," the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *rathādyat*.
The substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending (*sup*) is according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
[Thus we have] *raṃhā*.
From the word *raṃhas*, the suffix *yat* is added according to the rule *tatra sādhuḥ*.
The word *anāvaḥ* has its initial syllable udātta (accented).
Beginning with “*tvaṃ no agne*,” this hymn and the subsequent hymns are prescribed for the *prātaranuvāka*, in the *ṛtu* dedicated to Agni, in the *triṣṭubh* meter, and for the *ābhinava-śastra*.
It is stated in the Sūtra: “The four [hymns] beginning with ‘*tvaṃ no agne varuṇasya vidvān*’” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).
At the *avabhṛtha* sacrifice, Agni and Varuṇa are to be worshipped for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
In that context, "tvaṃ no agne" constitutes the two *yājyānuvākyā* verses.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "For the purpose of the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering to Agni-Varuṇa, [there are] the two [verses]: 'tvaṃ no agne' and 'varuṇasya vidvān'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.13).
When one should offer the *Agnihotra* while not having bathed, then there is the *Agnivāruṇī* sacrifice.
For this [sacrifice], these very same *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are used;

they are recorded in the text beginning with "Now they say: regarding him who has established the sacred fires," continuing with: "His *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* are 'O Agni, you who know the way of Varuṇa...'; 'O Agni, be our nearest protector... (AiĀ 7.9).

O Agni, you who are wise, may you ward off the wrath of the god Varuṇa from us; as the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and the brightly shining one, release us from all hostilities.

O Agni, you who know, may you ward off the wrath of the divine Varuṇa for us. As the best of sacrificers, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and the radiant one, release from us all those who hate us. 4.

O Agni, you who are all-knowing, knowing the means for accomplishing every human goal, remove—drive away—the wrath of the radiant Varuṇa and the bonds of capture pertaining to us that are wrought by Varuṇa. Furthermore, as the most excellent sacrificer, the best invoker, the supreme bearer of oblations, and the most brilliantly shining one, release us completely from all hatreds, sins, or hostile regions; set us utterly free.
*Heḷaḥ*: from the root *heḍ*, meaning "to disregard," with the suffix *kip*.
The form *śasi* [is derived as follows]:
in *śāsa*, because it begins with a vowel (*supvāt*), the syllable is unaccented (*anudāttatve*), and thus the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvaraḥ*) remains.
[The forms] are *yāsi* and *sīṣṭhāḥ*.

In this [form], the āśīr-liṅ (optative of benediction) occurs; the augment sīyuṭ is added after the suffix thās. Because of the rule “chandasyubhayathā” (in the Veda, [the suffixes] are optionally treated as both), the liṅ is considered sārvadhātuka, and thus there is no elision of the causative marker ṇi.
The root *yāsi* preceded by the prefix *ava-* signifies destruction.
*Mumugdhi* is the form of the root *muc-* in the imperative (*loṭ*).
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," the suffix *śap* is replaced by *śru*.
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and agne are well-formed when rapid.
2. Just as two horses [draw] a swift wheel, so too [the syllables] ṇa and aśva are like swift horses. 3.
[The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, ma, and sa are to be pressed together.
4. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa-tathya* | 5. *kha-ga-ca-ame tvam*.
Be thou for us, O Agni, our protector, most near to us at the dawning of this morning.
O Varuṇa, being gracious, sacrifice for us; accept our plea for mercy, and be easy for us to invoke.
O Agni, be our closest protector with your aid; be nearest to us at the dawning of this very night. Being generous, appease Varuṇa for us; grant us mercy and be easy for us to invoke. 5.

O Agni, such as you are, with your aid—that is, through your protection—being our nearest one, turned toward us, and standing close at hand, be most near to us at the dawning of this dawn, at the time of sunrise, for the sake of accomplishing the *agnihotra* and other rites.
Or rather:
through your coming (*ūti*), be our nearest protector.

Furthermore, O Varuṇa, appease—that is, remove or destroy—our *varuṇa*, meaning the disease such as dropsy caused by Varuṇa, or the obstructing sin. *Rarāṇaḥ*: rejoicing in the oblation offered by us.
Or rather:

Three are his supreme, true, and desirable births of the divine Agni for the sake of the sacrificers. Enveloped within the infinite [space], he has come—pure, bright, noble, and shining brilliantly. (7) Three are his supreme, true, and desirable births of the divine Agni. Enveloped within the infinite, he has come—pure, bright, noble, and shining brilliantly. (7)

Of that god Agni—who possesses other forms of self-conception—there are three births (*janimāni*) in the nature of fire, wind, and sun; these three are well-known, supreme, true (*satyā*), corresponding to reality, and desirable (*spārhā*), being sought after by all.
Or rather, there are indeed three births of Agni himself, as it is said: "Agni was first born from heaven" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.45.1).

He, the kinsman of sacrifice, awakens the human being; they lead him forward with greatness by means of a cord. He dwells in his dwellings; the god, bestowing gifts, has attained the wealth of the mortal. 9. He. awakens. the human being. kinsman of sacrifice. forward. him. with greatness. by a cord. they lead. he. dwells. in his. dwellings. bestowing. the god. of the mortal. wealth. has attained. 9.
"Yajñabandhuḥ": he whose binding or application is to the sacrifice, such as the Agnihotra and other rites;
that Agni "caitayat," meaning he knows or perceives "manuṣaḥ," those human beings who are engaged in ritual action.
With a great cord, that is, with the rope consisting of praise, they lead forth—that very Agni—unto the northern altar and other such places; the Adhvaryu and other priests cast him down there.
Accomplishing the desired goals within the *duryāḥ*, the dwellings of this mortal, this sacrificer, that Agni dwells and resides.
That radiant god, Agni, attains companionship with the wealthy man in whose house he resides.
The meaning is that, having caused abundant wealth to be given to the sacrificer, he became accompanied by it.
*Sādhana*:
[The root] *rādha* or *sādha* means "to accomplish" (*saṃsiddhi*). This is the form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) in the present participle (*śatṛ*).

May that Agni, who knows all, lead us toward the treasure allotted by the gods which belongs to him—that which all the immortals fashioned through their wisdom, while Dyaus the Father, the progenitor, and Satyamukṣan [bestowed it]. 10. He—may that Agni indeed lead us, knowing the way, toward the treasure allotted by the gods, which belongs to him; that which all the immortals fashioned through their inspired thought, while Dyaus the Father, the progenitor, and Satyamukṣan [poured it forth]. 10.

Knowing all, he who knows—let that Agni lead us swiftly toward and bring us that most excellent treasure, the wealth belonging to this Agni, which is to be honored by the gods, those worshippers of divine character. May all the immortal gods, through their wisdom—that is, by means of the ritual action characterized by the carrying of oblations—make him [Agni] the one who conveys the offerings.
And for that fire, heaven is the father—meaning its protector, its progenitor, and its bringer forth—as is heard in the Vedic text: "O Agni, you are the wise son of heaven" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 3.25.1).
Or alternatively:
The sun is the father and progenitor, possessing the divine nature of heaven;
for it is recorded in the sacred tradition that "from the sun comes fire.
The Adhvaryu priests and others sprinkle that true fire—which is reality itself—with oblations of clarified butter.
*Devabhakta* [is derived as follows]:
the root *bhaj* means "to serve"; the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the object (karmaṇi).
By the rule "the third [case ending] is used in the sense of the object," there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member of the compound.
*Ukṣan*:
from the root *ukṣ*, meaning "to sprinkle."
This is the form in the *laṅ* [aorist] tense;
the absence of the augment (*aṭ*) is due to the rule "in the Veda, [the augment is] optional" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

He was born first among the solid things; he, the great one, shone in the womb of this vast mid-world. Footless and headless, concealing his limits, the youthful one was in the lair of the bull. 11. He was born; first; among the solid things; the great one; he shone; in the womb; of this; vast mid-world; footless; headless; concealing; his limits; the youthful one; in the lair; of the bull. 11.
1. Having given *la* and *da*;
2. and those devoid of *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ra*;
3. by means of the characteristics of *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ha*, and *vi*.
Ṛgveda 2.63.1:

Agni, being the foremost and most excellent in the form of the Āhavanīya and other sacrificial fires, is born—that is, he becomes established—as the locus for the oblations in the *paśyās*, the dwellings of the sacrificers.

Likewise, he is established at the base (*budhne*) of that great (*mahaḥ*) enclosure (*vrajasaḥ*), namely the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and even there upon the earth, specifically in the celestial space (*dyoni*) such as the site of the northern altar (*uttaravedi*).
That [sacrificial animal] is Agni: with the omentum but devoid of feet, and with the head but devoid of the head.
He says that very thing:
"swallowing," [referring to] grasping the feet and the head at the beginning and the end.
The meaning is that his feet and head are imperceptible.
In the dark abode of the sky—the dwelling place of the rain-giving cloud—the youthful winds exist, employing themselves in the form of smoke;
or alternatively:

That first fire of lightning, which moves within the depths of the rivers, in the mid-air, and having ascended from the great, vast expanse (rajas)—or rather, from the source and place of splendor—moves about;

being footless and headless, devoid of feet and head, grasping and covering the very limits of its own self with its own brilliance, and again drawing those splendors together and mixing them within itself, it moves in the dark blue space of the sky, the abode of the bull-like cloud; that fire has now been born through the application of ritual action.
It is without feet.
The elision of the vowel *a* at the end of the compound is by the rule "pādasya lopo'hastvādibhyaḥ. [Thus we have] *gṛhītamānaḥ*. The root is *gṛh* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*).
The forms [are derived] from the śap and vikaraṇa suffixes; the form [is obtained] with the śānac suffix.
When the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka* has been applied to the śānac, the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*) prevails.
*Āyoyuvānaḥ*:
[derived from] the root *yu* in the sense of "mixing" (*miśraṇe*);
this is the form in the *śānac* suffix after the elision (*luk*) of the intensive (*yaṅ*).
The first syllable is accented acute (*udātta*) because it has been so practiced in recitation:
"The bold host has come forth first, with praise, at the womb of Truth, in the stall of the Bull—desirable, young, beautiful, and radiant. The seven dear ones have brought him forth for the Bull."

The host has come forth first, worthy of praise, in the womb of Truth, in the lair of the Bull—desirable, youthful, beautiful, and radiant. The seven beloved ones have brought him forth for the sake of the Bull.

O Agni, through your inspired praise (*vipanyā*), your first splendor (*śardhaḥ*) proceeds forth with excellence into the womb of the waters (*vṛtasya vyonā*), that is, into the place which is the womb of the rain-giving cloud (*vṛṣabhasya... vīḷe kulāyabhūte*), existing there in the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*) in the form of lightning (*vaidyutābhiḥ*).

In whom [resides] the desirable—the one desired by all—who is ever-youthful (*vyūvā*), beautiful (*vapuṣya*), lovely (*kamanīya*), and radiant (*vibhāvā*); to that *vṛṣṇe* (the showerer of rain), Agni, who rains down desired fruits—to him the beloved (*priyāsaḥ*) seven invokers (*sapta hotakāḥ*) generated [the hymn], they performed a song of praise.
[The root] *ṛ* means "to go."
In the *laṅ* tense, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs by way of transposition;
there is elision of the accent (*nighāta*).
[The word] *vipanyā*.
The suffix *in* is applied to the word *pana*.
The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*. It is acutely accented on the final syllable by the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
The acute accent (*udātta*) of the case-ending is due to the rule *udāttayaṇo halpūrvāt*.

In the compound *vipanyā ṛtasya*, according to the *saṃhitā* rule *iko'savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.127), even for a vowel other than *ik*, there is optionally a short vowel and an anusvāra (*anunāsika*). Here, our parents, the humans, sat down facing [the sacrifice], not failing in their devotion to the Truth (*ṛta*).

The human fathers, our ancestors, sat down here, not failing in their devotion to the *ṛta*. Invoking the dawns, they drove forth the cows from within the rock-fenced enclosure—the well-milking cows that were within the cave.

Our fathers, the men, sat down here, not failing in their devotion to the *ṛta*. They drove forth the cows from within the rock-fenced enclosure—the well-milking cows that were within the cave—invoking the dawns. 13.

1. Not in mahīṣu; not in mardīyeṣu. 2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Sa, the word "meghasya" is absent. 3. In Bha and Sa, there is the śavikaraṇa suffix. 4. In Ṇa, Na, La, and Sa, the word "yonā" is absent. 5. In Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, La, and Sa, the word "agnaye" is absent. 6. In Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Sa, the word "saṃhitāyā" is absent.
In this world, our ancestors, the Aṅgirases, having attained the *ṛta* (sacrifice), sat down facing Agni and proceeded toward him.

Those Aṅgirases forcibly [released] the cows from Vṛtra, who was the mountain-enclosure—Vṛtra being so called because he "chooses" (vṛṇoti), that is, he covers or obstructs; they were situated within him, inside that mountain-fortress. Furthermore, they brought out those well-milking cows, the "uṣtras," which had been carried off by the Paṇis, from that vessel.
What are they doing?
Invoking—that is, calling upon—the goddesses of the dawns, who destroy the darkness, for the sake of light.

The word *vatre* [is derived] from the root *vṛ*, with the suffix *ka* added according to the *auṇādika* rules; there is reduplication in accordance with the rule: “For roots beginning with *kṛ*, there is doubling.”
They, bestowing gifts, cleansed me; others among them proclaimed it on every side.
Beholding, they conceived of you; they discovered the first name of the Cow—the three times seven highest names of the Mother.
Or it appeared upon the nearby bank of that [river], manifesting with the ruddy luster of the sun.

They discovered for the first time the name of the cow; they found the thrice-seven highest names of the Mother. Knowing this, they followed her; the ruddy one became manifest through the glory of the cow. 16.

O Agni, the Aṅgirases, while offering praise to you, first perceived—the word "manvata" meaning they knew—the name, which is the mere sound that accomplishes praise, belonging to their mother, the progenitor, Vāc (Speech).
Subsequently, they perceived the twenty-one (triḥ sapta) meters belonging to that Speech, which are the means for accomplishing praise;
these consist of seven [metres] beginning with Gāyatrī and ending with Jagatī.
There are seven meters beginning with *atijagatī* and ending with *vyatiṣṭhanti*;
and seven beginning with *kṛti* and ending with *utkṛti*, including *sa*.
Thus, they found and obtained the three times seven supreme, highest meters.
The meaning is that they praised Agni with mantras endowed with such meters.
"Tat" means "then"; "jānatāḥ" means "knowing all"; "vāḥ" is a name for water.
The dawns have followed after him; they have praised him.
Then, together with the splendor and brilliance of the sun, the ruddy ones—those of ruddy color—have become manifest, they have appeared.
Or rather:

Those Aṅgirasas first conceived and uttered the ancient name of the cow: "Come, O fragrant one, you who have the scent of guggulu. They found the thrice-seven jewels that belonged to Mother Earth but had been carried away by the Paṇis;
then, recognizing the name thus uttered, the cows approached them.
They did not make a sound characterized by lowing;
at that time, they knew that the dawn had appeared. In one recension, the long vowel of the same quality as the preceding [vowel] is applied according to the rule "ava chandasi."
In both cases, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied and becomes udātta by the rule "aśaturanumaḥ nadyajādī.
[The form] *anūpata* [is derived from] the root *ṇu* in the sense of "praising" (*stutau*).
The form is from the root *luñ*. Due to its belonging to the *kuṭādi* group, there is no *guṇa* strengthening. Thus: *aruṇīḥ*.

Darkness perished; the sky shone bright; the light of Dawn arose. The Sun has ascended on high, beholding both the upright and the crooked among mortals.
The turbid darkness vanished; the sky shone forth. The radiance of the divine Dawn arose; Sūrya stood up on high, anointing all, beholding both the upright and the crooked among mortals.
The darkness—the gloom produced by night—was stirred up;
*dudhi* means "to impel.
At the time of the morning procession, being impelled by *uṣas*, it perished and vanished.
Then the sky and the intermediate space shone and blazed forth.
Then the radiance, the light, of the goddess Uṣas—she who is by nature divine—arose and ascended.
Then Sūrya mounted upon the great, vast, unaging mountains, or rather, he mounted upon his rays which are ever-moving.
Doing what?
Observing the upright, virtuous deeds existing among mortals—human beings—and the crooked, uneven deeds that are not straight, he presided over them; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

*neśat*. From the root *ṇaś* in the sense of "disappearance" (*adarśane*), in the *laṅ* tense, [the form is derived] according to the rule: "It should be stated that the substitution of *e* for the final vowel occurs after the roots *ṇaś* and *man*" (*pā. ma. 6. 4. 120. 5*). Thus [it is formed].
Since the suffix *śap* is marked as *pit*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains.
[The form] *rocate* [is derived from] the root *ruc* in the sense of "shining."
This is the form in the *laṅ* tense;
there is no loss of accent (*anighāta*) due to the division of the sentence.
1. *ca-pha*: thus it is threefold. 2. *ca-jānanti tāḥ*; *ṇa-jānantīti jānānāḥ*. 3. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha-bha*: they did not find the names. 4. *ta-na-gṛjanāni*.

From the beginning, having perceived the cattle, they have awakened; let them hold fast the most beautiful treasure. May all the gods in all their dwellings be present; O Mitra, may there be truth for the prayer, O Varuṇa.

From that very moment, having awakened, they have looked upon the cattle; from that very moment, let all the gods maintain their most beautiful treasure in every dwelling. O Mitra and Varuṇa, may there be truth for our prayer. 18.

Immediately after sunrise, the Aṅgirases, having awakened and knowing the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis and released from their confinement, searched for them along the backs of the cattle and beheld those cows in their entirety. Likewise, immediately thereafter, they held fast to the radiant treasure—endowed with splendor or shared by the gods—which had been seized by the Paṇis.
When the Aṅgirases had recovered the cows, all the gods worthy of worship came to all their dwellings, to every house.
