O Agni, may he indeed be fortunate and bountiful, who desires to gratify you with constant oblations and with hymns throughout his own life in his home; for him, every day shall be auspicious, and that sacrifice shall be successful. 7.

O Agni, that man who desires to gratify you with the oblation (*havis*)—which is the means for performing the Agnihotra and other rites—constantly (*nityena*), throughout his life (*yāvaj-jīvam*), according to his resolve; and he who desires to gratify you with hymns (*ukthaiḥ*) and liturgical recitations (*śastraiḥ*); may that very man be fortunate (*subhagaḥ*), possessed of good fortune, and endowed with noble generosity (*sudānuḥ*).
Furthermore, may he abide in his own dwelling (*duronē*), in his difficult-to-attain home, throughout his own lifespan (*āyuṣi*) known as a hundred years.
"May all—meaning every—one auspicious day belong to this sacrificer;
may his sacrifice—that is, his ritual—be effective as a means for attaining the fruit."
He desires to please (*piprīṣati*).
[The root] *prīñ* means "to satisfy.
The suffix *san* is applied according to Pāṇini’s Sūtra 3.1.7: *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*.
asat; [in the case of] *asti*, there is the augment *iṭ*;
[thus] *iṣṭiḥ*.
Is [the word] *vṛṣa* acute-accented by the rule beginning with "mantre vṛṣa"?
In the Ukha-saṃbharaṇīya sacrifice, "I praise thee" (*arcāmi te*) is the *yājyā* for Agni.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘I praise thy benevolence,’ ‘O swift one, come hither’—this is the sequence beginning with the stepping forward" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.1).
I honor your benevolent thought; let this song of mine reverberate near you, so that it may bring you close.
O you who possess noble horses and fine chariots, may we cleanse you; uphold sovereign powers for us and shake down riches.

I worship your benevolence, O terrible one; let it be directed hitherward. May this song of mine, like a beloved wife, resound together with you. We, possessing good horses and good chariots, would adorn you. Bestow sovereign powers upon us; shake them down for us. 8.
O Agni, I honor—that is, I worship—your *asumati*, your beautiful intellect that bestows grace.
Furthermore, this speech (*gīḥ*) being uttered here, approaching you again and again as "Vavātā," resounds in such a way as to be filled with resonance (*ghoṣi*).
(Note: Variants *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* do not contain the word *vi*.)
2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, and sa, the phrase "due to connection with *yad-vṛtta*, there is no *anighāta*" is absent.
3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, la, and ta, the term is *nipāta*.
4. In the manuscripts ta and la, it is "endowed with beautiful wealth" (*śobhanadhanayukta*).
5. When there is the cause for living (*jīvane*), namely *ta-na-pha-bha*, he who pleases you—may he (*saḥ*) be fortunate (*subhagaḥ astu*).
Or rather: he who pleases you in his own home, during his own life, that is, during his hundred-year lifespan. 6. *ṇa* means "let him stay" (*tiṣṭhatu*); *bha* means "let him stay" (*tiṣṭhatu astu*).
7. Kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-prīḍa | 8. Kha-ga-na-bha-la-sa-anugrahakarām | 9. Ṇa-arcāmi arcayāmi |

10. ṇa-vāvātā | 11. When *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *na* follow, [the suffix] *tvā* means "you"; when *gha* and *ṇa* follow, it means "again and again you. Facing you, let him—[the particle] *te* meaning "you"—praise you repeatedly.

We too, possessing our own horses— meaning we are endowed with beautiful horses— and having excellent chariots (this being an elliptical expression including sons, grandsons, and so forth), may we adorn you— that is, decorate you.
"Let us serve you," [they say], up to that point. But you, day after day, should bestow (*bhārayeḥ*)— that is, deposit (*nidhehi*)— powers (*kṣatrāṇi*) and riches (*dhanāni*) among us (*asme*).
*Ghoṣi*:
from the root *ghuṣ* meaning "to sound," with the *in* suffix added according to the *Uṇādi* rules.
It is acutely accented on the first syllable by virtue of the *nittva* designation.
Regarding *vāvātā*:
this is the form of the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) derived from the root √*vā*, meaning "to go" or "to scent," in its *yaṅ*-lopped (*yaṅluk*) form.
*marjayema*. [The root] *mṛjū* means "to cleanse" and "to adorn. This is the form of the causative (*ṇyanta*) in the optative (*liṅ*).
The absence of the vowel lengthening is a Vedic peculiarity.
May he attend upon you here, O dispeller of darkness, shining after the young men;
may we, playing and well-disposed, serve you, standing above the splendors of the people.
May many come here to you by themselves, O Agni, as evening falls upon you who shine brightly; may we, young and joyful in spirit, play around you, surpassing all people in glory.

O Agni, in this ritual action known as *rakṣohan* (the slaying of the Rakṣas), or rather, in this world, that man who, day and night (*doṣāvastaḥ*), constantly (*anu yūna*) blows (*dhaman*) upon you—shining (*dīdivāṃsam*) and blazing (*tvā*)—blows by himself (*ātmanā*) every day; he attends upon (*upacaret*) you most abundantly (*bhūri*) in such a manner.

Therefore, we— having overcome the splendors (*yumnā*), that is, the riches (*dhanāni*) of the people who are our enemies, and by your grace making them [our own]— and thus sporting (*krīḷantaḥ*), playing together with our sons, grandsons, and others in our respective homes, and being well-disposed (*sumanasaḥ*), that is, having auspicious minds, may we serve (*sapema*) you. Or alternatively, *doṣāvastar* is a vocative.
Of the night, which is the fault, of the darkness created by it, and of the one who covers with a garment—that is, the dispeller.
[This refers to] the third case ending of the word *ātman*;
[the suffix] is elided by the rule "supāṃ suluk... (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
In the case of mantras, there is the elision of the vowel *ā* according to the rule "āḍy-āder-ātmanaḥ," resulting in *doṣāvastaḥ*.
In the alternative view that this is a *dvandva* compound, the original accent of the first member is applied according to the rule "kārtakaujapādayaś-ca."
In the view that it is a vocative, the first syllable of the word following the vocative is optionally acute (ādyudātta) when it begins with *ā*;
thus, *sapema*.
[The root] *ṣap* [is used] in the sense of "to come together."
The form is [in] the optative (liṅ).
There is a nighāta [elision].
Whosoever approaches thee, O Agni, with good horses and fine gold on a chariot laden with wealth—
for him thou art a protector, for him a friend, he who has enjoyed thy hospitality according to human custom.

O Agni, whoever approaches you with good horses and fine gold on a chariot full of wealth—of him you are the protector, of him you are the friend; he who takes delight in showing you hospitality in due order. 10.

O Agni, that man who possesses fine horses (*svaśva*), is endowed with excellent gold (*suhiraṇya*)—that is, possessed of wealth suitable for sacrifice—and is accompanied by a chariot (*ratha*) filled with riches such as rice and other grains (*vasumat*), approaches you (*tvā*) for the sake of service, going into your presence;
you become his protector (*trātā*), the guardian from all misfortunes.
And whatever man, in due order, enjoys—that is, bestows—hospitality, which is worship worthy of a guest, you become his friend, a benefactor by granting him the fruit appropriate thereto.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ta, and Bha, there is *hatotuṃ saṃsaratām*; in Sa, there is *saṃsaratām*. 2. In Ṇa and Tvā, there is *tvām*. 3. In Ca and Pha, there is *ghuṣi*. 4. In La and Va, there is *vātā*. 5. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Ma, and Sa, the word *aniṣṭhāyām* is absent. 6. In Na, La, and Sa, the word *tvā* is absent. 7. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Ma, and Sa, there is *krīḍantaḥ*. 8. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, and Bha, there is *tvā*; in Ta, Na, La, and Sa, the phrase *tvā tvām* is absent.

He approaches. The compound [in *upāyāti*] is formed by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "saha supā" (Pāṇini 2.1.4). Since the suffix *tip* is marked with *p*, it is unaccented (*anudātta*), and thus the accent of the verbal root remains. By the rule "tiṅaścodāttavati," the movement [of the prefix *upa*] is unaccented (*nighāta*). *Ātithyam*: From the word *atithi*, in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*), the suffix *ya* is applied according to the rule "atitheryaḥ. This is the accent of the suffix. *Jujopat*: From the root *jopayati* in the *laṅ* tense, the *śap* suffix is elided by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. The augment *aṭ* is added. Because of the rule "chandasyubhayathā," the *tip* suffix is treated as an *ārdhadhātuka*, resulting in the elision of the *ṇi*. By the rule "abhyastānām ādiḥ," the first syllable is udātta. || 24 ||
Through kinship, I break down the great [fortresses] with my words; that [deed] has followed me from my father Gotama.
O most youthful Hotṛ, wise one, friend of the house, take note of this our splendor.

I break through with great kinship and with words; let that [be] from my father Gotama for my advancement. Do thou take note of this our splendor, O most youthful Hotṛ, O wise one, O friend of the house! 11.

O Hotṛ, invoker of the gods; O youngest, most youthful one; O Agni of excellent wisdom, through these words—these hymns composed in your honor—by that kinship, that bond of relationship which has arisen, I shatter, I destroy, the great Rākṣasas. Such speech, consisting of praise, reached me, Vāmadeva, from my father, the seer Gotama.
"O *damūnāḥ*—either one whose mind is subdued or one who destroys the enemies—such as you, 'know' (*cikiddhi*), that is, take note of, this 'our' speech, this statement consisting of praise."
Cikiddhi; [the root] *kit* means "to know";
it belongs to the *jauhotyādi* (third) class.
The form is *loṭi*.
[In the case of] *hotaḥ*,
because it begins with a *pāda*, there is optionally the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatvam*).

But in the case of the other two, because the rule "an unaccented vocative [is not treated as non-existent] when it is in grammatical apposition" prohibits the treatment of the first as being as if non-existent (avidyamānavat), there is no suppression of accent (nighāta) since they do not stand at the beginning of a metrical foot (apādādau).
They have no horses, no goats, yet they are swift; they are very kind, unwearied, non-cruel, and most tireless.
Those protectors of the people, sitting together in harmony, O Agni—O unerring one, protect us with them.
Without horses or goats, swift, very gracious, unwearied, non-hostile, most tireless—may those steeds of yours, O Agni, being united and having settled down, protect us, O unerring one! 12.
O unerring, undeluded, omniscient one;
or alternatively,
O Agni of unimpeded course, [protect] those who are sleepless and do not slumber.

"Jāgarūkāḥ" means being vigilant. "Taraṇyaḥ" means having the nature of constant movement, or those who rescue one who has fallen into distress. "Suśevāḥ" means very gracious. "Atandrāsaḥ" means not weary, that is, not lazy and free from all defects. "Avṛkāḥ" means non-violent. "Aśramiṣṭhāḥ" means most tireless. "Sadhryañcaḥ" means moving together in unison with one another. "Pāyavaḥ" means protectors. "Te" (those) such as these—"tava raśmayaḥ" (your rays)—"niṣadya" (having sat down), that is, having taken their place in our sacrifice, "naḥ" (us) "pāntu" (may they protect).
*asvamajaḥ*:
[the word] *sva-pitṛ* has the suffix *ṇini*;
the *avagraha* (word division) in the middle is Vedic.

*sadhryañcaḥ*. [This is derived] from *saha* preceded by [the prefix], followed by the root *añc*, with the suffix *kvip*. By the rule “*sahasya sadhiḥ*,” there is the substitution of *sadhi* for *saha*.

1. According to the reading of Sādhyādeśa, there is the udātta accent on *ta-* and so forth. 2. This [reading] does not exist in the versions of Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha. 3. According to Ta, it is from his presence (*sakāśāt*). 4. According to Na, La, and Sa, it is "Māṃ vāmadevam" (me, Vāmadeva). 5. According to Na, La, and Sa, the word "prāptam" (attained) is absent. 6. This is the consensus of Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Ma, and Sa. 7. The word "rakṣantu" (may they protect) is absent in Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṇa, Na, Ma, and Sa.

Because it is prescribed as having an udātta accent on the final syllable, when the *yaṇ* substitution occurs, it becomes *svarita* by the rule "udāttasvaritayoḥ". [The word] *amūḥ*: from the root *muha* in the sense of "bewilderment" (*vaicitye*); the substitution of *ra* for *ṭha* in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*) is Vedic. Alternatively, from the root *mṛd* in the sense of "binding" (*bandhane*), with the *uṇādi* suffix *rak*.

O Agni, those reeds which surrounded the son of Mamatā, the blind one, and protected him from distress—him, the doer of good deeds, the omniscient one protected; though the enemies sought to harm him, they did not succeed in harming him.

Those guardians of yours, O Agni, who protected the blind son of Mamatā from the evil-doer—him the All-Knowing One protected in his righteous deeds; even the enemies who sought to harm him could not deceive him. 13.
In this regard, there is this historical narrative:

Bṛhaspati, the younger brother of Ucathya, desired his elder brother's wife, named Mamatā, who was pregnant. He deposited his semen within her; while still in the womb, the embryo spoke to that semen.
"May my semen not waste away here; I shall dwell here.
Having been addressed thus, Bṛhaspati, his semen being obstructed, cursed the embryo in the form of that semen:
"Attain long-lasting darkness in the form of congenital blindness."
Then Dīrghatamas was born of her;
and having praised Agni for the sake of removing his blindness, he obtained sight.
This is what is now stated.

O Agni, those rays of yours—those protectors who, seeing [Dīrghatamas] as "blind," looked upon him with a compassionate gaze—protected Dīrghatamas, the son of Mamatā, who was blind and deprived of sight, from misfortune characterized by blindness, that is, from the curse, by preserving him through the granting of vision. You, the omniscient one (*viśvavedas*), have protected those rays with care, having embraced them, on behalf of the well-doer who performed the excellent deed of granting vision;
the successful attainment of their embrace is thus affirmed.
"Even though the enemies, desiring to deceive—that is, wishing to overcome him—did not indeed deceive this Dīrghatamas; they certainly did not prevail over him."
*Māmateya*:
[This is formed] in the sense of "the offspring of Mamatā" by the suffix *ḍhak* [applied] after feminine stems.
*Dipsantaḥ*.
In the root *dambhū* (to deceive),
there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* by the rule "sanīcantadhre°" and so forth;
furthermore, the vowel *i* is substituted [for the penultimate *a*] by the rule "dambha icca."
They played.

Because of the rule "An addition [to the list of roots] for śrindh, granth, dambh, and akṣī" (Kāśikā 6.1), there is elision of the penultimate vowel due to the *ki* suffix of the *liṭ* [perfect tense].
With you as our companion and protected by you, may we attain spoils through your guidance.
O upholder of truth, fulfill both the praises of our heart; make them come true.
Through you, may we be fortunate; protected by you, may we attain strengths through your guidance. O Lord whose heart is true, fulfill both our prayers without fail, for we follow you. 14.

"O Agni, whose coming is unobserved"—Yāska [says] in Nirukta 5.15: "He is called *ahayaḥ* because he has come. O such Agni, we, the singers of praise, being *sadhnyaḥ*—that is, possessing common wealth through your grace—and being *tvotāḥ*, protected by you, may we, by your *praṇītī*, that is, by your guidance and permission, *aśyāma*, may we attain *vājān*, foods.
O Satyatāti!
[The term] *satyatāti* means either "one who extends truth" (*satyaṃ tanoti*), or "that in which truth is extended" (*satyaṃ tāyate yasmin*).
O Satyatāti! O you two, the proclaimers of evil—both of you! [May there be] freedom from blame.

1. Because it is prescribed as having an udātta accent on the final syllable of the suffix *ta*. 2. The suffix *rak* [is applied] after *ta*. 3. From *ta* [meaning] "evil" (*pāpa*). 4. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *la*, there is *sa-śobhanacakṣu*. 5. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *bha*, there is *pālaya*. 6. The attainment of *parigraha* (possession/support) from *ta*. 7. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *bha*, there is *alakṣitagamana*; in *ta*, *na*, and *sa*, there is *alakṣitāgamana*. 8. In the versions *na*, *la*, and *sa*, both [terms] are absent.
[End of] Third Aṣṭaka, Fourth Adhyāya, First Pāda, Sūtra 4. Page 527.

"O Asudaya, slay the enemies, both those who are near and those who are far! Perform [them] *anuṣṭhuyā*, that is, in due order; accomplish the purpose set forth in this hymn (*sūkta*). *Sadhanyaḥ*: "Those who possess wealth" (*dhana*)—the suffix *ī* is applied according to the rule *chandasīvanipau*; then the *yaṇ* substitution occurs by the rule *eranekācaḥ*; and the *svarita* accent is applied by the rule *udāttasvaritayoḥ*. *Anuṣṭhuyā*: The suffix *ku* prescribed by the rule *apaduḥsuṣusthaḥ* occurs even after the prefix *anu-* because of the word "frequently" (*bahulavacanāt*). The third case ending is replaced by *yā* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. *Ahayāṇa*: From the root *hī* (meaning "shame"). The absence of the elision (*lubhāva*) of the *śap* suffix occurs by the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*. The absence of the augment *suk* occurs because "the prescription of augments is not mandatory" (*anityamāgamāśāsanam*).
With this fuel, O Agni, may we worship you; accept the hymn being recited.
Burn away the malevolent Rākṣasas; protect us from the malicious, from reproach, and from blame, O you who are as great as Mitra.

With this fuel, O Agni, may we worship you; accept the hymn being recited. Burn the malevolent Rākṣasas; protect us from malice, from reproach, and from blame, O you whose greatness is like Mitra’s. 15.

O Agni, with this fuel, with this kindling, with this hymn of praise, may we worship and serve you. Accept, receive this laudatory hymn being recited by us. Omit the *aśasaḥ*—those who do not praise, those who do not offer hymns; burn them, reduce them to ashes, O you who are the destroyer of the wicked. O Agni, you whose greatness is like that of Mitra, protect us from the malicious, from the reviler, and from disgraceful slander. *Gṛbhāya*: From the root *grah*, in the imperative (*loṭ*), the suffix *śāyac* is applied according to the rule "in the Veda, *śāyac* is also used for *śa*. Then *hya-hor-bheḥ* [the substitution of *bha* for *hya* and *hor*]. *Pāhi*: Due to the division of the sentence, there is no *anighāta*. *Nidaḥ*: From the root *ṇidi* in the sense of "censure," with the suffix *kip*. Because the rules regarding augments are not mandatory, there is an absence of the augment *suṭ*. The acute accent of the case-ending is by the rule "sāvekācaḥ... *Avadyāt*: By the rule "avadya-paṇya... the suffix *yat* is applied. The final syllable is acute by the rule "yayatoś-ātadarthe" (Pāṇini 6.2.156). In the *saṃhitā* reading of "mitramaho avadyāt," there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) of the *eṅ* vowel according to the rule "ayyāda-vadyāt. || 25 ||
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrtha Maheśvara bestow the four goals of human life.

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the third book in the *Ṛgvedasaṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
1. Complete with the *ta-na-bha* [signature]. Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Thus, the fourth chapter of the third Aṣṭaka has been explained with diligence by Sāyaṇārya; the fifth shall now be expounded.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
In the fourth maṇḍala, the first anuvāka contains ten hymns.
The fifth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with “vaiśvānarāya,” is the ṛṣi Vāmadeva’s composition; it is in the triṣṭubh meter and has Vaiśvānara Agni as its deity.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “vaiśvānarāya [is] the Vaiśvānara hymn.”
The application is inferential.
In unison with the bounteous Vaiśvānara Agni, how shall we offer great praise?
With his perfect and lofty tree-like pillar, he has propped up the firmament as a friend.

To Vaiśvānara, the bountiful one—may we, being of one accord, offer worship with great light to Agni. With his unyielding and vast power, he has propped up the firmament like a pillar supporting a bank.
"Being 'sajoṣāḥ sajopasaḥ'—that is, being of one mind and united in affection—we, acting as officiating priests, [ask]:

'To Vaiśvānara'—to the one related to all men, named after them; 'to Mīḷhuṣe'—the bestower of desired rain and other blessings; 'to Bṛhate'—the vast and great; 'to Bhāse'—the radiant; 'to Agni'—the divine one; 'kathā'—how, in what manner; 'dāśema'—should we offer?
By implication, it is understood that the oblation (*havis*) is meant."
Alternatively, the phrase "bṛhadbhāḥ" (of great luster) is to be connected with what follows.
It was asked, "When shall we offer? What is the excellence in that? To this, it is said:

That Agni who, being vast (*bṛhan*) and great (*mahān*), and being radiant (*bhāsamāna*), supports—by means of his own body which is *anūna* (unimpaired), *avikala* (complete), and for that very reason *bṛhat* (vast) and *prabhūta* (powerful)—the sky by means of his *vṛkṣatha* (that which is to be borne). The word "the sky" is to be supplied by implication; the meaning is that he pervades the world of heaven.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"The word *upamit* means 'obstruction' (*rodhaḥ*). It is called *upamit* because it is measured against (*upa-sam-mīyate*) or cast down [into comparison]; thus, it refers to a pillar (*sthūṇā*)."
Just as that [pillar] supports bamboo and other materials that obstruct the covering of grass and so forth, so too [does this];
or rather,
together with the hymn characterized as a "tree" which bears fruit and the like, it supports the heavenly world.

*stabhāyat*. The root *stambh* is a Vedic (sautra) root. In the *laṅ* tense, by the rule "in the Veda, the suffix *śāyac* may also [be used]," there is a substitution of *śāyac* even for the suffix *ah*.
The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, [grammatical operations] occur diversely).
What is it like?
It is like a bank (*rodhas*).
That which is measured (*mīyate*) in the vicinity (*upa*) is "that which is measured nearby" (*upamit*), namely, water.
Like a riverbank.
Do not revile him who, as a god, bestowed this great delight upon mortal man—
Agni Vaiśvānara, the wise, the immortal, the discerning, the most heroic among men, the youthful son of power.
Do not revile him who, as a god, bestowed this great gift upon mortal man—the self-sustaining, wise, immortal, and discerning Vaiśvānara, the most heroic and glorious Agni. || 2 ||

1. By Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Pha, Bha, and Sāyaṇācārya. 2. In Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, and Bha, the phrase *sajopasaḥ* is absent. 3. In Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha, La, and Sa, it refers to those connected with the rules (*vidhāna*). 4. In Kha, Ga, and Ca, there is an addition:
"O Hotṛ and the others, do not revile this Vaiśvānara; do not commit the act of reviling. This is for the purpose of praise.

That divine Agni, being made to give, possessing his own inherent power (*svadhāvān*) and endowed with the oblation characterized by the sacrificial offering (*havis*), has now given this mass of wealth—given in this manner—at present, to the mortal subject to death, to the mature one whose wisdom is fully ripened, for the sake of the great sacrificer. He is further distinguished as *gṛtsaḥ*: the wise one.
This is the name of Medhātithi.

*Amṛtaḥ* means immortal, whose nature is deathlessness; *vicetāḥ* means possessed of distinguished wisdom; *vaiśvānaraḥ* means being led by the Vaiśvānaras in the form of the Āhavanīya and other sacrificial fires; *nṛtamaḥ* means the best of leaders; *yajñaḥ* means the great sacrifice of fruits and so forth. This is a great name.
Agni is distinguished by qualities such as being the eater of food;
the sense is: "I have praised such a one."

The bull of mighty power, doubly strong, with sharp horns and a thousandfold vigor, having found the hidden track of the cow like one who knows the way, has uttered forth his great wisdom from within the mountain.

The one who possesses two-fold strength, the great one with sharpened points, possessing a thousandfold power, the bull, the mighty—having found the hidden track like that of a cow, Agni has indeed proclaimed this inspired thought as his vital secret. 3.

"Of double majesty," meaning sovereign in both the middle and the highest stations; "of sharp-pointed [flames]," meaning possessing keen brilliance; "possessing a thousandfold seed," meaning having manifold golden seed—or, the word *retaḥ* signifies essence, thus meaning "abounding in essence."
This Agni, a bull who showers down desires, powerful and possessing abundant wealth— like the footprint of a lost cow, that which is utterly hidden and most secret— he,
knowing specifically our intended great praise-song (*sāman*), has proclaimed that vast and great object of knowledge. He has spoken it forth.
May Agni, the bounteous giver with sharp jaws, consume them with his most piercing flame—
those who violate the ordinances of Varuṇa and the beloved, steadfast laws of the mindful Mitra.
May Agni, the one with sharp jaws and most fervent flame, devour them—he who is rich in gifts—whoever violates the ordinances of Varuṇa or the dear, firm laws of the mindful Mitra. 4.

That Agni who is *surādhāḥ*, possessing excellent wealth, being *tigmajambhaḥ* with sharp fangs, with *tapiṣṭhena śociṣā*—with most intense heat, a brilliance that excessively torments enemies—he *prabharbhāsate*, he severely rebukes those haters about to be mentioned; that is to say, he burns them.
The root *bhās* is used in the senses of "threatening" and "shining.
In the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood, the vowel *i* is elided by the rule "itaśca lopaḥ... [Pāṇini 3.4.97].
Then, the augment *aṭ* is added by the rule "leṭoḍaḍāṭau" [Pāṇini 3.4.94].
Regarding this, he asks: "Which ones? He says:
"Those who are haters" and "who are conscious," that is, "who know.
Both of these are adjectives [qualifying the haters].
They utterly destroy—that is, they excessively injure—the beloved, cherished, and firm abodes, stations of splendor, or ritual acts of both Mitra and Varuṇa.
The root *mī* is used in the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*).
According to the rule *mīnāter nigame*, there is shortening [of the vowel].
This is the accent of the *vikaraṇa* suffix.
1. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, mā: [these letters] signify censure. 2. Ca, pha, ma: [these letters] are associated with the nature of death.
3. Kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, bha: [these letters] signify "established."
4. *ca-pha*: one with much wealth; especially learned and possessed of knowledge.
5. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha*: "extremely hidden" (*atyanta-gopita*) is not present.
6. *na-la-sa*: "great" (*mahaṃ*) is not present.

7. In the versions with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, and *bha*, it reads *cetataḥ dveṣṭṝn*; in the version with *gha* and *pa*, it reads *cetataḥ dveṣṭāraḥ*; and in the version with *ta* and *sa*, it reads *cetataḥ*. 8. In the versions with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *pha*, *bha*, and *s*, it reads *tvām*; in the versions with *gha* and *pa*, the word *vā* does not exist. Ṛgveda 1.67.7–8.

Like sisters without brothers, like women wandering away from their husbands, like wives who are ill-behaved toward their lords—being wicked, false, and untruthful—they have produced this deep place. Like sisters (*abhrātaraḥ*) who are deprived of brothers, like *yoṣaṇaḥ* (women) who have departed from their husbands; [the lengthening of the vowel is absent due to the rule "vā papūrvasya nigame," which allows for the short vowel in such Vedic usage]. Just as they depart from the husband's house to the father's house, so too do they *vyantaḥ*: going away, meaning they wander on wrong paths, having abandoned sacrifices and other duties. Likewise, like *patiripo na janyaḥ*: women hostile to their husbands, they are *durevāḥ*: of evil course and bad conduct; therefore, being *pāpāsaḥ*: wicked, and *santaḥ*: existing as such, they are *anṛtāḥ*: devoid of mental truth, and *asatyāḥ*: devoid of verbal truth—those who offend both in mind and speech. They have *ajanata*: produced (in the singular form used by *vyatyaya*, a grammatical substitution), brought forth—that *gabhīram padam*: the deep, bottomless place, the station of hell, which is well-known as being experienced by the wicked. 1.1.5.5 || 1 ||

O purifying Agni, for me who am so small, you have not diminished this great thought, which is like a heavy burden. With boldness, bestow upon me that vast, profound, and sevenfold wealth—the great back [of the earth] touched with food. O *pāvaka*, O purifier, O *agne*, Agni! For me, who am *kiyate*—so very small—you have not *aminate*, diminished; you have not made it fail. Like a *gurum bhāram na*, a heavy burden that one is unable to carry, so too is this [wealth] difficult to sustain. Just as one might drop such a burden, so do I feel toward your work. To me, who am *aminate*—unharmed and unassailable—give *idam*, this well-known, *bṛhat*, abundant *manma*, wealth worthy of being meditated upon. That very wealth is further specified: *dhṛṣatā prayasā*, with food that is bold against enemies—a name for fire itself; joined with fire, it is *gabhīram*, profound and unfathomable by others; *yaham*, great; *pṛṣṭham*, the back [of the earth], fit to be touched; and *saptadhātu*, sevenfold, distinguished by the division of domestic and wild animals, according to the Śruti: "Seven are the domestic animals, seven the wild" (TS 7.2.2.1). The meaning is: "Give such wealth. Or, it may be construed thus: "Just as one gives another's heavy burden to someone else, so give us the wealth that ought to be given."

As if toward him, so indeed, having come together at the same time, may the purifying prayer reach him who is common to all. Upon the skin of the grass, he has brought forth the beautiful form of the dappled cow, fashioned as it were upon its surface.

1. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, and pratyāya occur. 2. [The letters] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, bha, and jana do not occur. 3. [The letters] gha, la, and sa are to be understood as such. 4. [The letters] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, bha, and ra occur, distinguished by the categories of domestic animals (*grāmyapaśu*) and wild animals (*āraṇyapaśu*).

Since Yāska stated in the *Nirukta* (7.23), "Even those called 'the fire purified by Agni' and 'the Sun' are denoted by the word *vaiśvānara* according to different opinions," here Vaiśvānara is praised in his aspect as the Sun (*ādityātman*).

May our own *dhītiḥ*—our thought, our praise—reach that very Vaiśvānara, who is established in the chariot of heroes, who is common to all and of one form, who is equal and similar [to all], and who purifies us; may it reach him through *ṛtā*, the appropriate rite, and indeed through *kṣapra*, the swift [path].
"May it attain him"—this is the meaning.

In the optative (liṅ) of the root *aś*, there is elision of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*” [Pāṇini 2.4.73]. There is an irregularity (*vyatyaya*) whereby the active voice (*parasmaipada*) and the middle person (*madhyamapuruṣa*) are employed.
Since the word *tat* was heard previously, the word *yat* must be supplied as an ellipsis.
The Vaiśvānara who is situated in heaven has a brilliant (*cāru*) orb that is *jabāru*—

meaning either "climbing while growing old" (*jaramāṇarohi*) or "climbing swiftly" (*javamānarohi*), as Yāska states in Nirukta 6.17— and he is *rūpaḥ*, beautiful, in the front, in the eastern direction.
Because it causes crops and the like to grow within itself, the earth is called *rasita*. From that [earth] comes *rasasasya*;
this is an elided simile (*luptopamā*).
Of the one who is as motionless as if sleeping; [the word] *pṛkṣaḥ* ends in *-mat*.
Because it is listed among the names common to both heaven and earth in the *Nighaṇṭu* (1.4.2): “*svaḥ pṛkṣaḥ*.”
Of the heavenly world being touched by Jyotiruttarā and the others, *adhi* means "upon" (*upari*), and *carman* means "for the skin" (*carmaṇe*) or "for movement" (*caraṇāya*).
The suffix *manin* is applied according to the *Uṇādi* rules;
the case-ending of the dative is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
It was fashioned by the gods;
"they [the gods] made it" is the connection with what precedes.
What of this my splendor is to be proclaimed? They speak of that which is hidden in secret, like a nest.
When he, like a bird, spreads out his wings over the cows, O Agni, he reveals the beloved footprint of the sun.
It is to be proclaimed: what of this splendor is hidden within me? They speak of it in secret when, like the waters of the cows, he guards the beloved form, the foremost step of the Bird. 8.
What is there to be said regarding this, my forthcoming speech?
The meaning is that only the truth is being spoken.
Of the cows...
This is a name for milk. Just as the milk belonging to cows that yield milk and so forth flows out like water (*udaka*), so do the milkers open it up (*apavṛṇvanti*) by means of the vessel.
*Niṇik*.

That which washes or purifies thoroughly is called *niṇik*, meaning milk. Such milk is said by the knowers to be placed (*upahitam*)—that is, deposited—within the cave (*guhā*) of this Vaiśvānara. Furthermore, he protects (*pāti*) the beloved (*priyam*), most excellent (*śreṣṭham*) station (*padam*) of the Earth (*bhūmyāḥ*), which is the form of the bird (*veḥ*) and is dear to all as their support. He is Agni.
This is that great, most wondrous power, whereby the auspicious cow follows after the bull;
established upon the station of Truth, she has been perceived as swiftly moving and hastening deep within the secret cave.

This—*ūm*—is that great face of the Great One, which the cow, full of milk, follows as she moves toward the sacred place of Truth. She has found him dwelling in the secret cave, moving swiftly, moving with rapid strides. 9.
1. Purifying *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*.
2. *Kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha* [are] moving; *na*, *sa* [are] moving; *rohi*. 3.
In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, the word "iti" does not exist.
4. This is an elided simile (*taluptopama*).
5. [The reading] *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha* is "of those who exude milk and so forth.
6. [The reading] *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha* states that "kiṃcāyam" is not present.

Of these [worlds], this very one—which is well-known, great (mahi), vast, and worthy of worship; which is the great (maha) host (anīka), meaning the solar orb in the form of a collection of the great gods; and which is Vaiśvānara himself—this is the remainder [of the sense]. That ancient (pūrya), or rather, filling (pūraka) orb, which the cow (gauḥ)—the producer of milk and other substances—is attended (sacate) for the sake of the Agnihotra and other rites, is situated above (adhi) in the place (pada) of the waters (ṛtasya), namely, in the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
Or rather, this is a supplementary explanatory statement (*anuvāda*).

I have known—that is, I have realized—that the Vaiśvānara is indeed the Sun: that which is *dvīyānam*, shining; which is in *guhā*, in the cave (the heart); which is *raghuṣyat*, flowing swiftly; and which is *raghuyat*, moving swiftly toward the solar orb.
Joining with his parents, he has perceived their secret and beautiful [essence] through his full powers;
seated near his mother in the highest station, the tongue of the bull, of the radiant and striving one, is extended.

Joined with his parents, he has remembered the secret and beautiful [truth] together with his mouth; at the highest station of the Mother, near the presence of the Bull, the tongue of the outstretched flame has become manifest. 10.

Then, having joined together, shining forth, and pervading the midst between his two parents, Heaven and Earth, he perceived with his own mouth for the sake of drinking the beautiful, delightful, secret milk hidden in the udder associated with the cow. He explains the very meaning already stated: He who is born from the two parents, Heaven and Earth, having united with them and being radiant, pervading their midst, perceived—that is, became aware of—the beautiful, delightful, and secret milk hidden in the udder connected to the cow, by means of his own mouth, for the purpose of drinking it. He clarifies this same point that has been stated.

The milk—which exists near (anti) the mother who produces it, such as the cow, in the supreme (parama) place, that is, the excellent station characterized by the udder—the tongue of Vaiśvānara, who is the showerer (vṛṣṇaḥ) of fruits, who is radiant (śociṣaḥ), and who is offered (prayatasya) in the form of the Āhavaniya fire and so forth, desires to drink it; this is the ellipsis.
Being questioned, I speak the *ṛta* with reverence and with a prayer for your favor, O Jātavedas, regarding all this that exists:
you are the master of whatever wealth there is in heaven and whatever wealth there is on earth.
I have spoken the Truth with reverence when questioned, O Jātavedas, through your grace—since you, indeed, rule over this wealth of his, whatever treasure exists in heaven or upon the earth. 11.
I, the sacrificer, being questioned and interrogated by others, speak the *ṛta*; I speak the truth.
What is that? It is said:

O Jātavedas—O Agni, knower of all beings or possessor of born wisdom—by your grace (*āśasā*), that is, by the means of your own praise, if this wealth should be obtained by us, you alone are its master; you alone are the lord of this wealth.
The sense is that one obtains that wealth through means such as sacrifice and the like, by way of commendatory statements (*arthavāda*).
What has been said is far too little;
for you are indeed the master even of that entire wealth which constitutes the whole universe.
He clarifies that which was stated generally as "the universe":

whatever wealth (*draviṇa*) there is in heaven (*divi*), in the celestial world, and whatever wealth is on earth—you are the lord (*īśvara*) of all that. This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*): "Wealth has arisen for the sake of sacrifice."
The sense is that sacrifice is impossible apart from fire.
1. That which is for the sake of the Agnihotra; 2. That which is for the sake of the Vārta;
3. That which belongs to him.

What is our wealth from this, and what is our treasure? O Jātavedas, you who are wise, declare it to us. We have reached the highest point of this secret path, yet we have not arrived at its final resting place.

What is our wealth? What indeed is our treasure? O Jātavedas, you who are wise, declare it to us—the highest point of this path that is hidden from us. We have not reached its foundation through our own negligence. 12.
Regarding that wealth for which ownership was declared by the preceding mantra—what is that wealth? What is the *draviṇa*, what means of attainment, is there among us that is to be given to us?
What is the *ratna*, and what delightful, beneficial wealth is there?
O Jātavedas, Agni whose wealth is born, you who are conscious, perceptive, and wise—discern that wealth and declare it clearly to us.
Alternatively, it may be construed as: "What wealth is there to be given? or "Of this heap of wealth, what is the value? (kadranam).

Reveal to us that which is hidden in the cave of this path—the way to the attainment of wealth—that which is secret, supreme, and most excellent, the goal to be reached; for we are empty, wandering toward a vacant place such as a home, while being censured by others for our motives.
The agentive suffix occurs in the sense of the object.
We have not gone; we have not reached it.
What is the boundary, what are the paths? How may we, like swift steeds, go toward your favor?
When will the goddesses, the wives of the Immortal, extend for us the splendor of the Sun?

What is the boundary? What are the pathways? And what is the desirable goal toward which we may go, like swift horses to the prize? When will the goddesses, the wives of the Immortal, the Dawns who have spread themselves out with the hue of the sun, come to us? 13.

What is the boundary? What is the established order of affection and so forth? And what is *vayunā*—the wisdom concerning the nature of things? What is *kadru*? And what is *vāma*—the collection of desirable objects? May we go toward and attain all this.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like the prize for the Raghvas; that is, like a battle for swift-moving horses and the like. Just so.

When—at what time—will the divine, shining Uṣas, the wives of the immortal Āditya, who protect and give birth to the Sun, extend themselves with the light of their manifestation for our worldly activity?
Thus, through this praise of the Uṣas in connection with the Sun, the praise of Vaiśvānara, the Self of All, is to be understood.
*tatanu*: from the root *tan* (to extend), in the *leṭ* mood; by the rule “*bahulaṃ chandasi*,” the suffix *plu* is substituted for the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*);
then reduplication and the *halādiśeṣa* [elision of all but the first consonant] apply.

With unassailable splendor, with a swelling body, with a face that turns toward us, O you who are heated by the fire—then, O Agni, what shall those weaponless ones say here? Let them lie down together.

With their lack of brilliance, with their hollows, with their backs, with their bellies, and with their backsides—being scorched by you, O Agni, what indeed do they say here? Let those weaponless ones consort with untruth. 14.
1. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, and ha are excluded.
2. In the manuscript *la*, the word "dhanasya" (of wealth) is absent.
3. In the manuscripts *na* and *sa*, the word "dhanasya" is absent.

4. [In the versions] kha, ga, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and sa, it says “that for us”; in ca and pha, it says “which for us. 5. In ta, it says “you are Jātavedas, you are Jātadhana”; in na and sa, it says “you are Jātadhana. 6. In kha, ga, gha, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the phrase “toward... likewise” does not exist.
7. Or, [the suffixes] *patnī* and *sthānīya* may follow *ta*, *la*, *pa*, and *layi*.
8. [The suffixes] *na*, *sa*, and *uṣas*; [and] *la* and *uṣas*. 9.
In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Pha, and Bha, the word "stutyā" (praiseworthy) does not occur.
Without *irā*, which is food; by that which is devoid of it;
by the fruitless, the hollow, the deceptive, and that which is to be departed from.
The meaning is "ascending.
By the word *kṛdhu*, which means "short";
for *kṛdhuka* is a synonym for "short," as it is stated in the list of names [of ants]: "The *kṛdhuka* is the *vamraka*" (Nirukta 2.2.6).
What do people say now in this world, O Agni, regarding you with such speech that is devoid of worship?
The meaning is that nothing at all is obtained by speech lacking an oblation;
rather, they are like those who are unarmed.
The word *āyudha* (weapon) indicates the means [of destruction].
May they, being devoid of such means as oblations (*havis*) and the like, encounter—that is, come into contact with—unreal suffering.
For the glory of this bull, as he was kindled, the face of the sun shone forth within the house.
Clad in radiant raiment, with a most beautiful form, he has gleamed like a dwelling-place for wealth, O bountiful one.
The face of this kindled bull, the Vasu, has shone for glory within the house; clothed in brilliance, beautiful in form, he has gleamed like a dwelling rich in wealth, abounding in boons. 15.
Of him who is kindled and being kindled—
the object of the action taking the agentive suffix—

of this Agni, the bull (*vṛṣṇaḥ*), the showerer of fruit, the dweller (*vasoḥ*), the one who causes [beings] to dwell, the face (*anīkam*), the mass of splendor, shines forth (*ā ruroca*) in the house (*dame*), that is, in the sacrificial hall, illuminating it on all sides.
For what purpose?
For the prosperity and ultimate welfare of the sacrificers.
That Agni is radiant.

Clothed in—that is, covering himself with—the nectar-like luster of his complexions, and for that very reason possessing a most beautiful form, he who is highly desirable (puruvāraḥ) by many priests and sacrificers shines forth. Like what? Just as fire, when clothed in the nectar-like luster of its own colors, shines with a most beautiful form.
The earth is [filled] with wealth such as horses and other riches, like a king [is surrounded] by ministers and others;
"the earth" refers here to human beings.
The sixth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “ūrdhva ū ṣu naḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and addressed to Agni.
It is listed in the Anukramaṇī as “ūrdhva ū ṣu ekādaśa.
This hymn is employed in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra during the Āgneya sacrifice when the metre is Triṣṭubh.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘“ūrdhva ū ṣu ṇaḥ,” “sasasya yadvīyuta,” and so on—these five [verses]’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
Stand up erect for us, O Hotṛ of the sacrifice, as the most excellent sacrificer among the gods;
for you surpass all thought, and you perceive the intention of the wise.

Upright! "Ūm!"—O Agni, Hotṛ of our sacrifice, stand as the most excellent sacrificer at the assembly of the gods; for you indeed surpass all thought, and you further even the inspired wisdom of the wise. 1.
O Hotṛ of the sacrifice, you who are the invoker of the gods associated with the ritual;
or alternatively,
in the word "hotar," the stem portion is a restatement (anuvāda).
O Agni, you who accomplish the oblation, you who are most worthy of sacrifice, stand up for us—stand truly upright.
The meaning is: may you remain perpetually elevated.
Where? That is now stated:
*Devatātā*, *devatātāu*:
the sacrifice is called *devatāti* because the gods (*deva*) are extended (*tāyante*) and spread out (*vistrīyante*) within it, O Agni;
in that [sacrifice].

For you indeed—you truly—overpower (*amyasi*) the entire universe (*viśvam*), all that is to be thought of (*manma*), namely the wealth of the enemies. Furthermore, even of the wise ones (*vedhasaścit*); *cit* is used here for the sake of honor.
You further and extend the *manīṣā*—the thought, the praise—of the praiser, the sacrificer, and others; the prefix *pra-* in *pratirasi* signifies "to increase" or "to cause to grow."
1. By the *kha-na-bha-uktha* [recitation].
2. In the *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa*, the word *samidhyamānasya* does not exist.
3. In the *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha*, there is the *phala* of the *vasu*s; in the *na-sa-phala*, there is the *phala*.

4. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ṛtvin, bhya, and jamānaiḥ. 5. In the sacrifice, the *manman* (the thought) of the *vedhas* (the wise one), the Brahman, is indeed directed toward the All; for it is truly for the purpose of invoking the gods.
They are spread out upon the grass.

The unerring Hotṛ has been seated by all the people—the joyous one, wise in the sacrificial assemblies. Like Savitṛ, he has raised his light on high; like a builder, he has propped up the smoke toward heaven. Unerring Hotṛ, Agni, the joyous one, wise in the sacrificial assemblies, has been seated by all the people. Like Savitṛ, he has extended his light upward; like a builder, he has propped up the smoke against the sky.

*Amūraḥ* means unerring; that is to say, bold. *Hotā* is the performer of the *homa* sacrifice. *Mandraḥ* means exhilarating or one who causes intoxication. *Pracetāḥ* means possessed of excellent knowledge. The divine *Agni*, among all the *ṛtvij* priests and among all creatures (*prajāsu*), has been firmly established (*nyasādi*) in the *vidathas*, that is, in the sacrifices which serve as the occasion.
Then Agni, having become thus, like Savitṛ the risen sun, has extended his radiance upward; that is, he rests with his face turned upward.

Moreover, like a pillar (metā)—just as a pillar supports a bamboo pole or similar structure upon which it is fixed—so this Agni supports the smoke, which has arisen from him, above the sky, holding it up over the world of heaven.

As he goes toward the well-warmed, ghee-anointed ladle, choosing the company of the gods while moving clockwise—the sacrificial post (*svaru*), newly born like a steed, well-placed and firmly fixed, anoints the victims. yatā | su'jurṇiḥ | rātanīm | ghṛtācīm | pra'dakṣiṇit | deva'tātim | urāṇaḥ | ut | ūm iti | svaruḥ | nava'jāḥ | na | akraḥ | paśvaḥ | anakti | su'dhitaḥ | su'mekaḥ || 3 ||
That which is *yatā* (restrained), *saṃyatā* (well-restrained), *sujūrṇiḥ* (having beautiful speed) or *suṣṭhu jīrṇā* (well-worn) or *purāṇī* (ancient),
the *ghṛtācī*— so called because it moves toward the clarified butter (*ghṛta*)— is the *juhū* (ladle). It is the *rātanī*, that which bestows wealth (*rāti*).
"Rich in the wealth characterized by oblations" means that it becomes filled with clarified butter (*ājya*).
"Thus performing the sacrifice for the gods," that is, making it extensive; "the *adhvaryu* priests have circumambulated you from the right"—thus he is called *pradakṣiṇit*.
He moves in a clockwise direction;
the elision of the letter *a* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
He is like a *svaru*—freshly born, produced at that very moment.
The word *svaru*, which denotes the chip of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śalaka*), here indicates the sacrificial post itself;
for this is evident from such passages as "The *svarus* with their chips [rest] upon the earth" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 3.8.10), where the word *svaru* signifies the sacrificial post.
The particle *na* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) also [is raised] upward. Because of the hearing of the prefix (*upasarga*), the verb "to raise" (*udyacchati*) is supplied; it becomes elevated.
Furthermore, *akraḥ* means "the one who strides" or "the well-established one"; *sumekaḥ* means "well-shining"; and *sudhitaḥ* means "well-placed," that is, the axe (*svadhiti*).
That [axe] also anoints—that is, moves toward—the cattle (*paśvaḥ*).
Or else: [the verse continues:]...
The *svaru* is well-placed; indeed, being raised up, it anoints the animal.
This is because of the Vedic revelation: "He anoints the animal with the *svaru*."

The sacrificial grass being strewn and the fire kindled, the Adhvaryu priest has stood up, well-pleased. Like a herdsman tending his cattle, the Hotṛ goes around three times, choosing the ancient path from of old. On the strewn sacrificial grass, while the fire is kindled, the Adhvaryu has stood upright, full of joy. Agni, like a herdsman or a Hotṛ, goes around three times, choosing the path from ancient times.
1. Kha, ga, ca: *mahanīyaḥ*; ṇa, na, bha, la, sa: *mahanīyaḥ*. 2. Ta, na, sa: in the case of those who have become *ṛtvij* priests.
3. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha: *svadhiṣṭhitam*.
4. Kha, ga, na, and dhūma arose; ca and pha arose as smoke; and sa was covered by smoke. 5. Gha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, pha, bha, and sa were ancient.
6. Kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, bha, and la came into being.

When the sacrificial grass has been spread upon the altar and the fire, beginning with the Āhavanīya, has been properly kindled, the Adhvaryu— the leader of the sacrifice— stands upright, having gratified the gods;
he stands as the Hotṛ, the performer of the oblation,
from of old (this being an ancient term).

The ancient *urāṇa* (the one who makes wide) is he who, even from a very small oblation, effects its expansion to a state fit for the gods. As the *Nirukta* states: "Urāṇa means making wide. And according to the *Śruti*: "Whatever oblation is prepared by the gods, that indeed increases in measure. Thus, it is appropriate for Agni to perform this act of expansion (*urvīkaraṇa*).
Such is this fire: like a herdsman who guards cattle, it encircles the cattle by turning around them three times;
for the fire is indeed carried around three times.
Agni, the Hotṛ-priest, goes forth by himself in measured steps—gladdening, sweet-voiced, and true to the cosmic order (Ṛta).
His flames run like swift horses; when he has blazed forth, all beings tremble with fear.

Agni, the Hotṛ-priest, goes forth by himself, measured in his suffering, delightful, sweet-voiced, and true to the Cosmic Order (Ṛta). His flames run forth like swift horses; all beings are struck with fear when he has blazed. 5.
He clarifies the very meaning already stated:
this Agni, the *hotṛ* who accomplishes the oblation, being by his own nature (*ātmanā*) of measured motion (*mitadru*), moves around (*pari veti*) the sacrificial animal.
Of what sort is he?
He is delightful, intoxicating, or one who causes joy; he is sweet-spoken, possessing pleasant words; he is possessed of truth, being rich in sacrifice.
Even the flames of that Agni, who possesses strength and oblations, are not [mere] lights—the word "na" (not) here carries the sense of "api" (even).
They run, that is, they go, on all sides.
Alternatively, the syllable *na* has the sense of a comparison;
thus it should be construed as "like swift horses (*vājinaḥ*), they run."
Because this one, shining brightly, blazes forth, therefore all beings—all created things—become afraid, filled with fear.
Auspicious, O Agni, is your face, O you of beautiful countenance; it is lovely even as you exist in your terrible and manifold form.
For your brilliance, most intense, cannot be obstructed by darkness, nor have the glooms ever brought blemish upon your body.

O Agni, fair of countenance, auspicious is your gathering together, you who are terrible yet lovely to the many; for they have not obscured your flame with darkness, nor have the soot-stained ones brought blemish upon your body. (6)

O Agni, whose flames are beautiful (*vsvanīka*), though you are terrible (*ghora*) and awe-inspiring (*bhītijanaka*), your form (*mūrti*)—which is manifold (*viṣuṇa*), pervading everywhere (*viśva*), and extending in all directions—is lovely (*cāru*), delightful (*ramaṇīya*), auspicious (*bhadrā*), and praiseworthy (*stutyā*). It is a sight to be beheld with perfect vision; that is to say, it becomes clearly visible. For your radiance (*śociḥ*), your brilliance, cannot be obstructed (*na varanta*) by the darkness (*tamasā*) of the nights.

And because those who destroy, such as Rākṣasas and others, do not place— do not bear, and do not perform— *vṛpaḥ*, meaning evil in the form of destruction and so forth, *in tanvas*, meaning in your body; therefore,
it connects with the word *saṃhak*.

1. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, and pradivaḥ; urāṇaḥ; uruvāṇaḥ—this is the name of the *adhvaryu*. 2. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pa, pha, bha, and sa: *madhuvacanaḥ*. 3. Ta: having the sense of comparison (*upamārthaka*). 4. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa: the elements (*bhūtāni*).

Whose birth was not obstructed by his progenitor, nor even by his mother and father; then, like a well-placed friend, the purifying Agni shone forth among the human tribes. 7. Whose birth was not obstructed from its source, nor even by his mother and father; then, like a well-established friend, the purifying Agni shone forth among the human clans. 7.

The gain—the gift characterized by cattle and other wealth, or his radiance—of that Vaiśvānara, the progenitor, the generator, the one who brings about [all things], is not withheld; it is not obstructed by anyone.
Furthermore, even his parents, Heaven and Earth, do not have the power to restrain him quickly when he is urged toward his desired mission.
Moreover, like a well-disposed friend, Agni, the purifier and cleanser, shines brightly among all human communities, within those connected to the mind.
The root *dīp* means "to shine.
The elision of the letter *p* is Vedic (*cāndasa*).
The use of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) ending occurs by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*).
By the excellence of their power (*liṅgabalātiśaya*), they flow with water from places such as the hollows of their trunks; they are *vrohitāsaḥ*, meaning red or crimson-colored;
and they are *vṛjvañcaḥ*, meaning "straight-going," for they move (*añcanti*) straight (*ṛju*) and without crookedness (*akuṭila*).
Moving well, going beautifully, the Varuṇas are radiant; they are bulls, youthful, and showerers [of benefits].
Because the long vowel is optionally prescribed by the rule "vā ṣapūrvasya nigame," there is no occurrence of the long vowel here.
"Vṛjumuṣkāḥ" means those with straight testicles; "vṛṣaṇāḥ" means virile. "Vdasmāḥ" means beautiful to behold.
Those flames of thine, O Agni, which move forward, all-conquering, unwearied, and fierce— like hawks hastening to their goal, they roar loudly like the host of the Maruts.
O Agni, those flames of yours which move forth—overpowering, tireless, and brilliant—like hawks hastening toward their goal, roar with great sound like the host of the Maruts. 10.

O Agni, indeed those rays of yours are well-known as "vayas"—overpowering, meaning they overcome enemies; "tveṣāsas," meaning radiant; "duvasanāsas," meaning worthy of worship; and "tava," meaning yours—those rays move toward their destination like falcons, that is, like horses. Of what nature are they?
Like the host of Maruts, the troop belonging to the Maruts, they possess a loud resonance; they become those of great sound, possessing exceedingly resonant voices.
The sacred prayer has been performed for you, O Kindled One; let the priest recite the hymn and sacrifice, O You who are distributed in many places.
Men have established Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, while the yearning ones, paying homage, offer praise to him who brings well-being.

The prayer has been performed; O kindled one, for you the hymn shall be recited. He sacrifices and bestows [the gift]. Men have established Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, paying homage, desiring [him], and seeking the praise of the living man. 11.
O Agni, being kindled by the fuel, for you—on your account—a prayer, that is, a hymn of praise, has been performed by us;
the Hotṛ priest recites, that is, chants, the *uktha*, which is the hymn in the form of a recitation.
The root *śaṃs* means "to praise.
The augment *āṭ* is applied according to the rule *leṭoḍaḍāṭau*.
The sacrificer worships you;

for that reason, bestow wealth upon us—grant it to us. [This is from] the root *dhā* (to give/establish); the absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "the augment *aṭ* is frequently omitted in the Vedic language" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*).

The word *vū* is a filler (*pādapūraṇa*). Furthermore, the human priests—those who desire wealth characterized by cattle and other such riches, who pay homage to and worship you, Agni, the Hotṛ of the gods who is worthy of praise (*śaṃsa*) for Vāyu—that is, for the human being; these men have sat down (*ni seduḥ*), meaning they serve you.
This seventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "ayamiha," is the seerly work of Vāmadeva and is addressed to the Aśvins.
The first verse is a Jagatī; the second through the sixth are Anuṣṭubhs; the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Ayamiha: [the first is] a Jagatī, [then] five Anuṣṭubhs."
The application of the *sūkta* is determined by its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*).
In the ritual of bringing forward the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), the verse beginning with "ayamiha" serves as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) for the Vaiśya.

Accordingly, it is stated in the Sūtra: "But for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, 'ayamiha prathamo dhāyi dhātṛbhiḥ' is the introductory verse at the establishment [of the fires]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 2.17).

1. Those increased by *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *ṇa*. 2. Those with *la*, *sa*, *sādhana*, and *muṣka*. 3. Those with *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* as the internal divisions (*vyadha*). Perform [this]. 4. For *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*, there is no "second and following" (*dvitīyādyāḥ*).
This [Agni], the most excellent sacrificer, worthy of praise at the rituals, was established here as the Hotṛ-priest by the creators;
he whom the Bhr̥gus, seeking wealth, have made to shine brightly like a wondrous disk among every people.

This one has been established here as the first by the ordainers, the Hotṛ-priest, most skilled in sacrifice, to be praised at the rituals—he whom the Bhṛgus, possessing wealth, have caused to shine forth brilliantly like a wondrous disk among every people. 1.

By the Adhvaryus performing the ritual for the sake of the sacrifice through the elements, this Agni—here in this sacrifice, the invoker of the gods, the most excellent sacrificer (*yajiṣṭha*), the one to be praised by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) during the sacrificial rites (*adhvara*), the foremost and chief of all the gods—is established (*dhāyi*), that is, placed and installed in his stations such as the Āhavanīya fire.

The form is the *luṅ* (aorist) in the passive sense of the root *dhā*. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule "in the Veda, [the augment is] frequently absent when not joined with *mā*. There is also the *nighāta* (elision of accent) by the rule "that which has an *atiṅ* [verb] preceding it [is unaccented]."
It has been stated, "This is Agni.
To the question "Who is this Agni?", he says: "Apravāna," meaning a certain descendant of Bhṛgu.

He and the other Bhṛgus, in the woods and forests, made him—who is wonderful, visible in many ways in the form of a forest fire, and who is the all-pervading Lord (*viśvam vibhum īśvaram*)—shine forth for every clan (*viśi-viśi*). By means of this repetition (*vīpsā*), the meditation of all people is implied. They caused that Agni—who is renowned as the bearer of oblations for the gods—to shine, endowing him with light for the sake of the entire clan, that is, for all progeny.
The word "yam" (which) is connected with the word "idam" (this), as in "yam idam" (that which is this).
Regarding the verse "agne kadā te": in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, within the *āgneya* hymn-form and the *ānuṣṭubha* meter, there are five verses beginning with "agne kadā te.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "Five [verses] beginning with 'agne kadā te'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).
O Agni, when will the manifestation of you, the god, appear in its proper sequence?
For mortals have indeed seized you, who are worthy of universal praise.
O Agni, when will the manifestation of you, the god, appear in its proper sequence? For mortals have indeed seized you, who are to be praised by all. 2.
O Agni, from this cause, when will your conscious splendor—the light belonging to you, the radiant deity—be continuous, ever-attendant?
There is the augment *leṭoḍāgamaḥ*.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision (*luk*) of the *vikaraṇa* suffix.
By the rule "bhūsuvostiṅi," there is the prohibition of *guṇa*.
For this reason it is also said:
"From what cause? It is said:
"Because (hi), for that reason, mortals—human beings—have seized, do seize, [and] will seize you, who are to be praised and extolled by all people."
In the word *grahibhāt* [from *grahibh- + liṭ*], there is the designation *bha* by the rule "after *hrasva* and *m*, [the suffix] *bh*";
and the augment *ruṭ* is applied by the rule "frequently in the Veda."
The observer of cosmic order, the wise one, like a dwelling surrounded by praises,
the bringer of laughter to all sacrifices within every home.
The upholder of *ṛta*, the wise one, who dwells around [all things] like a fixed abode through his hymns, the bringer of joy to all sacrifices, in every house. 3.
1. In the *tal-uṇ* [affix].
2. By virtue of being the carrier (*vāhaka*) of the letters *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *ha*.
3. Endowed with the letters *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, *sa*, and *dī* (the root *dīp*), they shone; that is, they caused to shine.
4. By the sound of *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *la*.
5. [The reading] "by *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *biḍbhiḥ*" does not exist.

Beholding Agni—who is truthful (*ṛtāvānam*), free from deceit (*amāyinam*), possessed of discerning wisdom (*vicetasam*), surrounded by the stars (*stūbhiḥ*) like a dwelling place (*dhāmiva*) accompanied by sparks, the illuminator (*haskatīram*) of all sacrifices (*adhvarāṇām*), and the bringer of prosperity (*vṛddheḥ kartāram*)—the officiating priests and others, in every sacrificial hall (*dame-dame*).
"They sang [the praises] of the swift one"—this connects with the preceding verse.

"The swift messenger of Vivasvat, who [rules] over all people; the Āyus have brought him hither as a banner, the Bhr̥gavāṇa, for every clan. (4) The swift messenger of Vivasvat, who [rules] over all people; the Āyus have brought him hither as a banner, the Bhr̥gavāṇa, for every clan. (4)
The Agni who surpasses all *carṣaṇīs*, that is, all progeny (*prajāḥ*), [and] the *āyavas*, that is, human beings—
[the word] *āyavaḥ* being read among the names of humans in the Nirukta (2.3.17) as "human beings" (*manuṣyāḥ*) along with *yadavaḥ*—
[who is] the swift, quickly-moving messenger of Vivasvat, the human sacrificer.
"Vivasvant" refers to human beings. "Ketu" means the one who makes known; "bhṛgavāṇam" means moving among the Bhṛgus.
The meaning is "the shining one."

The suffix *kvip* is applied by the rule "the suffix *kvip* should be stated after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*). From that which ends in *kvip*, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is added according to the rule "after [stems ending in] *i*. When the rule for the unaccented nature of *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes following a stem with a low-pitched vowel (*adupadeśa*) would otherwise apply, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is established because [the root] belongs to the class of *vṛṣan* and others, which is an open-ended group (*ākṛtigaṇa*).
For every people, for all progeny, they have brought him hither; they have brought him.
[The change from *ahar* to *ahaḥ* is due to the rule "hy-ama-hoḥ bhaḥ.

They have established that Hotṛ priest in succession—the wise one, the delightful, whose flame is purifying, the most excellent sacrificer, according to the seven stations. (5) They have established him, that very Hotṛ, in succession—the wise one, the delightful, whose flame is purifying, the most excellent sacrificer, by means of the seven stations. (5)
The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, being men, [worship] him in due order as the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods, who is *cikitvāṃsam*—that is, knowing.
[The root] *kit* means "to know";
the suffix *kasu* is used here for the perfect tense (*liṭ*).
The reduplication, the *halādiśeṣa*, the *pactva* (change to *k*), and the lengthening have taken place. This is the accent of the suffix (*pratyayasvara*).
They have established this very Agni within the altar (*vedi*).
Of what nature is he? He is *raṇva*, delightful; *pāvaka-śociṣam*, possessing purifying luster; *yajiṣṭham*, most worthy of sacrifice; and endowed with *sapta dhāmabhiḥ*, the sevenfold splendors.

Him, who dwells among the eternal mothers in the forest, who is sought after, who is unattached, who is wondrous, who is hidden in the secret place, who is easily found, and who seeks his goal wherever it may be—him [we invoke]. 6. Him. Among the eternal. Mothers. In the forest. Toward. Sought after. Unattached. Wondrous. Being. Hidden in the secret place. Easily found. Seeking his goal wherever it may be. 6.

1. [The variants] beginning with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, *bha*, and *pra*; and those beginning with *ca*, *pa*, and *pra*. 2. [The variants] beginning with *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, *sa*, and *a* do not contain the phrase: “or the agent of the *vṛddhi*. 3. [The variants] beginning with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *na* do not contain the phrase: “of human names... thus.”
4. *la*, *bhr̥gu*, and *āyu* [are the names of seers].
5. The suffix *manuṣya* takes the suffix *idam*.
6. The suffixes *ca* and *pha* take the augment *kip* optionally.
In the many eternal mothers, namely the waters— which are called "mothers" because they are the creators of the Sarayu and other rivers—
and in the forest, that is, in the multitude of trees.
The suffix *ā* is used in the sense of the object (*arthe*).

"Existing" (*santam*) means present; "lovely" (*vītam*) means desirable; "unresorted to" (*aśritam*) means not frequented by living beings out of fear of being burned—its meaning is that it is difficult to approach.

Wondrous and worthy of admiration, hidden in the secret cave, easy to find or easy to know, and bringing good fortune; [He is] one who accepts the oblation—consisting of fuel, clarified butter, sacrificial cakes, and so forth—from anyone anywhere seeking it, that is, from anyone desiring the sacrificial offering.
In the word *ka*, the vowel *va* undergoes *saṃprasāraṇa* according to Vedic usage, followed by the substitution of the preceding vowel; subsequently, the lengthening is applied by the rule *halaḥ*.
The connection with the preceding clause is: "they settled upon that Agni who has become thus."
In the *gāyatrī* metre of the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, there are five verses beginning with "sasasya yad viyutā" (RV 7.90.1–5).
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The five [verses] beginning with 'sasasya yad viyutā'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
O Agni, when you, being wise and knowing all, desire (*vei*) the visible duties of the messenger pertaining to the sacrifice (*adhvara*), or—
alternatively, *vei* may be a qualifier of the sacrifice itself.
Knowing the visible acts of the messenger connected with the sacrifice— the ritual of the most excellent sacrificer which produces the desired fruit—
and thoroughly cognizing the intermediate space situated between both *rodasī*, that is, between both heaven and earth; he is ancient from of old (*pradivaḥ*),
for this word is listed among the names of the ancient in the Nirukta (3.27.2) as "the question from of old."
Making even a small oblation vast and abundant—
as Yāska has stated, "urāṇa means making wide or making much"—
you, the most wise messenger of the gods, [know] the ascents, the ways of ascending, to the sky, to heaven.
The meaning is "places worthy of ascending. You go—that is, you proceed—to offer oblations to the gods.
The black one indeed comes before the ruddy ones, moving with flickering flame, the sole form among all forms;
when she who has not yet conceived bears the embryo, even as soon as he is born, you become the messenger.

The Black One; for you, O bright one, are the light before us, the moving flame, the sole marvel among wonders, since even while unimpregnated you take on the embryo. As soon as you are born, you indeed become the messenger. 9.
O Agni, this path (*ema*) belonging to you, the white and radiant one—
here the word *em* denotes the path of movement—
becomes black, that is, of a dark color.
Your light, belonging to you, shines before; your moving flame, which is by nature prone to wandering, is the splendor of the embodied— meaning,
of those possessed of form and brilliance.
Your form is indeed preeminent;
for you, whom the sacrificers—who have not yet approached you—indeed bear as a fetus, the cause of your birth, you, being born even from that very same womb, become the messenger;
you truly become the messenger of the sacrificer.
The sight of him as soon as he is born is vigor; when the wind blows after his flame, he bends his sharp tongue among the dry woods; indeed, he rends even solid things with his jaws.
The appearance of him who is born at once is vigor; when the wind blows after his flame, he extends his sharp tongue among the dry brushwood. Even solid things he rends asunder with his jaws. 10.
The vigor (*ojas*)—the brilliance (*tejas*)—of the fire that has just been born from the friction of the *aruṇi* wood is its manifestation;
the ellipsis is that it becomes visible to the officiating priests and others.
When the wind (*vāta*), the air, blows toward and follows the flame (*śocis*) of this fire, then this very fire applies its sharp tongue—the flame—to the *atasa* shrubs, which are clusters of trees.
Even solid things—solid objects in the form of food such as wood and the like—he tears apart with his jaws, that is, with his fiery energies;
the meaning is that he devours them.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, Bha, and Sa, the phrase “kāmayase ... jānan” (desiring ... knowing) is absent; [in these versions it reads] “na-vidvān jānan” (not-knowing, though knowing). 2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Na, Bha, and Sa, [the reading is] “yasya”.
3. In manuscript Ca, [the reading is] “dīptaṃ tejaḥ” (blazing splendor).
4. He makes the sounds *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *pha* vibrate.
When Agni, O youth, has quickly made his food ready with *tsu* and *tṣuṇā*, he makes it swift;
he joins the roar of the wind, and like a swift steed, he is urged on and incited.
When Agni has made his day swift with food, he makes it short; consuming [the fuel], he follows the roar of the wind. Like a swift horse, he is urged forward; the racer is driven on. 11.
Agni, who swiftly (*vitsu*) carries (*vakṣa*)— that is, consumes— the fuel (*vatsū*), such as wood and other materials, by means of his swift (*viṣuṇā*) mass of rays;
that great (*vahaḥ*) Agni makes himself (*ātmanam*) swift (*viṣum*) and acts as the messenger for the sacrificer.

Consuming the pieces of wood completely, the fire attends to—that is, serves—the *vmeḷi*, the strength, of Vāta, the wind; it does not [attend to] the *vāśu*. Just as one who praises a horse treats a horse, so the fire, being swift in its movement, makes its own ray *vājina*, that is, powerful.
And he fans or impels it.
The eighth hymn, "dūtaṃ vaḥ," consists of eight verses; it is the seer Vāmadeva’s composition, composed in the Gāyatrī meter, and has Agni as its deity.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "dūtaṃ vaḥ—eight [verses], in Gāyatrī.
In the first Chandoma of the ten-night *vyūha* sacrifice, this hymn serves as the locus for the insertion of the *jātavedasī* *nivid*.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "Or rather, [one recites] 'dūtaṃ va iṣyāmi mārutam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.9).
These first two hymns are prescribed for the Prātaranuvāka at the Agni-rite in the Gāyatrī metre.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'agne pāvaka' and 'dūtaṃ va'—these two hymns" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
I honor with my song your messenger, the all-knowing, the immortal bearer of oblations, the most excellent sacrificer.
I strive with my song for you—that immortal messenger, the all-knowing bearer of oblations, the most excellent sacrificer. || 1 ||

O Agni, I, the sacrificer, choose you with my speech—in the form of praise—to serve you, the all-knowing (*viśvavedasam*), whose wealth is everything (*viśvam samastam vedas*); you who are the bearer of oblations (*havyavāham*) for the gods; you who are immortal (*amartyam*), possessing the nature of not dying; you who are the most excellent sacrificer (*yajñiṣṭham*); you who are the one among the gods. I, the sacrificer, propitiate you with my voice consisting of hymns.
The meaning is "I cause to increase.
Yāska states: "The root *ṛñj* has the sense of adorning or preparing."
For he indeed knows the treasure-store, the great ascent to heaven;
may he bring the gods here to us.
For he knows the place where wealth is stored; the great one knows the ascent to heaven. He shall bring the gods here. 2.
For that very Agni, who is well-known, knows the bestowing of wealth—the granting of the desired fruits of the sacrifice;
the great and abundant Agni knows the ascent to heaven, the dwelling place of the gods;
that Agni [is present] here in this sacrifice.

1. *kha-ga-ca-na-bha-la-sa* [is used for] the *yajamāna*; *dūtam* [is used for] the messenger. 2. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-sa* [is used for] the two hymns beginning with *agne pāvaka* and *dūtaṃ vaḥ*. [Regarding] *na*: the *triṣṭubh* verse beginning with *pra yad vastriṣṭubham* and the *māruta* hymn beginning with *dūtaṃ vaḥ*.
In the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*), during the Agni-rite, in the *gāyatrī* metre, these two hymns beginning with this [verse] are used in the *ābhinasa* recitation.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "In the hymn beginning with *agne pāvaka dūtaṃ vaḥ*," and also [in the rule] regarding its being used as a *prātaranuvākyā*.

[The word *vakṣati* means] "he shall bring" (*vā devān indrādīn vā vakṣati*), that is, "let him bring. From the root *vah*, by the rule *liha-arthe aiṭ*, the affix *aiṭ* is added; for that [root], the suffix *tip* is applied. By the rule *sibbahulaṃ ha leṭi*, the suffix *sip* is applied, and by *leṭoḍaḍāṭau*, the augment *aṭ* is added. By *ho ḍhaḥ*, there is the substitution of *ḍha*; then follow the substitutions of *ḍha* for *ha*, *ka* for *ṭa*, and *pa* for *pha*. By the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*, there is the *nighāta* (suppression of accent).

He, the god, knows how to bring the gods to the dwelling of the one who follows the cosmic order; he bestows even dear treasures. 3. He knows, the god, the means of bringing [the gods] to the dwelling of the one who follows the cosmic order; he gives even dear riches. 3.

That shining god Agni knows—that is, he understands in due order—the *vāma*, meaning those who bow down, such as the sacrificers and others, so as to cause them to bow or offer salutations to the gods, Indra and the rest.

In the sacrificial hall (*dame*), for the sacrificer who desires the *ṛta*—that is, who seeks the sacrifice—he bestows, grants, and gives even the most cherished *priyāṇi vasu*, the desired riches such as cattle and other wealth.

He, the Hotṛ, being wise, goes between for his mission as messenger; he, knowing, knows the ascent to heaven. 4. He, the Hotṛ, he indeed, being conscious, goes between for his office as messenger; he, knowing, knows the ascent to heaven. 4.

Agni is the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods. He, that very same Agni, knowing—the one who understands—the mission of the gods, the work of a messenger; and knowing the ascent, the way of ascending, to the enclosure of heaven, the dwelling place of the gods; he moves, he goes, between heaven and earth.
The root *iṅ* means "to go. The suffix *iyan* is applied according to the rule *divādibhyaḥ iyan*. The elision [of the verb ending] is governed by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*.

May we be those who have honored Agni with offerings of oblations—those who, nourishing him, kindle him. 5. May we be those who have honored Agni with offerings of oblations—those who, nourishing him, kindle him. 5.
"May we be yours as sacrificers; may we become [your devotees]. This has been said. To the question "Who? it is replied:
The sacrificers, with offerings of oblations and gifts of sacrificial food, have worshipped Agni; they bring him pleasure.
Nourishing and increasing this very Agni, the sacrificers kindle him, making his flames blaze forth.
