They have become renowned through wealth and through great heroic powers—those who have won and who have offered worship to Agni. 6. They have become renowned through wealth and through great heroic powers—those who have won and who have offered worship to Agni. 6.
Let us, the sacrificers, speak aloud to Agni.
The form [in -ā] is due to the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
They have performed and maintain the services of worship; that is to say, they carry them out.
Having prospered, those who honor Agni are heard far and wide—meaning they are renowned and recognized—on account of wealth characterized by cattle and other such riches.
They shine forth with excellent heroic powers and with sons and other offspring endowed with beautiful valor.

1. [The reading] *la-anukrameṇa* is not found in manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Pa, and Bha. 2. [The sequence] *kha-ga-ca-pa-bha-'paścādīni* does not exist. 3. [The reading] *kha-ga-gha-ṇa-na-bha-la-sa-ārohaṇārtham* is not found in manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, La, and Sa. 4. [The reading] *kha-ga-ca-saparyām* is not found in manuscripts Kha, Ga, and Ca. 5.

[The word] *te* is not found in manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ta, Na, Pa, Pha, Bha, La, and Sa. May riches, desired by many, come to us day after day; may strengths rise up for us. (7) For us—riches; day after day; may they come together; desired by many; for us; strengths; may they rise up. (7)

May the desirable things—those riches such as cattle and other wealth being spoken of by the officiating priests and others—daily come together and flow toward us, the sacrificers who possess the two Vedas.

The locative case ending following the word *diva* is replaced by *śeṣa* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk...* and its udātta accent is applied by the rule *ūḍidampadādyappumraidyubhyaḥ*. When reduplication occurs by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ*, the syllable *sa-* of the subsequent portion becomes anudātta according to the rule *anudāttaṃ ca*.
May the *vājās*—the foods—impel us toward heroism for the sake of sacrifice.

He, the inspired poet among the peoples, pierces through the men with his might as if with a swift arrow. 8. He; the inspired poet; of the peoples; with his might; of the men; through; like a swift [arrow]; he pierces. 8.
The wise one (*vipraḥ*) is the intelligent one;
for *vipra* is a name for the intelligent, as it is listed among those names in [Nirukta] 3.15.1: "The *vipra* is the wise one" (*dhīraḥ*). He is Agni.
With all power— *śavas* being a name for strength, as it is listed among the names for strength in *Nirukta* 2.9.3—
"they are worthy of being destroyed as quickly as possible by the *carṣaṇīs*, that is, the human beings related to Manu."
"Evils" is the ellipsis.
*Vidhyati* means "he pierces"; *atividhyatu* means "may he destroy excessively."
‘Agné mr̥ḷa’: this ninth hymn consists of eight verses; it is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Vāmadeva, composed in the Gāyatrī metre, and has Agni as its deity. It is catalogued thus: ‘Agné mr̥ḷa’.
In the second Chandoma, this hymn is to be used as the introductory formula for the Jātavedas Nivid.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, may your host, the playful and merciful company of the Maruts, [be gracious]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.10).

O Agni, be gracious; you are great, you who have gone to this divine people to sit upon the sacred grass (barhis). 1. O Agni, be gracious; you are great, you who have come to this divine folk to take your seat upon the sacrificial grass. 1.
O Agni, be gracious to us; bring us happiness.
You are great; you are preeminent in power.
You have come to this divine person—the sacrificer who desires the gods—to sit upon the *barhis* grass at the sacrifice. You approach.

Among human dwellings, that invincible mortal has become the leader and the messenger of all. 2. He, among human communities, the invincible, the leader, the mortal, has become the messenger of all. 2.
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pha, and bha are indeed swift; na is not swift. 2.
The *gāyatra* [meter] belongs to Agni.
3. "O Agni, have mercy" is also recited in sequence.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on the *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic).
4. This hymn is used in the *ābhimāruta* śastra during the second *chandoma* of the ten-night (*daśarātra*) *avyūha* sacrifice;
and so says the Sūtra.

5. [The reading] *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha* ‘*prabhūto bhavasi*’ does not exist. According to *ka*. 3-69: *dūtabha*: he who is difficult for Rākṣasas and others to overcome (*durdabha*), difficult to seize (*durdaihasa*). *Mānuṣīṣu*: among human beings, those connected with humans; *viśvāsu prajāsu*: among all creatures. *Prāvīḥ*: one who goes with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa gantā*). *Amartyaḥ*: immortal by nature (*amaradharmā*). May that Agni become (*bhuvat*) the messenger (*dūtaḥ*) of *viśveṣām*, of all the gods.

He is led all around the sacrificial hall; the joyous Hotṛ at the divine rites. And as Potṛ, he sits down. He, Agni, is led all around the sacrificial hall (satra) by the officiating priests. Being led, that Agni—joyous (mandra), meaning delightful or worthy of praise—at the divine rites (diviṣṭiṣu), namely the sacrifices, becomes the Hotṛ. Moreover (uta), as the Potṛ, he sits down (ni ṣīdati) in the sacrificial hall.

And Agni is the leader at the sacrifice; and he is the master of the house in the home; and as the Brahman priest, he sits down. (4) Furthermore, Agni leads the *grās*—the wives of the gods—at the sacrifice (*adhvara*); or else, it means "he exists. Or rather, moving forward (*grās*), he becomes the Adhvaryu priest. And furthermore, that very Agni becomes the master of the house (*gṛhapati*)—the sacrificer—in the home (*dame*), the sacrificial hall. And furthermore, as the Brahman priest (specifically the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin), he sits down (*ni ṣīdati*).
You come as the invoker for the sacrificial rite, the one who speaks in favor of the people,
and [you bring] the oblations of human beings.
For you go to those who perform the sacrificial office.
The one who speaks up for the ancient ones;
the oblations.
And [the praise] of human beings.

O Agni, you indeed desire (*veṣi*) the oblations (*havyā*), that is, the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) of the *mānuṣāṇāṃ janānām*—of the human beings who are performing the sacrifice (*adhvarīyatām*). Furthermore, you are the *upavaktā*, the one who speaks the words such as "Lead me forward" for the sake of granting permission for all the rituals of the Adhvaryu and the others; you are the Brahman priest, according to the Vedic revelation:
"The Brahman priest indeed declares the knowledge of what has been born" (*brahmā tvo vadati jātavidyām*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.71.11).

You are the *upavaktṛ*, the supervisor (*upadraṣṭṛ*) or the *sadasya* (member of the assembly), for the sake of ensuring that all ritual actions are performed without deficiency; for Āpastamba has stated: "He indeed is the *sadasya* who becomes the supervisor of the ritual actions."

You perform the office of the messenger for him whose sacrifice you have accepted, in order to carry the oblation of that mortal. You indeed perform his mission as messenger, for you have accepted his sacrifice, so as to carry the oblation of that mortal.

1. *pa*-manuṣya-sambandhiṣu; 2. *pa*-manuṣya-sambandhinīnām; 3. *la*-janānāṃ yajamānānām; 4. *ṇa*-yad vā upavaktā; 5. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, and *sa*, the word ‘*vā*’ is absent.
O Agni, you [are the one] for the sake of carrying (*voḍhum*) the sacrifice (*adhvara*) and the oblation (*havya*) of whichever mortal (*martya*) human sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
From the root *vah*, the suffix *taven* is applied in the sense of the infinitive (*tumun*) by the rule "sesenase" (Pāṇini 3.4.9);
its initial vowel is acute by the rule "nnityādinintyam" (Pāṇini 6.1.197).
"jujoṣaḥ" means "you should serve."
The root *juṣ* means "to delight in" and "to serve.
It is in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood; by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the substitution of *ślau* for *śap* and reduplication.
The augment *aṭ* is applied by the rule "leṭo 'ḍāṭau."
"Of this sacrificer, you have indeed desired the visible and the act of giving."
Accept our sacrifice; O Aṅgiras, [accept] our worship. Hear our invocation. (7) Accept our sacrifice; O Aṅgiras, [accept] our worship. Hear our invocation. (7)
O Aṅgiras, O Agni, do you take pleasure in our sacrifice; enjoy, favor, and attend to it.
Enjoy our sacrifice and the oblation that is the means for its performance.
And hear—listen to our invocation, which is in the form of a hymn of praise.
This is the second person singular present indicative form of the root *śru*.
The suffix *sip* is applied;
by the rule "for *śru*, there is *śru*" (*śruvaḥ śruca*), the suffix *śru* is substituted for the root and the root itself undergoes the change to *śru*. Thus, *hir* is the substitute for *sip*.
The substitution of *dhi* for the suffix *hi* occurs by the rule "śruśṛṇukṛvṛbhyaśchandasi" [Pāṇini 6.4.102].

May your unassailable chariot encompass us from every side, O Lord, with which you protect those who offer oblations. 8. May your chariot, O Unassailable One, reach us from all sides—with it you guard those who give. 8.
O Agni, with that chariot by which you go in all directions toward every station, protecting the liberal patrons—the sacrificers who offer oblations—and guarding them from the inspired singers;
may that chariot of yours, difficult to overcome and invincible, reach and pervade us, the sacrificers, on every side.
The *parasmaipada* ending [is used] for the root *aś* by way of transposition.
"O Agni, him today"—this tenth hymn is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva, dedicated to Agni.

Thus says the Anukramaṇikā: "'agne tamadya' [is] a *padapaṅkti*; the fifth is a *mahāpadapaṅkti*, another is *uṣṇih*, the fourth is either a *ṣatpadā* or [the rest] up to the seventh; the third [of the seventh] consists of two pentads, a heptad, and a nonad; of the eighth, there is a pentad, a foot, a tetrad, a heptad, and an *aiṣabhra*."

This entire hymn consists of verses in the *padapaṅkti* meter, because it possesses the characteristics defined as: "four [verses] of five syllables each, one of six, and the fourth of four, or [alternatively], a *padapaṅkti*. The fifth verse, "tava svādiṣṭhā," is a *mahāpadapaṅkti*, because it possesses the characteristic: "five [verses] of five syllables each and one of six."
The verse beginning with "anyā śivā naḥ satyā" is in the *uṣṇih* meter.
The fourth, sixth, and seventh verses—"ābhīṣṭe aya," "ghṛtaṃ na pūtaṃ," and "kṛtaṃ ciddhi pmā"—these three are either *uṣṇih*s or *padapaṅkti*s.

Here, for the seventh and eighth verses, which are respectively *padapaṅkti* and *uṣṇih*, a different mode of division has been made to set aside the division of feet prescribed by the general rules (*paribhāṣā*).
On the tenth day, this hymn is the *ājya* recitation (*śastra*). It is stated in the Sūtra: "‘O Agni, [bring] him today with praises like a horse’—this is the *ājya*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.12).
In the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, one should return with the verse beginning, "O Agni, him today."
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should approach the fire with [the verse], 'O Agni, him today as with horses, with hymns... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.7).
This very verse is the *yājyā* for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering at the *paunarādheyika* rite.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'O Agni, him today as with horses, with hymns...'—these are the two *saṃyājyā* verses" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.8).

1. The means of accomplishment for the sacrificer (yajamāna-sādhana) consists of the syllables kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pa, la, and sa. 2. In the case of the syllables ta and la, there is the substitution of hirā. 3. In the case of the syllable va, there is the change to śru in its original form (prakṛti). 4. The syllables na, la, and sa do not exist in the word "te". 5. The syllables kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and duhi exist. 6. The syllables kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa do not exist in the word "āgneyam". 7. The *padapaṅkti* meter consists of the syllable ta. 8. This is because the characteristics have been stated as such for the syllables kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa.

O Agni, may we today succeed through our hymns in that [praise] which touches the heart—like a horse, like a blessed resolve—through our offerings to you. O Agni, may we today with our hymns succeed in that [praise] which touches the heart—like a horse, like a blessed resolve—through our offerings to you. 1.

O Agni, on this day, we— the officiating priests and others— strengthen you, the renowned one, with hymns (*stoma*) consisting of collections of praises that convey [the sacrifice] to Indra and the other gods;
we strengthen you like a horse that carries a rider, and like a mental power (*kratu*) that conveys the oblation and acts as its performer.
The meaning is "one who does a favor. Likewise, *bhadram* means "to be honored," *hṛdispṛśam* means "touching the heart" or "heart-pleasing"; the meaning is "exceedingly dear."
In the Paunarādheyikī sacrifice, for the principal offering, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "adhā hyagne";
for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in that same rite, the invitatory verse is "ebhirno arkaiḥ";
and for the principal offering, the offering verse (*yājyā*) is "āmiṣṭe adya."
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Now indeed, O Agni, at this auspicious season, we praise you today with songs and with these hymns" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.8).

For indeed, O Agni, you have become the charioteer of auspicious will, of effective power, and of the sublime cosmic order. 2. Indeed, O Agni, you have become the charioteer of auspicious will, of effective power, and of the sublime cosmic order. 2.
For indeed, O Vāyu, at this very moment you have become, and continue to be, the leader (netṛ) of our sacrifice through your wisdom.
According to the rule "chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ," the *liṭ* (perfect) suffix is used for the root *bhū* in the sense of the present tense; thus, *sip* is replaced by *thal*.
Although the augment *iṭ* would normally apply by the rule "ārdhadhātukasyeḍvalādeḥ," its absence occurs here due to the specific irregularity (*nipātana*) stated in the rule "babhūthātatantha."

Of what kind of sacrifice? Of that which is "auspicious" (*bhadra*), meaning worthy of worship; "skillful" (*dakṣa*), meaning prosperous; "righteous" (*sādhu*), meaning the achiever of desired fruits; "truth" (*ṛta*), meaning real; and "vast" (*bṛhat*), meaning great.

Through these our hymns, O Agni, be turned toward us like the light of heaven; be well-disposed toward us with all your gracious favors. 3. Through these | for us | with hymns | be | for us | turned hitherward | like the sun | the light | O Agni | with all | well-disposed | rays of light. 3.

O radiant one, like the sun in the sky, you who possess light and splendor—being well-disposed with all your manifold glories and powers, turn your face toward us through these our hymns of praise that are worthy of worship. Be present before us.

O Agni, praising you today with our songs, may we serve you with offerings. Your powers thunder forth like the roar of heaven. 4. O Agni, praising you today with our songs, may we serve you with offerings. Your powers thunder forth like the roar of heaven. 4.
1. There is no *na-la-sa* (negation) here.
Just as on this day, we—the officiating priests and others—praising you with these words consisting of hymns, may we offer oblations (*havīṃṣi*) to you.
Like the rays of the sun in heaven, your purifying flames (*śuṣmāḥ*) resound loudly.
Or rather:
like clouds from the sky, your flames resound.
For you, the most sweet one, even from afar, even from near at hand, even from the darkness of night—you shine for glory like a golden ornament close by. 5.
O Agni, most sweet to taste, with equal vision, you shine for glory now at daybreak and now at nightfall, like a golden ornament close at hand. 5.
O Agni, your most savory, most delicious, and most beloved radiance (*saṃdaṣṭi*)—your vehicle (*vahaḥ*)—is known even now from heaven; it is known even now from the speaker (*vaktoḥ*).
*Akta* is a name for night, as it is listed among the names for night in the Nighaṇṭu (1.7.4): "The night, the darkness, the wave.
[Thus,] it is known even now from the night.
The meaning is "day and night. From the verbal root *añj* (in the sense of manifestation, smearing, beauty, and motion),
the suffix *tumun* is applied by the Uṇādi sūtra "kicca," and its status as *kit* is also established.
The form *titutra* is an exception (*apavāda*) to this [rule]. By the rule *aniditām*, there is the elision of the penultimate *a*.
By the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, there is the substitution of *k* for the palatal (*cu*).
Like gold, he shines for the sake of beauty upon the object that rests near him;
"upāke" is a word for proximity, as it is listed among those names in the Nirukta (2.16.7): "āke upāke.
He shines, he gleams.
Like purified ghee, like a stainless body, like pure gold—O self-sustaining one, that [splendor] of yours shines forth like a golden ornament.
Ghee, not purified, is thy body; stainless and bright is thy gold. Like a golden ornament, it shines for thee, O self-dependent one. 6.
O Agni, you who possess the *svadhā* (the call of the ancestors).
The word *svadhā* denotes food.
O Agni, like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) that is purified and cleansed, your own form (*tanūḥ*), being full of food, becomes *varepāḥ*—that is, free from evil.
Pure, bright, and most delightful gold—your own, your well-known splendor—shines, gleams, and blazes like an ornament.
For even if enmity has been committed, O Agni, you drive it far away from the mortal; thus, O Giver, you protect the sacrificer.
For you have indeed driven away all-encompassing hatred from the mortal who thus sacrifices, O Agni, you who are true to the Cosmic Order (Ṛta).
O truthful Agni, whatever has been done by the sacrificer—even if it be an ancient act (*sanemi*)—drive away that hatred and evil from the mortal man.

*Note:* *Sanemi* is a name for "ancient" (*purāṇa*), as it is listed among the names for the ancient in the *Nighaṇṭu* (3.27.4): "sanemi, pūrvyam. *Dveṣaḥ* means "hatred" or "evil. *Martaḥ* means "mortal man."

1. *Gha*, *ca*, *pa*, *bha*, and *la*. 2. *La* means "near" (*arvāk*) or "in the vicinity" (*antike*). 3. *Kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, and *sa* signify the seasons (*ṛtavaḥ*). 4. *Gha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *pa*, *bha*, and *pa* signify "even though evil has been done" (*pāpaṃ kṛtam api*). 5. *Ta* signifies "advanced in age" (*pravayas*) and "without end" (*sanemi*). 6. *Kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* signify "from evil" (*pāpāt*), "men" (*manuṣyān*), "the sacrificer" (*yajamānāt*), and "thus" (*itthā satyam*). Regarding the word *itthā*, this is a name for Sāyaṇa, because it is listed among his names in the *Nighaṇṭu* (3.10.5) as "addhā itthā."
For indeed, [the word] *inopa* means "as if impelled"; the sense is "you cause to perish."
May our friendships with you gods be auspicious from this day forward;
may that be our kinship in this dwelling, in the possession of wealth.
May our friendships be auspicious with you, O Agni, among the gods. That is our kinship in this dwelling, at this very udder. 8.
O Agni, [place] our friendships, our acts of friendship, and our deeds related to friendship, among you—the radiant ones—among the gods.
By the rule "supāṃ suluk," there is the substitution of "śe" for the seventh-case plural ending.

May there be auspicious blessings; may there be propitious things. May that succession of friendship and ritual acts protect the inspired thought (*manīṣā*) of the singer in the presence of the gods. O you of many births, you who are praised, protect us with your power, as the sky [protects]. O pure one, great and most glorious one, grant us that abundant prayer which you, together with all the gods, desire. *Sā hi* (for she indeed); *agre* (in the beginning/presence); *gṛṇate* (to the singer); *manīṣām* (inspired thought); *kham* (the sky/heaven); *veḥ* (you protect/extend); *r̥pasā* (with power); *tuvijāta* (O you of many births); *starīḥ* (you spread out/protect); *naḥ* (us); *viśvairbhiḥ* (with all); *yat* (which); *vanas* (you desire); *śukra* (O pure one); *daivaiḥ* (with the gods); *tat* (that); *naḥ* (to us); *rāsva* (grant); *sumahaḥ* (O most glorious one); *bhūri* (abundant); *manma* (prayer).

O Agni, born many times through the friction of the two kindling-sticks (*araṇi*) in sacrifices and other rites, being praised by the officiating priests and others with *vepas*— that is, by the performance of sacrifice and other rituals, for "vepas" is listed among the names for ritual action in the Nirukta (2.1.5)—

you, being lauded with *manīṣā*, that is, with hymns of praise, by the sacrificer who performs it, protect— that is, open wide— the *kham*, the gateway to the world of merit to be attained by the sacrificer.
The meaning is "one who is liberated. From the verbal root *pū* (in the sense of the final rite), there is the suffix *laṇ*; the second person singular ending is *sip*.
By the rule *divādibhyaḥ śyan*, the suffix *śyan* is applied.
In this case, there is elision [of the suffix] by the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi. There is the substitution of ā for the vowel [of the root] by the rule "ādeca upadeśe'śiti.
And the replacement of the suffix si by hi occurs.
The word *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* indicates the rule of *nighāta* (elision of accent).
O Śukra, O blazing Agni, you [are] with all, with every one.
In accordance with the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, the substitution of *ais* for the case-ending *bhis* occurs.
Whatever wealth from the west you have won together with the gods, Indra and the others, bestow that upon the sacrificers.
The suffix *vanat* is in the present indicative (*laṭ*).
Of that, the *sip* [ending] undergoes elision of the vowel *i* by the rule "itaśca lopaḥ.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision (*ślu*) of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*).
The suffix *ślu* indicates reduplication (*dvirvacana*). By the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*, all but the first consonant is elided. By the rule *leṭo 'ḍāṭau*, the augment *aṭ* is added.
Because of the rule *yadvṛttānnityam*, there is an absence of the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
O Agni of great majesty and beautiful splendor, grant us—that is, give to us—abundant and plentiful *manma*, that which is to be meditated upon, as our wealth.
In the Mahāpitṛyajña, Agni Sviṣṭakṛt Kavyavāhana is to be worshipped.
He has two invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*).
Among them, "tvad agne kāvyā" is the second invitatory verse.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, from thee come inspired thoughts, from thee come prayers, as thou art born with power and strength" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.19).

From you, O Agni, are born poetic insights; from you, inspired thoughts; from you, effective hymns arise. From you comes wealth adorned with heroes, for the mortal who offers oblations and possesses such devotion. From you, O Agni, are born poetic insights; from you, inspired thoughts; from you, effective hymns arise. From you comes wealth adorned with heroes, for the mortal who offers oblations and possesses such devotion.

From you alone arise the foremost poetic compositions; from you arise the sacrificial acts related to the fire that carries the oblation and the channels for the gods, as well as the duties of the Adhvaryu priest.
From you alone arise the inspired thoughts in the form of hymns of praise.
From you arise the *ukthas*—the recited chants worthy of being bestowed.

*Itthādhiye dhīḥ*: *dhī* is a name for ritual action (*karman*). Since *itthā* is listed among the names for truth, [the compound means] "for the mortal, the human sacrificer who has given oblations to the one whose action is true. *Vīrapeśāḥ*: *peśas* is a name for form (*rūpa*).
This is the form *vikrāntarūpam*. Here, by the transposition of genders, the form becomes *vīrapeśāḥ*. *Draviṇam*—wealth such as cattle and so forth—*eti* goes forth or issues from you (*tvat*).
The meaning is that it arises.

1. To be churned by him (ta-mathanīya). 2. To be attained by the sacrificer (ta-yajamānena prāpyasya); not to be prayed for by the sacrificer (na-yajamānena prārthyasya). 3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pha, bha, and sa, the phrase “divādibhyaḥ... hirādeśaḥ” is absent. 4. In the manuscripts ca, ṇa, and na, it is “vāvanaḥ”. 5. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, bha, na, la, and sa, “manma” is absent. 6. In the manuscripts na, la, and sa, it is “bhavataḥ”. 7. In the manuscripts ca and pha, it is “tvadu tvattaḥ”.

From you is born the vigorous steed, the bringer of booty, the far-reaching one who grants aid, possessing true strength; from you comes wealth, impelled by the gods, the source of bliss; from you, O Agni, comes the swift and fleet-footed courser. From you [is born] the vigorous [steed]; the bringer of booty; the far-reaching; the grantor of aid; he is born with true strength. From you [comes] wealth; impelled by the gods; the source of bliss. From you, O Agni, [comes] the swift; the fleet; the courser.
"O Agni, you are a steed, powerful and a bringer of *vāja*—that is, a carrier of the food characterized by the oblation.
'The bringer of *vāja* for Agni' is his Vedic designation."
In the word *vāja*, the suffix *khac* is applied with *saṃjñā* as the governing condition according to the rule *bhṛt-ruji*;
the augment *suṭ* is added by the rule *ahar-dvi-pad-a-jantasya*;
and the acute accent (*udātta*) falls on the final syllable by the rule *citaḥ*.
The vast one,
the great performer of desired blessings, the performer of sacrifice,
or the performer of invocation— his son, whose vigor is truth and whose strength is truth, is born and produced from you.
Impelled by the gods, far from us [is] indolence;

far from us, O Agni, son of strength, [is] every evil thought, which I have cast away. At night you are auspicious; O God, you indeed bring well-being to him who strives for all. Far from us, indolence; far from us, wrath; far from us, every evil thought, which I have cast away. At night you are auspicious, O Agni, son of strength; O God, you indeed bring well-being to him who strives for all. 6.

O son of strength, O son of power! For fire is indeed born through the force of those who perform the friction; thus you are the "son of power. O Agni, you who are auspicious—meaning a bringer of welfare—and radiant by night, you who attend to us for our well-being and non-destruction, serving us on all sides.
The word *cit* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).
Since, for which reason, you protect—that is, you thoroughly guard—the sacrificers;
from them, from each of us, cast far away—*āre*, at a distance—the *amarti*, the desire for evil in the form of ignorance.
"Hunger indeed is evil thought," so says the Brāhmaṇa (Ai.
Brā. 2.2). O Agni, far away from us—that sacrificer who has brought for you, the fuel known as *samit*, the means for the oblation.
The root *hṛṣ* means "to take away.
The suffix *leṭ* is used in the sense of the potential (*liṅ*). From that *leṭ*, after the *tip* ending, the vowel *i* is elided according to the rule *itaśca lopaḥ*.
By the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi," there is the elision (luk) of the suffix śap; then the operations of reduplication and so forth are applied;
and by the rule "leṭoḍaḍāṭau," the augment aṭ is added.
The suffix *bh* becomes *ava*, according to the rule "haprahorbhaḥ."

Exerting himself in gathering fuel, he approaches your great majesty; *ā* here functions as a particle of emphasis. Honoring—that is, serving—your splendor, that sacrificer, having directed his attention toward the night (*doṣām*) and toward the dawn (*upasaṃ*), [approaches] the time of morning.
The meaning is "in both times.
*Indhānaḥ*—kindling you, making you possessed of radiance; *puṣyan*—thriving through offspring and cattle; *saḥ*—that sacrificer; *amitrān*—enemies; *ghnan*—slaying or harming; *rayim*—wealth;
*sacate*—attains or serves. [He is] always accompanied by cattle.

Even from great sin, O Agni, in the encounter with the gods above and even with mortals, may we, your friends, never suffer harm; grant health and prosperity to our children and descendants. (5) Even from great sin, O Agni, in the encounter with the gods above and even with mortals, may we, your friends, never suffer harm; grant health and prosperity to our children and descendants. (5)

O Agni, [protect us] from the sin committed by us in the presence— *abhīke* being a term for "nearness"— of the gods, Indra and the others, as well as of mortals, human beings; even from that great, vast, and extensive *enas*, sin, may we, your friends, your companions, your praisers, never at any time (*sadamit*) suffer harm or be destroyed.
O Agni, grant and bestow well-being—peace from misfortunes of evil form—and prosperity—the happiness produced by good deeds—for your son, your grandson, and your great-grandson.

Just as you, O Vasus, worthy of worship, once released even the Gaurī cow bound by the foot, so indeed release us from distress; O Agni, prolong our life further. Just as, O Vasus, worthy of worship, you released even the Gaurī cow that was bound by the foot, so indeed release us from distress; O Agni, prolong our life further.

O worshipful ones, worthy of sacrifice, and deserving of honor, O Vasus—those who provide dwelling—O Agnis, just as you indeed released even that Gaurī cow, though she was bound by her foot, so too do you completely release us from sin; may you utterly set us free. (The plural number is used for the sake of reverence.)
O Agni, by you may our life, which has increased further, be extended; let it be made to increase even more.

The third hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “pratyagniḥ,” is the seerly work of Vāmadeva; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Agni, or rather, its deities are the waters and others denoted by the specific wording of the respective mantras.
Thus it has been cataloged: “*Pratyagniḥ*: five [verses]; some say the deity is indicated by the characteristic marks [of the words].
The application is determined by these characteristic marks.

Agni has shone forth at the forefront of the dawning mornings that shine brightly, well-disposed toward the bestowing of treasures. O Aśvins, come to the dwelling of the pious man; the divine Sūrya rises up with his light. *prati agniḥ uṣasām agram ayat vibhātīnām sumanā ratnadheyam | yātam aśvinā sukṛto duroṇam ut sūryo jyotiṣā deva eti || 1 ||* Agni has gone forth toward the beginning of the dawns as they shine forth, benevolent toward the granting of jewels. Come, O Aśvins, to the house of the one who performs good deeds; the god Sūrya rises upward with his brilliance.

The benevolent Agni, whose mind is auspicious, shines forth toward the foremost point— that is, with reference to the preceding time— of the radiant, dawning Uṣases, who are like subordinate deities; he becomes magnified this very day, [bestowing] the bestowal of jewels (*ratnadheya*), meaning the manifestation of wealth.
1. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and sa are [the letters] to be excluded.
2. That which is preceded by kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, and bha; in the case of gha and pa, it is that which is preceded by those [same letters].
3. Kha, ga, gha, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha are the immediate [preceding letters].

O Aśvins, you two, come to the dwelling—the house—of the well-performing sacrificer; for "dwelling" (*duroṇa*) is a name for a house, as it is listed among the names for houses in [Nirukta] 3.4.7: "In the dwelling, the doors.
Go!
The Sun, the god who impels the officiating priests and others, rises upward, illuminating with his own splendor; the meaning is that he becomes manifest at the time of dawn.

The divine Savitṛ has extended his light upward, like a drop [of ghee] in a ladle, like a warrior eager for cattle. Varuṇa and Mitra follow their ordinance when they cause the Sun to ascend in heaven. ūrdhvam | bhānum | savitā | devaḥ | aśret | drapsam | darvivat | go'iṣaḥ | na | satvā | anu | vratam | varuṇaḥ | yanti | mitraḥ | yat | sūryam | divi | ā'rohayanti || 2 ||
The god Savitṛ, the impeller, has extended his light upward;

when the rays cause the sun to ascend in the sky, O shining god Sūrya, you— spreading out the web, that is, the collection of rays, for the purpose of taking up the essence which is the tongue of the world, and covering the night, the dwelling-place of nocturnal creatures, with its dark color, concealing it so as to turn it downward.
The meaning is "disregarding.
With the *vahiṣṭhebhiḥ*—horses most capable of carrying—you *yāsi*, you go along the path of travel.
Having established the direct (pratyakṣa) mode of address regarding Sūrya in the first half of this verse, he speaks in the second half to establish the indirect (parokṣa) sense.
Shaking off the two kinds [of darkness], the rays of the sun— the beams belonging to Sūrya— within the waters, that is,
within the intermediate space (for "āpas" is a name for the intermediate space, as seen in its list of synonyms: "ākāśam āpaḥ pṛthivī," Nighaṇṭu 1.3.8),
they have cast down— that is, they have driven downward— the darkness situated like a skin (camā) in the midst.
The meaning is that they treat [them] with contempt.
Unmeasured and unbound, this earth lies spread out like a hide;
who goes by his own power? Who has seen it? The pillar of heaven, firmly established, protects the firmament.

Unextended, unbound—how does this one, turned downward or upward, fall away? By what means does he go? By his own inherent power? Who has seen him? The pillar of heaven, firmly established, protects the firmament. 5.
The word *āyata* signifies "far away.
Its opposite is *anāyata*. While remaining *āsīnaḥ* (seated), this Sun, who is perceived directly and who possesses the conceit of being a disk (*maṇḍala*), is *anibaddhaḥ*—he is not bound by anyone.
Furthermore, even though this Sun is *nyaṅ*—facing downward—how is it that he is not *avapadyate*? That is to say, how is he not destroyed? [He is not.]
Furthermore, how does this one, lying flat—that is, standing with his face turned upwards—move by what power (*svadhā*)?
Here, the word *svadhā*, which denotes food, indicates its effect: strength.
Moreover, as the pillar (*skambha*) of heaven, the celestial world, joined with the firmament (*nāka*), the Sun protects the firmament, that is, the sky.
"Who has seen it in its true nature? Who perceives it?"—the meaning is that no one knows it at all.

The fourth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “pratyamṛkṣaḥ,” has Vāmadeva as its seer and is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter; it is addressed to Agni, or rather, its deity is determined by the wording of the mantras themselves.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “pratyamṛk.

Regarding the phrase “but [its] deity is indicated by the characteristic mark” (*liṅgoktadaivatam tu*), the word “but” (*tu*) indicates that this hymn also has its deity determined by the characteristic marks of the mantras.
The application is indicated by the internal evidence of the text.
The omniscient one has looked upon us, shining with splendors like the gods;
O wide-striding Nāsatyas, come to this sacrifice of ours on your chariot and shine forth!

Agni Jātavedas has shone forth toward the dawns; the radiant god has blazed with his great splendors. O Nāsatyas, you who traverse the wide expanse, come hither to this sacrifice of ours upon your chariot. 1.
The radiant god Agni, whose wealth is born (Jātavedas), becomes awakened in response to the Dawns who shine and blaze with their splendors.
O Nāsatyas, Aśvins, you two of wide stride, come hither by chariot toward this our sacrifice.

1. *ṇa*: the thread, the cord. 2. *gha*, *ca*, *la*: posterior. 3. *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ta*, *pa*, *bha*, *la*, *sa*: they said; *ca*, *ṇa*, *ja*, *pha*: they made. 4. *ba*, *pha*: facing upwards. 5. *ca*, *pha*: shoulder. 6. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*: by means of truth.
The divine Savitṛ has raised his banner on high, creating light for the whole world.
Sūrya has filled heaven, earth, and the mid-air, shining brightly with his rays.
On high has Savitar, the god, raised his banner, creating light for the whole world; Sūrya has filled heaven, earth, and the mid-air, shining brightly with his rays. 2.
Creating light—that is, brilliance—for the sake of every being and for the entire world, the impelling god Savitṛ has extended his upward-pointing banner, the radiant light.
Observing all things with particular clarity, Sūrya has filled both heaven and earth, as well as the intermediate space, on all sides with his own rays.
Bringing forth light with her ruddy glow, the great and wondrous Dawn, shining brightly with her rays,
the goddess Uṣas approaches on her well-yoked chariot, awakening us for a prosperous day.
Bringing [wealth], the ruddy one has come with light; great, wonderful, and shining with her rays, the goddess Uṣas goes forth on her well-yoked chariot, awakening us for the sake of fair fortune. 3.
Bringing wealth and bestowing it, the ruddy dawn is of a ruddy hue.
The second-case plural is used in place of the first-case singular; this is a Vedic usage.

Endowed with light and splendor, great and vast with her rays and beams, the wonderful and beautiful Dawn has come, shining brightly and knowing all. Furthermore, awakening the sleepers and making them wakeful, the radiant goddess Dawn moves upon her well-yoked chariot for the attainment of happy fortune.
May those most excellent carriers bring you both here—chariots and horses—at the dawning of the night.
For these Soma juices are for your sweet draught; O Bulls, rejoice at this sacrifice!

May those most excellent vehicles bring you both hither; may the horses [bring you] at the dawning of the morning. For these Soma juices are for you both to drink the honeyed draught; O showerers of blessings, rejoice at this sacrifice! 4.

O Aśvins, may those well-known chariots of yours—the swiftest, most excellent carriers, and the horses that move with speed—bring you both here to this sacrifice at the dawning of the goddess Uṣas, or at the time of her breaking forth; let them carry you and lead you hither from every side.
For, O showerers of blessings, O increasers of desires, O Aśvins, these Soma juices are for you both; rejoice and be gladdened at this sacrifice for the drinking of the sweet Soma.
1. Kha, ga, ca, na, pha, ma, and sa are facing forward; 2. La and bhūloka are also [facing forward];
3. Ṇa is at the time of dawn.
Unmeasured and unbound, this skin neither falls down nor lies prone;
by what inherent power does it move? Who has seen it? The pillar of heaven, firmly established, protects the sun.
Unextended, unbound—how does this one fall down, face downward or face upward?
By what inherent power does he go? Who has seen him? The pillar of heaven, firmly established, protects the light of the sun. ||5||
This Ṛgvedic verse has been explained previously.

The fifth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with *agnihotrā*, is the work of Vāmadeva; its metre is Gāyatrī. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “*Agnihotrā*: [this] is ten [verses], Gāyatrī. With the two verses beginning *ṛṣibodhataḥ*, Soma praised the divine Ṛk; with the following two, he requested the Aśvins and Āyu. Thus, in the two verses beginning with *bodhayat*, King Soma is praised; in the two verses beginning with *eṣa vām*, the Aśvins are praised; and the remaining six verses praise [Soma].
Therefore, those very deities [are worshipped] in sequence.
The application of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on its indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
For the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) of the sacrificial animal, [the verse] is “*agnihotrā naḥ*.”

The wise Lord of Strength, Agni, has stepped around the houses, bestowing treasures upon the donor. 3. Lord of Strength, the wise one, Agni, has stepped around the oblations, bestowing treasures upon the donor. 3.
*Vājapati*: the lord (*pati*) and protector of *vājās*, that is, of knowledges.
Regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa states: “The wise *vājapati* has gone around, for he is the lord of *vājās*” (AiB 2.5).

*Kavi*: one who sees beautifully or is wise. Bestowing—that is, granting—*ratnāni*, delightful riches, to the *dāśuṣe*, the sacrificer who has offered the oblation, *agni* has *pari akramīt*, he strides around the *havyāni*, the sacrificial offerings.
It pervades.
This one who is kindled before Sujñaya Daivavāta—resplendent, the subduer of enemies. 4. This one; who; before Sujñaya; before Daivavāta; is kindled; resplendent; the subduer of enemies. 4.
This fire, which is well-known and perceived through direct observation, [was kindled] for Sujñaya, the son of Devavāta;
Sujñaya was a certain performer of Soma sacrifices,
and it was upon him, acting as the cause, that this occurred.
In this context, the meaning is "for that purpose.

The Taittirīyas record the fact that Sujñeya was a performer of sacrifices: "Vāsiṣṭha Sādhyahavya asked Devabhāga: 'Since you have officiated as priest for Sujñeya, who performed many sacrifices... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.6.2.2).
On the *uttaravedi* situated in the east (*puraḥ*), in the eastern direction, it is "kindled," meaning it shines perfectly.
*Amitradambhana*: the destroyer of enemies; *sa agniḥ* (that fire) *bhavati ghumān*—the ellipsis being that it becomes radiant.

Indeed, what mortal hero could master this Agni—him who is thus, whose teeth are sharp, and who bestows abundance? (5) Indeed, what mortal hero could master this Agni—him who is thus, whose teeth are sharp, and who bestows abundance? (5)

The patron (*yajamāna*), who is mortal (*martya*) and subject to death, and who is valiant (*vikrānta*) in praise (*stuti*), may become the master (*īśvara*) through the grace of this Agni—Agni who has sharp fangs (*tigmajambha*), who possesses keen brilliance (*tīkṣṇatejas*), who is bountiful (*mīḷahuṣ*), the sprinkler (*sektr*) of desired fruits, and who is swift-moving (*īvata*). The particle *gha* is used for metrical completion.
The meaning is that by this [praise], the patron becomes capable of causing his own desired fruit to be realized.

Day after day they groom him, like a swift steed with a high back, like the ruddy one, like the child of heaven. 6. Him; like a swift steed; with a high back; like the ruddy one; like the child of heaven; they groom; day after day. 6.

The sacrificers daily—day after day—thoroughly purify and attend upon that Agni, who is like a swift-running steed on its back, who is like the child of heaven, the radiant sun, and who is ruddy and shining.

O Kumāra, son of Sāhadeva, take notice of me with your two bay horses; like one summoned, come forth toward me. 7. bodhat | yat | mā | hari'bhyām | kumāraḥ | sāha'devyaḥ | acchā | na | hūtaḥ | ut | īram || 7 ||
1. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-°ayīyaja*: at a sacrifice; 2. *pa-dambhaka*: deceptive; 3. *la-bhanena*: by speaking; 4. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bhajanīyam*: to be honored; 5. *kha-ga-ca-kurviran*: they would act.

The prince Sāhadevya—the son of King Sahadeva, the king named Somaka—when he perceived me, saying "Give a horse," with two horses [saying], "These two are your horses," then, being summoned by the prince, I did not emerge from my belly at that time because I had not yet reached full maturity.
And those two adorable bay horses were brought forward from the youth Sāhadevya; they were presented together at the gathering.
And those two sacrificial bay horses were brought from the youth Sāhadevya; they were led forth together. ||8||

Moreover, on the very day that I was summoned from the son of Sahadeva—the prince named Soma, the king worthy of worship—I seized those two famous bay horses, *harī*, which were well-trained and ready;
having obtained them from him, the seer who perceived the mantra, desiring the prince, accepted them with the words "Bodhat" and became joyful. This is the meaning.
O divine Aśvins, may this Kumāra Sāhadevya, the son of Somaka, have a long life through you both.
O divine Aśvins, may this Kumāra Sāhadevya, the son of Somaka, have a long life. ||9||

O two shining Aśvins, may this King Somaka—known by the name of Somaka, the son of Sahadeva, who gratifies you both—possess long life, that is, may he live for a hundred years. The kingship of Somaka is clearly established by the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with, "They indeed declared this to Parvata and Nārada regarding Somaka," and continuing with, "All were indeed great kings" (AiB 7.34).
O divine Aśvins, grant long life to that prince, the son of Sāhadeva.
O you two gods, Aśvins, grant long life to this Kumāra, the son of Sāhadeva. ||10||
O you two gods, the Ashvins, the radiant ones—you two—make that prince, the son of Sahadeva, the king named Somaka, long-lived, possessing a lifespan of a hundred years.
By means of this verse, the meaning is that one should pray for long life for this prince, saying, "O Ashvins, grant him your blessing."
The sixth hymn, consisting of twenty-one verses beginning with "ā satyo yātu," is the seerly work of Vāmadeva; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Indra.

According to the Anukramaṇikā, it is "ā satyaḥ saikendram" (beginning with "ā satyaḥ," with one [verse] for Indra). Since it is specified there as "Aindram" (addressed to Indra), it is understood that the governing rule for Agni has ceased to apply.
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), during the *maitrāvaruṇa* litany (*śastra*), this is the second *ahīna* hymn.
Accordingly, it is stated in the Sūtra: "The true one should come for the journey; the *maitrāvaruṇa* [recites] the second *ahīna* hymn" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.4).
This hymn is also used in the *niṣkevalya* litany on the ninth day of the *daśarātra* sacrificial session.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Niṣkevalya [chant] is: 'O True One, may I go to the earth; that is your organ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).

1. Invoked by *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*. 2. From *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *na*, *bha*, *sa*, and *somaka*. 3. *Gha* and *ṇa* are to be sacrificed. 4. From this *ta*. 5. In *kha*, *ga*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, the word "that" (*ataṃ*) does not exist. 6. Long-lived in *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*. 7. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *bha*, in *abhyūlahe*. Ṛgveda 2.71.562 [Maṇḍala 3, Anuvāka 5, Sūkta 1, Verse 17]
May the bounteous Lord, the drinker of the dregs, come hither with his swift steeds; may his bay horses run toward us.
For him, let the well-pressed Soma, most effective, be here as he is praised, bringing him hither.
May the true Maghavan, the drinker of the dregs, come hither; may his bay steeds run toward us. To him alone let the well-pressed, most skillful Soma-juice, being praised here, bring his arrival.
1. *Ṛjīṣī*: By the word *ṛjīṣa*, the pressed Soma that has lost its essence is denoted.
Possessing that, the true one, the truthful Maghavan—the wealthy Indra—*ā yātu*: let him come, let him approach us.
Furthermore, may Indra’s bay horses come swiftly to us;
we, the sacrificers, [invoke] for that Indra here at this sacrifice one who is well-skilled, meaning endowed with excellent strength.
We have pressed this Soma, which is perceived by direct perception, blind yet possessing the form of food;
may Indra, being praised by us, grant us his presence and come to us.
Like a steed at the end of its journey, come hither today to this libation to rejoice;
may the wise one, like Uśanas, proclaim a hymn of praise—a prayer for the conscious Asura.

O Hero, come hither from the end of this path; now, at this libation, may you rejoice to gladden us. Like Uśanas, the wise ordainer, he shall recite a hymn—a prayer—to you, the conscious Lord of divine power.
O Hero Indra, capable of overcoming enemies, now at this very *savana* called the midday pressing, release us—that is, liberate us—in order to exhilarate you, to make you rejoice.
Therein is an illustration:
just as men, having reached the end or vicinity of a path to be traveled, release their horses, so too [do we release you].

Like Uśanas Kāvya, like a wise creator, the praising sacrificer indeed recites for you, O Indra—the one who is observant and knows all—a *manman*, a thought to be meditated upon, an *uktha* in the form of a liturgical hymn, a song of praise, for you, the Asura among the Asuras, the destroyer of the Asuras. He performs this recitation.
Like a skilled craftsman, he accomplishes the secret rites when, drinking the pressed juice alone, he utters praise;
thus from heaven he brought forth the seven singers, and even the days themselves have made them their own, as they sing his glory.

The sage, accomplishing the secret rites of the assembly, when the bull, having drunk deeply of the libation, shall sing his praise—he has thus begotten from heaven the seven singers; praising him, they have made the days their own through his wisdom.

The poet, the wise one, like something hidden— *niṇyam* is a name for that which is concealed— he brings about the *vidathāni*, the things to be known, the multitude of tasks to be accomplished; Indra, the showerer of desires, when [he performs] the *seka*, the pouring of the Soma worthy of being served.
1. O powerful Indra, you who are not born from a womb!

2. As humans [behave] toward horses: with *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *bha*—as humans toward horses; with *gha*—as humans toward horses; with *ca*—humans [behave] unlike horses; with *ta* and *la*—horses [behave] like humans toward horses; with *na*—horses [behave] like humans. 3. *ṇa*: the classes of actions.
Drinking deeply, drinking according to his own will, he is especially honored;
the meaning is that he inspires faith in the drinking of Soma.
At that time, from yonder world of heaven, the possessor of the thunderbolt (vajī) truly, indeed, caused the seven rays—seven in number—to spring forth.
They generate [knowledge].
The rays, being praised by those who recite, have made manifest the *vayunā*—the insights of human beings—even from afar, having performed them through their radiant splendor.
With his rays, he has made this world beautiful to behold; the two worlds have shone with great light.
The best of heroes, for the sake of his worshippers, has dispelled the blinding darkness so that men may see clearly.

Heaven! That beautiful Veda which they have made to shine with great light through their hymns—that very light, indeed, the most heroic one has created for the sake of men’s vision, dispelling the blinding, turbid darkness from the dwelling place, so that it may be clearly seen in his protection. 4.

Or rather: when indeed they wove—that is, extended—the great, abundant *vaj-jyotis* (light in the form of splendor), and when that world of light (*vasu*) was known through its rays (*arka*), as something beautiful to behold (*vasu-dṛśīkam*), then the gods dwelt (*vavastuḥ*) in that heaven for the sake of residence and became radiant (*varurucaḥ*).
[The Sun] is the most excellent leader (*vanṛtamaḥ*).

He has made the paths easy for men to traverse upon their arrival at the sacrifice; he has specially provided for the vision of the people; he has dispelled the blind darkness, the enveloping glooms, and has destroyed all that is turbid.
Indra grew to immeasurable power; with his greatness, he filled both worlds. Even beyond that, his majesty extends further, for he has surpassed all existing beings.

Indra has grown; the impetuous one has increased beyond measure. With his greatness, he has filled both worlds, heaven and earth. Even beyond that, his majesty extends further, for he has surpassed all existing beings.
*Vaṛjīrpā*.
By the word *ṛjīpa*, the crushed Soma whose essence has departed is denoted.
Possessing that (*tadvān*), Indra—the Supreme Lord—has carried (*vavakṣe*, i.e., *uvāha*) his immeasurable greatness, which is devoid of limitation.
Moreover, by his greatness and by his own majesty, he filled both the *rodasī*, both heaven and earth;
Indra, as a bird (*vayaḥ*), has surpassed all worlds, having transcended them.
Even beyond all these worlds, the majesty of this Indra has shone forth, exceeding all measure.
The meaning is that he became superior.
Śakra, knowing all manly deeds, released the waters with his eager friends;
even the rock they split with their splendors, and the seekers of light uncovered the place rich in cattle.

Śakra, the wise one, has released all manly deeds; with his eager friends he has poured forth the waters. Even the rock they split with their splendors; the Uśijs have opened up the stall rich in cattle—yes, they have opened it. 6.

From the world of *kha-ga-na-ṇa-na-bha-sa*, Śakra— the capable Indra— knowing all the various deeds for the benefit of men, such as the slaying of Vṛtra and others, [acts] together with the Maruts, his friends who have become allies, who desire according to their wishes.
The instrumental case ending is used in the sense of the dative by means of the suffix *dhyāya*.
Indra emptied out the waters characterized by rain; that is to say, for the sake of the successful ripening of crops and other fruits, Indra gave the waters residing in the clouds to the Maruts.
Or alternatively:
Accompanied by his friends, the Maruts— who are full of desire and desiring [their tasks]— he [took] the waters from the sky;
for "āpaḥ" is a name for the intermediate space (antarikṣa),
where there is an inversion of case endings.
He became distinct and poured forth.
Those Maruts, by means of their words—forms of speech that are like rain—heated the path, the mountain, or the cloud;
for "asmat" is a name for the cloud.

They split it open; they escaped. Desiring it, those Maruts, the Uśijas, opened wide—the word *vavruḥ* means they covered or enclosed—the cow-pen belonging to the Aṅgirases, a stall filled with cattle.
When you struck down Vṛtra, who had encompassed the waters, at his downfall, the conscious earth rolled around you with the thunderbolt;
you, O hero, became the lord of the oceanic floods by your might, O bold one.
You struck down Vṛtra who had obstructed the waters; the earth, being conscious, favored your thunderbolt. You sent forth the oceanic floods, O bold hero, becoming their lord through your might.

O Indra, you protected [the world] preeminently from the Rākṣasas and others; with your thunderbolt, you struck down Vṛtra—the cloud that obstructed the waters, the waters characterized by rain—and drove him away. The earth, the ground, became conscious, endowed with sentience, through union with you.

O bold one, O hero of a courageous nature, O Indra of valorous stride, you, becoming the lord and protector of the worlds through your might and strength, have impelled forth the waters of the ocean—those floods situated in the firmament.
When you, O much-invoked one, shattered the mountain and brought forth the waters, that was your first deed;
as such, may you lead us to abundant booty, bursting open the cow-pens while being praised by the Aṅgirases.

When you, O much-invoked one, rent the mountain asunder, Saramā appeared before you, your ancient [path]. May he, our leader, burst open abundant strength for us, breaking through the cow-stalls while being praised by the Aṅgirases. 8.
O Puruhūta, you who are invoked by many, O Indra, whenever—aiming at the waters characterized by rain—you split the mountain, the cloud;

then Saramā, the divine hound, revealed to you in ancient times the wealth of cattle stolen by the Paṇis. Being praised with hymns by the Aṅgiras seers, shattering the cow-pens—the enclosures—you, the leader who brings us abundant food, have shown great favor toward us.

1. For those desiring *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-bha-kāma*. 2. Devoid of *ca-pha-ri*. 3. And your own, O *kha-ga-gha-pa-pha-bha-sa*. 4. An obstructer, O *kha-ga-ca*. 5. It became, O *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa*. 6. Wealth was carried away by *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-sa*; by *na-sa*, it was brought back. O you whose mind is on men, come toward the singer for his aid; O Maghavan, you who seek the light, help the suppliant with your protections.
At your invocation, the guileful Dasyu, lacking prayer, has perished.

Excellent! O Maghavan, you have indeed brought the lowly man under your protection in the struggle for light; do not neglect him who strives with his aids at your invocation. The sorcerer Dasyu, lacking prayer, has perished. 9.

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, you are called *nṛmaṇas* because you are honored (*manyate*) by men (*nṛbhiḥ*, i.e., humans). You went toward Kutsa, the wise and intelligent seer; furthermore, [you went] for the sake of attaining the light of heaven (*svarśatā*).

When his own wealth was at stake— that is, when the occasion for its acquisition or giving had arisen and the seer approached you— then, while Kutsa was imploring you for battle, you impelled him with *ūtis*, meaning protections consisting of the removal of calamities caused by enemies.
[He was] possessed of *māyā* (deceit), a deceiver, one who lacked sacred knowledge (*abrahmā*).

Knowing all the multitude of rites being performed by the officiating priests through the form of ignorance, you, the distinguished priest denoted by the word *brahman*, proceed in the same chariot with Kutsa, seeking help; you, the driver of Vāta’s two bay steeds,
desiring to secure straightaway prize-winning booty that cannot be seized, so that the pious man may be ready for the decisive day.

You come with Kutsa in the chariot, seeking aid; you, the goad, the master of the two bay steeds of the wind, desiring to win the prize straightway as if it were a fish to be caught, when the sage shall strive for the decisive day. 11.

O Indra, desiring to protect Kutsa, you who are eager for his aid— *vavasyuḥ* being used here with a transposition of vowels (*vyatyaya*) even in the sense of another's desire as seen in Vedic usage— you, the impeller (*todah*), the striker of enemies, the master of the two swift, wind-like bay horses (*haryoḥ*), go on the same chariot (*saratham*) with Kutsa, the royal seer named Kutsa;
[you take] that which is to be seized (*gadhyaṃ*).
"Seizable" (*gadhya*) is understood.
The *Nirukta* states: "Like straight-going [horses] seeking to seize booty (*vāja*), there is also a *nigama* [verse]" (Nirukta 5.15).

Just as one desiring to seize food (*vāja*) like booty, Kutsa—the wise seer (*kavi*)—yoking his two straight-moving horses to his own chariot, becomes capable (*bhūṣāt*) on that day for the crossing (*pāryāya*) or for the reaching of the further shore (*āpajji*).
On that very day, the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "With Kutsa, go against Maratha.
For Kutsa, strike down Śuṣṇa—the non-drying one—at the onset of the day; slay the Kṛyavas by the thousands. Instantly, with Kutsa, crush the Dasyus; with the great Sūra, overcome the adversaries.

For Kutsa, [you struck] Śuṣṇa; you struck down Aśuṣṇa. At the onset of the day, you crushed the Kuyava [demons] by the thousands at once. With Kutsa, crush the Dasyus! With the great [chariot], [you struck] the wheel of Sūrya in close combat. 12.
The meaning set forth in the verse *śuṣṇaṃ piprum* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.103.8) is clarified by these two verses beginning with *kutsāya*.
O Indra, for the sake of Kutsa—that is, for Kutsa—you [slew] Śuṣṇa;
"Śuṣṇa" is a name for happiness.
That indeed was done;
here there is an absence of lengthening.
You have struck down, you have cast down—that is, you have slain—the demon named Śuṣṇa.
Likewise, you carried this heaven to its full extent; at the first step in the forenoon, you slew Kuyava, the Asura named Kuyava.
Thus, with a thousand—that is, with many attendants—you [acted] instantly; at the very moment you slew Kuyava, you were joined by Kutsa.
"Kutsa" is a name for the thunderbolt.
Like Kutsa, hurl the thunderbolt at Kutsa;
with it, crush and slay the Dasyus, the enemies.
The suffix *vloṭ* is used in the sense of a factual event (*bhūtārtha*).
You have struck;
likewise, in the vicinity of the *vabhīka*—in battle—you have violently severed the wheel, the weapon of the impelling *sūra*, the Sun.

1. In manuscript *ta*, the phrase “the destroyer of enemies” (*śatrūṇāṃ hiṃsakaḥ*) is absent. 2. In manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa*, the term “equal chariot” (*samānaratha*) is absent. 3. In manuscript *na*, [the reading is] *preraṇāya*. 4. In manuscripts *ta*, *na*, and *sa*, [the reading is] *asminneva*. 5. In manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, and *na*, the word *api* has the sense of “also” (*apyarthaḥ*). 6. In manuscript *ta*, the phrase “Kutsa himself” (*kutsa eva*) is absent. 7. In manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, [it occurs] in the sense of a past action (*bhūte'rthe*). 8. In manuscript *ta* and *sa*, [the reading is] *sthitavānasi*; in manuscript *na*, it is *rakṣitavānasi*.

You subdued Pipru, Mṛgaya, and Śuśuvāṃs for Vaidathina, the son of Ṛjiśvan, in the contest for wealth; you cast down fifty thousand black ones, and like a builder, you shattered his fortresses with age. 13. You [subdued] Pipru, Mṛgaya, Śuśuvāṃs, for Vaidathina, the son of Ṛjiśvan, in the contest for wealth; you cast down fifty thousand black ones; like a builder, you shattered his fortresses with age. 13.

O Indra, you slew the Asura Pipru, who was swelling with power and named Pipru, and you also slew the Asura Mṛgaya, who was fully grown and named Mṛgaya. Furthermore, for the sake of Vidathināri—the son of Vidathin—namely King Ṛjiśvan, you brought him under control;
you cast down and destroyed fifty thousand black-colored Rākṣasas.
In that same way, you, by means of old age—decay—have shattered, as it were, the cities of Śambara before you, like the form of Arka, a particular stage of life.

The Sun, placing his body near [the earth], reveals that visible form of yours which belongs to the Immortal. Like a wild beast, like an elephant displaying its strength, like a terrifying lion, he bears his weapons. 14. The Sun; near; his body; placing; forth; that; of you; is perceived; the form; of the Immortal; like a wild beast; like an elephant; displaying; power; like a lion; terrible; bearing; weapons. 14.

O Indra, when you, the sustainer, placed your body in the vicinity (*upāke*) of the impelling Sun (*sūra*), then your immortal form (*varpaḥ*), free from death, became manifest (*vi ceti*). O Indra, it was not specifically known by those who know; for while all forms become obscured in the proximity of the Sun, the form of Indra, on the contrary, became especially radiant in the presence of the Sun. This is the meaning.

Moreover, O Indra, like a wild elephant—a specific kind of beast—wearing away the strength (*tarviṣīm*) of others, burning with weapons such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and wielding those arms, you became as terrifying as a lion.

Desires, seeking wealth, have gone to Indra, longing for the libation at the pressing of Soma as if for the winning of light; they are seekers of glory, striving with hymns, like a delightful home, like prosperity with fair dwellings. 15. To Indra. Desires. Seeking wealth. They have gone. To the winning of light. As if. At the pressing. Longing. Seekers of glory. Striving. With hymns. Like a home. Delightful. Like prosperity with fair dwellings. 15.

Desiring Indra for the sake of warding off fear from Rākṣasas and other dangers, dwelling with him, and subsequently desiring wealth, the worshippers went—have gone and continue to go—to Indra, who is possessed of supreme power.
In the sense of the present tense, there is Vedic elision (luk).
What kind of people are the praisers? 1. [The reading] is known in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, bha, la; it is not known in manuscript gha; manuscript na has [a different reading];
manuscript ta has the sense of the present tense.

Like those eager for battle in a contest for cattle, they desire this pressing of the Soma at the sacrifice; seeking glory, longing for the prize, they exert themselves with hymns and chants, praising and extolling him.
Then this Indra becomes like a dwelling place for their songs of praise, as if a home;
he is delightful, a beautiful friend, and like prosperity that is lovely to behold.

Let us invoke that Indra, who is easily invoked, he who has performed those many heroic deeds; he who, possessing desirable wealth, swiftly brings booty even from a secure place to a singer like me. 16. Let us indeed invoke for you that Indra, who is easily invoked, he who has performed those many heroic deeds; he who, possessing desirable wealth, swiftly brings booty even from a secure place to a singer like me. 16.
Indra performed those many well-known deeds, each one beneficial for humanity.
Moreover, Indra, whose wealth is desirable, swiftly brings to me, his singer who is like him, even that prize which is to be grasped and joined together;
O we who are singers, O patrons, let us invoke that very Indra for you, so that his invocation may be auspicious.

When the sharp bolt falls amidst the people in some sudden moment, when the terrible encounter with the enemy shines forth—then indeed, be the protector of our bodies. (17) When the sharp bolt falls within, in some sudden moment among the people; when the terrible encounter with the noble one occurs—then indeed, be the guardian of our bodies. (17)
O Śūra, O Vikrāntendra, whenever in any battle whatsoever that deludes all people and men, the sharp thunderbolt falls upon us in the midst of our ranks;
O Arya, O Lord Indra, whenever a terrible and fearsome encounter with our enemies occurs,
then at that time, be the protector and guardian of our bodies— be mindful of us!
Indeed, you have recognized us as those who must be protected from our enemies.

Become the protector of the prayers of Vāmadeva; become his friend, free from malice, in the winning of booty. We have come to you for your providence; O you of wide renown, be present for the singer at all times. 18. Become the protector; of Vāmadeva; of the prayers. Become; the friend; free from malice; in the winning of booty. To you; for your providence; we have come. O you of wide renown; for the singer; be present; at all times. 18.

[The syllables] called kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, bha, and la-sa [are used]. O Indra, may you become the protector (*avitā*)—the guardian—of the *dhīs* (actions or thoughts) related to me, the seer of the mantra of Vāmadeva. Being free from malice (*avṛka*), may you become my friend (*sakhā*) in the acquisition of booty (*vājasāti*), that is, in battle.

O Indra, having set our sights upon you—our supreme protector (*vpramati*) and possessor of transcendent knowledge (*prakṛṣṭajñāna*)—we have come to you. May you, O Indra, at all times (*viśvadha*), be one who possesses great power (*urkhāṃsaḥ*) through your vast command for the sake of the singer (*jaritre*). With these [songs] that belong to you, O Indra, we seek you, O Maghavan, in every battle.
May we, being masters, rejoice through many autumns and nights with our kinsmen, as if with the heavens through their rays.

With these men, O Indra, who are devoted to you—those liberal patrons, O Maghavan—in every battle, may we, overcoming our enemies like the heavens with their rays, rejoice through many nights and many autumns. ||19||

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, may we—these sacrificers together with our sons, grandsons, and attendants, accompanied by these men who are present before our eyes and endowed with wealth consisting of oblations offered for their own sake by liberal patrons (maghavadbhiḥ) desiring you for the sake of victory over enemies in every battle—shining like the heavens with both kinds of riches, like illustrious wealthy men, overcoming our enemies, may we rejoice and offer praise throughout all nights and many autumns.
The sacrificers at all times gladden Indra with hymns;
even so, for Indra, the bull, the vigorous one, [we offer] prayer and praise as the Bhr̥gus [fashion] a chariot.
May he never sever our friendship, for he is the fierce protector of our bodies.

Thus, for Indra, the bull, the vigorous one, we offer prayer and song, just as the Bhr̥gus fashioned a chariot. So that our friendship may never be severed, may he, the fierce one, be our protector and guardian of our bodies. 20.
Just as Indra would not quickly sever—would not separate—our friendships, our bonds, and our deeds;
and just as Indra, the fierce, the radiant, the protector of bodies, may be our helper and guardian.
In this very manner, we, the sacrificers, have performed (*akarma*) a prayer (*brahma*), that is, a hymn of praise (*stotra*), for Indra— the showerer of desires, the bull, the most constant youth—
just as the radiant Bhṛgus fashioned a chariot. This is the illustration.
The meaning is that the sacrificers praise Indra so that he may become the bestower of desired fruits upon them.
(Note: The phrase "by men... the sacrificers" is absent in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha;
the term "shining" is absent in manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, sa.)
3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the word *śatrūn* (“enemies”) is absent.
4. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and bha, the reading is *yajamānā*: [we] the sacrificers (*yajamānāḥ*), together with you, with our wives, sons, grandsons, and other attendants.
5. In the manuscripts na, bha, la, and sa, the phrase *kṣipram eva* (“very quickly”) is absent.
6. kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-na-pha-bha-sa-śarīriṇām | Ṛgveda 2.72.1:
O Indra, being praised and extolled, you have not made food swell for the singer, as the rivers swell with water.
O Lord of the bay horses, let our hymns be a new prayer for you; through this devotion, may we be charioteers who are ever victorious.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our inspired thought, may we be masters of chariots, ever victorious. 21.

O Indra, now indeed, swiftly praised by the ancient seers, now indeed being celebrated, and being extolled by us, do you cause food to swell for me, the singer who praises you—make it increase like rivers, as Agni makes the rivers swell.
O Lord of Bay Steeds (Harivaḥ), O Indra accompanied by horses named Hari, a new, more recent prayer has been made for you by us.

May we, possessing chariots like those who travel on chariots, being "Sadāsas"—those who always worship you with prayer in the form of wisdom and praise—be, or rather may we become, givers of food in the form of oblations for your sake.
The seventh hymn, consisting of twenty-one verses beginning with “*tvaṃ mahā~ indra tubhyam*,” is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Vāmadeva.
Regarding this, the table of contents (*anukramaṇikā*) states: “*tvaṃ mahā~ asikanyām ekapadā*.
In this [hymn], the verse “*asikanyāṃ yajamāno na hotā*” is a one-footed Virāj; the remaining twenty verses are Triṣṭubhs.
Indra is the deity.
This hymn is prescribed for the *niṣkevalya* litany on the eighth day of the ten-night *samūḷha* sacrifice.
And so it is stated in the Sūtra: “*tvaṃ mahā~ indra tubhyam* is the *niṣkevalya*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).
The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, is "Thou art great" (*tvaṃ mahān*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Thou art great, O Indra; to thee indeed belong the earths; [thine is] the whole... (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 3.8).
O great Indra, the earth indeed submits to your dominion by its own greatness, and the heavens acknowledge it;
you, having slain Vṛtra with your might, released the rivers that had been swallowed by the serpent.

You, O Indra, are great; indeed, the earth and the heaven have recognized your dominion with magnanimity. Having slain Vṛtra with your might, you released the rivers that had been swallowed by the serpent. 1.
O Indra, you are great and abundant;
"kṣāḥ" is the earth;
"kṣā" is indeed a name for the earth.
Endowed with greatness (maṃhanā), she indeed consented for your sake alone— that is, she approved of your own power (kṣatra).
And Heaven (dyauḥ) also consented to the power for your sake.

O Indra, you, by your own power and strength, slew Vṛtra—the Asura named Vṛtra who obstructs the worlds. Furthermore, [you rescued] those being swallowed, seized, and devoured by Ahi, that is, by Vṛtra.
The *kānac* suffix is substituted for the reduplicated perfect (*liṭ*).
"You have released" (*asṛjaḥ*) means you have let flow the waters of the rivers.

1. *ga* and *indra* [are present]; *na*, *sa*, and *he* [are present] before *indra*. 2. *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *bha*, and *andhasaḥ* [mean] of food. 3. *gha* [indicates] Vāmadeva as the seer (*ṛṣi*); *na*, *la*, and *sa* [indicate] that there is no seership (*ārṣam*) for Vāmadeva. 4. *la* [indicates] that which is to be inserted as a *nivid*. 5. *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *lokānām*... [the name] does not exist. 6. *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *apaḥ* do not exist. 7. *ṇa* and *ta* [indicate] "you have indeed created" (*asṛjaḥ* = *sṛṣṭavān asi*). "Thou hast indeed created the light; heaven trembled, and the earth trembled with fear at thy wrath. The well-being-seeking mountains yielded, the channels gave way, and the waters flowed forth."
At your birth, O Manyu, the heaven trembled and the earth trembled with fear at your own wrath. The well-watered mountains yielded, the desert wastes gave way, and the waters flowed forth.

O Indra, at your birth— your very manifestation— you, who are radiant with splendor, caused heaven and the intermediate space to tremble out of fear, that is, from the arising of terror due to your own wrath (the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative). They shook with the fear born of your anger.
The earth trembled; quaking, it shook.
The great mountains—meaning the clouds—were agitated.
The [clouds] prospered; that is, they were no longer obstructed by you, the regulator, for the purpose of bestowing rain upon the Maṣya and other regions.
Likewise, the clouds did not cause harm—that is, they did not inflict the suffering of thirst—upon living beings.
Furthermore, the clouds reached the *dhanvāni*, regions devoid of water.

O Indra, that Prajāpati—who is worthy of praise by the officiating priests and others, who possesses a beautiful thunderbolt (*suvatra*), and who is never fallen from his own celestial abode (*sadasaḥ*)—has, indeed, brought you forth;
"na" is used here in the sense of conjunction;
he has generated you, who are endowed with abundance (*bhūma*) through your greatness (*bhūmnā*).
The verbal root is *jan*, meaning "to produce."

The radiant *dyauḥ* (Heaven), your progenitor, that Prajāpati, thought: "May I be one who possesses excellent sons (*suvīraḥ*). Furthermore, the creator of Indra—that Prajāpati who is his progenitor—became the most skillful in action (*svapastamaḥ*), performing exceedingly beautiful deeds.
He who alone causes the multitude to tremble, Indra, the king of the peoples, invoked by many—
after him all rejoice as he approaches death, at the gift of the generous god who is praised.
He alone truly causes the earth to tremble; Indra, the king of the peoples, invoked by many. All rejoice in him as the truth—the gift of the divine, bountiful one who is praised. || 5 ||

He who is the king and lord of all *kṛṣṭīs*, that is, of all subjects; who is *puruhūta*, invoked by many; who is *eka* alone, the preeminent one among the gods—that very Indra drives away (*pra vyāvayati*), meaning utterly destroys, the fear arising from enemies that has already come into being (*bhūma*). All the sacrificers are *maghonaḥ*, that is, possessors of wealth characterized by oblations.
By taking refuge in the god who is equal to Indra, those who praise him—addressing this Indra, who is the kinsman of bounty—they truly rejoice and offer hymns of praise.
All Soma juices have become his; all the most intoxicating exhilarations belong to the Mighty One.
You have always been the Lord of treasures; O Indra, you have placed all peoples within your gift.

At once the Soma juices became his; at once all the most intoxicating draughts of the mighty one. At once you became the lord of treasures among treasures; O Indra, you have placed all the peoples under your dominion for the sake of giving. 6.
All the Soma juices of this Indra truly became abundant; "satrā" is indeed a name for truth—
it means they truly became plentiful.
Furthermore, the exhilarating Soma juices, which cause intoxication, have truly become the most intoxicating for this great Indra.
O Indra, you are the lord of wealth; not only the lord of wealth, but you truly are, indeed, the lord of all riches, such as cattle and the like. You remain so, verily.
O Indra, when wealth is to be given as the cause, you sustain all the tribes—the people who offer praise.
4.14.3 -> O Indra, as soon as you were born, you placed all the peoples under your dominion;
O Maghavan, increasing in power, you struck down the Asharya with your great thunderbolt.
O Indra, as soon as you were born, you placed all the peoples in their proper order; O Maghavan, with your thunderbolt, you struck down the serpent Ahi as he rushed forward from the heights. 7.
1. In the manuscripts ca, pha, and ‘indrasya’ is not present.
2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ta, and bha, it reads “atyantaśobhanakarmā” (one whose actions are exceedingly beautiful).
3. In the manuscript ṇa, it reads “dhārayasi rakṣakatvena” (you uphold [it] as a protector).
Moreover, O Indra, at the very moment of your birth, when the fear caused by Vṛtra arose, you sustained all created beings (*viśvāḥ sṛṣṭīḥ*) as their protector.
O wealthy Maghavan, aiming your thunderbolt (*vajra*) toward the downward-sloping,
water-filled regions, you cut apart, indeed you shattered, the demon named Vṛtra who was bellowing and obstructing the waters.
In the animal sacrifice to Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the verse "satrāhaṇam" is the invitatory prayer (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "satrāhaṇaṃ dādhṛṣiṃ tubham indraṃ sahadānuṃ puruhūta kṣiyantam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
[The verse is: "satrāhaṇaṃ dādhṛṣiṃ tubham indraṃ mahāram pāraṃ vṛṣabhaṃ suvajram."

The slayer of Vṛtra, the winner of booty, the giver of riches, the bounteous one, the bestower of great wealth—Indra, who is ever victorious, bold, impetuous, great, boundless, the bull, the wielder of the excellent thunderbolt; he who is the slayer of Vṛtra and the winner of booty, as well as the giver of riches, the bounteous one, the bestower of great wealth.
Satrāhannam, Dādhṛṣim, Tubhyam, Indram, Mahām, Apāram, Vṛṣabham, Suvajram, Hantā, Yaḥ, Vṛtram, Sanitā, Uta, Vājam, Dātā, Maghāni, Maghavā, Surādhāḥ. 8.
The slayer of many enemies, the utterly bold, the impeller;

the impeller of enemies, the great, the immeasurable. *Note: The term *tubhram* is interpreted here as derived from the root *tubh*, meaning "to impel" or "to drive. The commentary notes that *tumiḥ* is a verb signifying the act of impelling.*
The meaning is "devoid of destruction. We, the worshippers— this is the ellipsis— praise Indra, the showerer of desires (*vṛṣabha*), who possesses a beautiful thunderbolt (*suvajra*).
Indra is the slayer, for he is the one who strikes down Vṛtra, the Asura named Vṛtra;
and furthermore, Indra is the winner, for he is the giver of *vāja*, that is, food;
he is the possessor of excellent wealth (*surādhas*), the bountiful Indra who is the giver of riches (*maghāni*).
"Sing praise to that Indra"—this is the connection with the preceding [verse].
