In all these instances, because the word ends in a suffix having the sense of the present tense (*tṛn*), the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*; consequently, the accusative case alone is used.
This Maghavan, alone, is heard as one who overcomes Vṛtra and [brings together] the converging [hosts] in battles.
This one brings the prize for which he presses [the soma]; may we be dear to him in his dwelling. 9.

This one drives away the Vṛtras that face each other; he who is renowned alone as Maghavan in battles. This one brings the prize for which he presses [the soma]; may we be dear to him in his dwelling. 9.
Indra, the possessor of wealth, the bountiful one, is renowned as the preeminent leader among the prize-winners in battles; he is heard of as such.
We, O Indra, have surrounded the *vṛtaḥ*—the enemy armies so called because they "cover" (*vṛ*) the worlds. They are gathered together and come against us.

He drives them away; he destroys them. We are Indra. Whatever *vāja*—that is, food—he wins, he gives it to the sacrificer; he brings that *vāja*; he bears it in order to give that food to the sacrificer.
O singers, may we, as dear ones, remain beloved in the friendship of such an Indra, in his victorious power.

"He is heard of as he strives; moreover, he wins the cattle by battle. When Indra makes his wrath true, everything that is firm trembles in fear before him."

This one is heard of; indeed, he grows old, and even now he is young. And he drives forth the cattle by battle; when Indra makes his wrath real, everything that is firm trembles in fear before him. 10.
Moreover, Indra is heard of as "conquering," that is, he is renowned everywhere for conquering his enemies;
furthermore, he is heard of as "slaying," that is, he is renowned everywhere for destroying his enemies.
Moreover, Indra, by means of his victorious battle, makes the cattle—the enemy’s possessions—his own; he seizes them from the one who oppresses his foes.

Furthermore, when Indra makes his wrath truly real—that is, when he acts as an avenger of his enemies—at that time, he causes the entire world to tremble: both the firm and stable (the stationary) and the unsteady (the moving). That Indra attains from his mother, the progenitress, as much strength as there is.
From his father, he acquires as much strength as there is;
Indra, from whom— that Prajāpati who is the progenitor— this visible world was born, from that Prajāpati,
Indra repeatedly impels the vigor and all the strength of this world.
Like the wind impelled by thundering, roaring clouds, so Indra, impelled and urged on by his praisers, becomes summoned for the purpose of receiving the offering of oblations.
He makes the one who dwells in peace restless; Maghavan stirs up the dust in the thick of battle.
Shattering it like the sky with a thunderbolt, Maghavan bestows wealth upon his praiser.

He makes his own [people] abide and those who do not abide [in him] prosper; Maghavan sends forth the dust in a great mass, like the thunderbolt-bearing sky; and Maghavan shall bestow wealth upon his praiser. 13.

The generous (*maghavā*) Indra makes one person who possesses wealth (*dhanavān*), while he makes another person who dwells in poverty (*kṣiyantam*)—wasting away due to a lack of wealth—into one who does not dwell in poverty (*akṣiyantam*), being undecaying through wealth.
The meaning is that a certain man, having been destitute, became enriched with wealth by praising Indra.

Like the sky (*dyauḥ*) which possesses thunderbolts (*aśanimān*), Indra—the bountiful one (*maghavān*) who is especially a devourer (*vibhajanuḥ*) of enemies—drives away (*iyarti*) the gathered dust, that is, the accumulated evil, from the presence of his worshipper.
Moreover, the bountiful Indra bestows (*dhāt*) wealth (*vasau*) upon his worshipper; he places him therein.
This wheel of the sun strove to move; it has caused Etaśa, who was speeding along, to rest.
The black one, turning back, smears him at the base of the skin, in the womb of this mid-air.
This one has impelled the wheel of the sun; he has brought to rest Etaśa as he was speeding along.
The black, winding smoke besprinkles him at the base of the skin, in the womb of this region of space.
Regarding the meaning of *Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.61.15, “*etaśaṃ sūrye paspṛdhānam*,” a certain ancient narrative was previously indicated;
here too, in the first half-verse, “*ayaṃ cakram*,” that same narrative is indicated.
There was a certain king named Svaśva.
He worshipped the Sun for the sake of a son.
That Sun himself was born there in the form of a son and engaged in battle with the great seer named Etaśa.
At that time, the seer praised Indra for the sake of victory in the battle.
Being praised by him, that Indra protected him from the battle involving Sūrya, his own son.
We [the poets] impelled the wheel—the weapon—of Sūrya.
He brought to a halt, he restrained, he caused to cease Etaśa, the seer named Etaśa, who was rushing forth, moving toward battle.

Moving crookedly as it were, the dark-colored cloud, at the base—the root-source—of this water of *rajas*, from the essence of light. (Note: 1. The word "sakāśāt" is absent in the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, bha, and la;

6. He impels that with *kha-ga-gha-ṇa-bha-la*; he impels that from there with *ta-sa*. 7. He is praised with *kha-ga-gha-ṇa-ta-na-bha*; he is praised with *la*; he is heard with *sa*. 8. *na-la-sa*: “*etaśam*” does not exist.
He sprinkles this Indra, who stands in the womb, in his place, in the intermediate space;
let the impellers of the enemies and the non-gods protect him—this is the meaning.
Like a sacrificer, he [stands] at the *asiknī* river, like a *hotṛ* priest. (15) At the *asiknī*; the sacrificer; like; the *hotṛ*. (15)
This single line of the Ṛgveda is connected as an illustration with the preceding verse:
"In the night at Asiknī, the sacrificer is not like a non-sacrificer, [just as] the Hotṛ is not like a Hotṛ—that is, not like one who calls upon the gods.
Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
He sprinkles with Soma; the meaning is that he thereby sprinkles Indra. 23.

The wise ones, grasping [the Soma], desiring horses, seeking the bull, and striving for strength, yearning for wives, [grasp] the wife-giver who provides inexhaustible aid—we draw him forth as one draws a bucket from a well. 16. Grasping Indra for the sake of kinship, the inspired poets, longing for horses, seeking the bull, striving for vigor, desiring wives, [we grasp] the giver of wives, whose protection is imperishable; we draw him forth as one draws a bucket from a well. 16.

Desiring cattle (*gavyantaḥ*), seeking horses (*aśvayantaḥ*), desiring nourishment (*vājayantah*), seeking food (*vājam*), desiring wives (*janīyantaḥ*), we who are wise (*viprāḥ*) and singers of praise—through friendship (*sakhyāya*) with Indra, for the sake of companionship—we cause Indra to come hither; him who is the showerer (*vṛṣaṇam*) of desires, the progenitor (*janidam*) who bestows wives, and whose protection is imperishable (*akṣitotim*), meaning he who provides constant defense. Such is Indra whom we cause to approach.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"in a well" (*avate kūpe*).
*Avata* is a name for a well, because it is listed among the names for wells in [the Nighaṇṭu] as: "avataḥ, avaṭaḥ, kriviḥ" (Nirukta 3.23.7).
The treasury is not like a water-drawing vessel.
The meaning is that just as men draw near to a well to fill a water-drawing vessel with water, so do we draw near [to the treasury].³

Be our protector, O visible one; be our kinsman, our defender, and the comforter of those who offer Soma. Be the friend, the father, and the most fatherly of fathers; bestow vital strength upon the one who desires to create a world for them. 17. Protector. Of us. Be. Visible. Kinsman. Defender. Comforter. Of those who offer Soma. Friend. Father. Most fatherly. Of fathers. To create. Him. Verily. World. Desiring. Bestower of life-force. 17.

O Indra, you who are a kinsman (*āpiḥ*), one who has attained us (*āptaḥ*), and one who is beautiful to behold (*darśataḥ*)— as the protector of all, you who see— be (*bodhi*) our savior and guardian (*trātā*). Furthermore, you are the one who looks upon us (*abhihyātā*), the comforter (*marḍitā*), the bringer of happiness, the friend (*sakhā*) of those worthy of Soma (*somyānām*) such as the sacrificers who offer Soma, one of equal renown with Prajāpati, and a father (*pitā*) who protects.

He is not merely a protector, but the best among protectors, the most fatherly of fathers. (1) [Note: This Ṛgvedic verse is found in the recensions marked kha, ga, gha, ṇa, ta, pa, pha, bha, and sa as a single unit. (2) [Note:
The recensions marked kha, ga, gha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and sa include the word "jāyām" (wife).]
3. We do not abandon, nor do we forsake, Indra—the treasury of *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *ka*—as our foundation; rather, we share him for the sake of protection.

4. By virtue of being the protector of all (*gha*, *ṇa*, *ma*, *saṃ*), you are the preeminent guardian among the *ṛtvij*s and the creator of the ancestors; as the bestower of vital strength (*vayodhāḥ*), you [grant it] to the singer who desires the world, that is, the heavenly realm.
"Vaya" is a name for food;
therefore, be a giver of food.
O Indra, being praised, be our protector as a friend; grant vital strength to the one who lauds you, for we have performed service for you, O subduer, magnifying you, O Indra, with these ritual acts.
Friend, listen! Be our protector; being praised as our friend, O Indra, bestow vital strength upon the one who lauds you.
For we have performed service for you, O Indra, strengthening you with these ritual acts that are difficult to perform. 18.
O Indra, be our protector and guardian—be mindful of us who desire friendship with you as your friends.
Being thus praised, become our friend.
O Indra, bestow food and vital strength upon me who offers this hymn of praise.
O Indra, we—being "sabādhaḥ," that is, accompanied by those who press us hard—we indeed "ā cakrama," that is, we call upon you. Doing what?
"Mahayantaḥ," that is, honoring you with these "śamībhiḥ," that is, with these perceptible acts consisting of hymns of praise.
For the *puroḍāśa* offering to Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the *yājyā* verse is "stuta indraḥ.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "stuta indro madhavā yad vṛtraivā vasva indraḥ satyaḥ samrāṭ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
Indra, the giver of joy, has been praised when he alone slays many Vṛtras who are irresistible;
he is the dear singer for whom the gods guard his protection, not mortals.
Praised is Indra, the possessor of the Soma-drink, when he alone slays many Vṛtras that cannot be resisted.
His is the beloved singer, under whose protection neither gods nor mortals withhold desirable boons. 19.

Whenever indeed Indra, the possessor of wealth, being praised by us, becomes lauded, then Indra, alone and without companion, slays— that is, destroys— many *vṛtras*, meaning enemies who are "unassailable," that is to say, those who are difficult to overcome.
In the protection (*śarman*), that is, the refuge, of this Indra, the gods do not restrain—that is, they do not create any obstacle—for the singer who abides therein;
nor do mortals restrain him.
This singer, the praiser of this Indra, becomes beloved.
In the Ābhimāruta-śastra, "evā na indraḥ" is the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "He should conclude with 'evā na indro madhavā virapśī'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).

Thus may Indra, the bounteous, the exuberant, the unassailable upholder of the people, make our prayers come true. You are the king of all beings by birth; bestow upon us, O mighty one, glorious renown for the sake of the singer. Thus, Indra, the bounteous, the exuberant, the unassailable upholder of the people, shall make [our prayers] true. You are the king of all beings by birth; bestow upon us, O mighty one, glorious renown for the sake of the singer.

Virapśī, possessing manifold sounds; carṣaṇīdhṛt, the sustainer of all creatures; anarvā, unassailable—meaning not overtaken by any adversary; maghavā, the wealthy Indra; being thus praised by us, may he (evā) grant us (naḥ) our desired fruits which are true (satyā), that is, of the nature of truth.

O Indra, you are by birth the king and lord of all living beings; that fame and glory which is endowed with greatness, bestow that fame upon us, the singer and the worshipper, placing it preeminently within us. With the final verse, "Thus indeed [is] Indra, the bountiful, the exuberant," the concluding hymn is performed; for the Brāhmaṇa states: "Indra, the bountiful, the exuberant" (AiB 3.38), and so forth.

Now, O Indra, being praised, may you cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be chariot-borne victors, ever-conquering. 21. Now! Pressed! O Indra! Now! Being praised! Nourishment! For the singer! Like rivers! May you cause to swell! A prayer! Has been made! For you! O Lord of the Bay Steeds! New! Through devotion! May we be! Chariot-borne! Ever-conquering! 21.
Now, "O Indra, the pressed [juice]" is explained.

"This is the path" (*ayaṃ panthāḥ*) is the eighth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses in the Triṣṭubh meter. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "This is a dialogue between Indra, Aditi, and Vāmadeva.

Since it is established by the technical rule that "he whose words [constitute the hymn] is the seer (ṛṣi), and that which is spoken by him is the deity," the seers and deities in each respective case are to be understood accordingly.

In this hymn, a certain narrative in the form of a dialogue between Indra and Aditi is indicated in verse: while still in the womb, the great sage Vāmadeva, endowed with wisdom, formed the resolve, "May I not be born from the womb of my mother."
But having realized that this had come from the side [of her husband],
the mother reflected upon Śacī, Aditi, and Indrāṇī— the mother of Indra— for the sake of peace.
Aditi, accompanied by Candra, approached Garbhiṇī;
then Aditi, Indra, and Vāmadeva held a conversation.
By the sūtra "dialogue" (saṃvāda), this very discourse is indicated here;
for no specific speaker is mentioned here, as there is no mention [of one] in the instructional texts (upadeśas).
In reality, however, it must be understood that there is a difference in the speakers; this is the established principle.
In this hymn, Indra, Aditi, and the Sage have each spoken their own thoughts.
To Vāmadeva, who had lain in the womb for a very long time and had not yet emerged from his mother’s side,
Śatakratu addressed with the first verse.
With five half-verses beginning with the second, he spoke to the Vipras;
"na hī nv asya" consists of seven [half-verses], and "aditeḥ vacaḥ" is a half-verse.
"O Sage, the five verses beginning with 'mama cittaṃ yuvatiḥ' were indeed spoken by Vāmadeva for the pacification of misfortune; thus it is handed down in tradition."
Thus, because the meaning is not distinct from the action itself, the teaching is manifold;
however, because discrimination is clear, it has not been explicitly stated in the instructions.
"For the sake of attaining the state of a seer, a deity, or a perfected being, the purpose of discrimination has been declared" (Anubhūtiprakāśa 4.18).

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha, the word "prabhuḥ" is absent. 2. In manuscript La, it begins with "paridhi" and so forth. 3. In manuscript Ta, this is explained; in manuscript Sa, it was previously explained. 4. In manuscripts Ca and Ṇa, it takes the form of a dialogue.

This is the ancient path discovered of old, from which all the gods were born. From this very source let him be born, having grown strong; let him not, by such a course, cause his mother to fall. This is the path, discovered, ancient, from which all the gods were born. From this very source let him be born, having grown strong; let him not, by such a course, cause his mother to fall.
The words of Indra: "Ancient" means beginningless; "the path" refers to the way or course that is perceived through direct experience; "followed in succession" means obtained by all those being born.
From that womb-path, "all the gods" (viśve devāḥ) "were born forth," meaning they were produced with excellence.
Therefore, what need is there to say that humans are born from this path of the womb?
Thus, Vāmadeva— who has grown from this very path of the womb and has attained full development within the womb— may he be born, may he be born completely,
for the sake of falling upon her, that mother, *amuyā*.
The meaning is "for the sake of death.
*Mā kaḥ* means "let him not do."

I shall not emerge from here; this is difficult to traverse. I will go out sideways from this side. Many deeds yet unaccomplished remain for me to do; let him fight with one, let him question with another. I. Not. From here. Out. Shall go. Difficult to pass. This. Transversely. From the side. Out. Shall go. Many. For me. Unperformed. Deeds to be done. Let him fight. With one. Together. With another. Let him question. 2.
Vāmadeva replied to Indra, who had spoken thus:
"I shall not go forth, I shall not go forth, I shall not emerge from this path of the womb."
This path, which consists of entering the womb, is difficult to traverse; it is hard to reach,
meaning it is to be grasped with great difficulty and cannot be easily attained.
But I shall go forth, emerging from the side, not from the front;
the meaning is that I shall emerge by piercing the side without having emerged from the region of the womb.
Not only is this very thing being done by me, which has not been done by others, but there are many other deeds to be performed by me that have not yet been accomplished by my ancestors.
With him alone, my rival, let me contend;
with him alone, Yudhushnu, let me consult thoroughly.

I have sought after my mother as she went away; I shall not go after her, nor indeed shall I follow. In the house of Tvaṣṭṛ, Indra drank the Soma pressed by Śatadhanvan, the son of Cumuri. parā'yatīm | mātaram | anu | acche | na | na | anu | gāni | anu | nu | gamāni | tvaṣṭuḥ | gṛhe | apibat | somam | indraḥ | śata'dhanvyam | cumbauḥ | sutasya || 3 ||

1. In the *nalasa* recension, the *indravākya* is not present. 2. [The variants] *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* read *bhavanti*. 3. *la*: *kim*. 4. *ta*: *durgaham*. 5. *na*: *durbhahaṇīyam*. 6. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *pārśve*. 7. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*: "not done" means not done by a rival (*sapatnena*). 8. *ta*: "I ask. While I was still in the womb, Indra spoke to my mother as she was departing, passing away, and dying.
Even so, while now situated in the womb, it is not that I shall not follow, nor that I do not follow, the ancient path;
rather, I shall indeed follow it quickly.
Vāmadeva, having set aside his own failure to act, establishes Indra's failure to act by means of the second half of the verse.

Indra, being uninvited, drank the Soma—which was purchased with great wealth—belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ, who had pressed it in the house associated with him; that is, he forcibly consumed the Soma from the two *camū* vessels, the pressing-boards of the one who had performed the extraction.
This matter is elaborated at length in the section of the Maitrāyaṇīyas: "Tvaṣṭṛ, whose son had been slain, brought the Soma for Indra" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.4.12.1).
What has he accomplished? He bore a thousand months and many autumns. Indeed, there is no likeness of him among those who have been born or are yet to be born.

What [is he]? He is the one who, performing his work uniquely, has brought forth a thousand months and many autumns. Indeed, there is no measure for him among those already born or those yet to be born. 4.
Aditi bore this Indra for a thousand many months and for many autumns and years. She carried him.
It bears this form.
The meaning is that Indra, while remaining in the womb for many years, caused Aditi distress.
Being such as this, that Indra— *kiṃ yat* means "whatever," that is to say, even everything.
He performed a distinct and separate deed.
Aditi, the mother of Indra, unable to endure the reproach of Indra, speaks back to him:
"O Vāmadeva, among those who have been born, there is indeed no likeness—that is, no equal—to this Indra, even among the gods."
The particle *nu* serves to fill out the meter;
and furthermore (*uta*), among those gods and others who have been born, are to be born, or are yet to be born, there is no counterpart (*pratimāna*) to this Indra.
Thinking him as if lowly, the Mother hid Indra in a cave because of his heroic power;
then he rose up of his own accord, clothing himself in light, and being born, he filled the two worlds, heaven and earth.

As if despising him, the Mother [Aditi] concealed Indra with her power when he was cast down; then he rose up of his own accord, clothing himself in light, and as he was being born, he filled the two worlds.

Indra, who was born in a secret place within a secret, inaccessible cave-like maternity chamber, was regarded by his mother Aditi as merely a lowly embryo; yet, knowing him to be Indra, she brought him forth. By means of her own power and capability, she made him one who had attained supreme preeminence.
Then, immediately thereafter—

[The variants] "kha-ga-ca-na-bha-sa-kiyat" are found in MSS Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṅa, Bha, and Sa. 4. [The variant] "kha-ga-ca-ṇa-kṣepaṇam" is found in MSS Kha, Ga, Ca, and Ṅa. 5. [The phrase] "'devādiva' nāsti" (is not present) in MSS Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṅa, Na, Ma, La, and Sa. 6. [The word] "'upamānam' nāsti" (the word 'comparison' is not present) in MSS Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṅa, Na, and Bha. 7. [The particle] "hi" is found in MSS Kha, Ga, Ca, Na, Bha, and Sa. 8. [The letter] "ta" is for the purpose of completing the meter. 9. [The word] "'garbhava' nāsti" (the word 'womb' is not present) in MSS Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṅa, Ta, Na, Pa, Pha, Bha, La, and Sa. Indra, being born—that is, coming into existence—himself clothing himself in—that is, covering himself with—his own splendor.
The meaning is "bearing. He "arose" (udasthāt), that is, he stood out preeminently.
Furthermore, he "filled" (āṇuṇāt) the two worlds, heaven and earth, completely on all sides.
25 | These waters flow, sounding as they go, crying out like a woman whose husband has been slain.
Ask them: what is this they say? Why do the waters encircle the mountain as a boundary?

6 | These flow forth, becoming *alala*, like those observing the sacred law (*ṛtavarī*), crying out together. Ask these: what is it they say? To whom do the waters cling as a surrounding mountain-fortress? ||6||

"Alalābhavantīḥ": making such sounds as "alala"; "ṛtāvarīr iva": like those possessing water, these rivers; "saṃkrośamānāḥ": crying out, sounding in many ways with the joy produced by the spoken words that proclaim the greatness of Indra; they "arṣanti," meaning they flow. What do these rivers, being thus, "bhananti"—what are they saying, what sound audible to the ear are they uttering? O Seer, you must "vi pṛccha" them—ask them specifically. Thus, inquire into this matter.
The meaning is that when this is considered, these words become a statement regarding the very majesty of Indra.
Furthermore: "The waters (āpaḥ) resort to (rajanti) what enclosure (paridhim), what mountain (kam adrim), or what cloud (kam megham)?
The meaning is: the waters do not resort to any cloud whatsoever; rather, it is my son, Indra alone, who, having shattered the cloud that encloses the waters, causes them to flow forth.
Did they indeed proclaim these invocations to him? The waters desired Indra’s weapon.
Having slain Vṛtra with his mighty weapon, my son released these rivers.

What indeed? Is it that they proclaim these intimations to him? The waters desire to attain the slaughter of Indra. My son, having struck down Vṛtra with a mighty weapon, has released these rivers. || 7 ||
Aditi spoke, setting aside the view of Vāmadeva that when Indra slew the asura Vṛtra, he then incurred the eternal sin of Brahman-murder (*brahmahatyā*). [She said:
"The *nivid*s.
Certain words used in the *marutvatīya* litany that express praise for Indra—such as "the Maruts' hymn, O Maruts"—are designated by the term *nivid*.
Those *nivid*s say: "What indeed do they proclaim (*bhananti*) regarding Indra, who has incurred this sin in the form of *brahmahatyā* caused by the slaying of Vṛtra?
If one asks what they say, [the answer is:
then, considering Indra to be free from sin, the *nivid*s praise him."
How is Indra free from sin?
It is said:
the waters (*āpaḥ*) bear (*didhiṣante*), that is, they hold, the slaughter (*avadham*)—the sin consisting of the killing of a Brahmin and so forth—of this Indra in the form of foam.
"My son": my own son, Indra. "With great" means with abundant "slaughter. "Slaughter" (*vadha*) is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*);
having struck Vṛtra with the thunderbolt, he killed him.
Then he released these rivers, the waters, so that they might flow forth with full freedom;
that is to say, Indra released the waters, and their sin flowed away from him.

1. *ta-la-sa* do not have "eva". 2. *ta* reads *tiṣṭhati*. 3. *ṇa* reads *pūramāsa*. 4. *ta* reads *udakāvārakam*. 5. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-ma-sa* do not have "indram". 6. *ta* reads *yaḥ indraḥ*. 7. *ṇa* reads *samutsṛṣṭavān*.
At my very vitals the young woman spat upon you; at my very vitals Kuṣavā swallowed you.
At my very vitals the waters were gracious to the infant; at my very vitals Indra rose up with might.

Even from the vital organ, the young woman did not cast thee away; even from the vital organ, Kuṣavā swallowed thee; even from the vital organ, the waters were gracious to the infant; even from the vital organ, Indra rose up by his might. 8.
Due to a flaw in the hymn, the seer praises Indra:
"O Indra, like one who does not know the vital points, [you are] as if careless";
that is the meaning.
Your young mother Aditi cast you away;
moreover, a certain Rākṣasī named Kuṣavānākṣī, piercing your vital organs, swallowed you.
O Indra, as you were thus pierced in your vitals, the waters brought comfort and joy to you, their newborn child.
Like Indra piercing the vital points of Māgha with his own power, he rose up from the lying-in chamber by his own heroism; warding off the Rākṣasī, he stood there in pre-eminence.
O Maghavan, you struck him in his vital parts; having pierced his shoulders, you struck out his jaws. Thus, being struck down, he became inferior; you crushed the head of the Dāsa with your weapon.

Even as you struck him in his vital parts, O Maghavan, your fist shattered his jaws; though pierced, he remained superior for a moment, until you crushed the head of the Dāsa with your weapon. || 9 ||

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, even as you were striking, the Rākṣasa named Vyaṃsa struck your two jaws—having pierced them, he struck away your two jaws, the sides of your mouth. Then, O Indra, having been struck by the Rākṣasa, you became superior, possessing greater strength than Vyaṃsa; being thus, you crushed with your weapon, the thunderbolt, the head of the wretched Vyaṃsa.
The first-calf cow has brought forth for you the ancient, invincible, and most powerful bull, Indra.
The mother has praised her own son, who is eager to act and seeking a path for his own body.

The first-calf cow has well brought forth the ancient, unassailable bull, the powerful Indra, whom she, the mother, has praised for the sake of victory, as he himself seeks a path for his own body. 10.
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Sa, the word "kācit" does not exist.
2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, and Bha, it reads "sukhaṃ cakruḥ.
3. In the manuscripts Ta and La, it reads "vīryeṇa saha."
4. Pierced by *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *pha* at will, O Indra; pierced by *gha* and *ṇa* at will; pierced by *pa*, *bha*, and *ha* at will, O Indra; [pierced] by *sa* and *ha*, O Indra.
5. By *ṇa*, you, O Indra. Like a certain *gṛṣṭi* cow, she brought forth (*sasūva*) her calf.
Likewise, the mother Aditi, the progenitor of Indra, gave birth to Indra for the sake of wandering at will—that is, for free movement.

What kind of Indra? One who is *sthaviram*, mature in age; *tavāgām*, possessed of increased strength; *anādhṛṣyam*, unassailable by enemies; *vṛṣabham*, capable of impregnation; *tugram*, an impeller; *arīḷham*, unsubdued by enemies; one who seeks *gātum*—a path independent of others—for *tanve*, his own body.
Then the Mother indeed spoke to Mahiṣa: "O son, these gods are abandoning you.
Then Indra, about to slay Vṛtra, said: "O friend Viṣṇu, stride out even further!"
And the Mother looked upon the buffalo; "O son," she said, "these gods are abandoning you. Then Indra, about to slay Vṛtra, spoke: "O friend Viṣṇu, stride out even further! ||11||
Moreover, O my son Indra, those gods such as Valga and others are abandoning you,
leaving you behind— thus spoke Aditi, the mother of Indra, to Indra, the "Great Bull" (*mahipa*);
for *mahipa* is a name for the great.
He entreated him repeatedly;
then, O Viṣṇu, O friend, O Hari, you who are of a pervasive nature—desiring to slay Vṛtra, that is, wishing to kill him—stride out further, become exceedingly valorous; thus Indra spoke to Viṣṇu.
Who made his mother a widow? Who sought to kill you as you were wandering?
What god was there to grant you mercy when you seized your father by the foot and cast him down?
Who made your mother blind? Who desired to kill you as you were crawling? Which god was on your side with compassion, when, your eyes not yet closed, you grasped your father by the foot?
O Indra, because you, out of fear of being born from your father, seized your father by the feet and utterly destroyed him,
for that reason, what other god besides you made his own mother a widow by the slaughter of her husband?
And who other than you desired to slay you, whether you were lying down or moving about, or whether you were awake?
Who other than you, O God, was superior (*adhi*) in *mārḍīka*—that is, in bringing happiness to all creatures?

This meaning has been elaborated in many ways by the Taittirīyas in the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning with "The sacrifice meditated upon the sacrificial fee" (*yajño dakṣiṇāmabhyadhyāyat*), within the section starting from "The Ṛk and Sāman, indeed, [belong] to the gods" (*ṛksāme vai devebhyaḥ*, TaiSaṃ 6.1.3.6).
1. Kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-bha for moving about; ta-la-sa for wandering about.
2. Ta-suṣūva.
3. Kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa for the body.
I cooked the entrails for the sake of non-return; I found no comforter among the gods.
I saw my wife being carried away; then the falcon bore half of me away with honey.
Out of necessity, I cooked the entrails of a dog; I found no comforter among the gods. I did not honor my wife; then the falcon brought me the honeyed nectar. 13.
By this verse, Vāmadeva, indicating his own poverty, proclaims his supreme excellence:
"I am Vāmadeva; because of my lack of means of livelihood (*avatyā*), I cooked (*pece*) the entrails (*āntrāṇi*) and the intestines (*purītanti*) belonging to Śunaḥ, the son of Śunaka.
Among the many shining deities, such as Agni and others, I found no one other than Indra who was a *marḍitā*, a bestower of happiness."
Furthermore: Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
The fifth chapter of the third book has been explained with devotion by the wise one named Sāyaṇa; now the sixth chapter is being described.
In the second section of the fourth maṇḍala, eight hymns have been explained.
"Evā tvām indra" is the eleventh hymn, the ninth [in this section]. According to the conventions regarding the beginning of the maṇḍala, Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi) of this hymn.
By the paribhāṣā regarding the lack of specific instruction, the metre is Triṣṭubh;
Indra is the deity.
Thus it has been enumerated: "Evaikādaśa."

This hymn is used at the Mādhyandina-savana during the Maitrāvaruṇa-śastra in the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. For it is stated: "‘Evā tvām indra... sumanā upakaḥ’ is the *yājyā* verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.16). On the first day of the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava six-day periods, there is the Ahīna-hymn in the Maitrāvaruṇa-śastra; in its place, there are three Saṃpāta-hymns.
In this regard, this is the first hymn.
And it has been stated: “‘Evā tvāmindra yajña indraḥ’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).
O Indra, the gods—the ancient, undecaying fathers—released you like youths [are sent forth] for the sake of slaying the Asuras.

Then, O Indra, you who have truth as your source (*satyayoni*), you became the sovereign ruler (*samrāj*) of all the worlds. Targeting the waters (*arṇaḥ*), you slew the serpent Vṛtra, who was lying all around, encompassing everything.
"Viśvadhenāḥ": the nourishers of all; "vartanīḥ": the rivers that cause [water] to flow everywhere. "Prāradaḥ": you have performed a thorough excavation.
The meaning is that Indra, having slain Vṛtra, caused the waters obstructed by him to flow forth in the form of a current.
O Indra, you struck with your thunderbolt at the jointless place the insatiable, wide-extended, wakeless,
and unawakened serpent as he lay sleeping upon his downward slope.
Not being satisfied; spreading out; down.
Having slain Vṛtra, the most formidable Asura, Indra released the many hidden dawns and autumns—that is, the years—swallowed by the darkness; he specifically brought them forth.
Likewise, he released the rivers—the waters obstructed by Vṛtra.
Furthermore, Indra [released] the rivers (mīrāḥ), which were confined within the clouds, situated all around, and bound on every side by Vṛtra.
"Sīrā" is a name for rivers.
He pierced—that is, he opened—the earth by way of the earth-like path, in order that they might flow, for the purpose of moving.
With eloquent ones, you brought forth from his dwelling, like a treasure from a cave, that son of Amūhu who bestows gifts.
Grasping the serpent, the blind one saw; he seized him, and the joints of his body were loosened. He emerged, and they fell apart.

With the eloquent ones, you brought forth the son of Amu from his dwelling, even as a tawny steed; he opened his eyes, and grasping the serpent, he cast him out. He emerged, and his joints were set together. 9.

O *Harivaḥ*, you who possess horses known as *hari*, O Indra, with your *vagminaḥ*— the sub-tongues— you brought forth from his dwelling, that place called an anthill, the son of *Amū*, who was not giving and was cowering. You seized him from there.
Taking hold [of him] and being led by Indra, the son of *amu*, though previously blind, cast aside the serpent and beheld it clearly;
then he emerged from the anthill.
All his joints—the joints of his limbs that had become loose—were joined together, having been severed from the "pot" (the anthill) known as *ukhā*.
The meaning is that the joints of Amu’s son, which had been loosened by the *upajihvikā* [leeches], were set back together by Indra.
The inspired sage, knowing them, has proclaimed your many ancient deeds to the wise one—
just as you, O King, have performed your own glorious, manly acts for your own benefit.

The inspired sage, knowing them well, has proclaimed to you, the wise one, your many ancient deeds—just as they are, O King, your manly, rain-bestowing, and self-praising exploits that you have performed for the waters.

O King, O radiant Indra, you have pervaded—that is to say, you have performed—those deeds pertaining to you, which are worthy of a bull (vṛṣaṇyāni), self-praised (svagūrtāni), manly (naryāṇi), and beneficial to humanity (naryāṇi). Just as you have pervaded them, so have you accomplished them.

O *vipra*, O lord of the wise, Vāmadeva—knowing thoroughly (*āvidvān*) all those ancient deeds (*pūrvāṇi karaṇāni*) belonging to you, who are a knower (*viduṣe*) of everything—he proclaims (*prāha*) your glorious acts (*karāṃsi*) with excellence.

It has come to pass: O Indra, being praised now, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our inspired thought, may we be charioteers who ever win the prize.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being lauded, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds. Through our inspired thought, may we be masters of chariots, ever victorious.

O Indra, now indeed, you who were swiftly praised by the ancient seers and are now swiftly celebrated—being lauded by us—cause food to swell for me, the singer, like rivers; cause it to overflow, O Lord of the bay horses (Harivaḥ), even as fire causes rivers to swell. For you, a newer, more recent prayer has been fashioned by us.

Possessing chariots, we—being constant givers through our prayer, which takes the form of wisdom and praise, and always devoted to you—may we be, or rather become, givers of food in the form of oblations for that purpose.
‘Ā na indraḥ’ is the tenth hymn, consisting of eleven verses; it is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Vāmadeva, in the Triṣṭubh metre, and dedicated to Indra.
‘Ā naḥ’ is its entry in the Anukramaṇikā.
On the first day of the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas, this hymn is to be used as the Niṣkevalya Śastra by one who knows it.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*ā na indra* is the *niṣkevalya*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.5).
This is also the *saṃpāta-sūkta* in the Mahāvrata.
Likewise, it is stated in the fifth Āraṇyaka: “*ā na indro dūrād ā na āsāt* is the *saṃpāta*” (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.2.2).
May the fierce Indra come from afar or from nearby to grant us protection;
may he, the most powerful lord of men, armed with the thunderbolt, victorious in the clash of battles, overcome those who provoke conflict.

May Indra come to us from afar, may he come to us from near at hand; praised for our aid, may the fierce lord of men, with his most powerful [helpers] and thunderbolt in arm, come to the fray in battles, overcoming the enemies in the clash of arms.
May Indra—the performer of the desired deeds for those connected with the sacrificer who has praised him, the fierce and radiant one—come from afar for our protection;
may he also come from near at hand for our protection.
Of what nature is he?

In close and continuous battles, he who is victorious over his enemies, the destroyer of foes, with the thunderbolt in his arm and the thunderbolt in his hand—the lord of men, the protector of humanity through the door of prosperity—is joined, it is implied, by the Maruts, who are most exceedingly brilliant.
May Indra come hither with his bay steeds for our protection and for bounty;
may the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bounteous and exuberant one, stand by us at our sacrifice in the winning of the spoil.

May Indra come toward us with his bay steeds, turning hitherward for our protection and for bounty. May the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bountiful and exuberant one, stand by this sacrifice of ours in the struggle for booty.

May Indra— who is marked with the *la* syllable, who is near, who is turned toward us— come hither with his two bay horses (*haribhiḥ*), directed toward us for our protection (*avase*) and for wealth (*rādhase*).
Furthermore, may he come, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*), the possessor of riches (*maghavān*), the bountiful (*virapśī*), and the great one.
Since *virapśin* is listed among the names for the "Great" (*mahat*), [the meaning is as follows]:
when our enemies, the Asuras and others, encounter us in the contest for booty—that is, when war has come upon us—may he stand firm, taking aim at this sacrifice of ours.
O Indra, place this sacrifice of ours before you; you win for us our purposeful will.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, lead us to the acquisition of riches; with your aid, may we conquer the hostile army in battle.
O Indra, place this sacrifice of ours before you; O wielder of the thunderbolt, you shall grant us wisdom for the winning of riches. With you as our ally, may we conquer the enemy in battle. 3.
O Indra, you, placing us in front—making us your vanguard—shall win and fully enjoy this sacrifice being performed, our very purpose (*kratu*).

Moreover, O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), like a hunter pursuing deer, may we, your noble patrons and singers, conquer the battle against the enemy for the sake of gaining wealth—the prize of booty. May we be victorious!
In the Agniṣṭoma, at the midday pressing, the *śastra-yājyā* for the Maitrāvaruṇa is "uśannu ṣu naḥ.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'uśannu ṣu naḥ sumanā upākaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.16).
Desiring us, O self-dependent one, with a gracious mind, come near to us now for the well-pressed Soma.
Drink, O Indra, of this offered honeyed draught; let there be exhilaration through the intoxicating juice that flows along the back.

Desiring [it], O *uśan*, with the sound *ūm*, be well-disposed toward us in our proximity. O self-dependent Indra, drink now of the well-pressed Soma, of the offered honey-sweetness; let there be intoxication through the stalk-pressed juice. 4.

O *svadhāvan* (possessor of the *svadhā*-offering), O *annavan* (possessor of food), O *indra*, you who are *sumanāḥ* (well-disposed) and *sumanaskaḥ* (of beautiful mind), desiring (*uśan*) us most intensely (*u*), being right here (*upāke*) near us—drink (*pāḥ*) now (*nu*) quickly indeed the *madhvaḥ* (sweet), intoxicating *soma* of the *susutasya* (well-pressed) and *pratibhṛtasya* (presented) [juice].
By means of the *pṛṣṭhya*:
by the word *pṛṣṭha*, the hymn (*stotra*) sung by the *udgātṛ*s at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) is meant.
Be exhilarated—be greatly delighted—by that Soma juice, which is sweet through its connection with him, that you have drunk.
Him who has roared aloud with his swift heroes like a tree laden with ripe fruit, like a conqueror eager for gain;
him whom I address as Indra, the one invoked by many, even as a young man approaches a maiden with longing.

He who has been celebrated by all the seers, like a tree laden with ripe fruit, like a victorious hero, like a youth full of longing for a maiden—meditating upon him, I call hither Indra, who is invoked by many. 5.

1. Having directed the *ambhalakṣya* [toward] the letters kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha; having brought the letters ta, na, sa into alignment (*abhimukhīkṛtya*). 2. Ta is Mahendra. 3. Ta: may we be victorious. 4. By the word *pṛṣṭhya* consisting of the letters ta, na, bha, la.
"Pakka" means a tree with ripe fruit, like a tree.
Here, the word *sṛṇi* signifies a goad.
By this, his weapon alone is indicated.
*Sṛṇyaḥ* means one skilled in weapons, a conqueror—not merely a victor over enemies like a heroic man—who is praised in various ways (*vivarapse*) by new, ever-fresh seers (*ṛṣibhiḥ*).
O much-invoked one (*puruhūta*), I, the praiser, speak toward—that is, specifically address and praise—that Indra who is summoned by many.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
just as a mortal man, thinking "this woman belongs to me" while recognizing her as a woman, would not feel shame before her, so it is here.

Indra, who by his own power is lofty and great, born for victory like one impelled by the press-stones, fierce and terrible, has hurled his formidable, ancient thunderbolt; he is filled with wealth like a vessel brimming with water.

The mountain-like, self-strong, lofty Indra was born for conquest, fierce indeed from the very beginning. Like one who is terrible, he brandished his ancient, formidable thunderbolt, as the waters burst forth from a vessel filled with wealth.
O Indra, you are the mountain-like protector of the people; you behold the wealth, the riches, the dwellings, and the houses of all creatures.
Moreover, you are the one who turns back and wards off the gathered multitude of cattle.

The meaning is: "You become the liberator of the cows from the Asuras who seek to obstruct them. Furthermore, O Indra, you—being a leader (*śikṣāniḥ*) through your instruction, a guide and teacher of wisdoms, and one who possesses weapons (*prahāvān*) in battles—you are the one who leads and brings forth a vast heap, a great mass, of wealth (*vasvaḥ*).
By what power is he most mighty when [the wood] is dry, by which he repeatedly performs wondrous deeds?
Most effective in distributing much to the donor, he bestows wealth upon the singer for his sake.

By what power is he heard as the most mighty? It is by that power by which the sublime one, acting swiftly, makes even the most difficult thing easy for the liberal giver; he, the best provider of wealth, bestows riches upon the singer for his purpose. 9.
*Śaciṣṭhaḥ*: most wise, pre-eminently intelligent.
*Tat*: [the word] *tat* here involves a change of gender (from neuter to masculine).
*Tat sa indraḥ kayā śadhyā*: by what wisdom (*śadhyā*)—by what intelligence does that Indra [act]?
"Śacī" is a name for wisdom.
"Śṛṇve" means he is heard of.
The lofty, great Indra, by means of that wisdom, repeatedly performs various deeds.
That Indra is most capable of utterly destroying the greatest amount of distress for the liberal sacrificer who has offered oblations;
moreover, he bestows wealth, such as cattle and other riches, upon the singer who praises him.
Do not forget us; bring and give us that which is yours in abundance, to be bestowed upon the giver.
When a new gift is praised and a hymn is recited, O Indra, we shall proclaim it while offering our praise.

Do not forget us; bring it hither and grant that to us, so much as is yours to give to the donor. For this new gift of yours, when this hymn of praise has been recited, we shall proclaim it, O Indra, while offering our lauds. 10.
O Indra, do not forget us; do not harm us. Rather, bring [wealth] to us and be our nourisher.
O Indra, that abundant wealth of yours which is to be given to the donor—the sacrificer who has offered the oblation—is for the purpose of being bestowed.
The word "prevails" (pra bhavati) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
"To us"—that is, for our sake—bring and give that wealth.

O Indra, while we praise you in this *uktha*, in this present liturgical recitation called the *aikavalya-śastra*, for your sake, when the gift to be given—the sacrificial oblation—is being offered in the midst of this new and praiseworthy performance, we shall speak forth to you with excellence.

1. I look upon that wealth; 2. the word "ca" (and) is not present in the manuscripts Kha, Pa, Pha, and Bha; 3. the word "kayā" (by what) is not present in the manuscripts Kha, Pa, Pha, and Bha; 4. according to the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, Bha, and Ya, [the reading is] "ṛṣvaḥ" (lofty); 5. according to the manuscripts Ta, Na, La, and Sa, the phrase "mahān indraḥ" (great Indra) is not present; 6. according to the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, Bha, and Ya, [the reading is] "yad bhūri bahu api dhanam" (whatever abundant and copious wealth).

Now indeed, O Indra, being praised and now being extolled, swell nourishment for the singer as the rivers do; for you, O Lord of the Bay Horses, a new prayer has been fashioned. Through our devotion, may we be charioteers who are ever victorious. 11. (This verse was explained previously. 4.
‘Ā yātv indraḥ’ is the eleventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses; it is the Ṛṣi Vāmadeva’s composition, in the Triṣṭubh metre, and dedicated to Indra.
It is introduced with the words ‘Ā yātu’.
This is to be understood as [the stotra] on the first day of both the Pṛṣṭhya and the Abhiplava six-day periods.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Marutvatīya [śastra] begins with 'ā yātv indro 'vasaḥ' (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 7.5)."
May Indra come hither to us with wealth; praised here, may he come to our gathering.

May Indra come from heaven, from earth, swiftly from the ocean or from the watery realm; may he, accompanied by the Maruts, come from the light of heaven for our protection, or from afar, from the seat of Cosmic Order. 3. May Indra come hither from heaven, from earth, swiftly from the ocean or from the watery realm; may he, accompanied by the Maruts, come from the light of heaven for our protection, or from afar, from the seat of Cosmic Order.
May Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, come from heaven for our protection;
may he come swiftly from the earth,
or indeed from the ocean or the intermediate space.
The ocean is seen as having the name "Antarikṣa" (the intermediate space), for it is listed among its names in the Nirukta: "The ocean is the sacrifice, the *asagara* ocean" (Nirukta 1.3.15).
Alternatively, [let him] come from *purīṣa*, that is, from water;
for *purīṣa* is a name for water, as it is listed among its names in the Nirukta: "Honey, *purīṣa*, and the *pippala* fruit" (Nirukta 1.12.12).
May he come from the world of Svarṇara, from which the leader Nara [Sūrya] shines;
or may he come from afar, from the distance;
or may he come from the seat of Ṛta, the place of water, or from the world of the clouds.

Praise that Indra in the assemblies, who rules over vast and abundant wealth; he who, with Vāyu, conquers in the cattle-rich [battles] and boldly leads us toward greater prosperity. Of vast wealth, of great wealth, he who rules—him, indeed, praise you in the assemblies, Indra; he who with Vāyu conquers in the cattle-rich [battles] and boldly leads us toward greater prosperity.
Indra, who rules over *sthūra*— that which is firm— and *sthūla*, that which is massive, and over *bṛhat*, the great wealth (*rāyaḥ*) in the *vidathas*, that is,
in the sacrifices (for *vidatha* is a name for sacrifice)—
that Indra, indeed, that very Indra, we who are singers praise.
Indra, who with Vāyu—in the form of vital breath and strength—conquers and overcomes his enemies in the *gormatī* armies;

that bold and courageous Indra who fearlessly leads the singers toward and bestows upon them *vasyaḥ*, meaning more excellent wealth, such as cattle and other riches—it is that very Indra whom we shall praise: this is the connection of the section.

He who, supporting himself with reverence and praise, stirs himself forth, generating speech through sacrifices; may that Hotṛ-priest, striving with hymns toward the one of many boons, bring Indra hither to the sacrificial seats. 5. He who, supporting himself with reverence and praise, stirs himself forth, generating speech through sacrifices; may that Hotṛ-priest, striving with hymns toward the one of many boons, bring Indra hither to the sacrificial seats. 5.
1. [The variants] kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa read *adhvaraḥ*.
2. [The variants] kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-sa do not contain the word *tam indram*.

Supporting the worlds—that is, propping them up—he, being *ṛsānaḥ* (being propitiated or perfected), generates and brings forth the voice characterized by thunder for the sake of sacrifice (*yajadhyai*).
"Delight is the act of adorning," says Yāska.
Indra, who is possessed of many boons (*puruvāraḥ*)—meaning he is to be honored by many—and who is through *ukthas*, that is, hymns characterized as liturgical recitations (*śastra*), is in *namas*.
*Namas* is a name for food.
When the Daityas offer the oblation, [the sacrificers say] "homage to the sacrificers"; he impels—that is, sends forth—the food which is the means for the sacrifice and other rites.
Indra, being satisfied by the oblation, bestows food through rain; and by that food, the sacrifice is produced once again—this is the meaning.
Our Hotṛ-priest should bring that Indra forward—that is, make him face us—in the *sadanāni*, the sacrificial halls.
If, through inspired thought, those seeking inspiration hasten toward the pressing-stone in the dwelling of Auśija,
then may the invoker of the household, the bearer who brings us across in the secret enclosures, come forth with his glowing radiance.

Through inspired thought—when they, seeking wisdom, hasten hither and sit upon the pressing-stone within the secret lair of Auśija; he who is the invoker of the dwelling-place, the great bearer of oblations for us in the sacrificial rites. 6.

Desiring *dhiṣaṇā*, that is, seeking praise directed toward Indra; the *auśijas*, the officiating priests who are the sons of Uśij and who desire [the sacrifice]; their patron, the sacrificer, is the *auśija*. The people seated (*sadataḥ*) in his dwelling (*gohe*), in his house, [crushed] the mountain (*adrim*).
He who strikes down enemies is the Lord of the Mountains (Aḍrintra). When they approach that Indra with *dhiṣā*—that is, with praise—and with *saraṇyān* (swift movements), then let that Indra come.

Let him be our carrier (*vahni*) amidst our *savaraṇas*—the obstructions related to enemies. Let him be the invoker (*hotṛ*) summoned by the sacrificer dwelling in the *pastyā*, the house; he who is difficult to overcome in his wrath (*duruṣas*), the great Indra who is magnified.
"May he come," [he says].
Truly, the vigor of the bull Bhāvya accompanies the one who praises him for the sake of booty;
when he is in the secret dwelling of the son of Uśij, he goes forth to the sight, to the refreshment, and to the exhilaration.

Evermore, when the strength of the bull Bhāvrya accompanies him for the sake of the singer’s prize; when he is in the secret lair of Auśija; when he is set forth for the journey and for exhilaration. 7.
Of Bhāvra: Bharvara is the creator of the world, Prajāpati;
his son is Bhāvra.

That this very strength (*śuṣma*)—belonging to that Indra, the showerer of desires (*vṛṣṇi*)—attends (*siṣakti*) and serves the sacrificer who offers praise and performs the hymn; that indeed is the truth. That this food (*anna*) of the sacrificer Auśija prevails within the secret place (*guhā*), in the heart which is the seat of secrecy, for the sake of bearing it; that indeed is the truth. That it prevails in the sacrificer’s dwelling (*gohe*) for the performance of ritual action; that indeed is the truth.
For the sake of going forth, for the attainment of desires, and for intoxication and joy—if that [power] therein is capable and effective, then it is true;
the meaning is that Indra’s strength always protects the sacrificer.
1. Ca-puruṣiḥ | 2.

Kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa lack "yajñagṛheṣu" | When he uncovers the wide spaces of the mountain, he quickens the swift currents of the waters with his surrounding flows. He finds [the way] in the hiding place of the tawny bull, when the wise ones lead him forth for the sake of strength. yat | varāṃsi | parvatasya | vṛṇve | paryaḥ | bhiḥ | jinve | apām | javā~si | vidat | gaurasya | gavayasya | gohe | yadi | vājāya | su'dhyaḥ | vahanti || 8 ||
When Indra opens wide the expanses—the doors—of the mountain, that is, the cloud;
when he quickens—that is, causes to swell—the impetuous currents of the waters with milk;

and when the pious sacrificers, performing auspicious deeds, bring [offerings] for the sake of strength—that is, they reach Indra—then he finds those two animals in the cave: the bull of the *gaura* (wild ox) and the *gavaya* (wild cow). Thus he obtains both those beasts.
The phrase "all that exists" (tatsarvaṃ sat) is to be connected with what precedes it.
In the *Abhyudayeṣṭi*, for Indra the Bestower (*pradātṛ*), the *yājyā* is "Blessed are your hands.
And it is set forth in the Sūtra: "Long is your arm, O Aśvattha; blessed are your hands, well-fashioned are your palms" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.13).
O Indra, your two hands are auspicious, your two hands are beautiful, and they are well-fashioned, performing noble deeds.
Moreover, your two hands are the bestowers of wealth upon the praising singer, the sacrificer.
O Indra, what is the nature of your station, your dwelling place?
Why indeed, for what reason, do you not gladden me?
Why, for what purpose, are you not joyful—that is, why do you not rejoice—to give us wealth? Why are you not glad?
The invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the oblation of the animal sacrifice to Indra Vṛtrahan is “evā vasvaḥ.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “evā vasva indraḥ samrāḍyadvāgavadatyavicetanāni” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

Thus indeed is Indra, the true sovereign lord of wealth; may he slay Vṛtra and create wide space for us as of old. O much-praised one, grant us wealth through your wisdom; may I partake of your divine protection. Thus indeed is Indra, the true sovereign lord of wealth; may he slay Vṛtra and create wide space for us as of old. O much-praised one, grant us wealth through your wisdom; may I partake of your divine protection. 10.

1. Thus being praised in this manner, he who is *ta-pa* (the scorcher), *u* (indeed), *pūraṇaḥ* (the fulfiller), *satyaḥ* (truthful), *satyavān* (possessing truth), *vasvaḥ* (of wealth), *sannāt* (from the abundance), the *īśvaraḥ* (lord), *vṛtraṃ* (Vṛtra)— the demon named Vṛtra— *hantā* (the slayer), the *hiṃsitā* (destroyer), *indraḥ* (Indra), *pūrve* (formerly) for the sake of *manuṣyāya* (the human), the sacrificer, *varivaḥ* (wealth)— *kaḥ* (he makes).
The meaning is "he gives.
O Puruhūta—O Indra, you who are praised by many sacrificers—with ṛtā (truth) as the means, that is, through the act of praise, do thou śagdhi (grant) rāyaḥ (wealth) to us, naḥ (to us).
Of that daivya (divine), belonging to the gods, bhavasah (existence/wealth) being given by thee...
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
May I partake here; may I enjoy it.

Now indeed, O Indra, now being praised, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like the two rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be successful.

Not so! O Indra, being praised and now lauded, swell nourishment for the singer as the rivers swell; for you, O Lord of Bay Steeds, a new prayer has been fashioned. Through our devotion, may we be successful and ever victorious. 11.
This has been explained previously.
In that [section], there are eleven hymns in the third anuvāka.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "yanna indraḥ," is the ṛṣi Vāmadeva's composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
The Anukramaṇikā states: "yannaḥ."
This second *saṃpāta-sūkta* occurs in the *maitrāvaruṇa-śastra* at the midday pressing on the first day of both the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* and the *abhilava-ṣaḍaha*.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*evā svāmindra yanna indraḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).
Whatever Indra does not enjoy, whatever he does not desire—that, even though it be powerful, the Great One shall make favorable for us.
Maghavan, who comes bearing the prayer, the hymn, the Soma, and the recitations as if carrying a stone with his might—[he is the one].

Whatever Indra has enjoyed of ours, and whatever he desires, that shall the great and mighty one grant us—whether it be prayer, hymn, the Soma, or songs of praise—to him who goes forth bearing the thunderbolt with his strength.
May Indra—great, abundant, and powerful—enjoy (*jujuṣe*) our oblation consisting of food and the like, and desire (*vaṣṭi*) that oblation and so forth.
The particle *cit* has the sense of "also.

May he likewise accept (*ā karati*) this fourfold set: the sacred formulation (*brahma*) characterized by the sacrificial cake and other offerings, the collection of hymns (*stoma*), the pressed Soma, and the recited praises (*ukthā*). May he take possession of all this.
Maghavan means "possessing wealth.
Here, the word *aśman* signifies the *vajra*. Indra, who comes—that is, approaches—bearing and wielding the *aśman*, the *vajra*, and endowed with *śavas*, or strength.
The connection with the preceding clause is: "May that Indra accept it."
1. Ta-bhajeyam; 2. Gha-ca-na-atha; 3. Gha-na-turīyeḍanuvāke; 4. Kha-pa-pha-bha-sūktam; 5. Kha-ga-gha-ca-na-bha-sa—‘atra’ is not present; 6. La—aśmaśabdaḥ.
The bull, the most manly, the fierce, the most powerful, impels the four-cornered bull-hide with his two arms.
For the sake of glory, he grasps the Paruṣṇī river as if it were wool, whose joints are for the sake of the flowing stream.

The bull, the bestower of abundance, the four-cornered one, hurling [the bolt], the fierce, most manly, and powerful one—with his two arms, for the sake of glory, wearing wool, he who [climbs] the Paruṣṇī river, whose joints are for the sake of the swift chariot. 2.

Indra—the showerer of desires (*vṛṣā kāmānām*), the one who causes rain by means of breaking through the clouds (*vṛṣandhim*), the wielder of the four-edged (*caturaśrim*) thunderbolt (*vajram*) endowed with four streams (*aśmibhiḥ*) which he hurls at his enemies with his two arms—being fierce (*ugraḥ*) with exalted power, the most heroic leader (*nṛtamaḥ*), and possessed of skillful action (*śacīvān*), approaches for the sake of glory (*śriye*) the river Paruṣṇī, which is like a mountain and provides a covering (*ūrṇām*), while serving it as his refuge.
He who, for the sake of friendship, joined together the severed sections of the river that had divided the lands.
The god who, being born as the most divine, [endowed] with great spoils and mighty splendors,
holding the eager thunderbolt in his arms, caused the earth to tremble by his very nature.
The god who, being most divine as he was born, with great spoils and mighty splendors, holding the yearning thunderbolt in his arms, caused the earth to tremble with his mind. 3.
The radiant god, the most divine, the greatest giver, who as Indra was being born and is ever-born, has become joined with great spoils—foods—and with great, brilliant powers;
this is the sense of the ellipsis.

That Indra, holding and wielding the desired thunderbolt in his two arms, caused both the sky—the world of heaven—and the earth—the world of the ground—to tremble violently by means of his impetuous strength.
All the embankments and the many ancient floods, the lofty heaven, and the earth were stirred at his birth;
the radiant mother brings forth the measure of the cow, and may the winds blow around him as he moves.

All the embankments, the many downward slopes, the lofty heaven, and the earth trembled at his birth; she brings the measure of the radiant cow. May the winds now favor our course around the ocean. 4.
All, all the obstructions—
by the word *rodhas*,
elevated regions are meant— and mountains; as well as many, ancient, steep descents.
The meaning is "and the oceans.

Both the sky (*dyauḥ*), that is, the celestial world, and the earth (*kṣāḥ*) trembled—meaning they shook and quaked—at the birth (*janiman*) of Indra, while this great (*ṛṣvāt*) Indra was being born. Furthermore, the powerful one... (*śubhryā*)... [was] strong.

1. [The variants] kha-ga-gha-ṇa read *sevamānaḥ*. 2. [The variants] kha-ga-gha-ṇa-bha lack the word ‘ca’. 3. [The variant] la reads *unnatapradeśaḥ* (elevated places). 4. [The variants] kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-bha-la-sa read *arejata akampata*; *indraḥ* refers to the sun who goes through the sky (*goḥ*); *mātarā* means the two mothers, heaven and earth, who act as parents;
and *ā* is used in the sense of ‘and’.
He brings from all sides; he sustains.
Like men, the winds—driven by Indra—roar and resound throughout the intermediate space.
All these great deeds of yours, O Indra, the mighty one, are to be proclaimed at all the Soma-pressings;
for when you, O hero, bold and daring, having shown your courage, did with your thunderbolt and power drive away the Dāsas.

These, O Indra, are your great deeds, mighty ones to be proclaimed at all soma-libations: that you, O hero, bold one, having boldly displayed your courage, did with your thunderbolt and might strike down the serpent. 5.

O Indra, those various deeds of yours, though great and abundant, quickly become truly mighty. O Indra, whenever you— possessing the means of binding— released these rivers that were being bound by their embankments, you set them free so that they might flow at will along a long and extended course.
O Indra, possessor of bay horses, O Lord of bay horses, at this very time of release, those well-known goddesses,
the shining sisters— the rivers—
praise you with their protections (avobhiḥ) provided by you; they are full of praise for you.
The meaning is that people praise Indra through such deeds as filling rivers and so forth.
The drop has flowed like a surging river; may the power of the one who exerts himself reach you through the *śamī* wood.
Toward us, for the one who blazes forth, there is the impulse of the swift ray, the vigor of the bull for you.

Like an ant, like a stalk, like wine, like a river—may the power of the one who exerts himself at the sacrificial work come toward us; may the swift flame of the glowing one come from the twin [fires], like the mighty ray of the bull. 8.
O Indra, that exhilarating stalk, the Soma, has been pressed—that is, it has been squeezed;
it has prevailed—so is the meaning.
"Na" is used here as a particle of inquiry.
Now let the flowing Soma, like a river, draw you toward himself.
Let the pacifying power and the act of praise belonging to the one who is shining and striving—the one who praises—draw toward us that which is directed at us.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Like the rein—that is, the tethering rope for a horse—[the reins] of the swift-moving, quick-going steed [are] for you, possessing great strength;
that is to say, they are firm. Just like that [rope].
Perform for us the highest and most excellent heroic deeds, O ever-conquering one, all thy victorious powers.
Make the Vritras easy for us to slay; strike down the increasing mortal who pursues us.

For us, O Victorious One, make our manly powers most excellent and supreme; grant us all conquering strengths. Subject to us those who are easy to slay, O Vṛtra-slayer; strike down and increase the power of the mortal who seeks to harm us. 9.
O victorious Indra, you who are ever-enduring, grant unto us those most excellent, most abundant, most preeminent, and most glorious powers that overcome enemies;
O Indra, subdue for us our adversaries, making them easy to slay and bringing them under our control.
Furthermore, destroy—that is, annihilate—the weapon, the means of slaughter belonging to the mortal enemy who seeks to harm.
O Indra, listen to us; grant us manifold spoils of war.
Send forth to us all abundant blessings; O Maghavan, be a generous giver of cattle to us.
Hear us well, O Indra! Bestow upon us manifold spoils of war. Send to us all the fulfillments of our prayers. O Maghavan, be a true giver of cattle to us. 10.
1. *pa-pha* are being obstructed; 2. *na-la-sa-enāḥ*; 3. *na* was not envious; 4. *ta-* [belonging] to one whose nature is death.
O Indra, you—listen very well (*su*) to our (*asmākam*) own (*ita*) hymns of praise (*stutīḥ*).
Likewise, O Indra, bestow (*upa māhi*) upon us various (*citrān*) desirable (*cayanīyāni*) strengths (*vājān*), that is, foods (*annāni*).
Furthermore, O impeller, send forth all our inspired thoughts;
and moreover, O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, O Śakra, be well-disposed toward us as a giver of cattle.

Now indeed, O Indra, now being praised, swell for the sake of nourishment for the singer, as you have led us on. A new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds; through this inspired thought, may we be ever victorious charioteers.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; you have made it swell. A new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our inspired thought, may we be chariot-borne victors, ever-conquering. 11.
These have been explained previously.
The second hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “*kathā mahām*,” is the work of Vāmadeva; it is composed in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to Indra.
Regarding the verse “*ṛtasya hi*,” some hold that Indra is the deity here, while others maintain that the deity is *Ṛta*.
Thus it has been cataloged: “*kathā upanyāstindra ṛtadevyo vā*” (Is Indra the deity, or are the deities *Ṛta*?).

On the first day of the ten-night *daśarātra* sacrifice, during the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) at the *maitrāvaruṇa-śastra* of the *ābhiplavika* day, this third *saṃpāta-sūkta* takes the place of the *ahīna-sūkta*. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "How [is] Indra, the great, the sole breaker of forts? (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.5). This [sūkta] is also used in the *niṣkevalya* chant of the *mahāvrata*.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka by Śaunaka: “The hymn ‘How has the Hotṛ grown great? is the *saṃpāta*” (AiĀ 5.2.2).
How has the great Hotṛ grown strong, enjoying the sacrifice and the heights of Soma?
Drinking, urging himself on, and delighting in the plant, the lofty one has waxed mighty for the sake of shining wealth.

The story: He has grown great for whom? Delighting in the sacrifice of the Hotṛ, rising up, drinking the Soma, desiring it, enjoying the plant—lofty and pure, he has waxed strong for the sake of wealth. 1.
How, in what manner, and by what means could one increase Indra—who is already great and further augmented by his virtues?
The ellipsis implies: "our inspired hymn of praise. The sense is that this is because of the extreme greatness of his majesty.

That very Indra, being pleased (*juṣāṇaḥ*) with the sacrifice (*yajñam*)—the ritual performance—of some patron (*hotuḥ*), that is, the sacrificer who accomplishes the oblation (*homaniṣpādaka*), should approach it; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). An implied verb (*adhyāhāraḥ*) must be supplied because of the presence of the prefix (*upasarga*). Furthermore, drinking the Soma—the food characterized by Soma—which is "uplifted" (*ūdhah*), meaning highly increased or abundant, and tasting it, desiring (*uśānaḥ*) that very food, and enjoying (*juṣamāṇaḥ*) it, the great (*ṛṣvaḥ*) Indra [approaches] for the sake of radiant wealth (*śucate dhanāya*), such as gold and the like.
He carries—that is, he brings—the wealth characterized as described above to bestow it upon which sacrificer;
he holds within his belly even the food that has been drunk.
By these two statements, Indra’s inconceivable nature is made manifest.

1. kha-ga-ca-ṇa: our own praise alone; 2. kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha: external; 3. na-sa: ‘you’ is not present; 4. kha-ga-ca-ṇa: let it be determined; 5. kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa: for the sake of the characteristic of gold; ta: for the sake of the characteristic of the object of gold. Ṛgveda 2.76: Who has attained his shared feast? Who [attains] his common portion through his favors? Whose wondrous [deed] is known? When will he become the strengthener of the sacrifice of him who exerts himself?

Who has attained his shared banquet? Who has obtained it together with [his] gracious favors? Who has perceived what of him? What of him is wondrous? Through what aid will he become the strengthener of the one who exerts himself in sacrifice? 2.

Who is that man, a hero—meaning one who acts heroically toward hymns or enemies—who attains this *sadhamāda* belonging to this Indra? A *sadhamāda* is a battle, so called because they rejoice together (*saha mādhanti*) therein; or it refers to the drinking of Soma together. Who reaches that?
And who, through the *sumatibhiḥ*—the auspicious, gracious thoughts—of this Indra, attains an equal share?
Or when (*kad*) is his wonderful (*citram*), praiseworthy wealth (*dhanam*) perceived (*cikite*)?
The meaning is that no one knows the time of its bestowal.

When, or at what time, will the sacrifice of the one who praises, the one who recites the *yajus*, become for the increase—the strengthening—of the sacrificer, through your aid, that is, through your protection? May it be so.
How does Indra hear the oblation being poured? How does he, the knower of wealth, hear it? What are his ancient forms and manifestations? And how do they call him the fulfiller for the singer?
How does he hear? Indra hears the oblation being offered. How, while hearing, does he know his protections? What are his many maternal favors? And how do they call him a fulfiller for the singer? 3.
How, indeed, does Indra, who is endowed with supreme lordship, hear the singer who calls out to him?
And how does he know—while listening to the hymns—the protections belonging to this singer?
What, indeed, are his ancient gifts, those offerings belonging to Indra? (The sense is: "What [gifts] are there?"—this is the ellipsis.
How indeed do they speak of this Indra, the fulfiller who satisfies the desires belonging to the singer, the one who praises him?
May he who is diligent and meditating upon his wealth find it, even though he is oppressed;
may the god, the creator of the worlds, come to us through the truths, and may he, the lover of sacrifice, accept our homage.

How? Without hindrance; striving; may he reach his wealth, meditating upon it. May the god become one who knows my sacred rites; having gone toward them with reverence, may he take pleasure in them. 4.

How can the sacrificer—who is *sabādhaḥ* (oppressed) by rivals, *pīḍāsahitaḥ* (beset with affliction), *śaśamānaḥ* (exerting himself) in offering praise directed toward Indra, and *dīdhyānaḥ* (shining) through his ritual acts—attain *asya draviṇam* (his wealth), such as cattle and other riches? How indeed shall he reach it? (1. kha-ga-ṇa-bha omit 'bā'; 2.
kha-ga-gha-ṇa-bha read "of him who praises"; 3. kha-ga-gha-ṇa omit 'ba'; 4. kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-sa read "various"; 5. kha-ga-ṇa-bha omit 'ca'; he approaches).

Indra, having seized the vessel marked with the *habilakṣaṇa* sign, when he (*yat*) sought to serve me (*abhijujoṣat*), then the radiant god Indra became (*bhuvat*) the most excellent knower (*navedāḥ*) of my truthful hymns (*ṛtānām*).
Here, the particle *na-* situated within the word expresses excellence.
How could the god have relished the friendship of a mortal at the dawning of this beautiful dawn?
How, and in what manner, has the god taken pleasure in the friendship of mortals at the dawning of this dawn?

How, and in what manner, does his friendship extend to those friends who strive for a well-yoked desire toward him? 5. Kathā | kat | asyāḥ | uṣasaḥ | vi-uṣṭau | devaḥ | martasya | sakhyam | jujoṣa | kathā | kat | asya | sakhyam | sakhibhyaḥ | ye | asmin | kāmam | su-yujam | tatasre || 5 ||

O resplendent Indra, at the dawning of this Uṣas, at break of day, how, in what manner, and when will you take pleasure in—the friendship, that is, the service of a friend—belonging to a mortal, a human being who praises you?
Those singers who are well-yoked to this Indra...

This Indra, desiring to slay—that is, wishing to kill—the Rākṣasī who is *duhaṃ* (malevolent), *dhvarasam* (injurious), and *anindrām* (one who does not acknowledge Indra), sharpens exceedingly (*tetike*) his already sharp (*tigmāni*) weapons (*anīkāni*) for the purpose of striking her down (*tujase*). On those very Dawns (*upasaḥ*) characterized by that [destruction], even our debts (*ṛṇā cit*) oppress us;
Indra, the fierce one (*ugraḥ*) with upraised power, is the destroyer of that debt (*ṛṇayāḥ*).
The root *yati* has the sense of "killing.
Being "unknown" (*dūre ajñātāḥ*), that is, unexperienced, he "oppressed" (*babādhe*), meaning he afflicted them.

In the *Ṛtapeya* one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), before the insertion of the *nivid* in both the *Marutvatīya* and *Nikēvalya* recitations, two verses beginning with "For of Truth" (*ṛtasya hi*) are to be recited in sequence.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The hymn beginning with 'For of Truth are many boons' (*ṛtasya hi śurudhaḥ santi pūrvīḥ*) is the introductory hymn. [And further: "Those who go toward Truth, they indeed reach Truth; the swift ones of Truth are to be seized."
For the sake of Truth, the broad, vast, and deep Earth; for the sake of Truth, the two supreme milch-cows yield their milk.

Truth! He who goes toward these [worlds] wins truth alone. The swift one, seeking the splendor of Truth, is worthy of being grasped. For the sake of Truth, the two vast, deep, and wide worlds; for the sake of Truth, the two supreme milch-cows yield their milk. 10.

Moving forward, restraining [the enemy], and subduing him with hymns of praise, the praiser extols—that is, honors—the very one who encompasses the gods of Truth (*ṛtadeva*). He swiftly attains the power of that one who encompasses the gods of Truth;
"v" is used here as a particle of conjunction.
And he becomes desirous of water.

For the sake of the one who has encompassed the vast, extensive, deep, and unfathomable Earth and Heaven—the two worlds—for the sake of the one whose god is *Ṛta*, there are the two milch-cows, the gratifying ones;
for the sake of that very one whose god is *Ṛta*, they yield their milk in the supreme, most excellent [place]. The two worlds, Heaven and Earth, perform the act of milking.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being extolled, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our devotion, may we be skillful and ever victorious.

Now, O Indra, being praised and now being glorified, cause nourishment to swell for the singer like rivers; for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds, a new prayer has been fashioned. Through our devotion, may we be ever victorious and successful.
This has been explained previously.
The third hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “kā sustutiḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva and is addressed to Indra.
The tenth verse is an Anuṣṭubh, while the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs.
Thus, the Anukramaṇikā states: “kā sustutiḥ; the last [verse] is an Anuṣṭubh.”
The application is inferential.
What excellent praise shall turn Indra, the son of Śarva, toward us with his bounty?
For that hero, as the lord of cattle, bestows riches upon the singer; he is our protector, O people.

Who? A beautiful hymn. To Śarva’s son, Indra, let us turn him hitherward for the sake of bounty; for that hero is a giver of riches to the singer. He is the lord of cattle; may he remove our adversaries, O people! 1.

What kind of excellent praise (*sustuti*) could turn Indra— the son of Śarva, the son of Bala (meaning "the exceedingly strong one"), who is directed toward us (*vācīna*)— toward us for the sake of great wealth (*rādhase*), so that he might bestow wealth upon us? May he turn [toward us].

He is the one who brings forth people—the people who sacrifice; he is the hero, the valiant one; he is the lord of cattle, the protector of wealth from behind. That Indra bestows the riches belonging to the obstructing enemies upon us, his praisers who sing his praises; for he is indeed the giver to us.

1. To the god Kha-ga-ca-ṇa; 2. To the god Kha-ga-ca-ṇa. He is to be invoked in the slaying of Vṛtra; he is to be praised; he, Indra, is well-praised and true in his bounty. May that Maghavan bestow wide space upon the mortal who offers prayers and presses the Soma at his coming. He is to be invoked in the slaying of Vṛtra; he is to be praised; he, Indra, is well-praised and true in his bounty. May that Maghavan bestow wide space upon the mortal who offers prayers and presses the Soma at his coming.
That Indra, when the slaying of Vṛtras—that is, the striking down of enemies—has become the occasion, is to be invoked (*havya*) in the journey of battle;
that Indra is to be praised (*īḍya*);
and that Indra, being well-praised, becomes one whose wealth is true (*satyarādhāḥ*), possessing real riches to bestow upon the sacrificers.

Maghavan, the possessor of wealth, is that Indra; he bestows *varivas*—for *varivas* is a name for wealth—upon the mortal man, the sacrificer who presses the Soma, who desires the prayer and seeks praise.
