He grants it from all sides.

To him alone do the men hasten in the encounter; desiring to release themselves, they make him their protector, when both sides have come together in mutual conflict for the winning of sons and grandsons. To him alone do the men hasten in the encounter; desiring to release themselves, they make him their protector, when both sides have come together in mutual conflict for the winning of sons and grandsons.
Men, the leaders among humans, in the encounter of battle, call out variously to that very Indra alone.
Desiring to cast away their own bodies, exhausting themselves through austerity, the sacrificers make him, Indra, their protector, indeed making him their savior.

When, at whatever time, both parties—both the sacrificers and the chanters—having come together with one another, approach *Indra*, the giver who performs the act of giving; then, at that moment, when the acquisition (*sāti*) of offspring (*toka*), sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons serves as the cause, the men of both kinds, being human beings, make that very Indra their protector (*trātṛ*). This is the connection.

The people strive for mental power in the contest, O fierce one; seeking booty, they exert themselves against one another in the struggle for waters. When the clans have come together in conflict, then some among them, even in the encounter, call upon you as their Indra. kratuyanti kṣitayo yoga ugrāśuṣāṇāso mitho arṇasātau | saṃ yadviśo'rvavṛtranta yuṣmā ādime indrayante abhīke || 4 || The people strive for mental power in the contest, O fierce one; seeking booty, they exert themselves against one another in the struggle for waters. When the clans have come together in conflict, then some among them, even in the encounter, call upon you as their Indra.
He is the fierce one, the lord of overwhelming strength. The *kṣitayas*— meaning human beings— spreading abroad (*āśuṣāṇāsaḥ*),
when there is a mutual connection or union for the sake of obtaining water for the successful harvest of grain and other fruits (*arṇasātau*), desire *kratūn*, that is, ritual acts.
Whenever you shall fight against the clans, that is, the subjects, in close combat, [they] follow [you];
1. *kha* reads "anugacchanti"; *pa* reads "upāgacchanti". 2. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha* do not contain the word "sati".
[Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 4, Sūkta 24] The third Aṣṭaka, verse 607.
*Abhīka* is a name for battle.
*Sam adhvagrantha*: they come together; they meet one another. *Ādit*: at that very moment, *neme*: some fortunate warriors *indrayante*: they desire Indra in the battle.

Let the offering of the oblation set the senses ablaze; let the cooked rice and the sacrificial cake be presented. Let Soma swell with the waters of the cow; let him take pleasure in the bull for the sacrifice.

From him alone comes my power; from him they offer the sacrifice. From him alone may the cooked oblation exceed the sacrificial cake. From him alone may Soma flow forth for those who lack cattle. From him alone has he taken pleasure in the bull to be sacrificed.

At that very time, during the moment of battle, these other warriors indeed worship— that is, they honor— the powerful Indra, the possessor of sense-faculties (*indriya*). Immediately thereafter, on this very day, whatever sacrificer should press— that is, should perform the extraction of— *soma*, the food characterized by supreme excellence, for Indra, the god endowed with the highest purpose.
Likewise, he who shall cook the *paktyas*—the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and other such items—and perform the act of cooking;
and furthermore, he who [cooks] the *dhānās*—the barley grains suitable for roasting.
Here, the word *dhānā*, which denotes roasted barley, indicates barley in general.
He should roast; he should perform the act of roasting.

Indra, desiring the hymns (*ucathāni*)—the praises—of the yearning sacrificer who desires to offer praise, and being well-disposed toward them, bestows and maintains upon that sacrificer *śuṣmam*, a virile strength capable of raining down desires.

When the impetuous one, having discerned the conflict, rushed toward the long course of the race; when the noble one, with the Soma-pressers, sharpened the bull for the wife within the dwelling. When the impetuous one, having discerned the conflict, rushed toward the long course of the race; when the noble one, with the Soma-pressers, sharpened the bull for the wife within the dwelling.
When Indra, the destroyer of enemies (*ṛghāvā*), perceives—that is, specifically recognizes—the powerful mortal enemy as one to be overcome;

when the Lord (*arya*) Indra surveys the long, extensive battle (*āji*); then his wife, in the *durona*—the sacrificial hall—[is served] by those who press the Soma, with offerings that press the Soma, [and thus] sharpened—that is, made keen.
The meaning is: [she serves him] so that he becomes full of vigor through the drinking of Soma.
He calls out toward Indra, the showerer of desires; he utters a cry, he invokes him.

With the greater [portion] he pursued the lesser; though unsold, I desired to win it back again. He did not surpass the lesser with the greater; the skillful ones milk out the lowly sound. With the greater [portion] he pursued the lesser; though unsold, I desired to win it back again. He did not surpass the lesser with the greater; the skillful ones milk out the lowly sound.

In this context, certain verses are recited by the ancient teachers who are experts in the tradition (*saṃpradāya*) regarding the *Ṛgveda*. Those very [verses] are written here: 1. “He who accepts a price for a commodity that is greater [than its value], having gone back to the buyer, says: ‘This was not sold by me [at such a price]. 2. Thus, he desires the earth [as his reward] again to fulfill the price; yet that seller would not recover the price through a greater amount. 3. When one has previously sold [something], one does not obtain a better [price] if it is deficient; it should remain exactly as agreed upon at the time, and not otherwise. 4. If an agreement had been made that “this is indeed a sale,” then, for the sake of the price, a decision should have been reached after due deliberation. 5. “If such an agreement had been made then, one would have recovered the price. Thinking thus, “Therefore, an agreement must first be made by me in this matter,” Vāmadeva, having subdued Śakra with a great hymn of praise, was selling [him].
1. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, and Na, the word "somaṃ" is absent.
2. In manuscript Ta, "ṛghāvān" means "one who is violent.
3. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, and Ṇa, the reading is "asya."
4. Pha was here.
5. In the past, Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, and Sa were sold.
6. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, and Bha are not sellers.

7. *ta-na-bha-sa* for the statement (*vaktuṃ*); *la-kre-tuḥ*. 8. *kha-ga-ṇa-ta-na-bha-sa* for the origin (*kutaḥ*). 9. For the *kha-ṇa* [meter], there is certainty (*niścayaḥ*) without even deliberating upon this *āmetā*; for the *ga-ca* [meter], there is determination (*viniścayaḥ*) without deliberating upon this *āmetā*; for the *na-bha-sa* [meter], there is resolution (*nirṇayaḥ*) without even deliberating upon this *āmetā*.
10. It does not proceed from *la*.
11. One should reflect that it is not the time of *ṇa*, *ta*, or *bha*. This wheel is the *samaya*; it is said, "Who is this? and "What is this?"
And therefore, having observed that this meaning is for the most part the same as "he clothed," this point is established:
someone, while selling with a greater amount of goods, obtained (*acarat*)— that is, acquired— a smaller (*kanīyaḥ*), more meager (*alpataraṃ*) cloth (*vastaṃ*), meaning value, wealth, or price.
Furthermore, if the seller goes back to the buyer and says, "This object was not sold by me," and desires the completion of the price, he must pay the penalty.
The first person is used in place of the third person by way of transposition.
That seller does not overcharge for a smaller or lesser price with greater wealth; rather, he leaves the buyer empty-handed—that is, the buyer receives nothing more than expected.
Both the distressed and the incapable, as well as the skillful and the capable, milk the speech (vāṇam)—that is, they obtain exactly what was promised at the time of purchase.

Who will buy this Indra of mine for ten milch-cows? When he has struck down the Vṛtras, then let him give him back to me. 10 Who? This one. For ten. From me. Indra. Buys. With milch-cows. When. The Vṛtras. He shall strike down. Then. Him. To me. Again. Let him give. 10
Who buys—makes a purchase of—this Indra, who is my own and belongs to me, with the "milch-cows," that is, with the ten life-sustaining hymns numbering ten?
At that time, O buyers, this agreement is made among you:
when this Indra shall strike down (*jaṅghanat*) your enemies, the Vṛtras, then immediately thereafter, he shall give him back—that Indra—to me again.

Now indeed, O Indra, being praised and glorified, swell with nourishment for the singer like rivers; a new prayer has been fashioned for you, O Lord of the Bay Steeds. Through our inspired thought, may we be masters of chariots and ever victorious. 11. Now! Praised! O Indra! Now! Being glorified! Nourishment! For the singer! Like rivers! Swell! A new prayer! For you! O Lord of the Bay Steeds! Through inspired thought! May we be! Masters of chariots! Ever victorious! 11.
This has been explained previously.
The hymn beginning with “ko atha” is the fourth hymn; it consists of eight verses, is composed by Vāmadeva, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to Indra.
Thus it is cataloged: “‘ko atha,’ [consisting of] eight [verses].

In the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), on the fourth day, during the increase of the Stoma at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), this hymn is to be inserted after the *ārambhaṇīyā* verse in the Maitrāvaruṇa’s *śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "When the Stoma is increasing, who indeed is the other? (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.12).

Who today, being manly and desiring the gods, longing for it, has taken pleasure in the friendship of Indra? Or who, having pressed the Soma, praises him with great, final aid when the fire is kindled? 1 Who? Today? Manly? Desiring the gods? Longing? Has taken pleasure in the friendship of Indra? Or who? With great? For final aid? When the fire is kindled? Having pressed the Soma? Praises? 1
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and va are mentioned; [the syllable] la and va are not [mentioned].
2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, pa, pha, bha, and sa, the word "with praises" (stutibhiḥ) is absent.
(Ṛgveda 2.77)
On this day, what manly sacrificer—beneficial to humanity, desiring the gods, and longing for them—enjoys the intoxicating friendship of Indra?
Furthermore, which sacrificer, having pressed the Soma, praises Indra with great praise for the sake of great and supreme protection when the fire is kindled and blazing?

Who has bowed down with splendor, O Soma-loving noble one? Who becomes mindful, or who clothes himself in oxen? Who desires the alliance of Indra, who his friendship, who his brotherhood? And who seeks the protection of the Seer? (2) Who? Has bowed down? With splendor? O Soma-loving noble one? Mindful? Or? Becomes? He clothes himself? In oxen? Who? Of Indra? The alliance? Who? Friendship? Who? Brotherhood? Desires? For the Seer? Who? For protection? (2)
Which sacrificer bows down—that is, humbles himself—before the Soma-loving Indra with speech, that is, with praise?
Or who becomes "mindful" of Indra—that is, desirous of praising him?
And who clothes himself in the cattle, the cows bestowed by Indra?
The meaning is "he upholds.
Who desires *yujyam*, that is, assistance from Indra?
Who desires *sakhitvam*, friendship; who desires *bhrātram*, brotherhood—that is, the state of being a brother?
For the seer (kavi), for Indra who possesses transcendent vision, for his protection (ūtī) and for his satisfaction (ūtaye)—who [is there]?
The word "becomes" (bhavati) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Who today chooses the protection of the gods? Who prays for light from the Ādityas and Aditi? Whose pressed soma-stalk do the Aśvins, Indra, and Agni drink with their minds, finding it pleasing? Who? Of the gods. Protection. Today. Chooses? Who? The Ādityas. Aditi. Light. Prays for? Whose? The Aśvins. Indra. Agni. Of the pressed. Soma-stalk. Drink. With the mind. Finding it pleasing. 3.
Now, on this day, who among the sacrificers seeks—that is, prays for—the protection (*avaḥ*) of the radiant gods (*devānām*), Indra and the others?
Who invokes—that is, supplicates—the Āditya gods, Aditi the mother of the gods, light, and water?
And may the Aśvins, the two presiding deities, Indra, and Agni, being pleased by our mental hymns of praise, grant us freedom from distress (*avivenam*).
The meaning is "according to one's desire.
It refers to the *aṃśu*, that is, the Soma, which has been pressed (*sutasya*) and belongs to the sacrificer (*yajamānasya*).
The sense is "the Soma."
They drink; they perform the act of drinking.

1. *kha-pa-pha-bha-kraḥ* [is] *naryaḥ*. 2. *la-manuṣyaḥ* [is] beneficial (*hitah*) to the center (*nabhyo*). 3. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-na-pa-pha-bha-sa-* [is] for the purpose of offering (*arpaṇāya*). 4. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-kaḥ*: "Who maintains friendship (*sakhitvam*), who maintains brotherhood (*bhrātṛtvam*)?"—this is the meaning. Who desires (*vaṣṭi*) the alliance (*yujyam*) or assistance of Indra? Who [desires it] for the sage (*kavaye*)? 5. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-* [is] "the gods" (*devān nānbhi*). 6. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-* [and] "ca" does not exist. 7. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-* [is] "gods" (*devāṃ*). 8. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-* [is] "Soma" (*somam*).

Therefore, may Agni Bharata grant him protection; may he long behold the rising sun—he who says, "Let us press the Soma for Indra," for the manly hero, the most heroic among men. 4. To him, Agni Bharata shall grant protection; may he long behold the rising sun—he who says, "Let us press the Soma for Indra," for the manly hero, the most heroic among men. 4.
Bhārata: Agni is the bearer of the oblation (*havis*).
According to the Vājasaneyaka, "Having become the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he sustains the creatures; thus he is Bhārata.
May that Agni grant (*yacchet*) protection (*śarma*), that is, happiness, to this sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Furthermore, this fire might behold— that is, see— the sun for a long time (*v jyok*) as it rises while it is still shining;
that sacrificer (*yajamāna*) who says, "I shall press [the Soma] for Indra," meaning he declares, "I will perform the Soma-pressing for the sake of Indra"—
for what kind of Indra?
To the one who is the eye for men, the friend of men, the benefactor of men, and the most excellent leader among leaders of men.

Neither many nor few overcome him; Aditi shall grant him wide protection. Dear is the doer of good, dear is the one who honors Indra, dear is the one who offers well, and dear is he who possesses Soma. They do not conquer him, neither the many nor the few; Aditi shall bestow upon him wide shelter. Dear is the well-doer, dear is the one mindful of Indra, dear is the one who protects well, and dear is he who has offered Soma.
Whether they be few or many, even numerous enemy folk shall not overcome—that is, shall not harm—that sacrificer.
"To him who says, 'Let us press [the Soma] for Indra,'" thus it is connected with the preceding.
May Aditi, the mother of Indra, grant (*yaṃsat*) to that sacrificer wide (*uru*) protection (*śarma*), that is, happiness.
Furthermore, for Indra, the *sukṛt*—the sacrificer who performs auspicious sacrifices and other rites—becomes dear (*priya*) to him.
The *manāyuḥ*—one who desires praise directed toward Indra—also becomes dear to this Indra.
And the *suprāvīḥ*—the sacrificer who is a good protector or one who approaches [Indra] well—becomes dear to this Indra.
The Soma-offerer who possesses Soma becomes dear to Indra, the more excellent one.

This hero, the conqueror of the swift, makes the cooked offering his own exclusive possession through all [his powers]. Indra is no kinsman, no friend, and no relative to one who is ill-disposed; he strikes down those who speak evil words. *suprāvyaḥ* (well-protecting), *prāśuṣāṭ* (conqueror of the swift), *eṣaḥ* (this one), *vīraḥ* (hero), *suvaraiḥ* (with all [powers]), *paktim* (the cooked offering), *kṛṇute* (makes), *kevalā* (exclusive/own), *indraḥ* (Indra). *na* (not), *asuveḥ* (to the ill-disposed), *āpiḥ* (kinsman), *na* (not), *sakhā* (friend), *na* (not), *jāmiḥ* (relative), *duḥprāvyaḥ* (ill-protecting), *avahat* (he strikes down), *it* (indeed), *avācaḥ* (those who speak evil).
1. The phrase "among leaders" (*nāyakānāṃ madhye*) is absent in manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, and Bha.

2. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pha, and Bha, the reading is *dakṣāḥ*; in Gha, Na, Pa, and Sa, it is *lakṣyāḥ*. 3. The phrase "many are not" (*bahavo na*) is absent in manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, and Ṇa.
4. [The letters] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, sa, and śa are born from enemies.
5. Ta is for him (tasmai). 6. Kha, ta, pa, and pha belong to the auspicious path and so forth.
7. The sacrificer is joined with the mouth, the throat, and the mind; [the syllables] gha, na, ṇa, bha, and ma do not exist as "objects of Indra.
8. With the oblations (ta, la), he is one who thoroughly satisfies.

He is the hero, the courageous one, who swiftly and preeminently overcomes his enemies. This Indra is easily approached by the one who approaches him with oblations, or by the one who thoroughly satisfies him; for the sake of the *sutvan*, the pressing sacrificer, he makes for himself a *pakti*—that is, a nourishment that is exclusive and unique.
Furthermore, Indra does not become the "āpiḥ" (pervader or kinsman) of the "asukheḥ" (unhappy), that is, the non-sacrificer;
Indra does not become the "sakhā" (friend) of the non-sacrificer; nor does he become the "jāmiḥ" (relative or kinsman).
Moreover, for a man who is difficult to approach and devoid of praise, even the act of speaking to him becomes a source of injury.
Indra, the drinker of the pressed juice, does not associate with the stingy hand that offers no libation;
he seizes its wealth and strikes it down. He belongs exclusively to the one who presses and the one who cooks.

Indra does not form an alliance with the one who possesses no wealth, with the one who has no cattle, nor with the one who presses no soma, though he himself drinks the pressed juice. He seizes his property and strikes him down; he belongs exclusively to the one who presses the soma and to the one who cooks the offering. 7.
Drinking the pressed Soma, Indra does not approve of—does not praise—the friendship with the wealthy Paṇi, the greedy merchant who does not press the Soma and does not sacrifice;
that is to say, he does not consent to it.
Furthermore, he draws out—that is, he seizes away—the useless wealth, whether material riches or knowledge, of this non-sacrificer.
He strikes and destroys;

moreover, he manifests himself exclusively—that is, uniquely—not shared with others, for the sake of the one who presses the Soma, and for the sacrificer who cooks the oblations. He prevails and becomes manifest.
Those who are beyond, those who are below, and those who are in the middle— those going forth, those resting, those dwelling in peace, and those fighting— all men, seeking booty, invoke Indra.

Those beyond, those below, and those in the middle call upon Indra; those setting out, those resting, and those dwelling at home call upon Indra; both those fighting and those at peace, men seeking booty, invoke Indra. 8.
The superior and the inferior people invoke Indra;
the middling ones also invoke Indra alone;
those going forth for the sake of accomplishing their tasks invoke Indra alone.
Having settled and taken up residence, they invoke Indra alone;
the people dwelling in their homes call upon Indra alone;
and moreover, even those fighting and waging war invoke Indra alone for the sake of victory.
Seeking booty—that is, desiring to obtain booty—the leaders, men, invoke Indra alone.

The fifth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “*Ahaṃ manuḥ*,” is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Vāmadeva. Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*Ahaṃ manuḥ*: [it consists of] seven [verses]; with three [verses], the seer praised himself as Indra—or Indra praised himself; the last nine are either praises of the falcon. 1. *La*: “*Sakhā*” means a companion or ally. 2. *Ca*: The word “*janāḥ*” (people) is not present. 3. *Ca-Pha*: “*Indrameva*” (Indra alone). 4. *Kha-Ga-Ṇa-Na-Bha*: “*Janāḥ jayārtham*” (people for the sake of victory). 5. *Ca*: “*Udyogino janāḥ jayārthaṃ ca*” (and industrious people for the sake of victory).
In this context, Vāmadeva praised himself as being of the nature of Indra through these three verses beginning with "I am Manu";
or alternatively,
Indra himself praised himself.
Therefore, according to the view that this is a verse of Vāmadeva, the seer (ṛṣi) is Vāmadeva and the deity (devatā) is Indra;
according to the view that it is a verse of Indra, the seer is Indra and the deity is the Supreme Self (paramātman).
The meter (chandaḥ) is Triṣṭubh.
Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi) of the remaining verses.
In these remaining verses and the *taratsamandī* hymn, Brahman is praised in the form of Suparṇa;
therefore, their deity is the Supreme Brahman.
This hymn is [recited] at the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) during the *marutvatīya* litany in the *Iyena* one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*).
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "With the *Iyena* and *Ājira*, one should sacrifice with these [verses]: 'I am Manu, I am now the being... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.7).
I was Manu and I was Sūrya; I am the seer Kakṣīvat, the inspired singer. I brought Kutsa, the son of Archanānas, low; I am the sage Uśanas—behold me!
I was Manu; and I was the Sun. I am Kakṣīvat, the seer and the inspired singer.
Furthermore, I, crying out, led the waters—that is, the flowing streams—to every region.
O gods, beginning with Vahni, you follow my intention—that is, my resolve—with reverence.
Rejoicing, I shattered the ninety-nine fortresses of Śambara all at once;
the hundredth stronghold I gave away in its entirety when I protected Divodāsa, the son of Tṛkṣi.
I, rejoicing, have shattered the ninety-nine strongholds of Śambara all at once, and the hundredth dwelling as well, when I protected Divodāsa Atithigva in his total success.
Whether it was I or Vāmadeva, Indra, exhilarated and rejoicing in Soma, I simultaneously shattered the ninety-nine cities belonging to Śambara—
the Asura of that name— and I made the hundredth city, which was fit for habitation, an entry-point for Divodāsa.
In every way, at every sacrifice, when we protected Atithigva—the one who goes to the guests—and the royal seer named Divodāsa, then we shattered the fortresses;
this is the connection with what precedes.
May that hero prevail over the Maruts, and may the falcon prevail over the falcons through his swiftness,
when the fair-winged one, by his own inherent power, brought the god-pleasing oblation to Manu without wheels.

May he be foremost among the Maruts, O Maruts; may the falcon be foremost among the falcons for his swiftness, since that fair-winged one, by his own inherent power, brought the god-loved oblation to Manu without wheels. 4.
Now, the falcon (*śyena*) is praised with these [verses] beginning with this one:

O *marutaḥ*—O birds swift as the Maruts—that well-known bird called the falcon (*śyena*) shall indeed be superior in strength to all other birds, [that is,] to you. Furthermore, among the birds of his own kind whose flight is praiseworthy, let the falcon, being swift-flying and rapid-moving, be preeminent over them.

When the well-winged falcon, with his beautiful flight, brought—the word *svadhā* here signifying a chariot, as seen in such passages as “moving with a wheelless *svadhā*” (Ṛgveda 10.27.19)—the oblation characterized by Soma, which is dear to the gods (*devajuṣṭa*) and served by the gods, from the celestial realm to Manu Prajāpati; that is, he carried it away.

1. *ta-la-prairayam*. 2. The hundredth [verse] is to be recited with the syllables *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-ta-na-sa*. 3. [The name] *divodāsa* is absent from *kha-ga-gha-ṇa-la*. 4. *na-sa-yadāvam*. 5. The phrase “*puro vyairam*” is absent from *kha-ga-gha-ṇa-ta-na-sa*. 6. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-la-sa*: “May he be pre-eminent through strength (*balena*)”; let it be so. 7. The word “*manave*” is absent from *na-la-sa*. 8. The word “*prajāpataye*” is absent from *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-la-sa*. 9. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-pha-sa*: expressive of *bhaja*; *la-ra-sa*: expressive of *rasa*.
When Bharadvāja had ceased trembling, the mind-swift arrow was released from the path;
it sped swiftly with the honeyed Soma, and here the falcon won glory.
Bharadvāja: If, trembling, he was released from there by a wide path swift as thought, he sped with the Soma of honey; and here the falcon has won renown. 5.
When the bird, the falcon, from yonder world of heaven, flying about in agitation and terrifying the guardians of Soma, bore it away— that is,
seized the Soma— then he was released,
having been set loose along the wide path of the intermediate space, possessing a speed like that of thought.
Accompanied by the Soma, consisting of Soma, and by honey—that is, food—he went quickly; he departed swiftly.
Moreover, in this world, the falcon, the fair-winged bird, obtained fame—the glory resulting from the seizing of the Soma.
When there was the exhilaration of Soma, Indra— the straight-moving, unconfused, and wise one— abandoned (ajahāt), that is, struck down, the foolish enemies (arātīḥ).
The word *anṛāti* is neuter in gender.
The sixth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "garbhaṃ nu," is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
By this [meter], the Śakvarī consists of fifty-six syllables.
The deity is Śyena.
Since it was stated in the preceding hymn, "Or eight," Indra is the deity of this [hymn] as well. Thus it has been enumerated: "The five others [beginning with] 'garbham' are Śakvarīs.
This hymn is used in the Śyena sacrifice for the *nikkevalya* recitation.
But the Sūtra has already been cited previously.
As if dwelling within their womb, I indeed know all these generations of the gods;
though a hundred iron fortresses guarded me, I, being sinless, have escaped with speed.
While still in the womb, I indeed recognized all these generations of the gods; a hundred iron fortresses guarded me, yet half-way I became a falcon.

When the falcon cried out, half of heaven seemed to resound; when they bore the inspired singer away, Kṛśānu, the archer, drawing back his bowstring with his mind, released it for him with speed. ava | yat | śyenaḥ | asvanīt | ardha | dyauḥ | vi | yat | yadi | vā | ārtan | ūhuḥ | puraṃdhim | sṛjat | yat | asmai | ava | ha | kṣipat | jyām | kṛśānuḥ | astā | manasā | bhuraṇyan || 3 || When the falcon shrieked, half the sky rang out; when they carried the sage away, Kṛśānu, the shooter, drawing back his bowstring with his mind, sped it forth for him.
And then, at that time of the Soma's fetching, when the falcon made a downward-sounding cry from the sky,
or indeed when—
*vā* being used here in the sense of "and."
When the guardians of Soma scattered that Soma from this hawk,
at that time, when the archer— the hurler of arrows— [acted].

Now, therefore, let the heroic, valorous, and bountiful Indra take for himself the bright, pure Soma—contained in the jar, sprinkled with the milk of cows, swelling as it fills the vessel, radiant, prepared by the Adhvaryu priests, and offered as food characterized by the Soma; let him set aside the very best portion of the sweet Soma-juice for the sake of exhilaration, so that he may drink it.
(The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.)
The seventh hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “tvā yujā,” is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and has Indra and Soma as its deities.
Its Anukramaṇī states: “tvā yujā [is] Aindrāsoma.
Its application is indicated by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

With you as my ally, O Soma, Indra performed that deed for man; he made the waters flow easily, he slew the serpent, he released the seven rivers, and he opened the channels that were like sealed doors.

With you as my ally, O Soma, in that friendship of yours, Indra released the waters for the sake of man. He slew the dragon and set the seven rivers flowing; he opened the channels that had been closed up as if by a lid. 1.
O Soma, in that friendship of yours, with you as his ally and companion, Indra made the waters— those ever-moving waters characterized by rain— to flow for Manu, for the sake of mankind;
furthermore, he slew Ahi, the Vṛtra-asura,
and set the flowing rivers, the waters, in motion.
As if concealed, as if they were covered and hidden by Vṛtra—
the word *eva* here having the sense of "as if"—
he opened, that is, he unsealed, the *khāni*, the channels or openings of the streams.
With you as his ally, O Indu, Indra forcibly struck down the wheel of the Sun as it rolled upon the high ridge; it was established for the sake of all life, having cast off all oppressors.
With you as his ally, O Indu, Indra forcibly struck down the wheel of the Sun as it rolled upon the high ridge;
the great, all-sustaining [wheel] was cast away from the mountain peak. 2.

O Indu Soma, O Indra: immediately, with you as your companion and ally, one wheel of the two-wheeled chariot belonging to Savitṛ, the impeller, was suddenly torn away by forceful, overwhelming power. How was it? It was situated above upon the high, vast expanse of the intermediate space (antarikṣa). Furthermore, that all-pervading wheel belonging to the great, abundant, and malevolent Sun was carried off by Indra.
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, ta, ca, ta, pa, pha, bha, and sa do not contain the word *dhanavān*.
2. [The syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, bha, and sa do not contain the word *dattam*. 3. [This belongs to] Somarāja.
4. In the *kha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha* [syllables], there is no "a" at the beginning.

5. The *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *pā* [syllables] are for the sake of the vessel (*pātra*); the *na* and *sa* [syllables] are the vessel itself. 6. The *ta* [syllable] has Indra and Soma as its deity.
7. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha, and Tathā, the word *anukrāntam* is present; 8. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pha, and Bha, the word *sati* is present;
9. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha, the word ‘pūrva’ does not exist.

10. Of what kind is the wheel? It is joined with a high, broad, and great rim; it rolls on, existing, and is all-encompassing (*viśvāyu*). It was placed there eternally for the sake of destroying the great oppressor (*maho duhaḥ*), and was seized by Indra. He burned down the Dasyus in the mountains with his days long ago; he devoured them at close quarters today.
Like those who have made their way into a difficult dwelling, you have struck down many thousands with your arrow.
Indra struck them down; Agni, O Indu, consumed the Dasyus before midday in the encounter. Having made their way difficult in their own dwelling, he felled many thousands with his arrow as they fled.
In that close encounter, in the battle, Indra struck down and slew the Dasyus, the enemies;
Agni consumed and burned certain enemies.
Of what nature were Indra and Agni?
Before midday— that is, in the forenoon— before you drank [the soma], Śeṣa, having obtained strength from your drinking,
struck down, utterly destroyed, all the thousands— the many, the numerous, the countless thousands— of the Asuras as they were departing.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
In the dwelling, in the difficult-to-protect [place], they two—
by means of power intent on ignorance— deprived the earths of their luster.
O Maghavans, O wealthy Indra and Soma, you two who strike down enemies, all that which you have done in the manner described is indeed true.
The eighth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “ā naḥ stutaḥ,” is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “‘ā naḥ stutaḥ’ [is the hymn].
The application [of the hymn] is determined by its indicative marks (*liṅga*).

O Indra, being praised, come to us with strengths and aids, exhilarated by your bay steeds; passing even through many obstacles and all things, you who are extolled with songs of praise. 1. O Indra, being praised, come to us with strengths and aids, exhilarated by your bay steeds; passing even through many obstacles and all things, you who are extolled with songs of praise.

O Indra, being praised, come hither with thy steeds for our protection; pass across our many full libations— Yāska says in Nirukta 3.20 that "tiraḥ sat" refers to the libation— and come to our sacrifices for our aid, arriving with thy two bay horses for the sake of our preservation.
Of what sort is he?
Rejoicing, the Lord (Artha), being praised with hymns of praise (Āṅguṣebhiḥ) and lauded, possessing true wealth (Satyarādhāḥ).

For he indeed comes, mindful of men, being summoned by the pressers to the sacrifice; he who possesses fine horses, considering himself fearless, rejoices together with the heroes who have pressed the Soma. For he indeed comes, mindful of men, being summoned by the pressers to the sacrifice; he who possesses fine horses, considering himself fearless, rejoices together with the heroes who have pressed the Soma. 2.

Manly, worthy of men, well-disposed, and wise—knowing all and being invoked by the pressing priests, the officiating ṛtviks—may Indra come toward our sacrifice. (The words *hi* and *sma* are expletives. Accompanied by fine horses, fearless by nature, and being praised by the Soma-pressing sacrificers, that Indra who rejoices together with the heroic Maruts—he indeed takes his delight.
The connection with the preceding phrase is: "May that Indra come."

May he cause his two ears to hear for the sake of winning the prize; may he gladden us according to the desired direction. Raining down wealth for our prosperity, may the powerful Indra provide us with good paths and security. *śravaya it asya karṇī vājajityai juṣṭām anu pra diśam mandayadhyai udvṛṣāṇo rādhase turviṣmān karat naḥ indraḥ sutīrthā abhayaṃ ca.* 3. May he cause his two ears to hear for the sake of winning the prize; may he gladden us according to the desired direction. Raining down wealth for our prosperity, may the powerful Indra provide us with good paths and security.
1. There is no *na-la-sa* [sandhi] for "maghavānā. 2. *kha-pha-bha-sma* is indeed possible.

O singer (*stotar*), you—having listened to the praises (*juṣāman*)—should cause the fame (*śravaya*, i.e., make heard) of the hymns (*śravāṃsi*) so that Indra may be strengthened (*vājadhyai*) and so that he may be greatly exhilarated (*pra mandadhyai*) in all directions (*diśam*) that are frequented (*anu*). Make him hear the songs of praise.

The particle *it* is a filler. May the powerful *Indra*, exulting as he is being sprinkled with Soma, grant us for the sake of wealth (*rādhase*) excellent fords (*sutīrthā*) and freedom from fear (*abhayam*). May he bring these about.
He who comes with aid to the one who does not falter, to the inspired singer who thus invokes and praises him—
placing within himself the yoke-bearers, he whose arm wields the thunderbolt brings thousands and hundreds.

Excellent! He who, with his aid, goes to the one who does not press [the soma], to the inspired singer who thus calls upon him and praises him—placing swift steeds upon the yoke within himself—he, the thunderbolt-armed one, [bestows] thousands and hundreds. 4.

Indra, who has arms like thunderbolts and hands like thunderbolts—he who, for the sake of protection (*ūtī*), places upon the pole (*dhuri*)—the part of the chariot used for carrying—thousands (*sahasrāṇi*) of swift-moving horses (*āśūn*), numbering in the thousands and hundreds, which are well-known; he goes toward (*acchā gantā*) the wise one (*vipram*) who is imploring (*nādhamānam*) him for protection, who is calling out (*havamānam*), and who is praising (*gṛṇantam*) the sacrificer in this very manner (*itthā*).
(The word "he becomes" [*bhavati*] is to be supplied.)
The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "May that Indra create good fords and fearlessness."
O Maghavan Indra, under your protection may we, the inspired singers, be yours, praising you like the sun;
may we partake of the vast celestial wealth, rich in food, for the granting of poetic inspiration.

O Maghavan Indra, may we, the inspired singers, be yours when aided by you—praising you as Sūrya and sharing in the vast heavenly wealth, for the granting of poetic wisdom and of food in abundance. 5.

O bountiful Indra, O possessor of wealth, may we—your protégés, guarded by you, the wise sages who praise and extol you, the singers—be those who share in the granting of your riches. May we be those who partake of your wealth, which is vast, worthy of praise through its wisdom, abundant in food (or fame), and yours alone, for the sake of bestowing it upon us. May we thus remain as your devotees.
The ninth hymn, consisting of twenty-four verses beginning with “nakir indra,” is addressed to Vāmadeva as its seer, is in the Gāyatrī meter, and has Indra as its deity;
the eighth and twenty-fourth verses are in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Indra is the deity.

This triplet beginning with “divaścidvā” has Upas as its deity and Indra as its deity. Thus it is enumerated: “Nakiḥ [consists of] twenty-four verses; Viśva and Upastha are in the Gāyatrī meter; the others in the Brāhmaṇacchamsin’s litany are in the Anuṣṭubh meter. In the Atirātra sacrifice, during the third round (paryāya), this hymn is used in the Maitrāvaruṇa’s Śastra, excluding the final verse.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should recite the final verse [of the hymn] beginning with 'There is none higher than you, O Indra'. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4)
1. Kha, ga, ṇa, ṇa, ra, ya, vāhana; 2. Ca, ba, hu, dhana, sya; 3. Kha, ga, ca, pha, nimitta-bhūte.

O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, there is none superior to you, nor is there any greater than you; indeed, there is no one at all like you. 1. nakiḥ | indra | tvat | uttaraḥ | na | jyāyān | asti | vṛtrahan | nakiḥ | eva | yathā | tvam || 1 ||

O Vṛtrahan, O Indra, destroyer of Vṛtra—[in this world] there is none other [who is equal], such is the implication. There is no one superior (uttara), that is, more excellent than you. No one at all exists who is greater.
There is not even one who is superior to you or more highly praised.
O Indra, there is not even one such as you renowned in the world;
the meaning is that no one at all exists in the world equal to Indra.

Truly all the peoples have turned toward you as if toward two wheels; truly, you are renowned as great. 2. Truly, toward you, all the peoples have turned as if toward two wheels; truly, you are renowned as great. 2.
O Indra, the *kṛṣṭayaḥ* (the settled peoples) and the *prajāḥ* (the subjects), having taken you as their aim, have turned toward you with absolute truth (*satrā satyam eva vāvṛtuḥ*).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
*viśvā viśva* (all [the people]).
O Indra, you alone, indeed without any companion, fought in that battle against all the Rākṣasas and others who were harming and obstructing the gods, beginning with Indra;
likewise, you slew those who sought to harm.

Wherein, O Indra, you indeed set free the sun for the sake of the mortal, and by your powers you protected Etaśa. 6. Wherein | indeed | for the mortal | whom | did you release | O Indra | the sun | forth | you protected | by your powers | Etaśa || 6 ||
In whatever battle, O Indra, you indeed released the sun for the mortal man, the seer Etaśa;
[the word] *kam* is a filler.
At that time, by means of your powers—that is, your martial deeds—you protected Etaśa, the seer so named, with preeminent protection.

The Dawn has departed from the crushed place; I have emerged flushed with blood, since the Bull has loosened her. 10. Apa | uṣāḥ | anesaḥ | sarat | sam'piṣṭāt | aham | bimbyuṣī | ni | yat | sīm | śiśrathat | vṛṣā || 10 ||
Indra is the showerer of desires.

When he shattered—that is, destroyed—this cart associated with the Dawn, then the Dawn, the deity Uṣas, being terrified of Indra, fled away from that joined cart crushed by Indra; she departed and went far off.
The word "aha" is a filler.
This breath of hers lies well-crushed in the Vipāś river;
she has sped away to the far distance. 11. This, of her, breath, lies, well-crushed, in the Vipāś, by the light; she has sped away to the far distance. 11.
Well-crushed by Indra, thoroughly pulverized—this cart belonging to this Dawn has been shattered.
*Vipāś* is the name of a river;
upon it, on its bank, he lay down, he rested on all sides.

When this wagon was broken, O Upodevatā, you fled from afar, having retreated from the distant land; indeed, O Indra, by your wondrous power (*māyā*), you went around the Sindhu river, the Vibālī, and those who stand spread across the earth.

12. *uta sindhum vibālyam vitasthānām adhi kṣami | pari hyā indra māyayā || 12 ||* And [you went] to the Sindhu, the Vibālī, and those who stand spread across the earth; for, O Indra, you went around them by your wondrous power. 12.

O Indra, you encompassed by your creative power (*māyā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) the river Sindhu—overflowing with water, spreading out, and extending far—even as she lay upon the earth, and you brought her to rest on all sides. Furthermore, with bold courage, you seized the wealth of Śuṣṇa when you crushed his fortresses. And [you seized] the wealth of Śuṣṇa with bold courage; you seized it completely, since you shattered his fortresses. 13.

Moreover, O Indra, you who are bold—the bold one, the assailant—you completely crushed, that is, you forcefully struck down, the possession of Śuṣṇa, the demon named Śuṣṇa. When you thoroughly shattered his fortresses, his cities, then you completely crushed them; such is the connection.
1. There is no "Indra" [rule] for *sa-ga-ca-ṇa*.
2. Connection with *la-uṣas*.

And furthermore, O Indra, you struck down Śambara, the Dāsa, the son of Kulitara, from atop the great mountain—you cast him down and slew him. (14) And furthermore, O Indra, you—having brought down Śambara, the Dāsa, the offspring of Kulitara, from the great mountain—struck him down and killed him. (14) And furthermore, O Indra, you—having brought down Śambara, the Dāsa, the oppressor, the son of Kulitara, from the great mountain—the high peak—cast him downward and slew him. (14)

And indeed, O Indra, you slew hundreds and thousands of the Dāsa Varcin, more than five hundred, like the spokes of a wheel. (15) And furthermore, O Indra, you struck down the five hundred and the thousands of the Dāsa Varcin—those who were like the spokes situated all around a wheel—as if they were mere pins. (15)

O Vṛtra-slayer, you have led the blind and the lame along the two paths; that [deed] of yours cannot be fully praised. 19. anu | dvā | jaṃhitā | nayaḥ | andham | śroṇam | ca | vṛtrahan | na | tat | te | sujham | aṣṭave || 19 ||

O Vṛtrahan, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, you indeed led away the two—Jambhita, who was abandoned by all her kinsmen, and another, one-eyed and the other lame—who were both destitute; you guided them both, having spared them from their lameness.
O Indra, no one is able to pervade that happiness bestowed by you;
[no one can reach it], such is the sense.
Indra shattered a hundred stone-built fortresses for Divodāsa, who offered him oblations. 20. A hundred; of stone-built; fortresses; Indra; shattered; for Divodāsa; who offered him oblations. 20.

Indra [shattered] the hundred—numbering one hundred—fortresses of Śambara, those cities made of stone, constructed with rocks; moreover, O Indra, that which is your manly strength, your power, and your capacity, you have surely performed [in the past]. And now, no one whatsoever shall diminish or harm that strength today.
May Aryaman, the god, grant you what is desirable, O Āduri; may Pūṣan grant what is desirable, Bhaga grant what is desirable, and the god Karūlatī grant what is desirable. 24.
What is desirable, what is desirable—may the god Aryaman grant it; may Pūṣan grant what is desirable; may Bhaga grant what is desirable; may the god Karūlatī [grant what is desirable]. 24.
O Indra, destroyer of the enemies' fortresses, may Aryaman—the god so named who restrains the enemies—grant you every desirable and praiseworthy wealth that exists in the world.
Likewise, may Pūṣan, the nourisher whose teeth are severed, grant you desirable wealth;
and may Bhaga also grant you desirable wealth.

Now, is it not the case that this word *karūlati* must be connected with [the preceding term] because of its proximity? Or rather, it must function as an adjective qualifying all three, Aryaman and the others;
for how else could it qualify Pūṣan alone, since there would otherwise be a syntactic expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*)?
No;
for even when proximity (*sānnidhya*) and expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) are present, syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is impossible without compatibility (*yogyatā*).

Therefore, since Pūṣan alone is well-known in Vedic texts such as "Pūṣan has the portion of ground flour, for he is toothless" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.6.8.5) to be toothless, it is appropriate that he alone serves as the qualifier, even though he is separated [from the word].
"The word *vāma* means desirable" (*nirukta* 6.31); such passages from the *Nirukta* should be consulted here.
The hymn beginning with "kayā naḥ," consisting of fifteen verses, belongs to Vāmadeva; it is addressed to Indra and is in the Gāyatrī meter.

The verse beginning with "abhī naḥ" is a *pādanicṛt* gāyatrī, because it possesses the defining characteristic of that meter according to the rule: "Three [feet] of seven syllables each is a *pādanicṛt*" (Anuvāka 4.4).
Likewise, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: "In the hymn to Pañcanābhi, 'kayā' and 'pu' are *pādanicṛt*. The application of this hymn is based on its internal indicative marks (*liṅga*).
In the Agniṣṭoma, on the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the triplet beginning with "kayā naḥ" is the stotriya for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "Of the Hotṛ-priests, [the verse] 'kayā naścitra ā bhuvat'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
In the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, this same verse, "kayā naḥ," is the invitatory prayer (anuvākyā) for the oblation to Ka.

And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "By what [help] has the wonderful one come to us? Hiranyagarbha was manifested in the beginning" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.17). By what [help] has the wonderful one come to us for our aid, he who is the friend ever-increasing [our prosperity]? By what most powerful host? 1 By what? To us. The wonderful one. Has come. For aid. Ever-increasing. Friend. By what. Most powerful. Host. 1

May Indra—the one who is ever-increasing (*sadāvṛdhaḥ*), ever-growing (*sadā vardhamānaḥ*), wonderful (*citraḥ*), worthy of admiration and worship (*cāyanīyaḥ*), and our friend (*sakhā*)—be present before us (*ā bhuvat*) with what aid (*kayā ūtī*) for our satisfaction?
And by what most powerful (*śaciṣṭhayā*) means—that is, by what path (*vṛtā*) or action accompanied by wisdom—is he to be brought face-to-face with us?

1. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ṇa, na, and bha, the word "atha" is absent. 2. In the manuscripts kha, pa, pha, and bha, it reads "dārayitā indra. 3. In the manuscript ma, it reads "arīṇāṃ śatrūṇām. 4. In the manuscripts ga and ca, there is also the reading "bhago'pi. 5. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, and pha, it reads "atra. [The verse: Who among the exhilarating drinks is the true one, the most bountiful? May he intoxicate me with the soma-juice; may he break open even the firmest wealth. [Word-by-word gloss: Kaḥ | tvā | satyaḥ | madānām | maṃhiṣṭhaḥ | mat | sat | andhasaḥ | duḷhā | cit | ā | ruje | vasu || 2 || Who is the true one for you among the exhilarating drinks, the most generous? May he, being present, intoxicate me with the soma-juice; may he bring forth even the most difficult-to-obtain wealth. || 2 ||

O most generous one, worthy of worship, the truth itself, the very embodiment of reality—among the exhilarating draughts, what essence of the soma juice causes such intoxication? O Indra, may that which enables you to utterly shatter even the most firmly held wealth—the riches of the enemies—delight you.

Be truly our protector, the helper of us who are your friends and singers; may you be present with a hundred aids. 3. Be truly our protector, the helper of us who are your friends and singers; may you be present with a hundred aids. 3.

O Indra, you are the protector and guardian of your friends—those who share the same renown, the chanters and the praisers; with a hundred, that is, with many aids and protections, be well-disposed toward us, turn yourself toward us.
Turn toward us, as a wheel turns for a steed, with your teams of horses that bring joy to the people. 4. Toward us; turn hither; like a wheel; turned; for the steed; with the teams; of the people. 4.

O Indra, turn toward us with your teams [of horses]—toward us, the people of our own human race—as one turns a revolving wheel that has rolled away, or as one turns toward those who approach; come hither! Turn back toward us!

For you go down the slope of the seasons, O God, as if on a swift course; I have partaken [of the offering] together with Sūrya. 5. For you go down the slope of the seasons, O God, as if on a swift course; I have partaken [of the offering] together with Sūrya. 5.

O Indra, you indeed come—having arrived—to each and every steep descent (*pravat*), as if to your own footsteps or stations, belonging to the seasons, the ritual acts, and the sacrificers. The particle *ha* is used for emphasis. O Indra, I have partaken of you together with the sun (*sūrye sacā*).
When your indignations, O Indra, and your wheels have rolled together—then they were in you, and then in the sun. (6)
O Indra, those hymns of praise intended for you— when they have flowed forth and are being approved by us—
and when our movements and ritual acts have likewise flowed forth;
then, at that time, those hymns and those acts abide in you alone.
And immediately after that, they occur in the sun as well.
1. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, pha, bha, and sa are to be released.
2. [This applies to those] designated as being equal to pha and la. 3. Ga, ca, and pha belong to us, that is, to our relations.
4. There is no "pravarta" for kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, and sa.

And indeed, O Lord of Might (Śacīpati), they call you Maghavan, the giver who does not hesitate. And indeed, O Lord of Might, they call you Maghavan—the wealthy one, the giver to the singers, the bestower of desired things—who does not hesitate (*avidīdhayu*). *Vidīdhayuḥ* means "not playing" or "not shining"; *avidīdhayuḥ* means "one who shines. They call you such a radiant one; they truly proclaim this. Both particles *sma* and *hi* serve to emphasize the fullness of the sense.

And indeed, O Indra, you instantly bestow abundant wealth upon the one who exerts himself in praise and presses the Soma. (8) And indeed, O Indra, you instantly—*sadya it*—bestow even much wealth (*vasu*) upon the one who exerts himself (*śaśamānāya*), that is, upon the one performing praise; for Yāska has stated: "The word *śaśamānaḥ* means praising" (*Nirukta* 6.8). And upon the one who presses the Soma...
O Indra, here at this sacrifice, choose us—the sacrificers—for friendship, for companionship, for well-being, for non-destruction, and for great, celestial, radiant wealth. Enjoy [these gifts].
O Indra, favor us always with abundant wealth;
favor us with all your protections.
Know us at all times, O Indra, with abundant wealth; know us with all your protections. 12.
O Indra, you who are all-pervading, on every day, with great abundance and wealth, protect us, the sacrificers;
moreover, protect us with all your aids and defenses.
Open up for us those cow-filled enclosures, O Indra, with your newest aids.
Open up for us those cow-filled enclosures, as if for archers, O Indra, with your new protections. 13.
O Indra, with your new and fresh protections, like a shooter or a hero, open up for us those well-known cow-pens—stalls filled with cattle—and release the waters.
Boldly, our chariot, brilliant and unshakable, O Indra,
speeds forth, seeking cattle and seeking horses.
O Indra, our bold chariot, joined with you and never falling back, rushes forward, seeking cattle and seeking horses. 14.
O Indra, may this chariot—which is bold, the subduer of enemies, radiant, unshakable, seeking cattle, possessing kine, and possessing horses—belonging to us, go everywhere;
by means of that chariot, may you protect us. This is the sense.
Having seen the sun, one should descend from the chariot while reciting the verse, "Make us supreme" (*asmākam uttamaṃ kṛdhi*).
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having looked at the sun and muttered the mantra, 'Make us supreme,' one should descend" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.6.12).
O Sūrya, among the gods, establish for us supreme renown,
most exalted like the sky above.
O Sūrya, bestow upon us among the gods the highest, most exalted glory, reaching up above like the sky. 15.
O Sūrya, O impeller of all, O Indra, or O Āditya, among the *devas*—the shining ones such as Agni and the rest—make our glory (*śravaḥ*) most excellent, that is, supreme.
Therein is an illustration:
just as you made the sky (*dyām*), which is exceedingly great or capable of pouring forth moisture, the most excellent, situated above all the worlds; even so [make our glory supreme].
1. *la-aviddhi*: this is connected with what precedes. 2. *kha-ga-gha-ta-na-pa-pha-bha-sa-utpādaya*; *la-utpāṭaya*.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of twenty-four verses beginning with "ā tū na indra," is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Vāmadeva; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is addressed to Indra.
The other two hymns beginning with "ā kanīnakeva" have Indra and the Horse as their deities;
thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "In these twenty-four [verses], Indra and the Horse are praised.
The application [of the hymns] is thus established.
Come then to us, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra; come to our side, you who are great with your mighty protections.
Come hither to us, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra; come to our side, O Great One, with thy mighty aids. || 1 ||
O Vṛtrahan, O Indra, you who are the slayer of Vṛtras—that is, of enemies—come quickly toward us.
O Indra, you who are great and abundant, come to our side with your great protections and aids.
Even though you are swift and impetuous, O Wondrous One,
you perform wondrous deeds for our protection among those who seek wonders.
You are indeed a whirlwind, O impetuous one; O wondrous one, you come toward those who seek wonders; you bring forth wonders for our protection.
O Indra, you are wonderful, worthy of admiration, and worthy of worship. Although you are swift and tireless, you are also a prompt helper; indeed, you are the bestower of what we desire.
The particle *ā* is used here for emphasis.
Among our subjects—those women engaged in the art of painting—you provide wonderful and admirable wealth for their protection (*ūtaye*), making it available to them on all sides.
The syllable *gha* is for the purpose of filling out the meter.
With even a few companions, I overcome one who is more powerful in his might;
he who is with you, O Friend.
Even with few companions, you slay the more numerous and the most powerful by your might—those who are your friends and stand together with you.

O Indra, you, together with even the few and small friends who sacrifice, destroy—that is, you annihilate by means of your power and strength—the most numerous, leaping, and swelling enemy. (The root *śaś* means "to leap"; thus, "leaping" refers to one who bounds about. You slay and utterly destroy even the great foe through your might.
"Those sacrificers who have come together with you"— this is to be connected with the preceding [verse].
We, O Indra, are with you; we praise you aloud. Flow toward us, toward us alone!
O Indra, we are with you; we sing our praises to you. Protect each and every one of us! 4.

We praise you, you indeed, most intensely.
O Indra, you too, protect us—all of us—most excellently.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, come to us with your wondrous, blameless, and invincible aids.
O wielder of the stone, come to us with your wondrous, blameless, and unassailable aids. 5.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, you—accompanied by wondrous, praiseworthy, blameless, and unassailable protections that cannot be overcome by enemies—come hither to us.
O Indra, may we indeed be your companions for so much wealth of cattle, as your allies for bold conquest.
O Indra, may we, your friends who possess you, be accompanied by you for the sake of bold strength and for the acquisition of cattle. 6.

O Indra, may we, your friends and fellow-singers, being joined together for the sake of great, bold strength—that is, for food—become truly well-established as yours, belonging to you who are like yourself, possessing cattle, and endowed with kine.
For you alone, O Indra, rule over wealth consisting of cattle; as such, grant us great nourishment.
For you alone, O Indra, rule over wealth consisting of cattle; as such, grant us great nourishment. 7.
O Indra, since you alone are the lord and master of food consisting of cattle,
therefore do you grant us great nourishment.
They do not turn you away from another course when, O Indra, lover of songs, you wish to bestow wealth upon your praisers after being lauded.
They do not restrain you otherwise than this: that, being praised, O Indra, lover of songs, you shall bestow wealth upon those who laud you. 8.
O Indra, lover of songs, you who are the recipient of hymns and have been praised by us— when you desire to bestow wealth (*magha*) upon us, your praisers,
then no one can restrain you in any other way;
rather, all become entirely favorable.
The Gōtamas have sung aloud to you with their song for the sake of giving,
O Indra, for bold strength.
The Gōtamas have sung aloud to you with their song, O Indra, for the sake of giving, for bold strength, and for booty. 9.
