O Indra, being exhilarated by the Soma and rejoicing, you approached and utterly shattered the fortresses—the cities—that belonged to the Dāsa Asura. O Indra, we, your worshippers, proclaim with excellence those heroic deeds of yours performed therein.
The wise ones sing those manly deeds which you have performed for them, O Indra, lover of songs, when the juices are pressed.

Turn toward us, O Vasu; be well-intoxicated with this food, O Indra, drinker of Soma, from these Somas. 14. Turn toward us, O Vasu; be well-intoxicated with this food, O Indra, drinker of Soma, from these Somas. 14.
O Indra, you who dwell in the sacrifice, turn toward us—toward us who are the sacrificers.

Likewise, O Indra, drinker of Soma, exhilarate yourself well with the food of the Soma juices. May our hymn of praise reach you, O Indra; turn your two bay steeds hitherward. 15. Our hymn of praise, O Indra, shall offer itself to you; turn your two bay steeds hitherward. 15. *asmākam* | *tvā* | *matīnām* | *ā* | *stomaḥ* | *indra* | *yacchatu* | *arvāk* | *ā* | *vartaya* | *harī* iti || 15 ||

The word *matīnām* refers to hymns of praise, derived from the root *man* with the suffix *ktic* in the sense of an agent. O Indra, may our *stoma*, our hymn of praise, which is connected to us, draw you toward us; may it establish you among us.
And you, in turn, turn your two bay horses (*harī*) hither, so that they face toward us; perform this turning back.

Eat our sacrificial cake and take pleasure in our songs, as one desiring a bride takes pleasure in a young woman. 16. Eat our sacrificial cake; and take pleasure in our songs, as one desiring a bride [takes pleasure] in a young woman. 16.
O Indra, eat our *puroḷāśa*— that is, consume the food in the form of the sacrificial cake—
and likewise, take pleasure in and enjoy our *giraḥ*, our words in the form of hymns of praise.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Like a suitor:
just as one desiring women attends to the words of young women, so it is in this case.

We implore Indra for a thousand swift, harnessed horses; for a hundred [draughts] of Soma with its cups. 17. A thousand; of swift ones; of harnessed ones; Indra; we implore; a hundred; of Soma; with its cups. 17.
We, the singers, beg of Indra—who is endowed with supreme sovereignty—a thousand, that is, a thousandfold number of yoked, trained, and swift-moving horses.
Likewise, we beg for a hundred, that is, a hundredfold number of *khārīs* of pressed soma;
by the word *khārī*, which denotes a specific measure, the *droṇakalaśa* (soma-vat) is indicated here.
The meaning is that we request many sacrifices involving countless droṇa-measures of jars.

1. ta—residing at that sacrifice; 2. kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-pha-bha-sa—the word ‘ca’ is not present; 3. kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha—of the one who has been pressed; 4. la—the phrase ‘we ask for the droṇakalaśas’ is not present.

We bring to you thousands and hundreds of cattle; may your bounty come to us. (18) O Indra, we bring toward ourselves your thousands—that is, those numbering in the thousands—and your hundreds—that is, those numbering in the hundreds—of cattle; we turn them toward us. Likewise, may your wealth (*rādhaḥ*) come from you to us. (18)

We have received from you ten jars of gold; you are a giver of much, O slayer of Vṛtra. We have received from you, O Indra, ten jars—meaning as many as can be measured by jars—of gold, that is, of wealth most pleasing to us. O slayer of Vṛtra, O Indra, the destroyer of enemies, you are a giver of much; you are one who bestows abundantly.
O Bountiful One, give us abundantly;
do not withhold, O eloquent one, O lord of the wise! I praise you, O tawny one, whose horses are tawny-colored—I extol you preeminently.
O Giver of Cows, O winner of cattle, O Grandson, who does not cause the fall of those who praise you!
But rather, it means "as a protector.
O Indra, do not harm our cows by means of these two horses of yours; that is, do not let them perish.
Cows are scattered when they see horses.
The meaning is: "Let that not happen.
Like two small, crooked, and deformed wooden posts on a narrow path, those two brown ones shine amidst the processions. 23.
Like two young maidens, they shine upon the two separate, nine-holed, small wooden posts at the racing grounds. || 23 ||

O Indra, when [the world] is shattered, pervaded, expanded, new, newly born, small, minute, situated upon a wooden pedestal (*drupada*) in a forest of trees, or standing like a lovely young maiden, O Indra—your two brown-colored (*babhru*) horses shine with beauty, endowed with splendor, during their journeys to the sacrifices.
Regarding "young maiden" (*kanīnakā*):

"A maiden is lovely; she is so called because she is to be led as a bride to be purchased, or because she is led for the sake of love, or from the root *kan*, which means 'to desire'. Thus it is stated in the *Nirukta* (4.15).
They are sufficient for me against the one who possesses oxen, sufficient against the one who does not possess oxen; the two tawny ones are unfailing on the journeys. 24.
They are ready for me, for Ustrāyāman, and ready for Anustrāyāman; the two brown ones are unfailing on their journeys.
O Indra, O non-injurer, O non-injurer, O slayer of the serpent, O tawny one— may your two tawny-colored horses, when the journeys are undertaken, be sufficient for me, for Ustrāyāman—
one who travels in a chariot yoked with two oxen (*uṣṭra*).
May they be capable and adequate for my purpose.
"O Anusthāyinī, act so as to fulfill my requirements for me who am traveling along the very path. 30.3.
May Vidyātīrthamaheśvara, dispelling the darkness of the heart by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the third book (*aṣṭaka*) in the *Ṛgveda-saṃhitā-bhāṣya*, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of King Śrī Vīrabuka— the illustrious sovereign of kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path— under the patronage of Mādhava.
1. *ta-goṣaṇa*: 2. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa*, the word "in small quantities" (*alpake*) is absent.

3. In *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, it says "at sacrifices" (*yajñeṣu*); in *ta*, *la*, and *ya*, it says "at sacrifices and on journeys" (*yajñeṣu gamaneṣu*); in *na* and *sa*, the word "on journeys" (*gamaneṣu*) is absent.
4. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa do not contain the vowel *a*. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
In the fourth section (anuvāka), there are thirteen hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, "pra ṛbhubhyaḥ," consisting of eleven verses, is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Vāmadeva and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
According to the technical rules regarding the word "tu" and so forth, this and the subsequent hymns have Agni as their deity.
The table of contents (*anukramaṇikā*) here states: "To the *Ṛbhus*, eleven verses, or [twelve].
In the expanded (*vyūḍha*) ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), this is the *nivid* for the *Ārbhava* section within the *Vaiśvadeva* litany on the fourth day.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'To the *Ṛbhus*' and 'Forward, O bright one' constitute the *Vaiśvadeva*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).
I send forth my speech like a messenger to the Ṛbhus; I praise the barren cow that provides nourishment.
They who, impelled by the wind, with their swift-moving steeds, have in an instant encompassed the sky through their deeds.
Send forth your voice like a messenger to the Ṛbhus; spread out the cow for the sake of nourishment.
Immediately thereafter, they attained proximity with the gods—Indra and the others—namely, their shared station and divinity;
for it is said that because they had attained divinity without interval, the gods addressed them as "the youthful ones" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.3).
Furthermore, the wise ones— those who are steadfast and possessed of intelligence— bring and bestow nourishment consisting of cattle and other such things for the sake of the *manā*,
that is, for the sacrificer whose mind is intent upon it; or rather, they bring nourishment together with its objects for the *manas*, for the sake of the excellence of the mind.
Furthermore, those who made their parents young again, as if they were lying in old age like worn-out things—
may Vāja, Vibhvan, and Ṛbhu, accompanied by Indra and possessing the sweetness of honey, protect our sacrifice.

Furthermore: Those who made their two parents young again, though they had lain like old, worn-out sacrificial posts—they, Vāja, Vibhvan, and Ṛbhu, accompanied by Indra and possessing the essence of sweetness—may they protect our sacrifice. 3.
The *Ṛbhus*, who made their parents—the mother and father—who were like withered tree-stumps, worn out by age, and lying there, young again, always youthful, making them more vigorous than before.

May those three—the Vāja, the Vivā, and the Ṛbhu—sons of Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa, known as the Ṛbhus; accompanied by Indra (Indravantaḥ), being possessed of him as their benefactor; drinkers of the sweet essence (Madhupparasaḥ) of the sweet Soma juice, or rather those of enchanting form; may they protect, guard, or attend to our sacrifice (Naḥ yajñam).
That they protected the cow for a year, that they anointed me for a year,
and that they bore her light for a year— with those labors they attained immortality.
Because for a year the Ṛbhus guarded the cow, because for a year the Ṛbhus carved the flesh, and because for a year they carried away her hide—by those labors they attained immortality. 4.
"Saṃvasam": it is called *saṃvatsa* because living beings dwell together (*saṃvasanti*) within it; thus, it is *saṃvatsara*, the year.
For the duration of a year, the *Ṛbhus* protected—that is, they guarded—the cow that had died.
"By their own power"—that is, since this work exists;
and likewise, "year by year," the *Ṛbhus* fashioned the limbs of that very cow's flesh, making them distinct parts—since they did so;

furthermore, for the duration of a year, they brought forth her splendors, creating the beauty of her limbs—since they did so; through those *śamīs*, the ritual acts concerning the restoration of the dead cow to youth, they attained immortality, reaching the state of divinity.
This is because it was promised by the gods as a means for attaining divinity, according to the statement, “The cow is the Karvā.
Alternatively,
the word *saṃvatsam* here should be explained as meaning “together with the calf” (*vatsena saha*).
1. *Ta* refers to nourishment (*puṣṭi*) and growth (*poṣa*).
2. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa*, the phrase "for the sake of intelligence" (*matikṛte*) is absent.
3. In the versions *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, the word "sages" (*ṛṣayaḥ*) is present.
4. Those who consume the essence of the moon (*somarasa*)—that is, those who consume the essence of Soma (*pa-somasya rasaṃ bhakṣayitāraḥ*).
5. *Ta-la-kiṃca amuyā*: having scraped a limb with the hide of that dead cow (*ta-mṛtāyāḥ gostvacā*), they joined her flesh back together; this is the meaning.
Regarding the word *kurvan* (the phrase *kurvanniti yat* does not appear in the *Taittirīya* version).
6. By means of the attainment of divinity through [the syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, and bha:
the eldest said, "Let us make two cups"; the younger said, "Let us make three"; the youngest said, "Let us make four. Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the cups for you, O Ṛbhus, when you were heating [them].
The eldest said, "Let us make two cups. The youngest said, "Let us make three. The youngest of all said, "Make four," O Tvaṣṭṛ. Tvaṣṭṛ praised that speech of yours, O Ṛbhus. || 5 ||

Regarding the verse, “Make one cup into four” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.2): when the messenger of the gods spoke this in this world by means of the hymn concerning the attainment of divinity, then among them, the eldest Ṛbhu—who had been addressed regarding the attainment of divinity—said to the other two.
What did he say? It is explained as follows:
"Make two cups," he says;
"though there is only one, let us make it two.
Then [the other] says, "The younger one is right after that; let us make three cups."

The youngest among them said, "O Ṛbhus, let us make the fourfold [chariot]—that is, we shall make it fourfold. That very form of making it fourfold, O Ṛbhus, Tvaṣṭṛ praised as your own word—your speech.
For it has been stated that the rays themselves are the Ṛbhus; thus they are praised in that form.
This occurred when [they traversed] twelve empty days.
The meaning is that there are twelve constellations beginning with Ārdrā.
In the house of Vagodhya—meaning Agopya—the Sun's guest;
a guest who has arrived unexpectedly.
Hospitality (*ātithya*) is that action consisting of appropriate honor.
For that purpose, the *vṛbhavas*—dwelling, crying out, and living happily—delight themselves.
As it is said: "The house of him who does not give is as if he had no son" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.161.11).
At that time, they made the good fields uncultivated;
they turned the unplowed, empty fields into rivers and oceans by means of rain;
they caused the streams and rivers to flow forth.
At that time, the plants—the *oṣadhayaḥ*—stood upon the dry land, having resorted to a place devoid of water;
the waters stood in the low-lying places.
As it is said: "In the heights you made dry grass for him, and in the depths the waters" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.11).

May those who fashioned the well-rolling chariot, who [fashioned] the man-bearing cow, all-swift and multiform— may they, the skillful-handed ones, fashion for us wealth that brings the light of heaven, yes, wealth that brings the light of heaven.

May those R̥bhus who fashioned the well-rolling chariot that stands firm for men, and who [fashioned] the all-speeding, omniform cow—may they, the well-aiding, skillful-handed, and deft workers, fashion wealth for us. 8.
The *Ṛbhus* fashioned a chariot that was well-rounded, with good wheels—that is, one that rolls smoothly—and which stood upon the wheel of the leader among men.

And they fashioned a cow, a milch-cow, who impels all things, who is all-pervading, and who possesses many forms—or is named after this—just as it is fittingly said: "Bṛhaspati drove forth the all-formed one" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.161.6).
May those great Ṛbhus fashion for us wealth from wood; may they produce it from every side.
Of what sort are these Ṛbhus?

They are skillful in work (*svapasaḥ*), possessed of beautiful deeds, endowed with excellent strength (*svavasaḥ*), or possessing good protection, and having beautiful hands—that is, having skillful hands.
The gods indeed took pleasure in their work, contemplating it with wisdom and mind;
Vāja became the skillful artisan of the gods, Ṛbhukṣan that of Indra, and Vimbhvan that of Varuṇa.
For the waters indeed flowed forth for them, as the gods meditated with wisdom and mind; Vāja became the skillful worker of the gods, Ṛbhukṣan that of Indra, and Vimva that of Varuṇa. 9.
The gods, Indra and the others, accepted—the meaning is that they took for themselves—the *vapuḥ*, which is the work consisting of the construction of the sacrifice and so forth, of those *Ṛbhus*.
This is according to the manner stated in such mantras as, "Indra yoked his two bay horses; the Aśvins [yoked] their chariot" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.161.6).
Of what nature were they?
By means of their skillful action in the form of granting boons, and with a beautiful mind endowed with grace, they shine intensely.
He asks what is obtained through the favor of the gods:
"The strength (vāja) of one who performs good deeds (sukarman), whose activity is auspicious, is most excellent."
1. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, and sa, the word "twelve" (dvādaśa) is absent.

2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and sa, it reads "ariṣṭhāni"; in na and bha, it reads "ariṣṭhāni śūnyāni" (the ariṣṭhas are empty). 3. In the manuscripts ta and la, it reads "dhenuṃ viśvajuvam."

4. Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Ma: *dhenuṃ gāvam*; Ca, Dhe, Ņa, Gāṃ ca; Ta, La, Gāṃ vā; Na, Gāṃ ca; Sa, Vācam. 5. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, La, Sa: “*asurakṣaṇā vā*” is not present. 6. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, La, Sa: “*kuśalahastāḥ*” is not present.
7. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, and bhavataḥ [belong] to them; na and teṣām [do not]. 8. Ta, la, sukarmā, and śobhanakarmā belong to all the gods. They became related to all the gods.
Likewise, "Ṛbhukṣā," meaning "the most excellent for Ṛbhu," was related to Indra;
"Viśvāvasu" became related to Varuṇa. Why [is he] called "Hi"? Because he is a filler (pūraṇa).
Those who, exhilarated by their wisdom and hymns, fashioned for Indra the two well-yoked bay horses—
O Ṛbhus, bestowing prosperity and wealth upon us, grant us riches as you would a friend who dwells in peace.

Those who, with wisdom, gladdening themselves with hymns, fashioned for Indra his two well-yoked bay horses—O Ṛbhus, bestow upon us that increase of wealth and riches, as those who cherish their friend. 10.
O Ṛbhus, you who by means of *medhā* (wisdom) and *prajñā* (insight), and through hymns (*ukthaiḥ*) and praises (*stutibhiḥ*), joyfully and with delight fashioned the two bay horses (*harī aśvau*);

and you who for the sake of Indra fashioned those two well-yoked, well-fastened horses—O Ṛbhus, you, bestow upon us (*amme*) abundance of wealth (*rāyaspoṣam*), riches (*draviṇāni*) such as cattle and other possessions, and comforts; maintain these within us.
What is it like?
"Seeking security" means desiring safety; "like a friend" means as if toward a friend.
Here, just as there is only one named Ṛbhu, by association with him the others are also called Ṛbhus, according to the principle of the vital breath (*prāṇanyāya*).
O Maruts, you gods who are invoked for the drinking and the exhilaration of the soma, do not withhold it from us, for we are weary of our toil. O Rbhus, bestow upon us wealth in this third libation.
Today they have granted you exhilaration and the drink; O gods, it is not without toil that the wise man attains this. Therefore, O R̥bhus, bestow upon us now wealth in this third libation. 11.

‘Idā’ means ‘now,’ immediately after the preparation [of the Soma]. ‘Ahaḥ’ refers to the third pressing (*savana*) connected with the day of the Soma sacrifice (*sutyāha*). ‘Pīti’ is the drinking of Soma. ‘Uta’ means ‘also. And ‘madaḥ’ is the exhilaration produced by that. ‘Vaḥ’ means ‘for you. ‘Dhuḥ’ means ‘the gods bestowed.

[The gods did not bestow it] ‘ṛte’—that is, not for the sake of mere exhaustion, nor for those possessed of the nourishment of exhaustion; rather, they bestowed it ‘satyāya,’ for the sake of true being and consciousness. Since these [beings] were exhausted, therefore they bestowed it; such is the meaning.
O Ṛbhus, you who are great, establish—yes, firmly bestow—upon us, upon us, at this third libation, wealth and riches. Hold them fast for us.
The second hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “Ṛbhurvibhvā,” has Vāmadeva as its seer; it is dedicated to the Ṛbhus and concerns the Ṛbhus.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “‘Ṛbhurvibhvā’ [is the hymn].
In the expanded (*vyūḍha*) ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), on the fifth day, these [verses] are prescribed for the *vaiśvadeva-śastra* in the *ārbhava-kaṇḍa*.
Because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "I praise the people as Ṛbhu and Vibhvan" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).
1. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ta, Na, La, and Sa, the word *pūraṇaḥ* is absent.
2. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Pa, Pha, Bha, and Sa, the word *prajñayā* is absent.
3. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Ma, it reads *suyojamānāśvāḥ*; in manuscripts Gha, Ca, Pa, Pha, and Ta, it reads *suyojamānāśvāḥ*.

To him who is weary and burdened with toil, and to him who is unwearied and joined with austerity—O Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, Vāja, and Indra, come toward this sacrifice of ours for the bestowing of jewels! For now the divine Dhiṣaṇā has granted you drink; your exhilarations have gathered together. Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, Vāja, and Indra, come toward this sacrifice of ours for the bestowing of jewels! For now the divine Dhiṣaṇā has granted you drink; your exhilarations have gathered together. || 1 ||
Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, Vāja, and Indra—these gods, being bestowers of jewels (*ratnadheya*), come toward this sacrifice of ours, facing it; come near, approach us for the sake of bestowing jewels upon us.
If it is asked, "Since Indra alone is the lord of Soma, how can these others attain the sacrifice?", it is replied:
For now, indeed, at this very moment, your *dhiṣaṇā*—the goddess Speech belonging to Prajāpati—has established the drinking of Soma, which is connected to the pressing of Soma.
Regarding that, the Brāhmaṇa states: "He who [is] Prajāpati... [there these students... you alone [should instruct them] with these [verses]" (E.V.A. 3.30). He who... [text fragment].
O Ṛbhus, for you this sacrifice has been prepared. That sacrifice which, like a man, you have held within your bellies from of old— you who shine pre-eminently—
those Soma juices, seeking and serving you, have come forth toward you.
Moreover, O Vājas and R̥bhus, you all—having taken up [the implements]—have become, and indeed continue to be, the foremost, the most worthy of honor, or those who achieve preeminence.
O Heroes, this gift of treasures has been prepared for you by the worshiper, for the mortal who offers oblations.
Drink, O Vājas, O Ṛbhus; I have bestowed upon you the great third soma-portion for your exhilaration.

It has come to be: "Ūm!"—for you, who bestow wealth upon the one who performs the rite. Now, O heroes, grant riches to the mortal who offers oblations! Drink, O Vājas, O Ṛbhus! Great and all-encompassing is the third [portion] granted to you for exhilaration. 4.

O *Ṛbhus*, you who are leaders—by your favor, now at this very moment, at the third libation (*savana*), let there be a bestowal of treasure for me, the mortal sacrificer who honors you with praise and has offered the oblation; "vidhati" here signifies the act of serving. O *Vājas* (O *Ṛbhus*), for that purpose, drink! For that purpose, I give to you. What? The great, abundant third libation—that is to say, the Soma connected therewith. For what reason? For exhilaration, for joy, or for satisfaction.
May the Rbhuksans come to you like swift steeds, O great heroes, being praised for the sake of vast wealth;
may your exhilarating drinks reach us at the conclusion of the day, as these [songs] go forth to you like new [garments].

O Vājas, come hither to us; O R̥bhukṣans, great heroes, being praised, come for wealth. These drinks are for you at the arrival of the day; they have gone to our home like [cows] to their own stalls. 5.

O Vājas, Ṛbhukṣans, and Nara leaders, you who are our guides, come hither to us! What are you doing? Praising—that is, extolling—the great *draviṇas*, wealth (the genitive and accusative cases are used here for the same sense). That is, praising the great wealth. Furthermore, at the *abhipitve*—that is, at the arrival or gathering—at the third pressing (*savana*), these drinks (*pītayas*) come to you. Therein is an illustration: like cows that have recently calved (*navasvas*) returning to their home (*astam*). || 3 ||
O sons of strength, come hither to this sacrifice, being invoked with reverence;
being of one accord, drink of the honeyed draught for which you are praised, together with Sūrya—ye who are bestowers of treasures, accompanied by Indra.

O sons of strength, come hither to this sacrifice, being impelled by our homage; being of one accord, drink of the sweet [soma] of him with whom you are, O bestowers of treasures, accompanied by Indra. 6.

O sons of *śavas* (strength), or rather, those who do not cause its downfall— meaning, you who are powerful— being summoned by our homage (*namas*), that is, by our hymn of praise, come hither to this sacrifice. Come near!
What are you like?
"Sajopasah" means being joyful together with Indra;
"murasah" means wise.
It is now stated what the connection is between this copulative compound (*dvandva*) and these [rules]:
the word *yasya* and the word *ca* are well-known [from the preceding rules].
The intention is this: "Because you belong to Indra, through the fashioning of horses appropriate for him.

Since this is so, therefore, being "Indravantaḥ"—possessing Indra because he is pleased with you—and being "Ratnadhāḥ," givers of delightful wealth, you "piba pibata" (drink, drink) the "madhvaḥ," the sweet Soma.
In harmony with Varuṇa, O Indra, drink the Soma; in harmony with the Maruts, O lover of songs, drink it.
In harmony with those who drink first and those who drink at the appointed seasons, in harmony with the waters that yield treasures, drink in harmony.

In harmony with Varuṇa, O Indra, drink the Soma in harmony; O lover of songs, drink it in harmony with the Maruts, with those who drink first, with those who drink by the seasons, in harmony with the wives of the gods who bestow treasures—drink in harmony! 7.
O Indra, being in harmony with Varuṇa—the deity presiding over sovereignty—drink, that is, consume the Soma.
O Girvaṇas, O Indra who art to be praised and honored by songs, being united with the Maruts, drink, that is, consume the Soma.

Furthermore, [the phrase] "with the *agrepa*s," meaning with the first drinkers; and "with the *ṛtupa*s," meaning with the deities of the *ṛtuyāja* offerings; and "with the *grās*," meaning with the wives (*patnīs*).
The goddesses who are the protectors of women are the "wives" (*patnyaḥ*). With them.
"Menā grāḥ" refers to women, according to the *Nirukta* (3.21).
"Drink together with the Ṛbhus, who are bestowers of delightful wealth (*ratnadhābhiḥ*);
or alternatively," [the text continues].
This is a qualification of him by means of the wives of the clans;
or, "drink the Soma together with them in harmony."
Rejoice together with the Ādityas, O you who possess vigor; rejoice together with the mountains, O Ṛbhus.
Rejoice together with the divine Savitṛ, rejoice together with the rivers that bestow jewels.
Rejoice together with the Ādityas; O Ṛbhus, rejoice together with the mountains; rejoice together with divine Savitṛ; rejoice together with the rivers that bestow treasures. 8.
O Ṛbhus, being in harmony with the Ādityas, do you rejoice together;
likewise, being in harmony with the Parvatas—the specific deities worshipped on the joints (parvan)—do you rejoice together.
And so, being in harmony with Savitṛ, who is beneficial to the gods, and being in harmony with the Sindhus—the flowing deities who bestow jewels—do you rejoice together.
1. la-sa—because of the manifestation of that which is appropriate for it;
2. kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha-bha—by means of that; 3. kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha—of delightful riches.

Those who [are] the Aśvins, those who [are] the two parents, those who by their aid fashioned the milch-cow—the Ṛbhus—who [are] the horses, those who are fearless, those who separately [fashioned] heaven and earth—those far-reaching heroes who have created noble offspring. 9. Those who [are] the Aśvins, those who [are] the two parents, those who by their aid fashioned the milch-cow—the Ṛbhus—who [are] the horses, those who are fearless, those who separately [fashioned] heaven and earth—those far-reaching heroes who have created noble offspring. 9.
"The *Ṛbhus*, by means of their skillful action (*ūtyā*)—namely, the construction of the chariot—gratified the two Aśvins.
And they fashioned the two parents, who had become decrepit, into youths through their craftsmanship. And they fashioned the cow, by restoring her to life after she had died."
And those who fashioned the horses and pairs of horses;
who by their insights brought forth the cow from the barren rock, and who made the two who were aging into young men—this has been stated [in Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.161.7].
And those who made armor, shields, and breastplates for the gods.
And those who "separately" (*ṛdhak*) made "Heaven and Earth" (*rodasī*, i.e., *dyāvāpṛthivī*);

likewise, those "all-pervading" (*vibhvaḥ*) *Ṛbhus*, the "leaders" (*naraḥ*), performed "good offspring" (*svapatyāni*)—that is, deeds that are the means for their own falling [into action] or the means for attaining [their goals].
This connects with the word "not-impelled" (*neṣpr̥śāḥ*) later on.

O Ṛbhus, you who bestow wealth consisting of cattle, possessing vigor, rich in heroes, full of riches, and abounding in food; being joyous and leading the way, grant that wealth to us, as well as to those who praise your gift. 10. O Ṛbhus, you who bestow wealth consisting of cattle, possessing vigor, rich in heroes, full of riches, and abounding in food; being joyous and leading the way, grant that wealth to us, as well as to those who praise your gift. 10.

O Ṛbhus, you who maintain for me that which is rich in cattle, provided with cows, possessed of vigor, endowed with food, filled with excellent sons, replete with wealth such as houses fit for dwelling,
abundant in riches, and full of many people— O Ṛbhus, being the first drinkers and rejoicing, bestow upon us, O Agni, that wealth!
And those who praise the gift, the giving, or the Soma.
"Bestow [it] upon them"; or rather, "and those sacrificers who praise the gift (rāti), bestow it upon them as well."

You have not failed; we have not satiated you. O Ṛbhus, you have not been left unpraised in this sacrifice. Rejoice together with Indra, rejoice with the Maruts, and rejoice with the Kings, O gods, for the bestowal of treasures! 11. You have not failed; we have not satiated you. O Ṛbhus, you have not been left unpraised in this sacrifice. Rejoice together with Indra, rejoice with the Maruts, and rejoice with the Kings, O gods, for the bestowal of treasures! 11.

Do not be disaffected. And we have not failed to satisfy you; let us not leave you utterly unsatisfied.
Therefore, O Ṛbhus, being gods who are beyond reproach and blameless, rejoice together with Indra in this sacrifice; rejoice together with the Maruts.
O you who shine like kings and other gods, rejoice together and be satisfied.
For what purpose? For the bestowal of jewels—that is, for the giving of delightful wealth.
4 | The third hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with “*iha upa yāta*,” is the *ārṣa* of Vāmadeva; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and belongs to the *ārbhava* [laud].
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*iha upa nava*.”
This is the *ṛjīṣīyama-sūkta* for the Maitrāvaruṇa at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘Ā tvā vahantu... iha upa yāta’ is the recitation" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.5).
“Come hither, O sons of strength, O Ṛbhus, sons of Sudhanvan; do not stay away.”
In this libation of yours is the bestowal of treasure; may the exhilarations follow after Indra for you.
Come hither, O sons of strength, O R̥bhus, sons of Sudhanvan; do not stay away! For in this libation of yours is the bestowal of treasure; may the exhilarations follow after Indra for you. 1.

O sons of Śavas, O sons of Bala—those who are not his destroyers; O Saudhanvanas, sons of Sudhanvan; O Ṛbhus, come hither to this third libation. Do not stay away; do not remain distant. Following Indra, the bestower of delightful wealth, at this libation, may the exhilarating Soma juices reach you.
The word *anu* is connected with the verb;
the meaning is: "May they come toward you, O Indra. The particle *hi* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).
O descendants of Aṅgiras, here is the drinking of the well-pressed Soma, which has become a source of jewels;
for through skillful action and dexterity, you fashioned the single chalice into four parts.

O Agni, here has been the bestowal of treasure for the Ṛbhus; here was the drinking of the well-pressed Soma, since through skillful action and excellent workmanship, you fashioned the single chalice into fourfold.
O Ṛbhus, may that treasure-bestowing gift of jewels come to me here at your third libation;
or rather,
may the jewel of Soma itself come to you.
Because the drinking—that is, the consumption—of the well-pressed *soma* was obtained by Prajāpati; this is the meaning.
If one asks, "How so?", it is said:

Since, by means of skillful manual dexterity (*sukṛtyā*) and through the desire for the craft of constructing beautiful chariots and other works (*svapasyā*), you made the single chalice (*camasa*) fourfold, even though it was one. (Note:
1. The phrase "O Ṛbhus, you" does not appear in the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, sa.
2. The phrase "do not depart" does not appear in the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, sa.)
3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and ‘sa, the reading *saṃ madatha* does not exist.
4. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa, [the reading is] *indram*. 5. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, and sa, *ratnam āgamata*.
"You carved the chalice into four parts, O friend; you taught us and spoke.
Then, O Vājas, you became a troop of gods on the path of immortality, you skillful-handed ones."
"You have made the chalice fourfold; O friend, bestow [the wealth]!"—so he spoke. Then, O Vājas, you R̥bhus with skillful hands went upon the path of immortality to the host of the gods.
O Ṛbhus, you divided the chalice into four;
having divided it, O friend, O you who have become friends, you said, "Teach us how to partake of the Soma," thus you spoke. Then indeed, he did not speak anything unpleasant to us.
"What is it?
[The answer is: O Vājas, O Ṛbhus, you who have skillful hands—go, travel upon the path of immortality, that is, the path of heaven characterized by the nature of being deathless.
What is that immortality?
He approached the host, the assembly, of the gods beginning with Indra.
Of what material was this cup that you fashioned with fourfold skill through your wisdom?
Now press out all of it for exhilaration; drink, O Ṛbhus, of the honeyed Soma.

Of what was it made? Of wood, O Śilpa. A cup? Yes. This was it, which you fashioned into four with your skillful art. Now press it out; drink from it all for exhilaration, O Ṛbhus, from this honeyed Soma. 4.

Of what nature was it, O Śiva, and what was its essence? This was the cup. [The word] *āsa* is used here in the sense of a question. That single cup which they fashioned into four by means of the wisdom and skill belonging to the seers (*kavīnām*), those possessed of intelligence—now, at this pressing (*savanam*): *savanaḥ* refers to Soma, for it is pressed out; press that for exhilaration, O officiating priests! And you, O Ṛbhus, drink the draught of the sweet honey associated with Soma, the *somya*.
By your skillful power you made your two parents young; by your skillful power you fashioned the chalice for the drinking of the gods;
by your skillful power, O Ṛbhus, possessors of wealth and prizes, you provided the two bay steeds that carry Indra and bring swift gain.

By skillful power you made your parents young; by skillful power you fashioned the cup for the drinking of the gods. By skillful power, O Ṛbhus, you fashioned the two bay steeds, the swiftest, the carriers of Indra—ye who possess wealth as your prize. 1. O Vājas, ye Ṛbhus with beautiful hands, endowed with excellent hands—you have divided the cup into four parts.
Having done so, O friends, you spoke to the one who was like a friend, saying, "Teach him [the way] to drink Soma" through your favor.
Now, you have approached the path, the way to the immortal, to the heaven whose nature is deathlessness.

What is that immortality? It is the assembly, the gathering of the gods, Indra and the others, which you have reached. (The reading "na prāptāḥ" [you have not reached] does not exist. 2. The variants kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa do not contain the word "āsa."
3. [The reading] "madhāvinā" does not exist in manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa.

4. [The reading] "madhusama" exists in manuscripts kha, ṇa, and ma. O jewels among horses, O Ṛbhus, you who possess delightful Soma-food, by means of your skillful action (*śacyā*), you made your parents—young, indeed youthful—into two youths.
Likewise, by means of *śacī* (skillful power), they made the cup for the gods' drinking—that which is fit for the gods' drinking—into four parts; that is to say, they fashioned it into four.
By means of *śacī*, they fashioned the two bay horses (*harī*) through carving; that is, they brought them to completion by means of chiseling.
Of what sort were the two bay horses?
The two excellent archers, swift-moving, the bearers of Indra, those who carry Indra.
O Vājās, for him who at the close of days drinks the sharp [Soma] entirely for intoxication—
for him, O Ṛbhus, you bulls, rejoicing, fashion wealth consisting of all heroic sons.

He who presses [the Soma] at the arrival of the days—O Vājas, for his exhilaration, [make] the [Soma] strong and complete; for him, O Rbhus, you bulls, rejoicing, fashion wealth consisting of all heroes. 6.
O Ṛbhus, O Vājas, you who possess food— may that sacrificer for whom [this is prepared] at the arrival, that is, at the onset of the days, specifically at the third pressing (*savana*),
which is the intense and most delightful libation, [attain success].
*Savana* means that which is pressed; it refers to Soma.

One presses it for intoxication. For him, O *vṛṣaṇaḥ*—the showerers of fruit—rejoicing and delighting within, fashion and accomplish wealth consisting of many sons and all heroic offspring. "Fashion" (*takṣata*) here means to bring about or to perfect.

O Lord of the bay horses, you drank the pressed juice at dawn; the midday draught is all yours alone. Drink now with those who bestow jewels, for you, O Indra, have made your friends rejoice through their good deeds.

In the morning you drank the pressed juice, O Lord of the Bay Horses; at midday, drink all of it that is yours alone. Drink together with the Ṛbhus, the bestowers of treasures—those whom you, O Indra, have made your friends through their skillful deeds.
O Indra, Lord of the bay horses (Haryaśva), you drank the pressed Soma juice at every morning libation.
The midday libation belongs to you alone; it is yours and not that of others. Since the two libations have been mentioned separately, the third libation remains [implied].
At the third pressing, drink together with the *Ṛbhus*, who bestow delightful gifts;
O Indra, those *Ṛbhus* whom you made your friends through their excellent work (*sukṛtyā*).
Those gods who, through their skillful work, became manifest and settled upon heaven like hawks;
may they, the sons of Śavas, the sons of Sudhanvan, bestow treasure—those immortal ones who have become manifest.
Those who became gods through their good deeds have settled upon heaven like hawks; O sons of Śavas, O sons of Sudhanvan, bestow wealth, for you have become immortal. 8.
1. In manuscripts Na, La, and Sa, "aśvau" (two horses) is not present.
2. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Sa, "tam" (him/that) is not present.
O Ṛbhus! You who, through *sukṛtyā*—by means of excellent deeds—became gods (*devāḥ abhavata*).
By whom those of praiseworthy course were summoned—like special vultures in the sky, seated upon the celestial realm—O sons of strength, O powerful ones, do you bestow wealth and treasure!
O sons of Sudhanvan, you have become immortal gods.
That third treasure of all, which you have sought with skillful hands through your craft—this has been poured out for you;
drink it with exhilarating, invigorating draughts.

That third treasure, most pervasive, which you have won through your skillful work and deft hands—O Ṛbhus, that [gift] of yours has been poured out; drink it together with these exhilarating draughts that bestow power. 9.

O Rbhus, you who have beautiful hands—skilled-handed ones—you have fashioned the delightful gift of jewels; for you have prepared the third libation through your wondrous work. Drink together with those exhilarating powers of yours, which are associated with this libation—the Soma substance contained therein—which has been thoroughly poured out.

Although the mouth alone is the instrument for drinking, nevertheless, because satisfaction arises through seeing, hearing, and so forth, the eyes, ears, and other organs are also metaphorically designated as "vessels."
The fourth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "anaśvo jātaḥ," is the Ābhava hymn.
The seer is Vāmadeva.
This first verse is a Triṣṭubh; the remaining verses are Jagatīs according to the technical rule regarding those containing the word "pṛṣṭavant."
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: "The next [verse], 'anaśvo,' is a *triṣṭubh*.
This [verse] is the *nivid*-insertion for the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra* on the third day of the *ābhiplavika* period.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'anaśvo jātaḥ pavatau ya' is the *vaiśvadeva* [śastra]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.7).
The horseless, reinless, praiseworthy chariot with three wheels revolves through the mid-air.
Great indeed is that proclamation of the god, that you two, having become immortal, nourish the earth.

Without horses, born, without reins, worthy of praise, the three-wheeled chariot rolls around the realm. This is the great proclamation of your divinity, O Ṛbhus, that you cause the earth to flourish. 1.
O Ṛbhus, this chariot belonging to the Aśvins, given by you, was produced without horses, having become independent of any means of transport;

likewise, though without reins and free from a driver, it is worthy of praise (*ukthya*), possesses three wheels, and revolves throughout the mid-air (*rajas*). That great and abundant work of yours in the construction of the chariot is a proclaimer of your divinity, making known your status as gods.
And by whatever action you nourish—that is, make prosperous—the earth which [belongs] to whom; |||
1. In Na, La, and Sa, the phrase "the sons of Sudhanvan" is absent.
2. In Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Ta, Na, and Ma, [the text reads]: "Perform the third pressing accompanied by Soma and the Dānavas" (in Ta: "do not perform it"). 3. In La, it is devoid of the *graha* cups.
4. In the manuscripts Sa, Ga, Ca, and Ṇa, the word *amana* does not exist.
5. In the manuscripts Sa, Ga, Ca, and Ṇa, it reads *dyāvāpṛthivī vā* (not *na ca*).
Ṛgveda 2.82.
O wise ones, you who by meditation fashioned from thought a well-rolling chariot that does not weary horses—
O Vājas and Ṛbhus, we invoke you here at this sacrifice for the drinking of its libation.

Those of noble mind who fashioned the well-rolling chariot, which does not waver from the thought of the mind through meditation—to them indeed, O Vājas and Ṛbhus, we call you hither for the drinking of this libation at the place of sacrifice. 2.

The Ṛbhus, of pure mind and beautiful hearts, fashioned with their mental resolve—that is, through meditation and effort—this well-rounded chariot with its smooth-rolling wheels, which moves straight and without crookedness; they did this swiftly. Indeed, for that very purpose, O Vājās, O Ṛbhus, we announce you to this Soma for its drinking; we make you known here.
Therefore, O Vājas and Ṛbhus, your great power has become worthy of high praise among the gods;
for you fashioned your aged parents, who were worn out by time, into young men again so that they might move about.

Therefore, O Vājas, O Ṛbhus, your great power became renowned among the gods, O Vibhūs, since you fashioned your aged parents—who were worn out by time—into young men again for the sake of movement. || 3 ||
O Vājās, O Vṛbhas, O Vibhas—
this plural form is stated to be used for one another in relation to the others. That greatness, that majesty of yours among the gods became highly praiseworthy.
To this it is replied:
if you say that the parents, who were old and decrepit, having become youthful again, fashioned themselves for wandering—that is, for moving about as they desired—then [the meaning is] established.
You fashioned from a single chalice four vessels; by your insights, you brought forth the cow from the skin.
Then, through obedience, O Vājas and Ṛbhus, you attained immortality among the gods—this deed of yours is worthy of praise.

The single chalice you made became fourfold; by your insights, you brought forth the cow from the hide. Then you attained immortality among the gods. O Vājas and Ṛbhus, through your readiness to obey, that deed of yours is worthy of praise.
O Ṛbhus, you made that single cup—the vessel for drinking—into four branches;
"branches" (vayāḥ) means shoots;
you fashioned it as four-branched, having four parts.

Thus, by means of their insights and ritual acts, they fashioned forth a new cow from the hide; "fashioned forth" (*niravṛṇan*) is used here in place of "they completely produced" (*samastakuruta*). And for this reason, among the gods, they attained immortality.
O Vājās, O Vṛbhus, such is your deed;
"śruṣṭī" is a name for speed—
it quickly becomes praiseworthy.
1. A wheel with the excellent turning of *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha*; a wheel with the excellent turning of *sa*.
2. There is no "at will" (*yathēccham*) for *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*.

From the *Ṛbhus* comes wealth, most renowned, which the heroes, famed for their vigor, have generated; fashioned by *Vibhvan*, it is to be proclaimed at the assemblies—O Gods, he whom you protect is the one who observes all people. (5) From the *Ṛbhus* comes wealth, most renowned, which the heroes, famed for their vigor, have generated; fashioned by *Vibhvan*, it is to be proclaimed at the assemblies—O Gods, he whom you protect is the one who observes all people. (5)

From the *ṛbhus*, from the presence of the *ṛbhus*, [comes] that which is most preeminent in fame (*prathamaśravastamaḥ*)—wherein "fame" (*śravaḥ*) refers here to renown or wealth (*rayiḥ*). May that wealth be ours; this is the ellipsis. The *ṛbhus*—the leaders (*naras*) who are celebrated for their strength (*vājaśrutāmas*), having been manifested through the greatness of Agni’s power—generated (*ajījanan*) that wealth. They brought it forth.

Fashioned by Vibhvan, fashioned by all the Ṛbhus—this chariot of the Aśvins (or this ladle) is perfected through their craftsmanship; it is to be proclaimed, that is, to be praised preeminently, at the *vidathas*, the sacrifices.
O radiant gods, you who protect—that is, guard—this chariot (or ladle), it becomes *vicarṣaṇi*:
one who sees in various ways, meaning it becomes worthy of being seen.

He is the prize-winning steed; he is the seer through his inspired speech; he is the hero, the archer, invincible in battles. He bestows abundance of wealth and heroic might upon him whom Vāja, Vibhvan, and the Ṛbhus have protected. 6. He is the prize-winning steed; he is the seer through his inspired speech; he is the hero, the archer, invincible in battles. He bestows abundance of wealth and heroic might upon him whom Vāja, Vibhvan, and the Ṛbhus have protected. 6.
That steed, being swift and powerful, becomes one skilled in running;
that seer, possessing knowledge beyond the senses, becomes endowed with eloquence through praise;
and that hero, being courageous, becomes a hurler and slayer of enemies.
And he himself becomes invincible in battles and in the midst of armies; he cannot be overcome.
Yama indeed bestows—indeed, grants—the increase of wealth, the abundance of riches;
he bestows—indeed, grants—great heroic power, the state of being a great hero.
"That man whom Vāja, Vibhvan, and the Ṛbhus have clothed and protected"—
meaning "he who becomes exactly like them.
The intention [of using the plural] for another [deity] is due to the frequent usage of the term *Ṛbhu* as a designation for a portion of the plural.

A most excellent and beautiful form has been bestowed upon you; O Vājas and Ṛbhus, take pleasure in this hymn of praise! For you are wise, skillful, and inspired poets; we make ourselves known to you by means of this sacred prayer (brahman). śreṣṭham | vaḥ | peśaḥ | adhi | dhāyi | darśatam | stomaḥ | vājāḥ | ṛbhavaḥ | tam | jujuṣṭana | dhīrāsaḥ | hi | stha | kuvaryaḥ | vipaścitaḥ | tān | vaḥ | enā | brahmaṇā | ā | vedayāmasi ||7||
1. In manuscripts la, 0, and śrava, "agneḥ" is absent. 2. In manuscripts na, la, sa, and 'a, "agneḥ" is absent.
3. In manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pa, pha, bha, and sadasi, it reads "khyātaḥ"; in manuscript gha, "sa", and "sadābhikhyātaḥ"; and in manuscript ta, "sadābhikhyātaḥ".
4. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, bha, yaṃ: a cup (camasa) or a chariot (ratha).
5. Kha, ga, gha, ṇa, ta, na, bha: the giver (dātā); sa: then (tadā). 6. Ta: the activity (vyavahāra) of the Ṛbhus.
The most excellent, well-fashioned, and therefore beautiful form has been displayed for you; it has been placed upon you as a wondrous shape.
O Vājas and Ṛbhus, enjoy—that is, accept—the hymn of praise composed by us.
For you are renowned as wise, intelligent, poets, sagacious, and learned; we make you known through this *brahman*, this mantra consisting of a recitation (*śastra*).

Alternatively, those wise ones characterized as described above praise the limbs of the hymn and the vehicle; this is the ellipsis. We cause them to be known through the sacred word (*brahman*); that is, we make them manifest.
From your inspired wisdom, O wise ones, bestow upon us all manly enjoyments;
fashion for us, O Ṛbhus, resplendent strength, most excellent vigor, and desirable wealth.
O wise ones, from your inspired thoughts, fashion for us all manly enjoyments, brilliant strength, and most excellent, bull-like vigor; O Ṛbhus, fashion for us wealth and desirable treasures. 8.
O Ṛbhus, you [should grant] to us from our *dhiṣaṇās*—that is, from the hymns of praise which serve as the instrumental cause.
The word *pari* here restates the sense of the ablative case.
Alternatively, being wise and knowing all things, fashion and accomplish for us all those human-like enjoyments (*naryāṇi bhojanā*) that are beneficial to men and superior to our own thoughts.

Moreover, O Ṛbhus, fashion for us—our offspring and our food—splendid and radiant wealth in the form of gold and other riches, powerful strength, the drying-up power of those who are vigorous and virile, and supreme prosperity.
Bestowing offspring here, bestowing wealth here, fashion for us here a fame rich in heroes—by which we may distinguish ourselves above others. O Ṛbhus, grant us wondrous strength!
Bestowing upon us offspring here, wealth here, and here fashion for us a fame rich in heroes—O Ṛbhus, grant us that wonderful prize by which we may distinguish ourselves above all others. 9.
Rejoicing and delighting in this sacrifice of ours, fashion—that is, bring about—for us progeny in the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth;
fashion wealth right here in this sacrifice;
and fashion glory—fame endowed with the excellence of heroes and the like—right here in this sacrifice.
Furthermore, O Ṛbhus, grant us—that is, give to us—that wonderful (citra) food (vāja), by which we may surpass and be known as superior to others who are our equals.
1. In the manuscripts Na, La, and Sa, "abhavat" does not exist.

2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, and Bha, "yadvā...adhikāni" does not exist. 3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, and Bha, "saṃpādayata" does not exist; in Gha, it reads "saṃpāditavantaḥ."

4. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the word *ṛbhavaḥ* does not appear. 5. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the phrase *stutāḥ santaḥ prajāṃ* is absent; in manuscript na, *ramamāṇāḥ...rūpāṃ* is absent. 6. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and bha, the word *iha* appears; in manuscript na, *saṃpādayata* is absent.
The fifth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with “upa no vājāḥ,” is the ṛṣi Vāmadeva’s composition; it is addressed to the Ābhṛvas and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The fifty-fifth verse is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
Thus it has been enumerated: “upa no—aṣṭau [verses], ending with four Anuṣṭubhs.”
In the Vaiśvadeva-śastra on the sixth day of the ten-night *Dyūḍha* sacrifice, the first four [verses] are to be recited;
for it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Ārbhava [laud] consists of thirteen verses, beginning with 'upa no vājāḥ', and [ending with] four" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).

May the Vājas come near to us; O Ṛbhukṣans, you gods, come by the paths traveled by the gods, so that you, the joyful ones, may all establish yourselves at this sacrifice among these people on auspicious days.

O Ṛbhukṣans, O gods, come to our sacrifice with strength by the paths traveled by the gods, so that you all may take pleasure in this sacrifice of man on these auspicious days, as you have done for us before. 1.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, O Ṛbhus, O gods, come to our sacrifice (adhvara), that is, approach it,
by means of paths (pathibhiḥ) to be traveled by the gods (devayānaiḥ).

Just as (yathā), O delightful (raṇvāḥ) Ṛbhus, among these very (āsu) subjects (viśveṣu)— that is, among the sacrificers connected with Manu— you maintain (dadhidhve) our sacrifice on the auspicious days (sudineṣu) of the days (ahnām).
Just as you have attained a state of joy by means of this sacrifice, so may it come to the sacrificer.

May these sacrifices, dripping with ghee and pleasing to you, be dear today to your heart and mind; may the pressed juices, full and golden-hued, flow forth for you, and when drunk, may they exhilarate you for wisdom and skill.

May these sacrifices be pleasing to your heart and mind today—those which are beloved and clothed in ghee. May the pressed juices flow forth for you; may they, when full, bring exhilaration for your will and skill, and when drunk, provide delight.

"Today," on this day of sacrifice, "these"—namely these Soma juices which are the means of the sacrifice—"may they be for your heart," for your mind, for its delight. On this day, may the "acceptable" and sufficient Somas, "garmented in ghee"—that is, appearing radiant through the mixing substance—go to your heart. The "pressed" Somas, filled in the cups, are "offered forth" for your sake.
Or alternatively:
this is a form of the root *haryati*, which means "to desire";
they intensely desire you.
"Drunk for the sake of wisdom, for the sake of action, and for the sake of skill, may they cause us to rejoice."
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, just as you have received this triple increase ordained by the gods, so may this hymn of praise be offered to you;
like Manu, I pour out the Soma among all you people dwelling in the highest heavens.

The threefold increase; that which is ordained by the gods; even as for you, O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, [the gift] has been bestowed through our hymns—so do I offer the Soma to you among the later clans, as Manu did, together with all [the gods] who dwell in the high heavens. 3.

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha, the phrase “*dve vājāḥ*” is absent. 2. In the manuscript Pa and Bha, there is our own reading: *yāgam*. 3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha, it is *vājāḥ*. 4. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, and Pha, Bha, it is *te*; in Na and Sa, it is *ete*. 5. In the manuscripts Na, La, and Bha, it is *hṛdayāya*. 6. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Pa, Pha, and Bha, it is *savaneṣu*. 7. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Pha, and Bha, it is *balāya*. The meaning is: that which is the first, rising in heaven, accompanied by the three pressings (*trayasavana*), beneficial to the gods, known as Soma—the food beneficial for the gods or ordained by the gods—standing at the third pressing.
Just as this gift maintains you—
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, O Ṛbhus— just as this hymn of praise maintains you;
[so may it maintain you] in the lower regions.
The *uparās* are those who delight near the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*).

Among those *viśvas*, among the *bṛhadivas*, among the gods who bestow abundant gifts, I offer the Soma—just as Manu did—for your sake (*yuṣme*), together with me (*maccā*), in many houses, having set it forth; I sacrifice it.

Fat-horsed, with radiant chariots, indeed, you have become the goal-seekers; fair-cheeked, vigorous, and adorned with fine golden neck-ornaments—O sons of Indra, O grandsons of Might, your foremost [drink] has been recognized for your exhilaration. 4. Fat-horsed. With radiant chariots. Indeed. You have become. Goal-seekers. Fair-cheeked. Vigorous. Adorned with fine golden neck-ornaments. Of Indra. O sons. Of Might. O grandsons. Your foremost [drink] has been recognized for your exhilaration. 4.
O Vājins, O Ṛbhus, you whose horses are fat— meaning those who possess such fat horses—
and likewise whose chariots are radiant, meaning whose chariots are shining, and who have iron helmets;
*śipra* means either a cheek or a nose.
O you whose helmets are made of the essence of iron, who wear golden ornaments, and who possess splendid wealth—be present!
O sons of Indra, you who are to be protected like sons; O grandsons of strength, you mighty ones—for you, for your exhilaration, it has been recognized and followed:
the third libation, which is foremost among the gods and preeminent.

We invoke R̥bhu, O R̥bhukṣans, for wealth, for strength most powerful, for vigor accompanied by Indra—the ever-conquering one who possesses the Aśvins. 5. R̥bhu; O R̥bhukṣans; wealth; strength; most powerful; vigor; accompanied by Indra; we invoke; ever-conquering; possessing the Aśvins. 5.

O Ṛbhukṣans, O Ṛbhus, we invoke—that is, we call upon—your host: the Ṛbhu, who is widely shining; wealth in the form of riches (so called because they are the cause of it); most powerful in battle; a companion endowed with mutual cooperation; possessed of Indra; accompanied by Indra; most excellent in granting exhilaration at all times; possessing horses. We invoke your assembly.

O Ṛbhus, that mortal whom you and Indra protect—may he be a winner of spoils through his prayers; may he be a winner of horses. O Ṛbhus, that mortal whom you and Indra protect—may he be a winner of spoils through his prayers; may he be a winner of horses.

1. [The syllables] kha, ga, ṇa, na, and ma are present. 2. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and la are situated in the third *savana*; [the syllable] bha is situated in the third *savana*. 3. [The syllables] ga and ca do not exist among the gods.

4. With *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *bha*, they are excellent chariots (*suṣṭhu rathāḥ*); with *na*, *sa*, and *sapta*, they are chariots; with *pa*, they are excellent chariots. 5. With *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *bha*, they are like iron (*ayovat*) and possess portions that have become essential (*sārabhūtanāṃśikāḥ*); with *pa*, they are like iron and possess noses that have become essential (*sārabhūtanāsikāḥ*). 6. With *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, and *bha*, they are sons (*sūnavaḥ*), [that is,] children.
7. *Kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha-bha* is indeed the third libation (*tṛtīyasavana*).
O *ṛbhus*, whoever you and Indra, and whoever you and Aryaman protect and guard—that very person shall be so;
let it be thus.
The meaning is that no other may be superior.
May he alone be the winner (*sanitā*) through his insights and deeds;
may he alone be the one who shares in the distribution of wealth (*meghasātā*) at the sacrifice; and may he alone be joined with the swift, racing steed.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, you who are far-famed, come hither for our sacrifice;
as patrons, being praised, may you cause all our quarters to prosper.
O Vājas, O R̥bhukṣans, find for us the paths to sacrifice; O patrons, being praised, may you enable us to cross over all regions. 7.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, O Ṛbhus, discern—make known—the paths, the ways of sacrifice for us to perform;
that is to say, enlighten us. O wise ones, being praised by us, cross over all the quarters, all the directions, for our sake.
The remainder is explained by demonstrating its capacity.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, O Indra, O Nāsatyas, bestow upon us that wealth consisting of horses, surpassing all other men; O Maghavans, grant it abundantly.
O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, O Indra, O Nāsatyas, bestow upon us wealth and horses, more than all other people; O Maghavans, grant it abundantly. 8.
Having concluded this hymn of praise, you offer a desired prayer:

O Vājas, O Ṛbhukṣans, O Ṛbhus, O Indra, O Nāsatyas, Aśvins—you all, for us, for these people, for us human beings who are your worshippers, bestow that abundant wealth, that great riches, and many horses; O generous lords, grant them to us for the giving of wealth, pray for them together with perfect aspiration.

The hymn beginning with “*uta vām hi*” consists of ten verses (though six are used). Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*). Dadhikrā is the deity (*devatā*). The first verse is addressed to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*). Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*uta vām hi*—ten [verses]; dedicated to Dadhikrā; the first is for Heaven and Earth. The application (*viniyoga*) is determined by the indicative marks of the text.
For indeed, yours are those ancient gifts which Trasadasyu bestowed upon the many;
you gave him the winner of fields, the winner of fertile lands, and a fierce, overwhelming weapon to crush the Dasyus.

Moreover, indeed, yours are those ancient gifts which Trasadasyu bestowed for the sake of liberating many; you two gave him mastery over fields and mastery over fertile lands, a fierce and overwhelming blow against the Dasyus.
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa occur. 2. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and ma conclude the praise (*stuti*).
3. [The syllables] kha, ga, ṇa, and bha belong to the first *dyāvāpṛthivī* (Heaven and Earth); [the syllables] gha, ca, ta, pa, and pha belong to the second *dyāvāpṛthivī*.
The particle *uto* is used for filling the meter.
Since this [verse] refers to Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), even though the specific words for them are absent here, they are nonetheless to be addressed.

O Heaven and Earth, "from you two" (*vām*), from the presence of Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa, who is the giver (*dātrā*)—the agent of giving—"have been obtained" (*labdhāni*) "ancient" (*pūrvā*) riches, whether meaning former things or cities.
Whatever riches King Trasadasyu bestowed upon the many guests, the men—
the horses, being "winners of fields" (kṣetrasāḥ), because they win all lands and territories, were among those he gave.
They gave it to him.
Likewise [they gave] the *urvarās*.
An *urvarā* is all the earth that yields grain.
"He bestows that," thus he is the son of the fertile land (urvarā).
You two have given him;
you have given him a "ghanam"—a weapon fit for striking—for the sake of slaying the Dasyus.
What kind of weapon?
One that is "overpowering" (abhibhūta) and "overpowering" (abhibhavitṛ), "fierce" (ugra), and possessing "uprooted strength" (udghūrṇabala).
Or alternatively:
The latter half [of the verse] constitutes a single sentence: "You two have granted [these things]; you two have given a son characterized by non-blindness. You two have bestowed them.
The meaning is that they should grant those [gifts] to me as well:
"Or indeed, you two have granted the prize-winning steed, the one who overcomes many enemies, Dadhikrā, who belongs to all people;
the straight-flying hawk, the speckled one, the swift, the active one—like a noble king, a hero."

And you two have granted the prize-winning Dadhikrāvan, who is rich in many gifts, who belongs to all people, who is straight-flying, a hawk with speckled limbs, swift, worthy of being honored, and like a brave king over his subjects. 2.
Moreover, "vājinam" means the swift one;
or it refers to the deity in the form of a horse, because he is called Dadhikrā in the form of Aṅgiras.
His status as the lord of the Aṅgirases is recorded in the Brāhmaṇa: "Having become Miśra, he rushed toward them."
"Dadhikrā," the repeller of many—that is, the repeller of many enemies;
"Dadhikrā" is so called because he holds or bestows desirable things (*kāmatāti*).
He is this very god who has been described.
Oṃ: Pūraṇaḥ.
"Viśvakṛṣṭim": one whose "kṛṣṭis"—meaning all people who are to be protected or who are his servants—are universal.
"Ṛjipyam":
he who moves or reaches straight forward is called ṛjipya.

That "śyena" (hawk)—one whose movement is like that of a hawk, "pṛṣitapsu" (having bright-colored water or radiant form), "āśu" (swift) or "vyāpta" (pervasive), "aryah" (of the noble one), "cakrtyam" (of a habit to cut or destroy), "śūram" (heroic), and "nṛpatim na" (like a king among men)—the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, "dadathuḥ," they support and sustain that divine being.
He whom everyone, exulting, strikes down as he rushes along like a torrent across the boundary—
him who is celebrated on his back, like a sacrificial hero, who outstrips chariots and darts away like the wind.

Whomever he follows along his course like one rushing down a slope, everyone there welcomes him with joy on their backs—him who is eager, like a sacrificial steed, a hero swift on his chariot, darting forth like the wind. 3.
The connection is as follows: "whom—Dadhikrā—every (*viśvaḥ*), that is, every single (*puruḥ*) human being, *harṣamāṇaḥ*, meaning rejoicing or causing joy, *mardati*, meaning praises;
[to] that god, Heaven and Earth gave.
Thus the god is further specified.

"He who, like water flowing in due succession along a downward-sloping path that inclines in every direction, rushes and moves forward, and who, with his hind legs, strives and longs to leap across the quarters."

1. *ta-vāṃ* means "you two. 2. *ta-arthamanuṣyebhyaḥ* [means] "for the sake of men. 3. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, and *bha*, it is *dadathuḥ* or *dadāthām*. 4. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *bha*, the word *'hananāī'* does not exist; in *na*, it is *'ghātāīm'*. 5. *ta-ityarthaḥ* [means] "in this sense. The particle *hi* is a filler (*pūraṇaḥ*). 6. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, and *bha*, it is *dadhikrākhyā*; in *sa*, it is *dadhikrākhyam*. 7. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, *sa*, and *ta*, it is *ekam*. 8. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, the word *'vā'* does not exist. 9. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pha*, *bha*, and *sa*, it is *dīptasvarūpam*. 10. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *bha*, it is *ca*. 11. In the manuscripts *na*, *la*, and *sa*, it is *pravatā*. 12. In manuscript *ca*, it is *pravaṇeneva*; in *pha*, it is *pravaṇenaiva*. 13. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, the word *'gacchantam'* does not exist.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a hero who desires battle, one who is brave and powerful in the forest.
Or rather:
like the Adhvaryu and other priests desiring to enter the sacrifice;
like Vātaraṇa, who goes by means of a chariot; like Vātaja, who moves swiftly; like Vāyu itself.
The meaning is that we praise and uphold that God, just as all people praise the water, heroes, and winds when they are distinguished by the aforementioned specific qualities.

He who, restraining himself, moves apart from the assemblies while among the prizes, going away from the cattle; he who makes his strength manifest, perceiving the sacrifices, surpasses the steward of the living man.

He who, seizing the prize in battles, moves as a conqueror among the cattle, making his power manifest as he goes; he who perceives the assemblies and looks across the waters of the living man beyond the reach of the chariot-pole.
He who is indeed the god who [bestows] things to be grasped; for the Nirukta states: "The root *gadhyati* has the sense of the act of mixing."

The fruits are to be mixed; in battles, he who restrains [the enemy] while warding them off from all sides is the one who bestows wealth (*vasanutaraḥ*) and is the distributor (*saṃbhaktaraḥ*). In all directions, or among the cattle as the objects [of his action], he who goes forth is *vagoṣu*. *Vāvirñjīkaḥ* means one whose means are manifested, or one who has manifested his speech. *Vavidathā* refers to the *vidathāni*, things to be known; he has understood (*nicikyad*) them. This is a verb meaning "to see. Knowing the *varatiḥ*—meaning suffering, that which leads away from pleasure, or an adversary—he, the *pari*, goes around (*carati*) and overcomes (*tiraskaroti*) him from every side.
"To whom [is it] 'araṇi'? It belongs to Vāyu, the pervading one, the praiser; or to the human sacrificer.
And indeed, the people cry out after him in battles like after a thief who has plundered a mouthful;
he who stoops low like a weary falcon, [driving] toward glory and toward the herd of cattle.

And indeed, the people cry out after him in battles like after a thief who has broken through the mouth [of his lair]—him who, like a weary falcon swooping downward, speeds toward glory and toward a herd rich in cattle.
Indeed, they have even brought forth Dadhikrā in the battles, like a swift falcon that devours its prey;
seeing him, men cry out after him, and likewise the deer low toward him.
Moreover, he pursues the one who moves lowly and swiftly, like a hungry hawk swooping down upon its quarry.
Just as birds flee upon seeing him, so too [the connection is that] the cows,

the food, or the fame— like a herd of cattle— approach him with longing as they go toward him, lamenting for him. The Nirukta passage beginning with "api smainaṃ vaktramādhimiva vaktramādhinam" (Nirukta 4.24) should be considered here.

1. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa* read *śīghram*; *sa* reads *śāghrantām*. 2. *ta* reads *uktaviśeṣapaga*. 3. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha* read *tathāpyayama*; *pa-pha* read *tatrāpi yama*. 4. *kha-ga-ca-pha* read *āvirbhūtarathasārathidhanaḥ*; *na* reads *āvirbhūtadhanasādhanaḥ*; *bha* reads *āvirbhūtanāsādhanaḥ*; *sa* reads *āvirbhūtena sādhanena*. 5. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha* read *paritiraścarati sarvataḥ* (*kha* reads *sarvaḥ*) [and] *tiraskegataṃ*. 6. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha* read *āpaha*; *na-sa* read *vāpasya*. 7. *ta-la* read *yajamānasya*. Or, *āpaḥ* may be a qualifier of the deity. *Addhayaḥ*: the meaning is "manifested. 8. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa* read *kośānta*. 9. *ta* reads *imenapāṃkṣaṇāmiva*. 10. *ta-pa* read *saṃbandhaḥ*. It is not a filler (*pūraṇaḥ*). 2-83.
And indeed, they shall be the first to race among us, as if trembling with the lines of chariots;
like a bridegroom adorning himself, he makes a garland, repeatedly licking the dust, visible as he scatters his rays.

And indeed, as he is about to be the first to run forth upon these [tracks], he trembles with the rows of chariots; like a bridegroom adorning himself, he repeatedly licks the dust, visible as he scatters his brilliance. 6.

Moreover, indeed, among these armies of the Asuras, he who is about to rush forth—desiring to flow forward—as the foremost, the most excellent, and the chief, being joined with rows and lines of chariots, goes down deeply;
he runs hither and thither.
Like what? Like... (as follows).
It is said:
"A garland" (*sraj*). A garland is an ornament because by means of it form is created—that is, produced.
Making her [the reins]—acting as one who prepares them—one who is beneficial to the people (*janya*), like a horse;
*śumbhā* means "shining," as it becomes beautiful (*suṣṭhu bhavati*).
He beheld the bit (*kiraṇa*) that had entered the mouth.
Furthermore, when he fights against a thousand from every side,
then, while he is striving for victory, he becomes terrible— a cause of fear, difficult to withstand, and hard to restrain.
And indeed, people praise his impetuous speed, his overwhelming power over the peoples, and the swiftness of the eager one.
And of him they say, when they part in the encounter: "Dadhikrā has sped away with thousands."

Moreover, people indeed praise his impetuous speed, his overwhelming power, and his swiftness as he plows through the lands. And of him they say when they part ways in battle: "Dadhikrā has sped away with thousands."
Moreover, people indeed praise and celebrate both the overwhelming power, the invincible might, the speed, and the supreme victory of that Dadhikrāvan.
What kind [of being]?
Let us now praise that swift Dadhikrā; let us also celebrate him as belonging to heaven and earth.
May the dawns flushing at daybreak inspire me; may they carry me across all difficulties.
The swift Dadhikrā—him indeed let us now praise; let us celebrate him of heaven and earth. May the dawning Dawns inspire me; may they carry me across all misdeeds. 1.
Let us now swiftly praise that very god Dadhikrā, the swift-moving;
and moreover, from heaven and from earth, let us scatter his fodder.
May the Dawns, as they shine forth dispelling the darkness, bring me prosperity and protect my fruits.
May they carry across all difficulties; may they bring us safely to the further shore.
Furthermore, in mantras addressed to other deities, the praise of those other deities is contradicted by their state of being [merely] drinking-troughs for them.
Great is the might of Dadhikrāvan, the steed who attains the seasons, the possessor of many boons, the bull;
he whom Mitra and Varuṇa beheld shining among the many like Agni, the conqueror.

I celebrate the great steed Dadhikrāvan, who fulfills the seasons, the possessor of many boons, the bull—him whom you two, O Mitra and Varuṇa, bestowed upon the many, shining like Agni, the conqueror. 2.

I, the fulfiller of rites through my action, celebrate— that is, I perform most excellently— the praise of the great Dadhikrāvan, who attains the cosmic order (*ṛta*), who is the steed of the desert, who possesses many boons, and who is the showerer of benefits for the many.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two have bestowed—that is, you maintain—for the benefit of many men that deliverer from distress, who shines like Agni, standing resplendent like the blazing fire.
May he who has offered praise to the horse Dadhikrāvan at the breaking of the dawn, with the fire kindled at its head, be made sinless by the goddess Atri; may he be in harmony with Mitra and Varuṇa.
Whoever has performed [the rite] for Dadhikrāvan, the steed, when the fire is kindled at the dawning of the dawn—may Aditi make him sinless; may he be in harmony with Mitra and Varuṇa. 3.

The sacrificer who has performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan— the horse, the pervasive one, or the one who has spread forth— at the dawning of the dawn, when the morning has arrived and the fire has been kindled,
[has done so] with Mitra and Varuṇa, the two deities presiding over day and night.

1. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the word *mahaḥ* (of the great) is absent after *mahataḥ*. 2. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the word *araṇakuśalasya* (of one skilled in non-straying) is present. 3. In the manuscripts na, la, and sa, the word *purubhiḥ* (by many) is absent. 4. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the reading is *dadhikrāvṇo mahaḥ* (the greatness of Dadhikrāvan). 5. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and bha, the word *yuvām* (you two) is absent. 6. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, bha, and sa, the reading is *nārayitāram* (the non-leader). 7. In manuscript pa, the reading is *yaṃ dadhikrāvāṇaṃ dadathaḥ* (whom you two give as Dadhikrāvan). 8. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the reading is *aśvasyāsya* (of this horse).
May Dadhikrā—the one who is harmonious (*sajoṣas*), whose delight is shared (*samānaprīti*), and who is indivisible (*aditi*)—make that sacrificer sinless, free from evil.

We invoke for our well-being Dadhikrāvan, the source of food and great strength; we invoke the auspicious name of the Maruts which we have meditated upon, and Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, and Indra who wields the thunderbolt in his arm.

Of Dadhikrāvan, of food, of strength, of greatness—whatever we have meditated upon as the auspicious name of the Maruts—for our well-being, we invoke Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, and Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt. 4.

Of *iṣ*, the provider of food; of *ūrj*, the provider of strength; of *mahaḥ*, the great; of the divine *Dadhikrāvan*; and of the Maruts, who are the very essence of hymns—there exists a blessed and auspicious name and form which we celebrate. Furthermore, we invoke Varuṇa and the other gods, who partake of the offerings, for our well-being and security.
Both [worlds] invoke Indra alone as they rise up and proceed toward the sacrifice.

I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited horse. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives. (6) I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited horse. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives. (6)
"I have performed, and I shall perform, the praise of the divine Dadhikrāvan—
the victorious, ever-conquering, pervasive, and impetuous horse. May that deity make our faces— our mouths and senses such as sight and the rest— fragrant."
"May he extend—may he cause to increase—the lifespans for us, for our sake;
for the root *tṛ* has the sense of increasing when used with the prefix *pra*."

The fifth hymn, the eighth [in this section], beginning with "dadhikrāvṇa ita," is the ṛṣi Vāmadeva's composition dedicated to Dadhikrā. Of the eight verses, the first three are *gāyatrī* and the remaining are *jagatī*.
The verse "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" has Sūrya as its deity.
And likewise, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Of Dadhikrāvan there are five; the meaning is that the other four are Jagatī verses.
Or alternatively:
*Iṣaḥ*: desired, or one who is to be desired.
*Śravasyāt* / *śravasyet*: he should desire fame.
Furthermore, *turaṇyasat*: he should hasten.
He sits by means of his own radiance; thus he is *turaṇyasat*.

He is the true one (*satyaḥ*), being stretched out in the waters (*sarasi tāyamānaḥ*). He is the swift one (*dravaḥ*), the goer (*gantā*), the most rapid one (*dravaraḥ*), and the one possessing excellent speed (*prakṛṣṭavegavān*). He is the *pataṅgaḥ*; *pataṅgaḥ* is so called because of flying (*patanena*) or leaping (*utplavanena*). The act of flying is *patanam*.

The possessor of that [power], the swift-flying one, the excellently characterized *Dadhikrāvan*, the divine one, may produce— may generate— *iṣam* (food), *ūrjam* (strength), *svaḥ* (heaven), and *svargam* (the celestial world).
And indeed, the wind blows after his swift, rushing, and eager steed, as if after a full draught;
it follows Dadhikrāvan as he speeds with might along the curve of the path, like a swooping falcon.
And indeed, as he runs and hastens, the wind blows after him like a bird following a full [nest], as Dadhikrāvan—gliding like a falcon, leaping along his path—crosses over with his vital strength.

Moreover, indeed, following the course of this divine Dadhikrāvan—who runs swiftly, who hastens, who speeds along, and who is intensely desirous—just as other birds follow the flight or the wing of a bird that moves, so does every swift person follow him; that is to say, he is the swiftest of all. Furthermore, he is one who moves and carries others across.
This [verb] has the causative sense (ṇyartha) inherent within it.

Like a hawk, they go around—that is, on all sides—either the lap (the place where one rests) or the chest region, by means of *ūrj* (strength), whether as a cause or unknown; "they go together in a group" is the ellipsis.
And this vigorous steed, bound by the neck, at the flanks, and in the mouth, hastens toward the whip; Dadhikrā, exerting his strength, follows his will and springs along the curves of the paths.
