And this vigorous steed hastens toward the whip, though bound by the neck, the girth, and the mouth; Dadhikrā, exerting his full strength, stretches himself along the curves of the paths.

Moreover, that vigorous steed, the divine one characterized by speed, is bound at the neck—that is, at the throat which serves as the means of swallowing—and is bound at the *apikakṣa*, the region of the armpit, and at the *āsani*, the mouth.
For one whose limbs are bound, such bindings with nooses are possible in the aforementioned locations.
Being thus bound, he hastens—that is, he speeds—in accordance with the throw of the goad.

Furthermore, this god *adhikrāḥ*, having followed after his *kratu*—meaning either action or wisdom—and being one whose strength has increased (*saṃtavītvat*), follows the crooked bends (*aṅkāṃsi*) of the paths (*pathām*) and moves about, leaping everywhere (*āpanīphaṇat*).
This is the form of the root *phaṇati*, meaning "to go," in its *yaṅluk* (intensive without the suffix) state.
One should also consult the *Nirukta*, beginning with the passage: "Is he not the steed, the one who causes trembling? (*Nirukta* 2.28).

1. In manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, and Ṇa, it reads *turaṇyasat* [with the variant] *tvarayā sīdati*; in Ta, Na, La, and Sa, *turaṇyasat* ... *turaṇyasata* does not exist. 2. In Kha, Ṇa, Pa, and Bha, it reads *stūyamānaḥ*; in Ga and Pha, it reads *sūyamānaḥ*. 3. In Kha, Ga, and Ṇa, it reads *dadhikrā*. 4. In Na, La, and Sa, *dadhikrāvṇaḥ* does not exist. 5. In Kha, Pa, Pha, and Bha, it reads *anu*. 6. In Kha, Pha, and Bha, it reads *vāyeti*. 7. In Ta and La, it reads *śyenasyeva tasya devasya*. 8. In Kha and Pha, it reads *urapradeśam*. 9. In Kha and La, it reads *gacchatīti*. 10. In Kha, Gha, and Ṇa, it reads *balavān*. 11. In Ga and Sa, it reads *pragṛdhaḥ balavān*.
On the sixth day of the *daśarātra* sacrifice, during the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), this verse, "The swan seated in purity" (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*), is used in the *maitrāvaruṇa* litany.

Regarding this, the *sūtra* states: "Having called [the Hotṛ], he should ascend the difficult ascent (*durohaṇa*) with the verse 'The swan seated in purity,' foot by foot and hemistich by hemistich" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.2).
Śaunaka states its application according to the *smṛti*: "By means of the verse 'The swan seated in purity,' one makes the pure one speak."
"At the time of death, one should mutter the eternal Brahman" (Rigvidhāna 2.13).
The Swan dwelling in purity, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house;
dwelling among men, dwelling in the best, dwelling in truth, dwelling in the sky; born of the waters, born of the cows, born of truth, born of the rock—He is the Eternal Truth.

The swan; dwelling in purity; the Vasu; dwelling in the mid-air; the invoker; dwelling on the altar; the guest; dwelling in the house; dwelling among men; dwelling in the chosen place; dwelling in the cosmic order; dwelling in the sky; born of the waters; born of the kine; born of the cosmic order; born of the mountain; the Cosmic Order. 5.

By means of this solar verse—beginning with, "This golden person who is seen within the sun, with a golden beard" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.6)—it is established that the deity presiding over the solar orb as mentioned in such passages, the Supreme Self who is present as the witness of the wealth of all living beings, and the Supreme Brahman which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts, are all one and the same.

Haṃsaḥ: the meaning is "he goes" (hanti). He is the one who moves everywhere and at all times, the Sun who is to be meditated upon as a single entity through such modes of expression as "I am he," and who is expounded by the mantra of the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
And because he sits in the pure, radiant world of heaven (*dyuloka*), he is "Sitting in the Pure" (*śuciṣat*).
This is according to such scriptural passages as, "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7).
By this, the Sun, whose station is the sky, is established.
That very wind, situated in the middle, also says: "Vasu" means the one who causes all things to dwell; that is, Vāyu. And he is "antarikṣasat," moving within the intermediate space.
Now he describes the nature of that very [Agni] as the altar-ground (vedikā) of the earth:
"The Hotṛ"—the invoker of the gods or the performer of the oblation; "Vediṣat"—dwelling upon the altar in the form of the Gārhapatya and other fires;
"Atithi"—the fire who is always worthy of worship like a guest.
*duroṇasat*. *Duroṇa* is a name for the house; he resides there as the means for preparing cooked food and so forth.
By this, his nature as the mundane fire has been stated.
He is called *nṛpat* because he dwells (*sīdati*) among men (*nṛṣu*), that is, among human beings, in the form of consciousness.
By this, its nature as the Supreme Self has been stated. Furthermore, he speaks of its abiding state within the sun: "It is excellent."
He is called *varasat* because he sits (*sīdati*) in the desirable (*varaṇīya*) circle;
that is, the Sun.
For it is heard in the scripture: "This is indeed the best (*varaṃ*) among those seeking a boon (*sanvānāṃ*), in which this one shines while being invited. (4.20)
*Ṛta* is truth, Brahman, or sacrifice;
he sits therein, thus he is *ṛtasad*, Agni. *Vyoman* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
In this context, he who sits there is the wind, the "sky-sitter" (*vyomasad*). Now, the nature of the sun is described:
"born of the waters" (*abja*), meaning born in the waters.
It is born in the midst of water; it is born of the cow— that is, from the rays—
or in the weapon, according to the Vārttika.
2. Kha, ga, ṇa, na, pha, bha, sa: *śucirīya* (the one dwelling in purity) is the Sun;
*pa*: *pustaka* (the book). Of this mantra, only the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is seen: "O Haṃsa! The all-pervading Sun dwells in the pure, radiant heavenly world (*dyuloka*).
*Vasu* is the Wind, the dweller of all."
He who dwells in the intermediate space is indeed he who moves through the atmosphere in the form of wind.

The Hotṛ is Agni, the invoker of the gods. He who dwells on the altar is indeed he who stands upon the sacrificial ground in the form of the Gārhapatya and other fires. Ārti is Agni, who is always worthy of worship like a guest.
He dwells in the dwelling; he exists in the form of the common sacrificial fire within houses. He dwells among men; he exists in the form of the digestive fire within humans.
He dwells in the excellent; he exists within the desirable orb.
He is established in the sacrifice as *ṛtamata*, the one whose mind is truth; He is established as *vyomamata*, the one whose mind is the ether, existing in the form of the lightning-fire;
He is *abjāḥ*, existing in the water in the form of the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*).
Born of the rays—the rays of Savitṛ, the light in the cows—he rises; born of the Ṛta, he is truly born as that which is visible to all.
Born of the mountain, he has appeared upon the mountain of sunrise;
he abides in the form of Ṛta, which is Truth.
3. I am he who has *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *bha* as his final syllables; I am that very Sūrya. 4. [I am] Agni with *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *bha*.
5. [I am] established in *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*.
6. "In that dwelling" (ta-duroṇe).
7. Kha, ga, ca: by way of the nature of the *ṇa*, *ta*, *pha*, *bha*, *sa*, and consciousness (*citsvarūpa*); gha: by way of the nature of the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*).

He is born as *ṛta* (the Cosmic Order), which is Truth. He is "born of Truth" (*satyajāta*) because he is known by all; for unlike Indra and others, he is not hidden from view. Alternatively, he is born in the waters in the form of lightning or in the form of speech. Or, he is "born of the mountain" (*adrijāḥ*), being born on the mountain of sunrise. Such is the Sun of great majesty. He has established *ṛta*, the Truth, which is the reality of Brahman, the substratum of all. For he is indeed of that very nature. The fact that the Sun possesses the aforementioned nature is concluded in the Brāhmaṇa with the passage beginning, "The *haṃsa* dwelling in purity—this indeed is the *haṃsa* dwelling in purity" (Ai. Brā. 4.20). 14.
‘Indrā ko vām’ is the ninth hymn, consisting of eleven verses; it is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Vāmadeva, in the Triṣṭubh meter, and dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: ‘Indrā ko vām: eleven [verses], dedicated to Indra and Varuṇa.
When the Ābhilavika days have been reached, during the third pressing, these two initial hymns are used for insertion (āvāpa) in the Maitrāvaruṇa-śastra at the increase of the hair (loma-vṛddhi).
Because it is stated in the Sūtra: “In the hymn beginning with ‘indrā ko vām’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.9).
O Indra and Varuṇa, what hymn of praise, accompanied by oblations, shall the immortal Hotṛ offer to you for favor?
O Indra and Varuṇa, may that prayer, uttered with devotion, touch your hearts and awaken your will.

O Indra and Varuṇa, who has attained your favor? The mortal who, like an immortal Hotṛ-priest, brings a hymn of praise with an oblation—may he, full of resolve, speaking from us, and offering homage, O Indra and Varuṇa, touch your heart. 1.

O Indra! O Varuṇa! O Indra-Varuṇa! (The dual number is used for each pair in relation to one another. Which hymn of praise, accompanied by these oblations—namely, the sacrificial materials such as Soma, clarified butter, and other substances to be offered—has attained your favor (*sumna*)? That is to say, which hymn has reached your happiness? Who [has offered] this hymn endowed with oblations? Who has attained your favor?
The meaning is that he would obtain [the result] by means of the fruit.
Alternatively,
the word *haviṣmān* (possessing oblation) is to be connected with what follows later.

Possessing oblations (*haviṣmān*), joined with the sacrificial offering (*haviryuktaḥ*), immortal (*amṛta�*)—characterized by immortality—the Hotṛ priest, like Agni himself; just so, O Indra and Varuṇa, this hymn (*stomaḥ*) which is full of wisdom (*kratumān*), endowed with intelligence, uttered from us (*asmat*), proclaimed, accompanied by reverence (*namasvān*) and oblations (*haviṣmān*), or indeed possessed of salutations, may it touch (*apasparśat*) your heart (*hṛdi*); that is, may it reach your hearts.
Who is "Ma"? This is a praise of the hymn.

The mortal who has made Indra and Varuṇa his allies, the two gods, with a libation of Soma for the sake of victory—he slays the Vṛtras and his enemies in battles; or, with his great helpers, he becomes renowned.

O Indra and Varuṇa, that mortal who has made you two gods his allies, possessing milk for the sake of the sacrifice—he slays the Vṛtras and his enemies in battles; or through your great protections, he becomes renowned. 2.
O Indra and Varuṇa, the two gods Indra-Varuṇa!
The word *ha* is a filler or indicates what is well-known.

He who, being mortal—subject to death—and possessing offerings characterized by sacrificial food (*paryasvān*), makes himself a friend (*āpī*) to the one who is bountiful (*makhivāya*) and a giver (*dandhū*). (He does so) for the sake of union.
He destroys the obstructing evils of mortals;
likewise, he slays the enemies in battles.
The word "vā" has the sense of "and."
With great protections—that is, with great aids—he, O men, is heard far and wide; he becomes renowned and famous. 1.
Born of truth (according to *ta*).
2. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*: truth is indeed unassailable; *pha*: truth is indeed inexpressible.
3. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, bha: He is immortal (*amṛta*), meaning free from death; he is not like the sacrificial fire (*agni*) which serves as a means for attaining heaven.
4. Kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, sa: This one. 5. Kha, pa, pha, bha: Endowed with sacrifice (*yajña*).

6. [A sound] uttered with *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, or *bha*; [a sound] uttered with *ta* or *pa*; [a sound] joined with *na* or *sa*. 7. [A sound] merely touching (*spṛśat*) *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, or *bha*.
8. The word *ha* [is used] after *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, or *sa*; the word “or” (*vā*) does not exist.

9. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and āpi formed a circle with their kin; pa, āpi, and cakre formed a circle with bandhu (ndhū). 10. And by means of kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, ga, and rakṣaṇa, he was indeed heard far and wide.
(Ṛgveda 2.84)
May Indra and Varuṇa bestow that treasure upon the men who labor diligently;
when they, as friends for friendship's sake, rejoice with well-pressed Soma and abundant food.
O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow treasure upon the men who labor with devotion; when you two friends, for the sake of friendship, delight yourselves with the pressed Soma juices and abundant food.
Those two, Indra and Varuṇa— indeed,
they are well-known—
are the two gods who bestow delightful wealth upon us, the mortals, the descendants of Manu, who are striving and praising them as singers. They are the givers of that treasure.
The word "bhavataḥ" (you two become) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

If you two, being "sakhāyā" (friends)— either friends with each other or friends of the sacrificer— for the sake of "sakhyāya" (friendship), that is, for the performance of friendly acts, "mādayethe" (rejoice) with the "sutebhiḥ somaiḥ" (pressed Soma juices) while being "suprayasā" (possessing excellent Soma offerings),
then you two become the givers of "ratnānām" (jewels).
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two fierce ones, hurl your most powerful thunderbolt at him who is ill-disposed toward us, the wolfish one who seeks to deceive; strike him down with your overwhelming might.
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two fierce ones, bestow upon this man your most powerful flashing bolt; against him who is evil-minded toward us, a wolf-like deceiver, measure out your overwhelming power.
"O Indras, O two Indras; O Varunas, O two Varunas; O Ugras, O two Ugras.
In all these instances, the dual number is used in reference to each other, as in "of Mitra and Varuna" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.66.1).
Or alternatively:
Due to the nature of Vedic language (*chāndasatva*), the suffix *ānaṭ* is applied even when separated [by other words].
"In this enemy, lay down the *didyu*, the blazing; the *ojiṣṭha*, most intensely brilliant; the *vajra*, the weapon.
The meaning is: "Impel it for the purpose of slaying."

"Whosoever is our enemy—evil-minded, a wicked sinner, a *vṛkati* (one who excessively fails to give), and a *dabhīti* (a harmful assailant)—upon that enemy, you two must exert *abhibhūti* (overpowering) *ojas* (strength); that is to say, you two must display such power."
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two are the precursors of the thoughts of all that exists, like two bulls [desiring] a cow.
May she yield for us, as if having come, like a great cow with a thousand streams, with her milk.

O Indra and Varuṇa, you two are the inspirers of the thoughts of all that exists, like two bulls [of a cow]. May she yield for us, as a great cow having gone to the pasture, yielding with her milk in a thousand streams. 5.
1. *na-la-sa-* "he" does not exist. 2. *ta-tā* "ha". 3. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa-* "śaṃsamānebhyaḥ" does not exist.
4. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and sa, the word ‘māyetām’ is absent. 5. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and he is absent.
6. In the manuscripts kha, ṇa, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, [the rule applies] to a separated [element]; in the manuscripts ta and la, it applies even when there is an intervention.
7. *kha-ga-ṇa-bha* with *ojas* is the shining, blazing *didyu-* (missile); *ta-te* with *tejas* is the *vajra*; *ca-pha* with *ojas* is the shining, blazing *didyu-vajra*.
8. *kha-ṇa-bha-yu-vam*; *na-la-sa* lacks "the two youths" (*yuvaṃ yuvām*), like *pa*.
O *ha*, Indra and Varuṇa—O Indra and Varuṇa—you two, the two of you, become (*bhūtam*) the ones who gladden (*pretārā*) and satisfy this hymn (*dhiyaḥ*).
The two bulls are like those of a cow;
may that cow, which is the form of praise, milk for us—that is, she may yield—our desires; she should fulfill them.
Like a great cow, vast and yielding a thousand streams of milk, [the earth] is characterized by grass and fodder such as *yavasa*.

For our offspring, for our well-being, for our progeny, for the fertile fields, for the sight of the sun, and for manly vigor—may Indra and Varuṇa be with us here with their protections, O givers of strength, in the pursuit of what is desired.

O gods Indra and Varuṇa, for our welfare regarding our kinsmen— our children, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons— and regarding the fertile fields, the crops, and the lands that serve as the instruments [of our sustenance], for the sake of the long-lasting vision of Sūra, the impeller, the Sun— that is,

for long life— likewise, O showerers of blessings, for my manly power, for virility, and again for the capacity for procreation, you two, O wonder-workers who destroy enemies, being present with our protections, [grant this] when there is the great encompassing movement [of the sun].
Or rather, this is a name for the night;
for during the night, they may serve for the slaying of enemies.
We choose you two, the young ones, for protection and for prosperity—you who are abundant, possessors of nourishment, and well-resting.
We choose you, the heroes, most liberal givers, dear and worthy of praise, who bring well-being like father and mother.

For we choose you two alone for protection and for prosperity—you who are abundant, who delight in cattle, who are easy to approach, O heroes, most liberal givers, and bringers of well-being like father and mother. 7.

O Indra and Varuṇa, seeking cattle and nourishment, we [come] from here to you two— *hi* being a filler for the meter— to you both alone, for the sake of prosperity and for the ancient protection (*avasa*) granted by you.
The connection is "we choose.
*Prabhūtī* means the two who are powerful; *svāpī* means those who have become excellent kinsmen.
*Āpiḥ* is a name for a kinsman.

Or rather: O you two who are thoroughly pervasive, heroic, valorous, most worthy of honor, and preeminent— you two, we choose for ourselves, we pray to you from all sides, for the sake of the common harvest and for our beloved [offspring],
just as parents, being sources of well-being (*śambhū*), [choose] for their son.

1. By means of the sign of grass and so forth (*pa-tṛṇādinimitta*). 2. *Ta-lagatbī* means having the habit of going. 3. In *na-la-sa*, "he" does not exist. 4. And *va* refers to the grandson (*pautra*). 5. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa*, "tathā" does not exist. 6. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa*, "ca" does not exist. 7. *Ta* means the third (*tṛtīya*). 8. In *pa-bha-maha*, it means "here" (*atra*). 9. *Ta* means surrounding (*paritastakana*). 10. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha*, it means "relative" (*bandhu*). 668. *Vakramamāṇau* means two who are going.
The word "bhavatām" (be yours) is the ellipsis.
May "ūtībhīḥ" (with fresh aids), that is, with protections, "asmatrā" (toward us), "niyutaḥ" (harnessed horses) and "rāyaḥ" (wealthes) "sacantām" (attend upon us).
Come to us, O Great Ones, with your great aids—Indra and Varuṇa—to win the prize in battle!
May we be the winners of that strength of yours which sports in the fray against the seekers of booty.

O ye two great ones, come to us with your mighty aids, O Indra and Varuṇa, to the winning of the prize! When the twice-born ones play boldly in the battles, may we be the winners of that contest through you both. 11.

O you two, the great ones—the mighty Indra and I, Varuṇa—come hither together with your vast protections and aids. Come to the battle for booty, or to that conflict which serves as the cause for obtaining wealth; come to the fray among the armies where the *didyavaḥ* (missiles) fly. *Didyavaḥ* is a name for weapons.
The weapons belonging to the enemy play against him; may we, through your favor, O you two, become winners and sharers of such a battle as that.
The tenth hymn, consisting of ten verses, begins with “mama dvitā. Trasadasyu, the son of Purukutsa, is the royal seer (rājarṣi).
In the first six verses, which are praises of himself, the seer himself is the deity.
The deities for the remaining four [verses] are Indra and Varuṇa;
the metre is Triṣṭubh. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “*mama dvitā daśa*, *tramadabhyuḥ*, [and] *paurukutsyaḥ palācca* are hymns of self-praise.”
The application has been stated; thus it is in the hymn.
My kingdom is twofold, that of the all-active Kṣatriya; as all the immortals attend to our will, so do the gods attend to the will of Varuṇa, the king of the highest Kuṣṭi, the son of Vṛtra.

Mine is the kingdom, the dominion of the Kṣatriya who provides all sustenance. All the immortals follow our will, even as the gods follow the will of Varuṇa; I rule over Kuṣṭi, the highest and most excellent.

Of the *kṣatriya*, one born of the *kṣatriya* caste; of the *viśvāyu*, one whose lifespan is the whole [of existence]. "My" (*mama*) is a designation for myself in this way. "Twofold kingdom" (*dvitā rāṣṭram*) refers to the kingdom that has become twofold through the division of heaven and earth.
"May Trasadasyu [be] for me; may all the immortal gods be such as they are for us"—that is to say, so that the kingdom and the subjects [may be ours].
Of Varuṇa, the restrainer, or one who has the form of Varuṇa; of Kuṣṭi, a human being, or one possessing [the power of] him; of Upama. This is a name for "nearness."
He chose the one nearest to all:
this was the name of form (rūpa).
All the gods attend upon—that is, serve—the ritual act (kratu) of me, who possess form.
And I am the King;
the root *rāj* signifies the act of ruling.
I become the Lord of All.
Or alternatively, it should be construed as:
"O King, you are like Indra in battle."

1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha, and Cakra, the reading is *mārṇā*; in Gha, Na, La, Sa, Cakra, and Māṇau, it is *māṇau*. 2. In Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha, and Sa, the reading is *āvartāmati*. 3. In Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pha, and Bha, it is *tato’smadīye vājasātau*; in Pa and No, it is *’smadīye vājasātau*. 4. In Na, La, and Sa, the word *ayuddhasya* does not exist. 5. In Ca, Pa, and Pha, the reading is *rājarṣi*: [then] *ṛṣiḥ*. 6. In Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, Bha, and Ma, it is *jātyupakṣampa*. 7. In Pa, it is *asmadīyā*. 8. In Kha, Ga, Na, Ṇa, Pha, and Bha, it is *sarvaiścaryakarmā*. 9. In Ta, it is *sarvameśvaraḥ*.
I am King Varuṇa; for me those primordial powers of Asura were maintained. The gods follow the will of Varuṇa; I rule over the people and over Vṛtra, the highest.
I am Varuṇa, the king. To me these first divine powers were entrusted. The gods follow the will of Varuṇa; I rule over the people, over the highest Vṛtra.
"And I alone am King Varuṇa.
For me, for my sake alone, they— the gods— held, that is, maintained, those well-known *asuryāṇi* powers, which destroy the Asuras, as the foremost and principal."
The rest has been explained.
I am Indra and Varuṇa through your greatness; you have established the two wide, deep, well-fashioned realms.
Like Tvaṣṭṛ, knowing all beings, you have brought the two worlds together and sustained them.
I am Indra, I am Varuṇa—by my greatness, I have set in order the two vast and deep realms, well-established. Like Tvaṣṭṛ, knowing all beings, I have brought together and sustained the two worlds. 3.
"I am Trasadasyu; I am Indra, and I am Varuṇa as well.
By my greatness, I alone am those two vast, deep, and unfathomable (or spacious) realms—the two well-formed and beautiful regions of dust, heaven and earth."
Knowing this, I, like Tvaṣṭṛ and like Prajāpati, have set all beings in motion;
and I have sustained the two worlds, heaven and earth.
I, swelling like waters, have moistened them; I have supported heaven in the seat of Order.
By Order the Son of Aditi, protected by Order, has spread out the earth in threefold layers.

I, the son of Aditi, true to the *ṛta*, have caused the swelling waters to flow; I have supported the heaven, seated upon the seat of *ṛta*. By means of *ṛta*, I, the son of Aditi, who am faithful to *ṛta*, have spread out the earth in threefold layers. 4.
"I alone caused the swelling waters to flow; I poured them forth.
Thus, while the seat—the place or cause—of *ṛta* (water or the sun) existed, I supported the sky, the world of heaven.
Or alternatively:
In the place that is a reservoir of water (1.
*ta-ye*), the two worlds (*rodasī*) shine with dust (2. *ta-rajasī*).
3. While the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), shine forth with the letters *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, I have supported them—that is, I have held them fast.
Furthermore, like Tvaṣṭṛ, the wise Prajāpati, I have set all beings (*viśvā bhuvanāni*) in motion. 4. For the sake of that [purpose].
I have supported the heaven and the sun. By means of *ṛta*—that is, by water as the causal sign—I, the son of Aditi, became the possessor of *ṛta*.
Furthermore, I have specifically expanded the earth, the pervasive sky, which is threefold and of three kinds.
"For my sake alone did the Supreme Lord create the three worlds, beginning with the earth."
Men seeking heaven, striving for booty, and gathered in battle, invoke me;
as Indra, the bounteous lord, I stir up the fray, a vigorous steed, with power that overcomes the dust.
Men with good horses, seeking booty, call upon me when they are hemmed in in the clash of battle; I, Indra Maghavan, create the fray, for I, possessing overwhelming might, stir up the dust.

Men who are leaders—warriors with beautiful horses (*svarśāḥ*), seeking booty (*vājayantaḥ*) and desiring battle—follow me alone; this is the ellipsis. Being chosen by me, they call upon me alone in the encounter, in the battle, for the sake of combat.
Being Maghavan, the possessor of wealth, and being Indra, I create and bring about the battle;
possessing overwhelming power, with a strength that surpasses others, I stir up and drive forth the dust.
I have made all those things; no one can restrain my divine, irresistible power.
When the Soma juices exhilarate me and the hymns of praise, both the boundless realms tremble with fear.
I am he whom no one can restrain—the divine, irresistible power of the gods—when the Soma juices have exhilarated me and when the hymns have done so; then both the boundless realms tremble with fear.
I, Trasadasyu, have performed all those well-known deeds.
No one can restrain my divine power (*sahaḥ*), that strength belonging to the gods, which is irresistible and unyielding;
for the Soma juices have exhilarated me.

And because even the hymns and recitations have exhilarated me, therefore both worlds—the two regions of heaven and earth—tremble and shake in me, who am boundless and whose reach extends to the furthest distance.
All beings have known this of you; as such, O Ordainer, you proclaim these deeds to Varuṇa.
You have shattered the Vṛtras, having struck them down; you, O Indra, have released the obstructed rivers.
They know all those worlds as his; you proclaim them to Varuṇa, O Ordainer. You have shattered the Vṛtras, having struck them down; you, O Indra, set free the obstructed rivers. 7.

1. *ta*—He is the possessor of truth (*ṛtāvā*) and the possessor of sacrifice (*yajñavān*). 2. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha-sa*—Only that which is capable (*samartham eva*). 3. *ca-pha*—Manifesting even the three worlds (*lokatrayam api prakhyāpayat*). 4. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha*—Me alone (*mām eva*). 5. *na-la-sa*—"Arana" does not exist. 6. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-bha*—Of others (*anyeṣām*); *sa*—of these (*eṣām*). 7. *ta*—"Sahas" does not exist. 8. *ta*—Causing them to rejoice (*amādayan*). 9. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-bha*—Because (*yasmāt*). 10. *kha-ga-gha-ca-pa-pha-bha*—On the near shore (*adure pāre*); *na*—not in "adare"; *sa*—on the far shore (*dare pāre*). 11. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha*—But both (*ubhe tu*). 12. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-bha*—Both heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivyām ubhe*). 13. *la*—Fearing (*bibhyataḥ*).
From here onwards is the praise of Indra and Varuṇa. O Varuṇa, "of that" (tasya) refers to you;
the genitive case is used in the sense of the object.
All those various beings, all the classes of living creatures, know you—
O Vidhātar (Ordainer)! This is a name for the one who praises.
O singer, you have offered praise to Varuṇa; O Varuṇa, you are praised.
O Indra, you are heard of—indeed, you are renowned—as one who has struck down, that is, slain, the Vṛtras, the enemies.
Moreover, O Indra, you released, that is, caused to flow, the rivers that were obstructed, which by their very nature are prone to flowing.

Our fathers were there; they were the seven seers when Durgaha was awakened. They sacrificed for Trasadasyu, him who was like Indra, the subduer of Vṛtra, the god of half-divine nature, for this [earth]. 8. Our fathers were there; they were the seven seers when Durgaha was awakened. They sacrificed for Trasadasyu, him who was like Indra, the subduer of Vṛtra, the god of half-divine nature, for this [earth]. 8.
While Purukutsa’s consort was imprisoned in the house of Durgaha,
she saw that her husband was without a kingdom and, desiring a son for him, [acted].
He even conquered the Seven Sages who had arrived there by chance;
and they, being pleased, again spoke highly of Indra and Varuṇa.
Commanded by Indra, Varuṇa, and the others, she gave birth to Trasadasyu;
knowing this ancient history, one should recite this verse here.
Now, here in this land of our own sovereignty, upon this earth, these were our fathers, our protectors, and our progenitors; they were.
These renowned sages, while Purukutsa—the son of Durgaha—was awake, offered up Trasadasyu from the firm bond of this [earth] for him, through the grace of Indra and Varuṇa.
Of what sort was he?
They gave us a son who is a conqueror of Vṛtra, a slayer of the enemy Vṛtra, a demi-god (ardhadeva) existing in the midst or proximity of the gods;
or rather,
they gave us a son who stands like Indra, having become the very center of the gods.
"Of whomsoever half belongs to Indra, therefore Indra is the most abundant among the deities," so says the Taittirīyaka (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.4.8.3).

For Purukutsānī has served you both, O Indra and Varuṇa, with offerings and with prostrations. Therefore, they have established King Trasadasyu—the slayer of Vṛtra, the god-like one—as her lord. 9. Purukutsānī; for; you two; she has served; with offerings; O Indra and Varuṇa; with prostrations; then; the king; Trasadasyu; of her; the slayer of Vṛtra; they have established; the god-like one. 9.
O Indra and Varuṇa, Purukutsānī—the wife of Purukutsa and a seer—did not offer worship to you two;
she was indeed displeasing with her oblations, sacrificial offerings, prostrations, and hymns of praise.
Then, for this Purukutsānī, you two bestowed as a gift Trasadasyu, the king, the slayer of Vṛtra, the demi-god, the son of Utlakṣaṇa. Thus they have given him.
1. In manuscripts sva, ga, ca, ṇa, and ma, the word "ataṃ" does not exist. 2. In manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, bha, and ā, the word "āśrutān" appears.
3. In manuscripts kha, ga, ca, and pha, it reads "syandanasvabhāvān meghān apputān"; in ṇa and sa, "syandanasvabhāvān apputān"; and in pa, "sindhūn medhān apputān".

4. When *kha*, *ga*, *ta*, *bha* are situated in *bandhana*, and *ṇa* is situated in *sthāna*. 5. [The sequence] *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha* is "without a king" (*arājaka*); *na*, *ma*—that is *āpa*. 6.
*kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha* belong to Purukutsa.

7. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha read *prati*. 8. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha read *dṛcā iti*; na, bha, sa read *dṛcād iti*. 9. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, sa read *ca*.

10. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha, the word "utpādakāḥ" (producers) does not exist. 11. Among the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, Bha, and Sa, [the reading is] "devānāṃ madhye" (in the midst of the gods).
12. In the manuscripts Ca, Pha, and Bha, [the reading is] "indrāvaruṇā" or "indrāvaruṇau" (Indra and Varuṇa).
13. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, pa, pha, bha, and sa please [the gods]. May we, having won wealth, rejoice with the gods through oblations, as cattle rejoice in pasture.
O Indra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us forever that cow which does not kick away.
O King! May we, having won the prize, rejoice with the oblation, O gods, as with fodder and cattle. O Indra and Varuṇa, grant us every day that cow which does not shrink away. 10.

May we rejoice in wealth through our riches, O you two, as those who have won and shared it among us. May the gods delight in the oblation, and the cattle in pasture and fodder. O Indra and Varuṇa, you two who are the slayers of all [enemies], grant us that cow, the bestower of joy, and wealth every single day—every day being the meaning of the indeclinable *viśvāhā*. What kind of cow? One that does not kick out, one that is not harmed. Or rather, *viśvāhā* is an indeclinable; the sense is "at all times. 36.
‘Ka u śravata’ is the eleventh hymn in the seventh [maṇḍala].
Purumīḷha Ājamīḷha, the son of Suhotra, is the seer (ṛṣi).
Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandas).
The deities are the Aśvins.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: ‘Ka u śravat... purūmīḷha; Ājamīḷha and Sauhotra [composed] the two hymns for the Aśvins.
These two hymns beginning with this [verse] belong to the morning litany (prātaranuvāka) and the Aśvina-śastra, in the Aśvina sacrifice, and are composed in the Triṣṭubh metre.
This is because it is formulated in the Sūtra as: "‘The cow—who indeed will hear the question? (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.15).

Who among those worthy of sacrifice is most renowned for hearing? Which god takes pleasure in the one who offers praise? To whose heart shall we bring this divine, most beloved hymn of praise, accompanied by excellent oblations, among the immortals?

Who? "Ūm"—let him hear! Which one among those worthy of sacrifice? Which god accepts the one who offers praise? Whose is this divine hymn, most beloved among the immortals, that they may place in their hearts—this well-praised song accompanied by excellent oblations? 1.

Among the gods worthy of sacrifice and deserving of worship, which god would hear the hymn? Which god [would hear] the praise-song of the one who is inclined to worship? Which god would take pleasure in it—that is, would favor it?

In whose heart shall we place this most beloved, dear goddess—she who is radiant, worthy of excellent oblations, or endowed with beautiful offerings—and this beautiful hymn of praise? Among the immortals, whom as the best, or whom as the one to be approached, shall we choose? Between the two Ashvins, which god shall be our master? Thus [they ask] regarding the flow of the libation.
Who is merciful? Who is most accessible? Among the gods, who is most beneficent?
Which chariot do they call swift-horsed and rapid, which the Daughter of the Sun has chosen?

Who is merciful? Who is the most accessible? Which among the gods is the most beneficent? Which chariot do they call swift with its racing horses—the one that the Daughter of the Sun has chosen? || 2 ||

1. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa omit *hāvaṣām*; ṇa omits *yuvām*. 2. ta reads *modante*. 3. kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa omit *na*. 4. la omits *śobhanāṃ stutim*. 5. ta omits *thāyayema*. Ka. 2-85: Who is gracious? Which god is gracious? Who would make us happy? Which god is most ready to come? Who comes most readily toward our sacrifice?
Among the gods of gods, which god is *śambhaviṣṭha*: the one who most effectively brings about happiness?
Who is it that possesses such distinguished qualities as those mentioned, [and] who might he be among the two Aśvins? This is the sense.
Which chariot do they say has swift-running horses? They urge it on.
That chariot which the daughter of the Sun chose as her husband, and which she shared with the Sun—
that chariot they call swift.
For you two come quickly even from afar, like Indra brandishing his power;
born from heaven, divine birds of beautiful wings—by what power among powers do you become most mighty?
Come quickly indeed! Like Indra, may we brandish our power against the high heavens. Born from heaven, divine birds of beautiful wings—by what power among your powers do you become most mighty? 3.
"Quickly" means swiftly.
"Hi sma" are particles used for filling out the meter.
"Īrvataḥ" means of those who possess movement, those who are coming; "dyūn" means days; "sudhyā-sambandhinaḥ" means related to the pure mind; "prati gacchathaḥ" means you two go toward [those days].
Indra [displays] his own power, as if at the end of the night that causes great trembling; the word "displays" is to be supplied.
Just as Indra goes at the time of dawn on a fine day, so too do you two go—this is the meaning.

Born from heaven, come from the celestial world; you two are divine, being those who exist in heaven; you two possess beautiful flight (suparṇā). Among your own deeds or powers (śacīnām), by what power (kayā śacyā) do you two become most powerful (śaciṣṭhā)—that is, most capable or possessed of beautiful deeds?
Who indeed surpasses you? By what means, O Aśvins, do you come when invoked?
Or who, in the encounter, has offered you great honor? O lovers of sweetness, O Dastras, protect us with your aid.

Who has become your favor? By what means, O Aśvins, will you come to us when called? Who among you two, even from afar, will protect us in the encounter? O lovers of sweetness, O destroyers of foes, grant us your aid! 4.

What is your shared intention? What praise—meaning that which measures the presence of your qualities for the sake of discernment—might it be? By what hymn, being invoked—that is, being called upon—do you two come toward us? Come to us!

O you two, in the face of even the great *tyajas*—for *tyajas* is anger, so called because it is cast off (*tyajyate*) and abandoned by all—who could be its endurer? *Vām* means "of you two"; *abhīke* means "in one's own region" (or presence); and *mahas-cit* means "even of the great. *Tyajas* is that which is abandoned; *kaḥ* means "who would be. *Soḍhā* means "an endurer. Thus, who could be the endurer of such anger?
O makers of the sweet draught, O dispensers of water of sweet flavor; O destroyers of enemies, O Aśvins, protect us with your aid—that is, with your protection.
Guard us!
Protect us!
1. *ta-mṛḍāti* means "may he be gracious. 2. *ta-la-dravad-aśvam-āśum* means "and [he who has] a swift horse that runs swiftly.
3. *kha-ga gha-ca-ṇa-bha-yuvām-āgacchatam* means "O you two (the letters Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Bha), come hither."

4. Kha, ṇa, pha, and bha are being offered (*hūyamānā*); *hūyamānāu*; ga, ca, and *hūyamānā* are being offered; *hūyamānau*; na, la, and sa are being offered. 5. Ga, ca, ṇa, bha, and ma are the honeyed (*madhvī*) honey (*madhu*).
6. Kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, and pa for protection (*rakṣaṇāya*); bha, la, and sa for protection (*rakṣaṇayā*).
Your broad chariot reaches far across the stations when it turns from the ocean toward you.
O lovers of sweetness, with honey you are sweet; the drops of honey have moistened you, and they have cooked for you your two nourishing portions.

Broad is your chariot; it reaches every station when it turns back from the ocean for you. O lovers of sweetness, with honey you are sweet; let your honey flow in abundance, as they cook for you the prepared sacrificial foods.

O Aśvins, your chariot goes around the world of heaven, reaching as far as the vast and abundant expanse; for from here, from the ocean— that which serves as the means of flowing— or from the intermediate space, it turns toward you, moving directly in your presence.
The Adhvaryu priests sprinkle the two [cups] characterized as *mādhvī* with sweet liquid (*madhu*), that is, with honeyed milk; they sprinkle the sweet Soma juice (*madhu*).
Since, from every side (*sīm*), the cooked grains (*pṛkṣaḥ*)—that is, the ripe barley—reach you both (*vām*), therefore it turns toward you.
May the Sindhu pour its juice for you both; may the swift, unaging horses go around. That very swift vehicle of yours approaches, by which you two became the lords of Sūryā.

The Sindhu, indeed, and the Rasā shall sprinkle your horses; the glowing birds shall fly around from the red-dappled steeds. That swift vehicle of yours was well-known, by which you two became the lords of Sūryā.
O you two, may the Sindhu—the flowing river, the cloud, or the water—sprinkle [you] with its essence (rasa).
With fervor (ghṛṇā) and vision (dīdhi), the birds-like seekers or horses, being radiant (aruṣāsaḥ), go around (pari... agman) on every side.
Your vehicle, the means of motion, the well-known chariot, is swift (ajiram).
"Quickly bring this!"— it is understood that "su" means "well. "By which chariot you two become the protectors and bearers of Sūryā"— that is the chariot.
Whatever you two have here together for our nourishment—may that benevolence of yours, rich in booty, be ours.
Protect the singer; O Nāsatyas, our desire rests upon you both, directed toward you.

Here, here! That which is yours for common nourishment—this is that very benevolence of yours toward us, O you who possess the treasure of strength. Protect the singer; for our desire rests upon you, O Nāsatyas, directed toward you. 7.

O Aśvins, because of that, or by whatever good thought (*sumati*), being of one mind (*samanas*)—that is, having a common purpose—at this very sacrifice here, I unite you both with that good thought for the sake of nourishment (*pṛkṣe*) through praise. This [praise] is now being performed. 1. (Variant readings):

*kha-ga*—the two who possess the aforementioned characteristics and are the creators of sweet water; *ca-ṇa-pha*—the two who possess the aforementioned characteristic and are the creators of sweet water; *pa-bha*—the two who are the creators of sweet-tasting water.
2. *pa*—[I offer] the Soma-juice to you both.
3. Those that attain *ta* remain [separate]; those that attain *la* become mixed. 4.
In *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *sa*, the form "of you two" (*yuvayoḥ*) does not exist.
5. In *kha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, there is *dīdhyāḥ*.
6. *ta-la-vetāraḥ* means "those who go.
7. *ta-kṣipram* means "quickly.
8. *ca-tadu*; *pha-tadu saḥ*.
9. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the phrase "yat... sumatyā" is absent. 10. In the manuscripts kha, pa, pha, and bha, it reads "yat yayā sumatyā.
*Sumatiḥ* means "excellent praise"; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "may [that] be fruitful for us alone (*asme*)."
O you two who possess the prize as your treasure and the delightful horses—
for according to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (9.3.4.1), "The goat is indeed the prize" (vāja)—
may you two carry, that is, protect, me, the singer, the one who praises.
O Nāsatyas, O Aśvins, our desire has indeed resorted to you both, directed toward you alone, having reached you.

The twelfth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “*taṃ vāṃ rathaṃ*,” has Purumīḷha and Ajamīḷha as its seers; Triṣṭubh is the metre; the Aśvins are the deity. This is indicated by the phrase “*taṃ vāṃ*. Its application is prescribed for the *prātaranuvāka* (morning litany) and the *āśvina-śastra* (Aśvin recitation).
We invoke today that chariot of yours, O Aśvins, which has a broad path, the gathering place of the cow,
which carries Sūryā in its seat, which is yoked by song, most abundant, and seeking wealth.

We invoke today that chariot of yours, O Aśvins, which has a broad path and meets with the kine—that vehicle which carries Sūryā, which is sought after by songs, most abundant, and desirous of wealth. 1.
O Aśvins, we, your praisers, invoke your chariot today on the day of the Soma-pressing.
Of what kind is it? It is one of broad course, possessing celebrated speed, the bringer of the gathering of cattle. That chariot which carries—that is, sustains—Sūryā.
He who possesses the *vandhura*—the wooden seat on the chariot that serves as its support—is "possessed of the *vandhura*" (*vandhurayuh*).
He is the bearer of hymns (*girvāhasam*), the carrier of praises and songs of praise; he is most abundant (*purutamam*) and the possessor of wealth (*vasuyum*, i.e., *vasumantam*).
O Aśvins, you two win that glory through your divine power and your skillful deeds; O sons of Heaven, nourishments attend your wondrous form when the great steeds draw your chariot.

O Aśvins, you two win that glory through your divine powers; O sons of Heaven, you obtain it by your mighty deeds. Your wondrous form is accompanied by nourishing foods when your lofty steeds draw your chariot.

O Aśvins, you two, the sons of Dyaus—the offspring of the Āditya, or rather, the protectors from falling from the heavenly world—ye two are indeed deities (devatā). [The word *devatā* here functions as a dual noun with a case-ending suffix.]
You two enjoy (vanathaḥ) that well-known glory (śriyam) through your deeds (śacībhiḥ), whether understood as actions or powers.
Alternatively,
the root *van* has the meaning of "giving."
Your two bodies, O you two, are attended by nourishing foods characterized by Soma; that is, when the great, towering horses carry you both upon the chariot—
or rather,
when the flowing streams carry you both on the chariot.

Who—namely the sacrificer—shall today perform praise for you two with hymns (*arkaiḥ*), with mantras, having offered oblations and presented the Soma, either for protection, or for the drinking of the pressed juice?

O Aśvins, who, offering homage and performing obeisance, would turn [you] toward the sacrifice for the ancient enjoyment of the eternal water or the sacrifice? O Aśvins! Who would cause [you] to return?

O Nasatyas, you who exist in many places, come near to this sacrifice with your golden chariot. Drink indeed of the Soma that gladdens; bestow treasure upon the person who honors you. hiraṇyayena purubhū rathenemaṃ yajñaṃ nāsatyopayātam | pibātha it mardhanaḥ somyasya dadhatho ratnaṃ vidhate janāya || 4 ||
O Nāsatyas, you who exist in many forms, come to this sacrifice with your golden chariot;
[come] for the sake of the sweet juice of the Soma-related [offering]. (The genitives are used in the sense of the accusative.)

Or else, you bestow the essence of Soma upon the person who serves and attends to you; you bestow—that is, you grant—the great, delightful treasure, wealth. This is a form of the root *dhā* (to give) in the *leṭ* mood.

Come to us from heaven and from earth with your golden, well-rolling chariot! Let not others who seek the gods detain you; for your ancient kinship has been established. Come to us from heaven and from earth with your golden, well-rolling chariot! Let not others who seek the gods detain you; for your ancient kinship has been established.
Come toward us— come from the sky, from the world of heaven, and from the earth—
with what means? With a golden, most delightful, and well-rolling chariot.

O you two, other sacrificers seeking the gods and desiring you both, let them not restrain you; let them not impose a restriction. Since from of old, the ancient bond—the hymn of praise—has been joined together as that which precedes all others, therefore come hither.

1. *na-u-sa-*: The word *aśvinau* does not exist [in this context]. 2. *ta-*: It proceeds [as follows]. 3. *ta-bahubhavantau*: [The two] becoming many. 4. *ca-pa-pha-*: *nāsatyā*, [meaning] the two Nāsatyas. 5. *kha-ga-*: By means of the golden (*hiraṇyayena*). 6. *ta-loṭi*: [This occurs] in the imperative (*loṭ*) mood. 7. *pa-rūpam*: The form [is as follows]; *it* is a filler. 8. *ga-sakāśādvā atra*: Or, in this case, from the presence (*sakāśāt*) of *ga*. 9. *pa-ramaṇīyena*: By means of that which is most beautiful (*ramaṇīyena*). 10. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-rū-bha-sa-*: Desiring you both (*yuvām icchamānāḥ*).

O *dasras* (wondrous ones), measure out for us great wealth consisting of many heroes, for both [families] are known to you. When the leaders, the *aja-mīḷhas*, have offered praise to you, O Aśvins, they have come to this common laud. Now, O *dasras*, quickly bestow upon us great wealth consisting of many heroes—wealth that is vast—for both [families], among these very people. When the leaders, the priests related to Purumīḷha, have offered praise to you, O Aśvins, they have come; likewise, those related to Ajamīḷha have also come together with them to this great song of praise. "Here, here," as before, is explained. This hymn, "This light" (*eṣa sya bhānuḥ*), consists of seven verses. It is the thirteenth hymn; the first six are *jagatī* meters and the seventh is *triṣṭubh*. The seer is Vāmadeva, the son of Maṇḍala-draṣṭṛ; the deities are the Aśvins. It is indicated by the phrase "This *triṣṭubh*-ending. It is to be recited in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* according to the respective meters. Thus it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "He has awakened... this light" (*āśva. śrau. 4.15*). This light rises up; the chariot is yoked, the one that travels all around, upon the ridge of this shining heaven. Upon it are three pairs of wings; the fourth part, the tooth, of the honey, roars aloud. This light, that very radiant sun, rises upward. And the chariot belonging to you two, which moves everywhere, is yoked upon the ridge of this shining sky. Upon it are three pairs of wings; the fourth part, the tooth, of the honey, roars aloud. 1. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha-bha*: O *dasras*, O *dasras*, the two who destroy; *pa*: O *dasras*, the two who protect enemies (the destroyers). 2. *ṇa*: "Here, here" is explained as before; *ta-na*: this is explained; *pa*: the commentary on the entire mantra of the manuscript exists. 3. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha*: "Upon the ridge" (*sānavi*) is yoked.
It should be connected [to the verb] as “it rises” (*udīyati*) or “it is perceived” (*virūpyate*) in the elevated region.
Upon this chariot—on its upper part—there are three pairs, that is, threefold wing-joints;
for the joint is fashioned in three ways.
For it is heard in scripture: "This food, drink, and solid food.
Indeed, the word *mithuna* (pair/mating) is seen in the Taittirīyas with respect to all three categories of objects: "The mother, the father, and the son—that indeed is the pair (*mithuna*).
*Diti* is the third.
The substance that is the substratum of the essence is called the *padārtha* (category), which is golden and is Diti.
Belonging to the honey—the Soma juice—it is the fourth, filled with honey, and shines forth in three ways (*trirūpate*).
The powerful, honey-sweet steeds of the Dawn rise up at her dawning, like chariots;
uncovering the hidden darkness, they spread out the bright light across the mid-air.

Upward rise for you two the food-offerings rich in sweetness; chariots and horses [come] at the dawning of the mornings. Uncovering that which was enveloped, they spread the bright light like the sun across the mid-air.
The *pṛkṣas*—the nourishing ones, threefold in nature, rich in sweetness, and endowed with the essence of Soma—are your chariots harnessed with horses for the two battles.
Or rather:
the sweet, nourishing chariots and the swift horses go forth, facing upward, at the dawning of the *uṣas*s, when they break forth.
Doing what?
Dispelling—that is, removing—the darkness that surrounds and pervades them on all sides; and, like the sun (svaḥ), spreading forth the bright, radiant realm (rajas) and splendor.
The particle "ā" is used here in the sense of "and."
Or rather:
spreading the dust of the atmosphere, which is bright and radiant.
Drink the honey with your honey-drinking mouths; moreover, harness your dear chariot for the sake of the honey.
You quicken the tracks and the paths with honey; O Aśvins, you carry a honey-filled gift.

Drink the honey with your honey-drinking mouths; moreover, harness the chariot for the sake of the beloved honey. You quicken the tracks with honey and you cleave the paths; O Aśvins, you carry the honey-filled gift.
Drink the sweet Soma juice with the honey-drinking mouths that are worthy of drinking Soma.
Moreover, yoke your dear chariot for the sake of obtaining sweetness; [yoke it] with horses, and—[the ellipsis being] "come to the path," namely, to the house of the sacrificer.
"Jinvathaḥ": you two gladden the paths, the ways of travel, with honey;
or rather, you gladden the speech, the word, and the path, the track, the sky.
O Aśvins, you two bring and sustain the honey-sweet draught.
1. *la*, *vā*, and *ra* are one hundredfold.

2. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *ṇa* are threefold. This vessel, this food, and this eating are ordained as a triad; for it is heard in the scripture that this food and eating are ordained as threefold: namely, drinking, chewing, and eating. *bha*, *la*, and *sa* are threefold.

"Threefold": (In the *sa* manuscript, 'tredhā' is absent) this food—consisting of eating, drinking, and chewing—is ordained as threefold; for so says the Śruti: "O you who chew! (In the *ta* manuscript, this occurs in the *Taittirīya*;
in the *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *pha*, and *ma* manuscripts, it appears in the *vyucchiteṣu* sections).
5. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, sa, and ‘ā’ do not exist. 6. O Aśvins!
Those swans of yours which are honeyed, unfailing, golden-winged, carrying you along, and awakening at dawn—
Leaping up, exhilarated, you who touch the exhilarating [draught], like bees to honey, you go to all the offerings.

Like swans—those which are yours, full of sweetness, never-failing, golden-winged, carrying [the offerings], awakening, leaping upward, exhilarating, touching with joy, you go to all the libations like bees to honey. 4.

The *haṃsāsaḥ* are those who travel swiftly on the path; the *madhumantaḥ* are endowed with sweetness; the *asidhrāḥ* are non-injurious; the *hiraṇyaparṇāḥ* have beautiful and delightful leaves; the *uhuvaḥ* are carriers; the *upabudhaḥ* are those who awaken above; the *udprutaḥ* are those who cause the waters to overflow; the *mandinaḥ* are exhilarators; the *mandispṛśaḥ* touch the exhilarating Soma.
Such are the horses, those which are mine—like honey, as it were, they extend [their power] like honey;
these are the horses of the Aśvins.
The sun, resorted to by the gods, having yoked his chariot, travels along the path;
O Aśvins, you two perceive—make known—by means of *svadhā*, that is, food characterized as Soma, all the paths in their proper sequence for your arrival.
O Aśvins, we have proclaimed this prayer for you, who possess the chariot with its noble horses that is ageless;
the chariot by which you instantly traverse the realms toward the one who brings oblations, the swift and generous patron.

I have proclaimed your praise, O Aśvins, as one who fashions the prayer. That chariot of yours which possesses good horses and is ageless—by means of it you traverse the regions in an instant toward the one who brings the oblation, the swift, the liberal patron. 7.
O Aśvins, I, the sustainer of wisdom, am the upholder of sacred rites; I proclaim and praise you both.

That chariot of yours—which possesses fine horses, is undecaying, unwearied, eternally new, or rather, ageless—by means of which chariot you traverse the worlds (the *rajas*) at that very moment, O bounteous ones.
By means of that chariot, come toward us—to reach us—to the one who possesses oblations, who is joined with the soma and other offerings, who is a crosser, a deliverer, swift-moving, and a provider;
[the words] "come" are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In the fifth Anuvāka, there are thirteen Sūktas.

Among them, the first Sūkta, "agne piba," consists of seven verses; it is the Ṛṣi Vāmadeva’s composition, in the Gāyatrī metre, and has Indra-Vāyu as its deity throughout, though the first verse is dedicated to Vāyu alone.
And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "The [hymn] for Agni is in the Vāyavya [meter], but that for Indra and Vāyu is Gāyatra.
The application of the hymn is based on its internal indicative marks (liṅga).
The first two [verses] are the invitatory and offering verses (yājyā) for the draught of Soma for Indra and Vāyu.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* [verse] 'O Agni, drink of the offerings' (*agne piba maghānām*) is to be recited without pausing" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).
O Agni, drink the pressed juice of the patrons; O Vāyu, at the sacrifices for heaven, for you are the one who drinks first.
O Agni, drink the pressed juice of the liberal patrons; O Vāyu, at the sacrifices for heaven, for you are the one who drinks first. 1.

O Vāyu, you first—before Indra and the others—drink the pressed juice, the essence extracted by pressing, of the *maghūs*, the sweet-flavored Soma juices, accompanied by the *manvan* finale. Where? That is stated: in the *diviṣṭis*, the sacrifices that lead to heaven, the celestial realm.
Or rather: for us, on the occasions of going to *div*, the heavenly world—
you indeed, you truly, are the one who goes before.
The word *hi* serves to indicate the well-known fact from other mantras such as "O God, you hold the first draught" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.52.1).

That Vāyu has the first drink is clearly known from the Brāhmaṇa passage: "The gods, indeed, did not agree upon the first drinking of King Soma, [saying], 'I shall drink first'" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 2.25).
For there, Vāyu, having run the race first, obtained the drink.
O Vāyu, with your hundred aids, accompanied by your teams and with Indra as your charioteer, sate yourselves with the pressed soma.
With a hundred aids for us, O Vāyu, accompanied by your teams and with Indra as your charioteer, satisfy yourselves with the pressed juice. 2.

1. *pa-aśvinā* means "possessing horses. 2. *ta-pa-aśvinā* means "possessing horses. 3. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-pa-jha-svaśvaḥ* means "one who has excellent horses. 4. *pa-yāthaḥ pariṇo gacchathaḥ* means "you two go around us. 5. *ta-abhiprāmum* [refers to the verse]. 6. *ta-kṛtsnaṃ sūktam* [refers to] the entire hymn. 7. *ta-kevalā vāyavyā* [refers to] those dedicated exclusively to Vāyu. In Ṛgveda 2.86: O Vāyu, accompanied by your team (*niyutvān*), having yoked them, and with Indra as your charioteer—that is, with Indra as your companion—you come hither for the sake of a hundred, that is, immeasurable, *abhidh*—meaning *parṇaya*, which refers to desires—as the instrumental cause; this is the ellipsis.
And having arrived, may you two—Indra and [Vāyu]—satisfy yourselves with and drink our own pressed Soma, the son of our son.

Regarding Indra’s partnership, it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa: “Of that [Soma], Indra became the fourth part, and Vāyu the three parts”; or, “The collectors indeed say that in the fourth part alone they reach a consensus, by which very portion Indra, acting like a charioteer, conquered” (AiB 2.25).
May a thousand bay steeds bring you both, Indra and Vāyu, toward the offerings for the drinking of Soma.
O Indra and Vāyu, may a thousand bay steeds bring you hither toward the sacrificial food for the drinking of Soma. 3.
O Indra and Vāyu, these thousand bay horses—meaning a thousand in number—come toward you, hastening toward the sacrificial food (*prayaḥ*).
Here, the word *hari* is a general term for horses. May they bring you both hither for the drinking of the Soma.
O Indra and Vāyu, come to this chariot with its golden seat, which touches the heavens and is well-adorned for the sacrifice.
The chariot with its golden seat, for Indra and Vāyu, well-fashioned; for you two indeed occupy it, which touches the heavens. 4.

O Indra and Vāyu, you have indeed mounted the chariot that has a golden seat (*hiraṇyabandhura*), is equipped with a golden supporting frame (*hiraṇyanivāsādhārakāṣṭha*), touches the sky (*divispṛś*), and possesses a beautiful sacrifice (*svadhvara*). Since this is so, the meaning is "therefore come hither.
Alternatively, it may be explained as "you have mounted toward the beautiful sacrifice" (*svadhvaraṃ pratyāsthātha*).
The triplet beginning with “rathena pṛthu” constitutes the second Aindravāyava cup at the Prauga-śastra on the fifth day of the ten-night sacrifice.
This is stated in the Sūtra: “rathena pṛthupājasā vahavaḥ sūracakṣasaḥ” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.13).
Come to the donor with your chariot of broad splendor;
O Indra and Vāyu, come here!
Upon your broad-shining chariot, come to the donor; O Indra and Vāyu, come hither! 5.
O Indra and Vāyu, with your broad-shining, mighty-strength chariot, come unto the donor, the sacrificer who bestows gifts;
for that purpose, come hither to this sacrifice.
O Indra and Vāyu, this [soma] has been pressed; drink it together with the gods in the house of the donor, being in harmony with them.
O Indra and Vāyu, here is the pressed juice; drink it together with the gods in the house of the donor, being of one accord. ||6||
O Indra and Vāyu, this Soma has been pressed and poured out;
drink that Soma together with the gods, being of one mind and equal delight, in the house of the donor—the sacrificial hall of the giver of the oblation.

1. [The variants] kha, ga, ṇa, na, bha, la, and sa do not have *naḥ* (us). 2. [The variants] ta and pa read *somapītaye pānāya* (for the drinking of the Soma); [the variant] pa reads *somapītaye pānāya abhi*. 3. [The variant] pa reads *śobhanayajñavantam* (possessing a beautiful sacrifice). 4. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and bha read *sthitau* (in the two who stand). 5. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, ma, and sa do not have *ā garta* (to the seat). 6. [The variant] la reads *samānaprītau santo* (being those of equal delight). May there be your arrival here, O Indra and Vāyu; may there be your release here for the drinking of the Soma. *iha* | *pra'yānam* | *astu* | *vām* | *indravāyū* | *vi'mocanam* | *iha* | *vām* | *soma'pītaye* || 7 ||
O Indra and Vāyu, let there be your departure—your coming—to this sacrifice here;
in this very sacrifice, let there be the unyoking of your horses for the drinking of Soma.
Although the two statements have the same meaning in terms of their conclusion, there is no contradiction, as they serve the purpose of expressing reverence.

The second hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with "vāyo śukraḥ," is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; it is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Vāmadeva and is dedicated to Indra and Vāyu (*aindrāvāyavam*).
The first verse is dedicated to Vāyu alone.
The index (*anukramaṇikā*) states: "The four [verses] beginning with 'vāyo' are dedicated to Vāyu; they are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter."
The application of the hymn is based on its internal indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
In the first ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), on the fourth day, the first verse is used in the *prauga-śastra* for Vāyu;
this is prescribed by the Sūtra: "O Vāyu, the bright [oblation] is offered to you; partake of the uninvoked invocations" (*vāyo śukro ayāmi te vihi hotrā avītāḥ*, Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).
O Vāyu, the pure [soma] is offered to you at the forefront of the sweet [juices] during the rites for heaven.

O Vāyu and Indra, you two who are powerful, lords of strength, come together in one chariot with your teams of horses for our protection, to drink the soma. Vāyo, Indraśca, śuṣmiṇā, saratham, śavasaḥ, patī, niyutvantā, naḥ, ūtaye, ā yātam, somapītaye. 3.

O Vāyu and you, Indra, you two are lords of power, lords of strength, full of vigor, mighty, possessed of teams of horses—meaning you have horses known as *niyuts*—and you have mounted a single common chariot; this is the sense of the remainder.
Come here for our protection, for the drinking of Soma, for the consumption of Soma.
Or rather: [the same].
And the two sentences: "He has mounted and is seated upon the chariot," and "He has come."

O Heroes, Indra and Vāyu, those teams of yours which are much-desired for the donor—bestow them upon us, you two who are the bearers of the sacrifice. 4. Those teams of yours which exist, O Heroes, much-desired for the giver—those, O Indra and Vāyu, you who convey the sacrifice, bestow upon us. 4.

O leaders, O you who carry the sacrifice, O Indra and Vāyu, those teams of horses which are much-desired—longed for by many—are ours; bestow them upon us, the sacrificer who has offered oblations, for my sake. Grant us those teams of horses.
The third hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “vihi hotrā,” belongs to Vāmadeva and is dedicated to Vāyu.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “vihi [pañca], five [verses]; dedicated to Vāyu.
The application of the hymn is established by its internal indicative marks (liṅga).
The second [verse] belongs to the Vāyu-deity in the Prauga-śastra on the fourth day of the Daśarātra;
thus it is stated in the Sūtra: “vihi hotrā avītā vāyo śataṃ harīṇām” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.11).

Accept the invocations; protect the inspired songs as if they were the wealth of a noble lord. O Vāyu, come with your bright chariot for the drinking of the pressed soma. 1. Accept the invocations; protect the inspired songs as if they were the wealth of a noble lord. O Vāyu, come with your bright chariot for the drinking of the pressed soma. 1.
O Vāyu, come hither, come hither; consume [the offering].

The *hotrās*—the oblations of Soma that accomplish the sacrifice—which have not been tasted (*avītāḥ*), meaning they have not been consumed by others before; [you who are] like a shaker (*vipaḥ*) of enemies, O King.
Furthermore, [grant] the riches (*rāyaḥ*), the wealth of me, the noble (*aryaḥ*) worshipper.
The word "having accomplished" (saṃpādya) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. O Vāyu, come with the gladdening chariot for the drinking—that is, the consumption—of the pressed Soma.

These two dark ones, the repositories of wealth, adorned with every beauty, have extended themselves. The fourth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “idaṃ vāmāsye,” is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is addressed to Indra and Bṛhaspati.

The application of this hymn is determined by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

This oblation is for your mouth, O Indra and Bṛhaspati; this dear hymn and the exhilarating draught are recited for you. (1) This is for you two; for your mouth, the oblation; the dear [hymn], O Indra and Bṛhaspati; the chant and the intoxication are being recited. (1)
"O Indra and Bṛhaspati, I cast this dear oblation in the form of Soma into your mouth"— this is the ellipsis.
And the *uktha* (recitation) and the *śastra* (chant), which produce exhilaration, are being praised.
This Soma is poured out for you both, O Indra and Bṛhaspati—
delightful for exhilaration and for drinking.
The application (viniyoga) of this [verse] has been stated together with the preceding mantra:

O Indra and Bṛhaspati, we invoke you with songs when the Soma is pressed, for the drinking of this Soma. (5) O Indra and Bṛhaspati, we, with songs, call upon you at the pressing for the sake of drinking this Soma. (5)

drink the Soma.
"And having drunk, may you both become exhilarated.
The fifth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "yastastambha," is the work of Vāmadeva; it is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
The tenth [verse] is in the Jagatī meter.
The tenth, consisting of two pādas, has Indra and Bṛhaspati as its deities; the remaining nine are dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Of the eleven [verses], one is dedicated to Bṛhaspati; the others are dedicated to Indra, and the penultimate is in the Jagatī meter."
In the *ābhipūlika* Ukthya sacrifice, during the third pressing, this hymn is for the purpose of insertion (*āvāpa*) in the *stomavṛddhi* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest.
Thus says the Sūtra: "He who established [the world], he who split the rock" (*āśva. śrau. 7. 9*).
In the first Bṛhaspatisava, this hymn belongs to both the *marutvatīya* and the *nikkevatya* recitations.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The hymn beginning with *yastastambha dhunetayaḥ* is for the opening of the *sūktamukhīya*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 9.5).
"He who by force propped apart the ends of the earth, Bṛhaspati, dwelling in the three seats, with his roar;
him the ancient seers, the inspired poets, meditating deeply, have placed in front—the one with the melodious tongue."

Bṛhaspati, who by his might suddenly propped apart the ends of the earth, he who has three abodes—him, the one with the pleasant tongue, the ancient seers, the inspired sages, meditating, have placed in front.

Bṛhaspati— the god who is the protector of the great sacrifice of the great god— by his power (*sahasā*), that is, by his strength, propped apart, that is, firmly established and restrained, the ends of the earth (*jmaḥ*), meaning the ten directions.

Abiding in three places, existing in three locations—he stands thus by means of his roar; that God, the ancient seers, the perceivers of the supersensuous, shining brightly, the wise ones—the sacrificers and others—have placed him in front, establishing him before them through hymns and the like.
He whose tongue is gentle, whose tongue is gladdening, whose tongue is delighting.

Drive away the fires; being exhilarated, [attain] that which is well-manifested. O Bṛhaspati, those who have extended toward us—that spotted, well-established, unburnt enclosure—O Bṛhaspati, protect its womb. 2.

O Bṛhaspati, those whose movement is a shaker—that is, whose gait is one that causes the enemies to tremble—such [beings], being exhilarated and gladdening you, O one of beautiful wisdom (*supraketa*), may they protect us; and those officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who belong to us, who extend themselves toward you or offer praise, may they protect this form, the womb, the cause, the sacrifice, or me, the sacrificer. Protect them!
The source is distinguished as follows: the speckled one, pouring forth fruits, well-stepping, having the nature of gliding, unburnt, unhurt, and wide.
The two verses beginning with "bṛhaspate yā" are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the omentum (*vapā*) and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Bṛhaspati;
for it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning with 'bṛhaspate yā paramā parāvat'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
O Bṛhaspati, those who touch the Truth have sat down at that supreme place which the cattle proclaimed from afar.
For you, the dug-out wells, milked by stones, flow with honey on every side toward the overflowing abundance.

O Bṛhaspati, from that which is the furthest distance, those who touch the *ṛta* have descended for you; dug out by the pressing-stones, the wells flow with honey on every side toward your overflowing abundance.
O Bṛhaspati, that which is well-known as the supreme, most excellent, and farthest distance— situated beyond the firmament,
that is, heaven— or rather, with a change of gender, it is the highest place.

Therefore, from this direction, for the sake of the goal—[expressed by] "ā ā"—your horses, which touch the *ṛta* (the cosmic order), that is, those touching the sacrifice, have sat down; they have settled down.
For you, the wells have been dug.
This is a simile based on comparison:

just as dug wells flow out from all sides, even so the Soma juices, milked from the stones and pressed by the pressing-stones, flow forth—sweet as honey—with a loud and distinct sound, such that there is a resonant hymn of praise.
Bṛhaspati, being first born from the great light in the highest heaven,
seven-mouthed and born with many powers, blew away the darknesses with his roar, as he possessed seven rays.
Bṛhaspati, being first born from the great light in the highest firmament, seven-mouthed and many-born, blew away the darkness with his roar, he who possesses seven rays. 4.

This god Bṛhaspati, the presiding deity of the mantras, being born first—manifesting at the very beginning—from the great, luminous, and blazing Āditya in the supreme, unsurpassed firmament, with seven mouths consisting of the seven meters, is many-born in manifold ways.

With the *suṣṭubh* chant, with the quality of the *ṛc*, and with his roar, he shattered the enclosure of Vala. Bṛhaspati drove out the lowing cows that had been hidden by the slayer; bellowing loudly, he released those that were crying out.

He, with the well-praising [hymn], he, by means of the quality of the *ṛc*, shattered Vala, the enclosure, with his roar. Bṛhaspati, loudly bellowing, drove forth the lowing cows that were eager for the draught. 5.
That Bṛhaspati, together with the Ṛk-hymn possessing beautiful praise, with the radiant quality, and with the roar—the sound—of the Aṅgirases, [opened] the enclosure.

Phalibheda;

The second [verse] is the filling one with sound. That very god, bellowing loudly, has driven out the lowing cows—those who yield milk known as "enjoyment" for the sake of the *habhya* vessels, impelling the oblations of milk and other offerings.
‘Evā pitre’ is the *yājyā* for the oblation in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Bṛhaspati;
this is because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘Evā pitre viśvadevāya vṛṣṇe viśve adya maruto viśva ūtī’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
In the Agniṣṭoma, this very verse serves as the *dhāyyā* in the Vaiśvadeva-śastra.

Thus may we worship with sacrifices, reverence, and oblations the Father, the Bull who belongs to all the gods;
O Bṛhaspati, may we, possessing good offspring and heroic sons, become masters of riches.

To him, the father, the one belonging to all the gods, the showerer [of benefits], let us do honor with sacrifices, with reverence, and with oblations. O Bṛhaspati, may we, possessing good offspring and heroic sons, be masters of riches. 6.
To the *pitṛ*, the protector; to the *viśvadeva*, whose form consists of all the deities.
He is called a *viśvadeva* because the gods are the objects expressed by mantras, and he is the presiding deity (*abhimānin*) of those mantras.

To the bull (*vṛṣṇe*), the showerer, the divine Bṛhaspati—to him we shall serve (*vidhema*) with sacrifices (*yajñaiḥ*) performed in the manner described, with oblations (*havirbhiḥ*) characterized by clarified butter and the like, and with reverence (*namasā*) consisting of praise.
O Bṛhaspati, may we be possessed of good offspring (*suprajāḥ*), endowed with heroic sons (*vīravantaḥ*), and become masters (*patayaḥ*) of riches (*rayīṇām*).

He who well maintains— that is, supports, cherishes, and praises— the god Bṛhaspati, the protector of the great (bṛhatām), whose characteristics have been described above, and who serves him as a domestic priest (purohita) by means of excellent oblations, hymns of praise, clothing, and so forth; and who honors and bows down to him, giving him the first portion— that is,
