Thus do the Bhojas, thinking of their own wealth, approach the wealthy ones for the sake of receiving gifts.
Within the unadorned [space], the merchants sleep, awakening in the midst of darkness.
Shining forth, making even the wicked take notice, the wealthy Dawns have come to bestow their bounty. Let the stingy niggards sleep on, unawakened in the midst of the darkness.

Now, on this day, the Dawns— shining forth, driving away the darkness, wealthy with riches— make themselves manifest for the sake of bestowing bounty, that is, for the granting of wealth such as Soma and other gifts, to the liberal patrons who are the sacrificers; they do so in the midst of the darkness, in the wondrously marvelous gloom, meaning in the deepest, most intense obscurity.
There, let the Paṇis, those merchants who give nothing here, remain unawakened; let them sleep.
Whether it be an ancient divine path or a new journey for you, O Dawns, may it be so today; by which path Navagva and Daśagva attained their state, you,
truly awakening us for the sake of life characterized by cattle and for the purpose of movement— walking, going, and other such activities— proceed forth.
Who was she, which among them was the ancient one, by whom they ordained the ordinances for mortals?
The auspicious Dawns move toward what is auspicious; those who have grown old together are not distinguished [as separate].

Which one among these is the ancient one? Which of the ordinances did the Ṛbhus establish? When the auspicious Dawns move in splendor, they are not distinguished as different; they are alike and ageless. 6.
Among these Dawns, which one indeed has arisen today, and which is the most ancient?
By which [Dawn] did the Ṛbhus perform their various tasks, such as the fashioning of the cups and other vessels for the Ṛbhus?
And those Dawns which are radiant, moving with splendor, and creating beauty and light.

They are ageless, unbroken, and eternally new; they cannot be distinguished because, being identical and similar, they maintain one and the same form on all days. Therefore, these very ones of today are those same ones of old; as such, the dawns move everywhere.

3 *Samanā*: equal from all sides; 4 *sarvataḥ*: everywhere; 5 *samānāḥ*: equal; 6 *purastāt*: in the east, in the eastern direction; 7 *samānataḥ*: from the equal region, from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); 8 *samanā*: equally from all sides; 9 *prathānāḥ*: spreading forth; 10 *ṛtasya*: of the sacrifice (*yajña*), of the seat (*sadas*) of Truth (*ṛta*).
Therein, the first [refers to] the officiating priests, the sacrificial oblations, and so forth—this is for the sake of being perceived.
2 *Budhānāḥ*: awakening, causing to awaken.
This [root] has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) inherent within it.
Thus, the great beings (*mahābhāvāḥ*), the *uṣas* (dawns), are being praised (*jarante*).
The emissions (*sargāḥ*) of the cows are like the creation (*sṛṣṭi*) of waters.
For it is heard in the Śruti: "The 'emissions' (sarga) of the cows are not rays" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.52.5).
Just as those [rays] are praised everywhere because they are beneficial by their very occurrence, so too do these Dawns move together, being alike and of uniform color.

Taking up the black darkness with their radiant, bright bodies—pure and shining—the Dawns move forth together, all alike, of uniform color, and unafraid. Taking up the black darkness with their radiant, bright bodies—pure and shining—they move forth.
They indeed move forth together, all alike, of uniform color, and unafraid; taking up the black darkness with their radiant, bright bodies—pure and shining. 9.
"tāḥ" refers to those very dawns. "id" is a filler particle. "nu" means "then. "Samanā" means "equal" or "identical," having the sense of being gathered together in one place.
Equal, uniform, of immeasurable color, or of unassailable color, or indeed of limitless color, they move about from all sides. What are they doing? They are crying out "Amba! (O Mother! to you.

This is great; it is exceedingly great. Taking up—that is, concealing—the black and dark form with their shining, radiant bodies—their own forms—they are bright, glowing, pure, and resplendent, or rather, illuminating.
O daughters of heaven, shining forth, O goddesses, bestow upon us wealth accompanied by progeny.
Awakening from this pleasant place, may we be masters of heroic vigor.
O daughters of heaven, shining forth, bestow upon us wealth accompanied by progeny, O goddesses. Awakening from this pleasant place, may we be masters of heroic vigor. 10.

O daughters of heaven—acting as the daughters of the radiant Āditya—O shining ones who manifest special splendor, bestow upon us wealth consisting of progeny, that is, riches accompanied by sons and the like. O goddesses, from a pleasant source, may we, awakening you and causing you to awaken, become masters of heroic vigor;
may we be the protectors of wealth together with our sons and kin.
When it has dawned, he should mutter: "taddo divaḥ."

1. Equal in *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *la*; equal in *ca*; equal in *ta* and *pa*; equal in every respect through equality. 2. *Ta*: from the atmosphere with one foot. 3. In *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, "from every side" (*sarvataḥ*) is absent. 4. In *kha*, *ga*, *pa*, and *bha*, [they are] swelling through equality (*samena*). 5. In *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, [the sequence is] beginning with the officiant (*ṛtvij*); in *la*, beginning with the glory of the officiant (*ṛtvigyaśa*); in *sa*, beginning with the power of the officiant (*ṛtvigvaśa*). 6. In *kha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, those are indeed those. 7. In *kha*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, "of unassailable color" (*aṃhisitavarṇāḥ*) is absent. 8. In *ca*, it is the form of darkness (*tamas*). 9. In *ta*, "making true" (*kurvatyaḥ satyāḥ*). 10. In *pa*, "may we become" (*bhavema*). [End of] the supplement.

To you, O daughters of heaven, shining brightly, I address these words, O Dawns, whose banner is the sacrifice: may we be glorious among the people; may both Heaven and the Goddess Earth grant this. 11. To you, O daughters of heaven, shining brightly, I address these words, O Dawns, whose banner is the sacrifice: may we be glorious among the people; may both Heaven and the Goddess Earth grant this. 11.

O daughters of heaven, O radiant dawns! To you—that fruit which is to be described by the first quarter-verse of the latter half—I, whose banner is sacrifice (yajñaketu), meaning one for whom the sacrifice itself is the guiding light, speak; that is, approaching you, I address you. Now, much is being said.
May we, while offering praise, be possessors of glory, renown, food, or lordship among our fellow men.
May Heaven and the Goddess Earth uphold that glory.
‘Prati vyā’ is the seventh hymn, consisting of seven verses; it is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Vāmadeva, composed in the *gāyatrī* meter, and has Uṣas as its deity.
According to the *Anukramaṇikā*: “‘Prati vyā,’ [seven verses], *gāyatra*.
This is to be recited during the *prātaranuvāka* at the *uṣasya* rite, in the *gāyatrī* meter, and in the *āśvina-śastra*.
For it is thus prescribed in the Sūtra: "Then Upastha [recites] 'prati vyā sūnarī' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.14)."
The noble lady, the daughter of Heaven, has appeared, shining forth from her sister. 1 She, the noble lady, the daughter of Heaven, has appeared, shining forth from her sister. 1

May she, being thus praised—she who is noble (*sūnarī*), the excellent leader of living beings (*suṣṭhu prāṇināṃ netrī*), the mother (*janī*) who brings forth fruits, and the sister (*svasuḥ*) of the night which is established in its own state—at the upper part of the night, at the time of its conclusion, shining forth (*vyucchantī*) and dispelling the darkness; as it is said: "The sister [stands] by her elder brother" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.124.8)—may that Dawn (*uṣas*), the daughter of the radiant sun (*divaḥ duhitā*), be seen by all. *Praty adarśi*: she is perceived by everyone.

Like a dappled, ruddy mare, the mother of cows, the observer of cosmic order—Uṣas has become the friend of the Aśvins. 2. Like a horse; variegated; ruddy; mother; of cows; observer of cosmic order; friend; has become; of the two Aśvins; Uṣas. 2.

Like a horse, she is variegated (*citrá*) and worthy of praise (*cāyanīyā*); she is formless (*á-rūpī*) yet radiant (*rócamānā*). She is the mother (*mātā*), the fashioner (*nirmātrī*), of the rays (*raśmīnām*) of light; she is *ṛtāvarī*, possessed of sacrifice (*yajñávatī*). Dawn (*uṣás*) has become, and continues to be, the friend (*sakhā*) of the Aśvins—sharing the same renown and being praised together with them.
Because she is praised together with the Aśvins and with Dawn, their mutual friendship exists.
And you are the friend of the Aśvins; and you are the mother of the cows; and, O Uṣas, you rule over wealth. 3.

1. Making the sun shine with distinction, they shine forth as they dispel [the darkness]. 2. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and la read *bruvantaḥ*; in pa and sa, *stuvantaḥ* is absent. 3. In pa, *annasya vā* is absent. 4. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, and bha read *dhārayatām*; *ca* is a filler. 5. In sa, it is *vāmadevyam*. 6. In ta, it is *prastūyamānā*. 7. Kha, ga, ṇa, and bha read *uṣā uṣasaḥ*; gha reads *uṣasaḥ*. And furthermore, you are the friend (*sakhā*) of the Aśvins;
and furthermore, you are the mother (*mātā*) of the rays (*raśmīnām*) of the cows.
Moreover, O Uṣas, you are the mistress, the sovereign, of wealth and riches.

O you who ward off hatred, O conscious one, O bestower of joy, we have awakened you with our hymns of praise. 4. Warding off hatred, you, the conscious one, O bestower of joy—we have awakened you with our hymns of praise. 4.
*Yāvayaddveṣasam*: one who causes hatred to be driven away; that is, one from whom hatreds and haters are being driven away or separated, or by whom hatreds are made distinct.
For enemies intent on killing at night indeed flee at the approach of dawn;
such a one, O possessor of true speech (*sūnṛtāvarī*), makes you known—
*sūnṛtā* being a name for speech.
O Goddess, we have awakened you—who possess those [qualities]—with hymns of praise; that is, we extol you with our laudations.
The auspicious rays have shone forth like herds of kine; Dawn has filled the wide expanse. 5. The auspicious rays have shone forth like herds of kine; Dawn has filled the wide expanse. 5.
The auspicious and praiseworthy rays have shone forth; they are visible like streams of water, like showers of rain. This Dawn has filled the wide expanse with her great splendor.

O radiant one, you have filled [the world]; you have dispelled the darkness with your light. O Uṣas, protect us according to your own nature. 6. You have filled; O radiant one; you have opened wide; with light; the darkness; O Uṣas; according to; your own nature; protect. 6.
O Night, you shine forth; filling the world with splendor, you dispel the darkness of gloom with your light. Furthermore, afterwards, protect the *svadhā*—the food characterized by oblations.
"Thou extendest unto the sky"—this verse is the invitatory prayer (*anuvākyā*) for Uṣas at the oblations to the gods.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Thou extendest unto the sky with thy rays, bringing hither nourishing foods" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.14).

O Uṣas, thou extendest unto the sky with thy rays, and unto the wide, beloved mid-air, with thy bright, glowing luster. (7) O Uṣas, thou extendest unto the sky with thy rays; thou extendest unto the wide and beloved mid-air with thy bright, glowing luster. (7)
O Dawn, with your rays you extend across the sky;
with your rays you extend across the vast and beloved mid-air.
Being endowed with a bright and flaming radiance, you act in this manner.

1. *ta-sakhā* means "having him as a friend. 2. In the versions *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha*, the word is *īśvarī*; in *la-sa*, it is *īśvaraḥ*. 3. *pa-la-yavayadveṣasam*. 4. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-la-sa*, the particle *vā* does not exist. 5. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-bha*, the meaning is "they fled" (*palāyanta*). 6. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha*, the address is *he sūnṛtāvari*. 7. In *pa*, it means "possessing truthful speech" (*satyavāgavatī*). 8. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha*, the reading is *gavāṃ sargā na udakānām* ("the streams of cows, that is, of waters"). 9. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-la-sa*, the word *anu* (meaning "afterwards") does not exist. 10. In *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-la-sa*, the phrase *ā dyāṃ...* does not exist. (Ṛgveda 1.66)
The eighth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "tad eṣasya," is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva; it is in the Jāgata meter and is dedicated to Savitṛ.
Thus it is enumerated: "tad eṣasya [is] Sāvitra, in the Jāgata [meter].
On the third day of the Ābhiplavika rite, this hymn is used as the Sāvitra Nivid insertion within the Vaiśvadeva Śastra.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "With 'tadasya ghṛtena dyāvāpṛthivī,' [he offers] three [oblations]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.7).
We choose that very great and ancient power of this Savitṛ, the wise Asura;
may he himself grant protection to the donor, and may the great god raise us up through the nights.
We choose that great boon of the god Savitṛ, the wise Asura—the protection by which he himself bestows [favor] upon the donor. May that great god extend it to us through the nights. 1.
We choose— that is, we pray for— that great, worshipful, and desirable wealth of Savitṛ, the impelling deity.
[This is] the strength of his vital breath (*asu*).
Therefore, [the word] *vpracetasaḥ* means "of one with excellent intellect"; it is connected with the word *devasya*. Being endowed with that wealth (*vyena dhanena*), [he attains] *chardiḥ*.

This is a name for the house; it refers to the collection of wealth characterized by the house. The god Savitṛ himself (*ātmanā*) bestows (*vyacchati*) that protection (*chardiḥ*) upon the sacrificer who has given the oblation (*vāśuṣe*). He does so by means of nights (*rātribhiḥ*), which are the "speakers" (*vaktubhiḥ*).
This is also an elliptical expression for sacred knowledge (*brahman*).
"By all days," that is, on all days, may he grant us "awakening"— the meaning is that he may cause [our intellect] to arise;
or alternatively,
*chardi* is a name for splendor (*tejas*).
"May that splendor rise," so [he says].
The upholder of heaven, the lord of creatures, the seer, puts on his tawny mantle;
far-seeing, spreading abroad and filling all, Savitar has brought forth auspicious light from the middle realm.

The upholder of heaven, the lord of creatures of the world, the seer, the far-seeing one, puts on his tawny mantle. Spreading it out and filling the wide space, Savitar has brought forth praiseworthy bliss.
The sustainer (*dhartā*) of heaven (*divaḥ*), that is, the supporter of the celestial world,

and not only of heaven but indeed of the entire universe (*bhuvanasya*), Prajāpati— the protector (*pālayitā*) of creatures through light, rain, and so forth, the wise (*kaviḥ*) god— puts on (*muñcate*), that is, covers himself with, the golden armor (*piśaṅgaṃ drāpiṃ*), at every rising.
The far-sighted one, the seer of all things—he, the very God, spreading abroad his splendor and filling it everywhere, has generated abundant, praiseworthy, and laudable happiness.
1. *kha-ṇa-na-bha-la-sāvitraṃ* is that which has the *sāvitrī* as its *nivid*; *sa-sāvitraṃ* is that which is to be recited with the *sāvitrī*.
2. *kha-ga-ṇa-bha-la-sa* [is used] for *prakṛṣṭamaḥ*; *gha* [is used] for *prakṛṣṭasya*; *ca* [is used] for *prakṛṣṭamasya*. 3. *pa-devaḥ savitā* (the god Savitṛ).
He has filled the celestial and terrestrial realms; the God makes his song for his own law.
Savitṛ extends his arms for our impulsion, settling the world by nights and setting it in motion.

He has filled the celestial and terrestrial realms; the God makes his fame known for his own righteous law. Savitṛ extends his two arms for this purpose of impelling, settling the world with his rays while setting it in motion. 3.
This god Savitṛ has illumined the celestial realms belonging to the Vasus, the earthly realms, and the intermediate spaces—the three heavens and the earths.
For it is heard in the Śruti: "He, the supporter, has sustained the three earths" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.27.8).
The god,
filling the quarters with his own rays,
makes for himself— his own— to sustain the wealth [of the world], a song of praise; he creates a hymn of glory.
Vasavitṛ, at the impulse—that is, at the occasion of permission—extends his own two arms toward us;
that is to say, he stretches them out.
What is he doing?
With rays (*aktubhiḥ*), making the world beautiful, establishing it in its respective functions, causing it to flourish, and impelling it; or alternatively, since *aktubhiḥ* is a name for night,
the meaning is that he acts in this manner during all days, as characterized by those nights.
Unassailable, he has illumined all beings; the god Savitṛ protects all creatures.
Having impelled them for the sake of the progeny of the world, he who maintains his vows rules over the great field of action.

Unassailable, surveying all living beings, the divine Savitṛ protects the winds. With arms extended for the sake of the creatures of the world, he who maintains the sacred law rules over the great realm of movement. 4.
The god Savitṛ, who is invincible and unharmed by others, has become the one who gazes upon the worlds. Illuminating the *vratas*—the actions of living beings—he protects them from all sides.
He extends his two arms toward the offspring of the world, toward those born of the lineage;
the meaning is that he grants permission for their respective duties.
Because all activities are dependent upon the sun, the Śruti declares: "Savitṛ indeed is the lord of all productions" (Ai. Brā. 1.16).
He whose vows are firm—that is, whose actions are steadfast—by acting thus, he shines forth (*varājati*) as the sovereign (*varāja*) over the great *vajma*, the moving world.
Savitar, by his greatness, thrice encompasses the mid-air; he pervades the three regions and the three luminous spheres.
He impels the three heavens and the three earths; with his threefold laws, he protects us by his own self.

Savitar, by his greatness, thrice encompasses the mid-air; he pervades the three realms, the three luminous spheres, and the three heavens. He impels the earth and the three [worlds]; with his three vows, he protects us himself.

1. Related to that earth. 2. Ga, ṇa, bha: let it be. 3. Kha, pa, ma: for the subjects, for their subjects; ga, ca: for Prajāpati, for his subjects; ṇa: for the offspring of Prajāpati, for their subjects.
4. [The letters] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, bha—this means "he causes to permit.
This [sun], by Savitṛ, [traverses] the threefold intermediate space (antarikṣa). It is called *antarikṣa* because the world (*jagat*) exists within it, having been contained therein.

Being the subduer, the one who overcomes, he strikes—that is, he pervades—by his greatness (*mahitva*), [the worlds] known as Vāyu, Vidyut, and Uruṇya, which are divisions of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), according to the Śruti: "He [attains] the world of Vāyu, he [attains] the world of Varuṇa" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.3), and so forth.
He strikes the three realms (*rajāṃsi*), the three non-self worlds consisting of the triads of earth, intermediate space, and heaven.
Previously, a specific sub-division of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) was mentioned; here, however, it is mentioned in its general form, so there is no tautology.
He strikes the three *rocanā*—the shining ones—which are the fires, winds, and other luminaries, by virtue of being the master of the three aforementioned locations.
Previously, a specific sub-division of the intermediate space was mentioned.
Now, the internal distinction between deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) is stated:
he traverses three heavens called Indra, Prajāpati, and [the third], that is, the three worlds;
likewise, he traverses three earths.
He destroys the worlds, which are intermediate divisions of the earth.

Thus, the divine Vyāsa protects us—us, his own people—by means of the three divine activities known as heat, rain, and cold, solely through his own mind and by his own grace; may he protect us. May he gladden us with wealth and other blessings throughout the nights and the days—that is, on all days. May he bestow upon us, the ashes [of our sins], riches accompanied by progeny; that is to say, may he pervade us and grant them to us. || 4 ||
The ninth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “*abhūdu vaḥ*,” is the *sāvitra* hymn of Vāmadeva.
This first verse is a *triṣṭubh*, while the remaining verses are *jagatīs* according to the rule that the rest are *jagatīs* when the final verse is a *triṣṭubh*.
Thus, the *Anukramaṇī* states: “*abhūdu vaḥ*: six verses, ending in *triṣṭubh*.”
In the Agniṣṭoma, this [hymn] containing the Sāvitra Nivid is used for the Vaiśvadeva Śastra.
Thus says the Sūtra: "abhūreva ekayā ca daśabhiśca svabhūte" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.18).
The first [verse] is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) for the Sāvitra cup-offering.
And so says the Sūtra: "While performing with the Sāvitra cup, [the priest] says: 'Savitṛ, who has become our father, is now to be praised by us. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.18)

Savitṛ has indeed become worthy of our praise; he is now to be invoked by men this very day—he who distributes treasures to human beings, bestowing upon us the most excellent food and wealth. He has become the god Savitṛ, worthy of our desire; indeed, he is now to be praised by men this very day—he who distributes treasures to human beings, so that he may grant us the most excellent food and wealth.
That god Savitṛ has become manifest;
therefore, indeed, he is now to be praised by us.
Now, at this time of sacrifice, during the third pressing (tṛtīyasavana), he is to be invoked—that is, to be praised—by men, our own Hotṛ-priests.

That god who distributes delightful treasures (*ratna*)—meaning pleasing riches—for the sake of men, the offspring of Manu, that is, for those performing sacrifices; may that god bestow upon us here, in this ritual act, the most excellent and praiseworthy wealth characterized by cattle and the like, so that he may grant it to us.
Thus he has become one who is to be praised and invoked.

For you have first bestowed immortality upon the gods worthy of sacrifice; you have fashioned the highest portion. Then, O Savitṛ, you unfold the gift for humanity, providing successive spans of life. devebhyaḥ | hi | prathamam | yajñiyabhyaḥ | amṛtatvam | suvāsi | bhāgam | uttamam | āt | it | dāmānam | savitar | vi | ūrṇuṣe | anūcīnā | jīvitā | mānuṣebhyaḥ ||2||
"First indeed to the gods":
the word *hi* indicates well-known fact.

To the gods—those worthy of sacrifice, those entitled to sacrifice—you grant (*suvāsi*), that is, you authorize, the highest, most excellent portion characterized by Soma and other offerings, which is the means for attaining immortality.
O Savitṛ, immediately after [the beginning], you reveal—i.e., you manifest—the giver of gifts, the giver of oblations;
for the sake of human beings, the sacrificers, the lives that follow one after another in succession.
The succession consists of father, son, and grandson.
Such lives as these you shall later unfold.

1. The syllables *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa* are the *dhanas*. 2. *Kha* and *pha* belong to Sāvitra; this is the *nivid-vāna*; this is the *sanividvānīya*. 3. *Ta* is equal to [the preceding]. 4. *Ṇa*: "To the Mānavas worthy of sacrifice. 5. *Kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*: "Of us. 6. *Ta*: characterized by *soma*, *ājya*, and so forth. Whatever we have done through lack of thought among the divine folk—with feeble skill, with abundance, or with human nature—O Savitṛ, among both gods and men, do thou here impel us to be sinless.

Whatever we have done through lack of thought among the divine folk, with feeble skill, with abundance, or with human-like power—among both gods and men, O Savitṛ, may you here grant us freedom from sin. 3.

O Savitṛ, we have committed an offense through lack of worship and lack of wisdom toward you, the divine among men— whether by those who are wretched and weak, such as sons and others, or by those who are arrogant and powerful, through the intoxication of wealth (meaning *prabhūtyā*) and through human-like behavior (*puruṣavat*). Whatever sin we have done...

Not only what was done by you alone, but whatever we have done out of ignorance and so forth toward the gods, others, or humans—regarding this action, please grant us leave, making us free from guilt and sinless.
At the oblations of the *devasuvām*, the invitatory verse for Savitṛ of true instigation is "na pramiye.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "na pramiye savitur daivyasya... tadbṛhaspate prathamam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).
The divine power of Savitṛ is not to be measured; it is that by which he shall sustain the entire world.
That which he, the self-strong one, impels from the expanse of the earth and from the vault of heaven—that word of his is truth.
No, it is not to be measured; that of the divine Savitṛ is such that he will sustain the entire world.
That which he, with beautiful fingers, impels within the expanse of the earth and within the armor of heaven—that of him is truth. 4.
That work of the divine god Savitṛ is not to be measured, nor is it to be measured away, nor is it to be harmed;
the meaning is that it does not become subject to injury.
The suffix *ken* is used in the sense of "that which is to be done."
Alternatively,
in the phrase "of the divine" (*daivyasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*);
and that [genitive] has the sense of the object (*karma*).
The meaning is "divine action. To the question "How is it not to be harmed? he says:
"In such a way that it will sustain—that is, it sustains—the entire world."
That action which consists of the sustaining of the universe is not to be measured;
likewise, he who has beautiful fingers—characterized by lovely digits—with his hand, [acts] over the vastness of the earth. (The word *ākāra* is used here in the sense of "extent" or "dimension.")
He impels and sends forth [the rain] from the earth into the wide expanse;
likewise, he impels it from the sky, from the realm of heaven, into the wide expanse.
That deed of this god is called true and unassailable.

1. [The reading] *tathājñānādibhiḥ* is found in manuscripts *la*. 2. [The reading] *apāpān* (meaning "sinless") does not exist in manuscripts *na*, *la*, or *sa*. 3. [The reading] *ca* is found in manuscript *ta*, and there is also a *sūtra* [to this effect]. 4. [The reading] *vyādhikaraṇe* is found in manuscript *ta*. 5. [The reading] *yaḥ* is found in manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ma*, *la*, and *sa*; [the reading] *yam* is found in *ta*; [the reading] *yat* is found in *na*. 6. [The word] *prerayati* ("impels") does not exist in manuscripts *na*, *la*, or *sa*.
From the great mountains, O Indra, you have brought forth these dwellings for the eldest [beings]; you fashion them as abodes full of nourishment.
Just as they fly apart in various directions, even so do they stand still at your command, O Savitar, for your impelling.

To those whose chief is Indra, to the great mountains, to these dwellings—you bestow them as prosperous abodes. Just as they, flying forth, have spread themselves out, even so, O Savitṛ, do they stand for your impulsion. 5.
O Savitṛ, you impel us— who have Indra as our eldest—
that is, those for whom Indra, endowed with supreme lordship, or Indra himself, is the eldest, the most excellent, and the most venerable—
from the great mountains; you send us forth as superior to them.
Furthermore, for these sacrificers, you send forth habitations—dwellings such as villages, cities, and the like—possessing houses.
Just as they fly forth and go, they separate themselves;
yet, by your very impulse (savāya), that is, by your permission, they stand thus, remaining exactly according to the fixed order without transgression.
O Savitṛ, those beautiful rays of yours which day by day bring us prosperity—
may Indra, Heaven and Earth, Sindhu, Aṅgiras, and Aditi with the Ādityas, grant us protection.

O Savitṛ, those who three times a day, well-adorned, send forth prosperity for us day after day—may Indra, Heaven and Earth, Sindhu with her waters, and Aditi with the Ādityas, grant us protection. 6.
O Savitṛ, those libations (*savāḥ*)—that is, the *soma* juices—which belong to you for the sake of the sacrificers;
[here] the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative:
[namely,] the *somān*.
Or rather:
they press [the Soma] three times a day against the pressings of morning and so forth, accompanied by the *savas*.
Not only on a single day during the three pressings, but day after day (*divedive*), they press it—that which produces good fortune (*saubhagam*).
From them—Indra, may he grant us protection;
may Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivī) grant it; and may Aditi, together with the Ādityas, grant protection, along with Sindhu—the river distinguished by its waters—and the deity presiding over Sindhu.
Having stated the inclusion of Indra and the others in the Sāvitra hymn, their invocation is not contradicted.
The tenth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “*Ko vaḥ satrā*,” is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Vāmadeva and has the Viśvedevas as its deity.
Of these, the first three verses—beginning with the eighth—are *gāyatrī*s;
the remaining verses are *triṣṭubh*s according to the rule regarding unspecified meters.
And thus it is recited in sequence: “What [is] yours? Ten [verses] for the Viśvedevas, ending with three Gāyatrīs.
The application is based on indicative marks (liṅga).

1. Those who are endowed with fear (*saṃbhāmān*) regarding the worlds (*jagatīrādīn*), such as Kha, Ga, Ṇa, and Sa; and those who are endowed with fear (*sa-saṃbhāmān*) regarding battles (*saṃgarādīn*).
2. Living beings (*prāṇinaḥ*) who go toward Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Bha, and Gha.
3. By you (*tvayā*) [who possess] Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, and Bha.
4. *pa*—thus it is for you.
5. *na*, *la*, and *sa*—the term "dyāvāpṛthivī" does not exist [here]. 6. *ta*—because it possesses the nature of a particle (*nipāta*); *pa*—because it is devoid of the nature of a particle.
7. [The syllables] *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ta-na-bha-la-sa* have the Viśvedevas as their presiding deities.
Who is your protector, O Vasus? Who is your defender, O Heaven and Earth, O Aditi?
Protect us from the more powerful mortal, O Varuṇa and Mitra! O Gods, who among you grants wide space at the sacrifice?

Who is your protector, O Vasus? Who is your defender? O Heaven and Earth, O Aditi, protect us from the more powerful mortal, O Varuṇa, O Mitra! O Gods, who among you bestows wide space at the sacrifice?

O Vasus, you gods who cause all things to dwell, who is your protector? The intention is: "Since you are the Vasus (the bestowers of dwelling), who is there? And who is your benefactor, the one who shares with you?
Or rather:
among you, O Heaven and Earth, who is the protector (*kakhātā*) and which god is the warder-off (*varutā*) of sufferings, or the one to be chosen? O Heaven and Earth, protect us, guard us.
"O Aditi, the indivisible one.
This is also an epithet for Heaven and Earth;
there is an inversion of the number.
If this were an address to separate deities, then there would be no *nighāta* (anudātta accent).

This is because, according to the rule "an address that precedes [another] is as if non-existent," the preceding word is treated as non-existent, and thus this very [word] begins the *pāda*, just as in the examples:
"O Aditi, Mitra, and Varuṇa, be gracious" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.27.14) and "The Ādityas, Rudras, and Vasus, the bounteous givers" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.66.12).

Since it functions as an adjective in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), its *nighāta* accent is established by virtue of that apposition, just as in the case of "O Agni, O Purifier, with your light" (*agne pāvaka rociṣā*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.26.1).
Therefore, it is an adjective qualifying the pair "Heaven and Earth.
O Varuṇa, O Mitra, may you two protect us from a more powerful mortal, from a man who would seek to overcome us.
O gods, who among you provides— i.e., bestows— *varivas*, wealth, at your sacrifice (*adhvara*)?
Or rather,
who among you maintains *varivas*?

Those who follow the holy ordinances, the radiant ones who shine forth, the unerring ones—those wise ones, whose thoughts are fixed on Truth, have distributed them with vigor; they shine with beautiful splendor.

When the wise illuminators, the ordainers whose thoughts are fixed on the Eternal Law, shine forth, they have established their pure abodes; radiant and beautiful, they have spread out with unclouded light. || 2 ||

Those gods who praise and bestow upon their worshippers the ancient, meritorious abodes or stations; and those who are the dispellers of sorrows, the unmixed, the immortal, and the undeluded, who shine forth and drive away the darkness— those gods, the ordainers and makers of fruits, the eternal ones, have distributed and bring about what is desired through their power.
Furthermore, those of true insight, whose actions are real, who are formidable and beautiful to behold, they shine forth; they radiate light.
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Pa, Bha, and La, the phrase "‘akaḥ... varūtā’ does not exist. 2.

In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Pa, Bha, and Sa, it reads "saṃcārayitā"; in Ca, "saṃcarāyitā"; and in La, "saṃcarayitā. 3. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Pa, Bha, and La, it reads "mantreṇa"; in Sa, "mantraṇe."
4. Like *cetivat*.

5. Regarding "in a coreferential [compound] with *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *pa*, *sa*": since it is a coreferential [compound], and because of the prohibition of the treatment as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*) when [the suffix] *-ta-* is based on a name that is coreferential. 6. Protect him who bestows—that is, gives—wealth (*dhana*).
7. Those who take refuge in *kha*, *ga*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*; those who destroy *gha* and *na*.
With hymns, I invoke for prosperity the river Arditī, for friendship with the Goddess Svasti.
May both Day and Night protect us, and may Dawn and Night make us free from blindness.

I praise with hymns Aditi for prosperity, the Sindhu river, and the Goddess Svasti for friendship; so that both Day and Night may protect us, and Dawn and Night may grant us sightlessness-free vision.

I praise with hymns—that is, I extol with mantras—that goddess Aditi, who is to be approached by all, the undepressed mother of the gods; that goddess Sindhu, whose nature is to flow; that goddess who is honored as the lord of rivers; and that goddess named Svasti, whose name signifies a happy dwelling, for the sake of friendship and favor.
Just as both days—the two deities Heaven and Earth—may protect us thoroughly, so do I praise them.
May the two deities presiding over day and night, Upas (Dawn) and Naktā (Night), who are invincible and cannot be deceived, grant us their favor.
The word "desired" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
May Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Agni, the lord of nourishment, grant us a path, a prosperous course;
and may Indra and Viṣṇu, being praised, now extend to us wide protection and secure refuge.
Aryaman, Varuṇa, and Agni, the lord of nourishment, have made known the path, the way to well-being. O Indra and Viṣṇu, being well-praised, grant us powerful protection and a secure refuge.
The divine Aryaman discerns—that is, makes known—our path, the way beginning with sacrifice;
likewise Varuṇa discerns it.
He is the lord and protector of *iṣ*, that is, of the food characterized by the oblation.
Agni discerns the path—the way to heaven and the like—which leads to well-being and happiness.
O Indra and Viṣṇu, being well-praised, grant us a desirable, powerful shelter—a home or a state of bliss—endowed with human-like qualities and accompanied by men.
(The particle *u* is a filler.)
May we obtain the protections of the mountain-dwelling Maruts, of the god Trātṛ, and of Vṛṣabharga.
May Pātpati deliver us from the distress caused by our kinsmen, and may Mitra, as one who loves friendship, protect us.

May the protection of Parvata, of the Maruts, and of the divine savior Atri-Bharga preserve us. May Mitra protect us from the distress caused by enemies, and may he deliver us from that which comes from his own kin. ||5||

1. *ta* reads *aditim aditim*; 2. *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *ca* read *īḷe*; *gha*, *pa*, and *pra* read *īḷe*; 3. *kha*, *ga*, and *ṇa* read *prāstoti*; *ca* reads *prāstod iti*; *na* lacks the word *'staumi*; *bha* reads *prastaumi*; *sa* reads *stauti*.
O Agni, I choose for myself the protections of Parvata—the friend of Indra, the deity named Vetta—and of Bhaga, the brother and protector of the Maruts.
Furthermore, may Varuṇa, the Lord, protect us from the sin arising from human society; may he guard and preserve us.
And furthermore, may Mitra and the son of Mitra protect us, us, with a friendly disposition.
Now let us praise the two goddesses, Heaven and Earth, with the serpent of the deep and with these desired offerings of water;
like two seekers of gain on a journey to the ocean, they have opened themselves up like the flowing sounds of the heated milk.

Now let us praise Heaven and Earth with the Dragon of the Deep; let us praise the Goddesses with our desired offerings. Like those seeking gain at a gathering, the rivers, sounding like the heat of the cauldron, have opened wide their paths as if toward the ocean.

O you two, Heaven and Earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), I praise you both quickly with these desirable objects of attainment that have been reached— along with the divine Ahibudhnya, the one dwelling in the depths— with songs of praise. Desiring to win wealth, seeking to share it, for the sake of traveling— that is, for the journey into the midst of the ocean— I praise you just as one praises the ocean itself.
Because these gods, whose own sound is the *gharma*—that is, those of radiant voice—open up the rivers (*nadyaḥ*) as if from behind the scenes;
or else, it is a prayer that "may those gods open up the rivers.
Therefore, the connection is: "I praise [them]."
May the divine Aditi protect us; may the protector among the gods guard us ever-vigilantly.
For we must not neglect the sustenance of Mitra and Varuṇa, nor the summit of Agni.
May the goddess Aditi protect us; may the god, the savior, protect us without ceasing. For we must not violate the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa upon the summit of Agni. 7.
May the goddess Vaditi, the undepressed mother of the gods, together with other gods such as Mitra and others, protect— that is, preserve— us. Likewise, may the god Trātṛ, the protector—
the meaning being Indra— protect us.
May he too, guarding the rampart and remaining vigilant, protect us.
And we, having reached the lofty summit of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni—that food characterized by Soma and other offerings—do not deserve to harm it; indeed, we are worthy [of it];
we become capable [of protecting it].
The meaning is: "By what performance has he been made worthy? (i.e., increased in worthiness).
May Agni, the lord of wealth and the one worthy of honor,
grant us those riches of good fortune.
Agni rules over the acquisition of wealth; Agni [rules] over great good fortune. May he grant all those things to us. 8.
1. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pha, bha, la, sa belong to the mountain friend.
2. Pa and devī are for the shining one; he is [the letter] ha. 3. Kha, ga, ca, la—“not like the ocean” (samudraṃ na) is absent.
4. May the goddess Ca-pha, shining brightly, together with the gods, protect us—may Aditi guard us.
5. Likewise, may the god Pālaka, [represented by] Kha-ṇa-bha-la-sa, and Ca-pha-devatrātā, protect us as well. 6. Ka-kha-ga-gha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-la refers to the Arhats.
Agni, the god, is the lord—meaning he has the power—to bestow a wealth consisting of a multitude of riches;
likewise, Agni is the lord of great good fortune.
Therefore, may he grant us those riches and that good fortune.
O bountiful Dawn, bring us many desirable things, O giver of joy, O possessor of strength!
O bountiful Dawn, O bringer of true wealth, bring hither many desirable things for us, O thou who art rich in spoil. 9.
O Dawn, O bountiful one, O possessor of wealth, O thou whose nature is pleasant truth and speech, O goddess rich in food, bring hither and bestow upon us many desirable treasures worthy of choice.
Therefore, may Savitṛ, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman,
and Indra come to us with bounty.
May Savitṛ, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra come to us with bounty. 10.

With that wealth and bounty by which Savitṛ, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, and Indra each come individually to the sacrifice—may those gods bestow that wealth and bounty upon us most excellently; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
The hymn beginning with "mahī dyāvāpṛthivī" is the eleventh in the seventh [maṇḍala]; it is the seerly composition of Vāmadeva and is addressed to Heaven and Earth (Dyāvāpṛthivī).
Since it was stated previously that "the three ending in Gāyatrīs," the first three verses, starting from the fifth, are Gāyatrīs, while the remaining ones are Triṣṭubhs.
The Anukramaṇikā states: "mahī sasa dyāvāpṛthivīyam."
When the ten-night sacrifice has been arranged, on the fifth day, during the Vaiśvadeva Śastra, the first four verses of the *dyāvāpṛthivī-nivid-dhānīya* hymn are to be recited.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The four straight verses beginning with *mahī dyāvāpṛthivī* are the *viṣṭut-vimvā*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8).
May Heaven and Earth, the two greatest worlds, be present here with their radiant luster and pure hymns;
when the two most excellent and vast ones are established, they shall sprinkle [the sacrifice] with speech through their far-reaching protections.

"O Earth! O Heaven and Earth! Be here, O two eldest ones, with your splendor, through pure and radiant hymns. When he, the bellowing bull, builds up these two most wide and vast expanses, he roars aloud with his far-reaching movements. || 1 ||
In this sacrifice, O Heaven and Earth— the two great, vast, most excellent, and praiseworthy ones— joined with radiance and endowed with shining hymns (*arkas*) or oblations such as Soma,
may you both be present; for, since the Bull, the showerer Parjanya, establishing, defining, and fixing you both, the Heaven and Earth, which are most extensive, superior, and vast, on every side.

Together with these *pramathānebhiḥ*—those who crush (*prathamānaiḥ*), those who go (*gamanashīlaiḥ*), or those who are joyful (*harshimaih*)—he calls out, he makes a sound. The particle *ha* is a filler.
Therefore, the connection is: "May you two arise from that."
The Goddess, worshipped by the gods who are worthy of sacrifice, stands unimpaired and enduring;
she, the observer of Truth, firm, mother of the gods, the leader of the sacrifice, with her radiant hymns.

The two goddesses; by the gods; she is worshipped; by those worthy of sacrifice; undecaying; they have stood firm; pouring forth; observers of cosmic order; steadfast; having the gods as their sons; leaders of the sacrifice; with radiant hymns. 2.

The two goddesses, worthy of sacrifice, who are to be worshipped, who do not diminish offspring, who are non-violent, who nourish, who pour forth, who are observers of cosmic order (*ṛtāvarī*), who possess cosmic order, who are firm, who are free from malice, who do not commit injury, who have the gods as their sons, who are the progenitors of the gods, the two leaders and conductors of the sacrifice, Heaven and Earth—joined by the gods who are worthy of worship, by the radiant hymns or oblations that cause them to shine—they stand; they remain present.
He indeed was the skillful one among the worlds, he who brought these two, Heaven and Earth, into being.
He, the wise one, by his power has brought together the two wide, deep, well-established, and pillarless realms.

He alone was the skillful craftsman among all beings—he who generated these two, heaven and earth; the wise one, by his power, has joined together the two wide, deep, well-established, and pillarless realms. 3.
He alone, being well-performing (svapāḥ) through auspicious deeds, dwells within the worlds.
He is he who generated these two, Heaven and Earth;
and he, Prajāpati, the wise one, by his skillful power (śacyā), properly impelled the two vast, deep, immovable, well-formed, rootless, and supportless expanses—the intermediate regions.
He indeed is our own protector.

Now, O Heaven and Earth, together with the wives [of the gods], providing nourishment, well-pleased, far-reaching, and worthy of universal worship—do you both protect us with great defenses. Through our prayer, may we be chariot-borne victors, ever-conquering.

O Heaven and Earth, with your vast protections, accompanied by your consorts, providing nourishment, well-pleased, far-reaching, and worthy of all worship—protect us through our prayer! May we, as masters of chariots, be ever victorious. ||4||

1. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha-satyavatyau* | 2. *pa-dīpayadbhiḥ* | 3. *pa-arcanīyaiḥ* | 4. *pa-śobhana-rūpe rajasī bhuvane* | O two *rodasī*, Heaven and Earth, who together with your wives (*patnīvadbhiḥ*), accompanied by your wives, with great (*bṛhadbhiḥ*) protections (*varūthaiḥ*), houses, or riches, desiring food for us (*iṣayantī*), being in harmony (*sajoṣāḥ*), united with one another, wide-reaching (*urucī*), pervasive (*uru*), worthy of sacrifice (*yajate*), and true (*satye*), protect us thoroughly (*ni pātam*). The rest, beginning with *dhiyā*, is understood.
The triplet beginning with "pra vām," composed in the Gāyatrī meter, is to be inserted as the Dyāvāpṛthivya Nivid in the Vaiśvadeva Śastra during the expanded (vyūḍha) Daśarātra sacrifice.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The two triplets beginning with 'pra vām mahi dhavī'... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.11).
We bring forth a great hymn of praise unto you two, O mighty ones; we approach you, the pure ones, for glorification. (5)
To you two, O Heaven and Earth, the resplendent ones (*ghavī*), we bring forth with excellence a great, abundant hymn of praise (*upastuti*).
O pure ones, we approach you for the sake of glorification (*praśastaye*).
Since the prefix *upa* is heard, the appropriate verb is to be supplied.
The remainder of the sentence is "let us approach."

Purifying each other’s bodies by their own inherent power, you two rule over the purpose of the sacrifice from of old according to the eternal Law (Ṛta). 6. *Punāne* (purifying), *tanvām* (bodies), *mithaḥ* (mutually), *svena* (by their own), *dakṣena* (power), *rājathaḥ* (you two rule), *ūhārthe* (for the purpose of the sacrifice), *sanāt* (from of old), *ṛtam* (the eternal Law). 6.
O two goddesses, you two rule over the sacrifice or the sacrificer, purifying and cleansing each other mutually with your own bodies, forms, and inherent power (*dakṣa*).
Alternatively,
it may mean that you two purify and cleanse each other mutually through portions of your respective bodies.
The distinction is this: Heaven [supports] the earth with its own rain, and the earth, through its own smoke situated in the moon, supports heaven;
thus you two eternally, at all times, carry the *ṛta*, the sacrifice, for the sake of its elevation.

The two great ones have furthered the truth of Mitra; crossing over and fulfilling the *ṛta*, you two have encompassed and protected the sacrifice. 7. "The two great ones," "of Mitra," "have furthered," "crossing over," "fulfilling," "the *ṛta*," "around," "the sacrifice," "down," "you two have protected. 7.
The two great ones, Heaven and Earth, have accomplished the desire of Mitra—that is, of the worshipper who has become a friend.
Crossing over *ṛta*, that is, food, and carrying it across, fulfilling and completing the sacrifice, you two have established yourselves around it; you take refuge in it on every side.
The twelve-verse hymn beginning with "kṣetrasya patinā" is the seerly work (ārṣam) of Vāmadeva.
The first, fourth, sixth, and seventh verses are *anuṣṭubh*s; the fifth is a *purauṣṇih*.
For its definition is: "If the first [pāda] is a *purauṣṇih* [it is a *purauṣṇih*]."

The remaining three verses are *triṣṭubh*s. 1. *pa-rathyaḥ*: May we, possessing chariots (*rathavantaḥ*), through our prayerful hymn (*dhiyā stutyā*), be ever-winning (*sadāsāḥ*)—that is, may we always be those who devote ourselves to you. 2. *ta-vyūḍhe*. 3. *ta-rājathaḥ*: You two are sovereigns (*īśāne*). 4. *kha-ga-ca-pha-svasvaśarīraikyādinā*. 5. *ta-sādhadhaḥ*: You two accomplish (*sādhayathaḥ*). 6. *kha-na-la-sa-āśrayataḥ*.
The first [verse] has the deity Kṣetrapati; the fourth has the deity Śuna; the fifth and eighth have Śunāsīra as their deity; the sixth and seventh have Sītā as their deity.

Thus says the Anukramaṇikā: “The first three belong to Kṣetrapati; one following belongs to Śuna; the next is a Purauṣṇih addressed to the Maruts; the two penultimate verses belong to Śunāsīra; those two are in the Anuṣṭubh metre, as are the first and the fourth.”
For the purpose of plowing a field, one should offer oblations or recite this hymn verse by verse.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the hymn beginning 'By the Lord of the Field, we... (RV 4.57), one should offer oblations or recite it verse by verse" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.10.4).
In the *asuryāma* sacrifice, there are four *atiriktokthas* following the *āśvina-śastra* of the *hotṛ*.
Among them, the first is the *paridhānīyā*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*kṣetrasya patinā vayam* is the *paridhānīyā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.11).
Through the Lord of the Field, our benefactor, may we be victorious;
having nourished our cattle and horses, may he be gracious to us in such a state.
Through the Lord of the Field, as if through a benefactor, may we conquer. May he grant us cattle and horses for our nourishment; may he be gracious to us in such a state. 1.
We, the sacrificers, [worship] with the god who is the Lord of the Field.
Some say Rudra is the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati), while others say it is Agni;
or rather, some speak of a certain independent being as the Lord of the Field.
The word "iva" has the sense of "only" (evārthe);
thus, it means "by that alone which is for the welfare of all living beings.
Alternatively, it means "as if by a friend."
Just as one accomplishes one's own task through the assistance of a friend,
so do we conquer; we conquer the field.

That god shall increase our cattle and horses—or rather, he shall bring us wealth characterized by cattle and horses; this is the sense. Because of the presence of the prefix *upa*, the verb "to join" (*yunakti*) is supplied. That very god, when such wealth as described above is to be given, shall be gracious (*mṛḷāti*) toward us, that is, he shall make us happy.
One should understand the etymological explanation [of this] as given in the Nirukta, beginning with "kṣetrasya patinā" (Nirukta 10.15).

The *paridhānīyā* for the Maitrāvaruṇa at the Aśvamedha, when there is an *atiriktoktha*, is [the verse] "kṣetrasya pate madhumantam ūrmiṃ. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *paridhānīyā* is 'kṣetrasya pate madhumantam ūrmiṃ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.11).
O Lord of the Field, milk for us a honeyed wave, as a cow yields her milk—honey-distilling, well-purified like clarified butter; may the Lords of the Eternal Law (Ṛta) be gracious to us.
O Lord of the Field, milk for us the honeyed wave, as a cow yields her milk—sweet-flowing, well-purified like clarified butter. May the Lords of Truth be gracious unto us. 2.
O Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapati*), just as a cow (*dhenu*) yields milk (*payaḥ*), so do thou pour forth for us a swelling wave (*ūrmi*) of water endowed with sweetness (*madhumantam*).
It is like clarified butter (*ghṛtam*); this is a simile meaning water that flows with honey (*madhuśrutam*) and is well-purified (*supūtam*). Such is the sense.
May the lords or masters of the *ṛta* (the cosmic order) or of the sacrifice, or of the waters, have mercy upon us and grant us happiness;
or rather,
the genitive case here refers to the action of the *ṛta*.
May they grant the *ṛta*;
the root *mṛḍ* here has the sense of giving.
1. Ta and te.
2. By means of a friend characterized by kha, ga, ṇa, pha, bha, la, or sa; or by means of a friend characterized by na.
3. With the assistance of ta.
4. Herein, regarding the field:
5. [The letters] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pa, bha, when augmented, produce the son (or the purified); pha, when augmented, produces the well-purified purifier.
6. [The letters] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, that.
Regarding the *paridhānīyā* verse for the *atiriktokthya* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin:
"The *paridhānīyā* is 'madhumatīroṣadhīrvāva āpaḥ' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.11)," as it is so prescribed in the Sūtra.
May the plants indeed be honey-sweet, may the waters be honey-sweet, and may the intermediate space be honey-sweet.
May the Lord of the Field be honey-sweet; may we follow him unharmed.
Sweet are the plants; sweet are the heavens; sweet are the waters. May the mid-region be sweet for us. May the Lord of the Field be sweet for us; may we follow him unharmed. 3.
May the herbs—the *oṣadhīs* such as rice (*vrīhi*), millet (*priyaṅgu*), and so forth—be full of sweetness (*madhumatīḥ*) for us (*naḥ*).
Likewise, may the heavens (*dyāvaḥ*); for since it has been stated that there are three heavens, the plural number is appropriate.

Likewise, may the waters and the mid-air be sweet for us; moreover, may the Lord of the Field also be full of sweetness. Unharmed—that is, not being injured by others—may we follow after this Lord of the Field and move about together with him.
"Śudeva means 'one whose deity is Śuna,'" says Śaunaka.
Therefore, Indra and Vāyu are [the deities] of Śuna. "Vāyu is Śuna; Śīra is Āditya because he moves through the intermediate space," says Yāska (Nirukta 9.40).
O you two, Śuna and Sīra, may you both take pleasure in this my speech which I am about to utter. With that milk which you created in heaven, sprinkle this earth.

Turn toward us, O auspicious Sītā; we pay homage to you, so that you may be fortunate for us, so that you may bear us good fruit. 6. Turn toward us! O auspicious one! Be [favorable], O Sītā! We revere you, so that you may be a bringer of fortune to us, so that you may be a bearer of good fruit for us. 6.
O auspicious one, O cool one, you who are born near us, turn toward us;
we pay homage to you, we praise you,
so that you may be auspicious to us, possessing beautiful wealth.
Just as you are one who bears good fruit for us, so do we pay homage to you.

May Indra grasp the furrow; may Pūṣan follow and guide it. May she, rich in milk, yield for us [milk] year after year. 7. May Indra grasp the furrow; may Pūṣan follow and guide it. May she, rich in milk, yield for us [milk] year after year. 7.
May the god Indra take hold of the furrow and the wooden beam that supports the furrow;
may the god Pūṣan guide and restrain that furrow;
may that heaven, rich in milk, yield its abundance.
When [it is asked], "When?", that is explained:
in each successive year, in each successive year.
The application of these two ṛcs is stated in the verse: "O Śuna and Sīra, [accept] this... and so forth.

May our ploughshares furrow the earth auspiciously; may the farmers come toward us auspiciously with their draft-animals. May Parjanya [bestow] auspiciousness through honey and waters; O Śuna and Sīra, bestow auspiciousness upon us. 8. Auspiciously. For us. Ploughshares. May they furrow. The earth. Auspiciously. Farmers. Toward [us]. May they come. With draft-animals. Auspiciously. Parjanya. Through honey. With waters. O Śuna and Sīra. Auspiciousness. Upon us. Bestow. 8.

1. Kha, ga, ṇa, bha, sa—Śaunaka reads *he śunāsīrā*; gha, ca, pha, la—Śaunaka reads *he śunāsīrī*; ta—Śaunaka reads *he śunāsīrāḥ*. 2. Ta reads *vāyuḥ*; the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*) say "Indra and Vāyu" or "Vāk and Āditya. 3. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, pha, bha, la, sa—there is no "*he śunāsīrau*. 4. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, la, sa—[the reading] *sītādhārakāṣṭhām*. 5. Pa—*udakavatī no 'smākam*. 6. Ta—*duhyate*. 7. Ga, ca, ṇa—*uttaram*. [Note: *bhūmi vphālāḥ* means "ploughing-shafts for breaking the earth"; *śunaṃ vi kṛṣantu* means "may they plough for our prosperity"].
May the plowmen (*kīnāśāḥ*), the protectors of the oxen, go toward the draft-oxen so that there may be well-being (*śunam*).
May Parjanya sprinkle [the earth] with sweet milks—that is, with waters—so that there may be well-being.
O Śunāsīrau—whether Indra and Vāyu, or Vāyu and Āditya—bestow and maintain happiness (*śunam*) upon us.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "samudrād ūrmiḥ," has the Jagatī meter for its first verse and the Triṣṭubh meter for the remainder.
Its deity is either Agni, Sūrya, or Ghṛta.
Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi).

Here is the table of contents (anukramaṇikā): “*Samudrād ūrmiḥ* consists of eleven verses; it ends with a *jagatī*, belongs to Soma, or to Vāyu, or to the Cow, or it is a praise of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
This hymn is the *ājya* [offering] at the Viṣuvat day.

And thus says the Sūtra: “From the ocean, the wave—the clarified butter, the well-pressed [Soma]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.6). When the ritual formation is expanded, we ten sacrificers shall proclaim and praise the name of the clarified butter.
In this sacrifice, with salutations or with oblations, let us maintain [the rite].
May the exalted god Brahmā hear—indeed, listen to—this which is being recited and praised.
He who has four horns.
He is one whose four horns consist of the four Vedas;
this applies in the case of the Sun (Āditya).
In the other cases as well, the word *śṛṅga* (horn) is to be explained according to the etymologies stated by Yāska.
The fair one, the god of ruddy hue—he has impelled this work, that is, he has impelled or brought forth the world; the meaning is that he carries it out.
Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, and seven are his hands.
Bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals.
Three are his horns, four his feet, two his heads, and seven his hands. Bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals. 3.

Although this mantra should be explained in five ways because the hymn (*sūkta*) has deities such as Agni and Sūrya as its subject matter, it is nevertheless explained here with reference to Agni and Sūrya as the illuminators, according to the method of the *Nirukta* for passages not explicitly discussed therein.
Of this Agni who is the essence of sacrifice, there are four horns—the four Vedas—which occupy the position of horns.

Although Āpastamba stated, "We shall explain the sacrifice; it is ordained by the three Vedas" (Paribhāṣā 1.3), nevertheless, because the Atharva Veda alone—without depending on the others—is the expounder of all rituals to be accomplished by a single performance, it is said [in the Ṛgveda] that it has "four horns" with reference to that. "Three are its feet": the three *savana*s (pressings) are its feet.
They are called "feet" because they are the means for setting the ritual in motion (*pravṛtti*).

There are two heads: the *brahmaudana* and the *pravargya*. It has been stated that these consist primarily of the *iṣṭi* and *soma* sacrifices. There are seven hands, which are the seven meters (*chandas*).
The hands are the primary instrument for performance;
likewise, the meters (*chandas*) are the primary instrument for pleasing the deities—this is the conventional usage regarding the hands.
"Bound in three ways" means bound in a threefold manner by the *mantras*, the *brāhmaṇas*, and the *kalpas*.
Its bond is its state of being produced;
it is a bull, the showerer of fruits, and it roars loudly—
it makes a great sound.
He resounds with the utterances of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, in the form of praises to Śambhu, and with the Dhruvas such as the Hāgupta;
thus the great God has entered mortals.
This "entry" is figuratively expressed because [the deity] is to be accomplished by mortal sacrificers.

Regarding this, Yāska has declared: "The four horns are said to be the Vedas" (Nirukta 13.7), and so forth; that should be reflected upon here. Now, it is explained according to the solar interpretation: the four horns of this Āditya are the four quarters.
These are metaphorically called "horns" because they serve as supports.
It has three feet;
the three Vedas function as its feet, since they are the means for its movement.

For instance, beginning with "In the forenoon, the god moves in heaven by means of the Ṛg-verses," and concluding with "By means of the three Vedas, Sūrya goes to the zenith" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.1), his movement by means of the three Vedas is indeed recorded. There are two heads: day and night are the two heads.
He has seven hands; he has seven rays. Or rather, there are seven hands because the seasons are sixfold in their characteristics and one is common to them all.
He is bound in three ways, meaning he is connected to the three locations—earth and so forth—in the form of fire and the other elements.
Bound by the three divisions beginning with summer, the rainy season, and winter, the bull, the showerer, roars aloud.
1. [In the versions] kha, ga, ca, and ṇa, it reads "we praise."
2. Or [the syllables] are of the nature of the four Vedas, with *ta* as the lord of the directions (*digapāṇi*).
3. Like *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*.
4. *Kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *ṇa* are also in the subsequent [groups]; *la* and *sa* are also in the intermediate [groups].
5. The color of gold;
6. by way of *ca*, *pha*, *sa*, and *pha*;
7. of the three colors beginning with *ta* and *sa*.
8. *ta*-hand; 9. no activity of the hand;
10. not in the *mantras*, *kalpas*, or *brāhmaṇas* of *la*.
11. Pa praises [it]. 12. This god is the great-souled deity who is the essence of sacrifice (*yajñātman*).

In place of the passage beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and ending with "should be seen" (*draṣṭavyam*), the reading found in manuscript Pa is: "In this way, it should be applied by means of reasoning to the position of Sūrya and the others."

13. Because *kha*, *na*, and *eva* have the meaning of "not hearing"; because *ga*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa* have the meaning of "hearing"; because *ca*, *ṇa*, and *pha* have the meaning of "relying"; and because *ta* alone has the meaning of "relying. 14. By virtue of *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa* being mutually identical in nature, one produces sound through the gateway of *vṛthā* and so forth.
"That great god has entered into mortals with his mighty power;
Sūrya is the self of all that moves and stands"—so indeed it is heard in the Śruti (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.115.1).
The same should be applied to one's own position and others as well.

However, the Grammarians (Śābdikas), taking the verse to refer to the Śabdabrahman, explain "four horns" as the four classes of words—namely, nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles—and so forth. Others, however, interpret it according to their own views.
All of that is to be seen here.
The gods discovered the clarified butter (ghṛta) hidden in three ways by the Paṇis within the cow;
Indra produced one part, Sūrya produced another, and from Vena they fashioned the third through their own inherent power.

In three ways—beneficial, hidden by the Paṇis, and within the cow—the gods discovered the clarified butter. Indra produced one part, Sūrya produced one, and from Vena they fashioned the third by their own inherent power. || 4 ||

The gods (devāsaḥ) discovered—that is, they obtained—the clarified butter (ghṛtam), which is radiant or consists of essence, hidden, deposited, and guarded in three ways among the cows by the Asuras with their hands; that is, it was placed in a threefold manner according to the distinction of milk, curd, and ghee.
Among those, Indra produced one [form], the milk;
Sūrya produced another.

From the "venā" (the one who moves), that is, from Agni or Vāyu who possesses movement, the gods fashioned forth (*niṣṭakṣuḥ*) a single clarified butter (*ghṛtam*), by means of *svadhā*—that is, with food as the cause, or as the substance, or as the instrument.
These flow from the heart, from the ocean, through a hundred enclosures, so that the enemy may not perceive them. I behold the streams of clarified butter; in their midst stands the golden reed.
These flow from the heart, from the ocean, in a hundred streams; they cannot be looked upon by an enemy. I gaze upon the streams of clarified butter; in their midst stands the golden reed. 5.

These waters, or streams of clarified butter, flow downward; they fall with a hundred paths, moving in immeasurable ways. From the heart—that is, from the ocean which reaches to the heart—namely from the intermediate space, they flow so that they cannot be seen by the enemy, by Vṛtra, the adversary who obstructs the release of water; they flow in such a way that they remain invisible as they are seen.
I gaze upon those streams of clarified butter; I behold them.
Where is that [tree] said to be?
It is the golden (hiraṇyayaḥ) or gold-like (hiraṇmayaḥ) cane (vetasaḥ), born from the waters and established within them; the ellipsis is that it exists in the midst of these waters.
Here, by the final quarter-verse, "I behold the streams of clarified butter," the fire established as the locus of the oblation—either the sacrificial fire or the sun—is described.
The streams flow perfectly like milch-cows, purified within the heart by the mind;
these waves of clarified butter rush forth like wild beasts springing forward with speed.
Like rivers, the streams flow together, being purified within the heart and the mind; these waves of clarified butter surge forth like deer rushing toward their prey.
1. *ta-tattanmiyantayā* | 2. *ta-na-abādipakṣe'pi* | 3. *ga-ca-nāmāruyātopasarganipātāśca* | 4. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha-etayataḥ*; *pa-la-sa-ekāntamataḥ*; *bha-ekāyataḥ*.

Upon this fire flow—indeed, they stream—perfectly the streams of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Like what? Like rivers, like pleasant-flowing streams (*dhenāḥ*). They are purified, being cleansed by the mind within the heart—that is to say, by the consciousness situated in the middle of the heart, which is accompanied by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This very point is stated: these waves, the essences of the clarified butter, move; they fall from the ladle onto the fire. Like what? Like deer fleeing from a swift archer, as they enter the thicket (*kakṣa*); by this, their swiftness is expressed. 1. *ghṛtasya dhārāḥ*: "streams of clarified butter" 2. *antarhṛdā*: "within the heart" (with *hṛdā* understood as *hṛdayena*) 3. *ardhanti*: "they go" or "they move" (from root *ṛ*) 4. *kṣipaṇoḥ*: "of the one who throws" or "the archer" (from root *kṣip*) 5. *īṣamāṇāḥ*: "fleeing" or "escaping" (from root *iṣ*) 6. *mṛgā iva*: "like deer" 7. *kakṣam*: "thicket" or "bush" (referring to the grass or undergrowth) 8. *śaidhyam*: "swiftness" (from *śīghra*) 9. *anena*: "by this" (referring to the comparison) 10. *uktaṃ bhavati*: "is expressed" or "is said" (passive construction) (Note: The commentary explains that the streams of ghee are compared to deer fleeing from a hunter; the speed with which they reach the fire is likened to the deer's rapid entry into cover.)

Like the surging waves of the ocean on its course, the mighty streams of clarified butter fall down, destroying obstacles; like a ruddy steed, they break through the barriers, swelling the earth as they flow.
Like the currents of the Sindhu river on their course, the mighty streams of clarified butter fall down—unfailing, like a ruddy steed breaking through the barriers, swelling with its waves. 7.
Like waters from the Sindhu, the flowing river, the streams of clarified butter—swift-moving (*śṛghnāsaḥ*), as the Nirukta states:
"‘Āśu’ and ‘Śu’ are names for one who moves quickly" (Nirukta 6.1);
like the wind, possessing great velocity (*vātapramiyaḥ*), mighty (*yahvāḥ*)—fall, that is, flow, over the fire.
In the interpretation that "ghṛta" means water, the word "iva" (as if) in the phrase "sindhor iva" (as from the ocean) would be redundant.
From the atmosphere, which is the means of flowing, streams of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and streams of water, characterized as described above, fall—that is, they go—to the earth.

Furthermore, breaking through the *kāṣṭhās*, the boundary-marking enclosures, by means of its waves—that is, its essences—and swelling—that is, increasing—through the state of being clarified butter, it becomes full.
In the case where [the subject] is water, having traversed the quarters (kāṣṭhāḥ) and remaining there, it pierces the directions with its waves and billows, becoming swollen.
Therein is an illustration:
like a "formless" (arupaḥ) steed—a shining horse characterized by pride and the habit of moving.
Just as he becomes both piercing and swelling, so it is.
Like beautiful women smiling as they go to a gathering, the streams of clarified butter approach Agni with kindling wood; and Jātavedas, taking pleasure in them, eagerly accepts them.
Like beautiful women smiling as they go forth together toward a gathering, the streams of clarified butter reach Agni as kindling wood; enjoying them, Jātavedas takes delight in them. 8.
The streams of clarified butter flow toward that Agni, just as women with one mind flow toward a husband;
they cause him to be immersed.
What are they like? They are like young women.
The auspicious ones, of beautiful form, smiling and laughing;
moreover, those very kindling-sticks (samidhas), truly illuminating and reaching out, pervade [the fire].
Jātavedas, delighting in or enjoying those very streams (dhārās), desires them.
In the view that the word *ghṛta* (clarified butter) means water, either Vaiśvānara Agni or Āditya is understood by the two words *abhijātavedas*.
Toward that deity the streams of water flow and descend;
he desires them.

1. *ta*—streams of clarified butter (*ghṛtadhārā*). 2. *ta*—furthermore, with the inner heart (*antarhṛdā*). 3. *kha-ca-ta-pha-bha*—the quarters (*kāṣṭhā*: accusative plural *kāṣṭhān*). 4. *ta*—just as the quarters (*yathā kāṣṭhā*: nominative plural). 5. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa*—he indeed surpasses them (*sa tā vā hy atīta*); *ta-na-sa*—and he does not perish (*ca tā hy atīti*, [variant] *na hyati*).

Like a hunchbacked woman going to the wedding procession, I gaze upon the ointments as they are being applied. Where the Soma is pressed, where the sacrifice is, there the streams of clarified butter flow toward it. Like a hunchbacked woman, for the sake of going to the wedding procession—Oṃ!—I gaze intently at the ointment as she is being anointed. Where the Soma is pressed, where the sacrifice is, there the streams of clarified butter flow toward that place.
Like an unmarried maiden— a young girl—
just as she goes to the wedding, to obtain her husband, manifesting her *añji*, that is, her ornament or her radiance; even so do these [waters],
like maidens, manifest their *añji*, the manifestor of his form, as they go toward the sacrifice, the clarified butter, or the sun, which has become their own husband.
I behold, I look upon, the streams of clarified butter.
It is well known that the blazing of the terrestrial fire and the fire of clarified butter occurs through the medium of clarified butter and water.
Furthermore, those streams flow toward—that is, they go toward—that sacrifice where Soma is pressed and where the other sacrifice is performed.

Flow toward our excellent praise; [win] the race for cattle. Bestow upon us auspicious riches. Lead this sacrifice of ours to the gods. The streams of clarified butter flow sweetly. 10. Flow toward! Excellent praise! For cattle! The race! Upon us! Auspicious! Riches! Bestow! This! Sacrifice! Lead! To the gods! Our! Streams of clarified butter! Sweet! Flow! 10.
O my priests, flow toward or cause [the sacrificer] to reach the *ājī*—the herd of cows or that which pertains to the cows—and [bestow] excellent praise (*suṣṭuti*).
Here, by the word "cows" (*go*), waters or rays are meant;
their collection is intended.
While we are performing the sacrifice, bestow and maintain auspicious riches;
for through praise, one shall indeed obtain the fruit. Furthermore, lead—bring before us—this our sacrifice to the deities, the gods who are to be worshipped here.
Just as the streams of clarified butter are full of sweetness, so do they flow and proceed.
The first verse of the subsequent hymn, beginning with “*dhāmante*,” is prescribed for use during the *sarjana* and *apākaraṇa* rites;
for after stating the opening phrase “*dhāmante viśvam*,” the *sūtra* concludes with the rule: “*ṛcāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.5.7).
1. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pha, bha, la, sa, and enaṃ.
2. [The syllables] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, and sa manifest the consonants (vyañjana).
3. Or where [the syllables] kha, ga, ca, and ṇa [occur]; bha, la, and sa are the points of entry (avatāra).
4. From Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha, La, and Sa, [the syllable] tāyāt.
5. Pha and He are the streams (dhārāḥ). Flow toward us, rain down upon this collection of water consisting of cow-products, and sing for you both.
In Kha, Ga, Ṇa, and Pa, the word āji means "from all sides" (āsamantāt); in La and Sa, it means "from all sides."
6. The letters *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa* do not exist [in the sense of] "as it is" (*yathā tathā*). 7. *ta*—these are the verses (*dṛcāḥ*):
"Upon your abode the entire world is supported; within the ocean, within the heart, and within life."
In the encounter of the waters, in the assembly, may we obtain that honeyed wave which has been brought by you.

Upon your abode the entire world is supported. Within the ocean, within the heart, within life, and at the meeting-point of the waters—may we attain that honey-sweet wave of yours which has been brought forth there. 11.
